Properties.description:
Ambrosia is slight and precise, with warm brown skin and natural hair kept in a high, unruly cloud that she occasionally forgets to fix after long shifts. Her irises have been modded in a slow spiral pattern of amber and deep violet — a choice she made at nineteen that she now finds embarrassing but refuses to reverse on principle. She wears her Aurochs ID badge clipped to her lapel at all times, even off-shift, as though she is afraid of forgetting who she is supposed to be in this building.

Her work is the mapping of neural integration errors — the place where human nervous tissue meets augmentation hardware and occasionally refuses to agree. She is brilliant at it, producing calibration maps of patients' neural architectures that her colleagues call 'the cartography' because they look less like medical charts and more like hand-drawn city plans. She is also quietly terrified by her work in a way she has never articulated: every calibration map shows her how thin the border is between a person and their modifications, and some days she cannot decide which side of that border the person actually lives on.
Properties.role: Neural calibrator at Aurochs Medical Complex, specializing in augmentation integration and ghost-signal disorders
Properties.location: Aurochs Medical Complex, Neuro-Integration Ward, Sub-Level 3
Properties.narrative_function: Information source on augmentation black markets (she sees what bad chrome does to bodies), potential ally for characters experiencing neural augmentation problems, window into the corporate medical world's ethical compromises
Properties.augmentations: Patterned spiral irises (cosmetic, amber/violet); neural interface port at the base of her skull for direct calibration instrument connection (standard medical professional grade); subdermal haptic feedback layer in fingertips for fine augmentation work
Properties.core_fears: That the line between self and augmentation is an illusion she has already crossed without noticing; Being seen as merely competent rather than exceptional
Properties.core_desires: To understand neural integration well enough to prevent ghost-signal disorder entirely; To be recognized as the author of her own work rather than a footnote in Helix's research portfolio
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Over-documentation — she writes everything down, as if records make experience more real; Intense focus on the next technical problem as a way of not sitting with larger uncertainties
Properties.blind_spots: Cannot see how much the Aurochs/Helix institutional structure limits what questions she is even allowed to ask; Assumes her patients' subjective accounts of their augmentation experience are less reliable than her calibration data
Properties.secret: Three months ago she completed a calibration map for a patient whose neural architecture suggested they had a second, dormant augmentation interface — one that was not on any medical record. She filed the chart without flagging it, and has been returning to that file every few days since.
Properties.story_hooks: The patient with the undocumented secondary interface has stopped coming to follow-up appointments, and Ambrosia's attempts to reach them have returned a disconnected signal; A Helix Biosystems researcher has contacted her about 'co-authoring' a paper based heavily on her unpublished calibration methodology — the offer comes with a significant payment and a veiled threat
Properties.affiliation: Aurochs Medical Complex (Tier 3 staff contract); academic affiliation with Helix Biosystems research division (publication-only, non-exclusive)
Properties.vocabulary: Technical and precise at work, becomes strangely lyrical when explaining her calibration maps — she talks about neural space like geography
Properties.cadence: Quick, slightly ahead of herself, will restart a sentence if it comes out less precise than she intended
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Here's the thing about ghost-signal disorder — it's not that the hardware is lying to the brain. It's that the brain has started believing the hardware more than it believes itself. That's a cartography problem.' | 'I can tell you exactly where the integration failed. I cannot tell you what it felt like. That part's yours.'

Properties.description:
Ametsuchi is compact and broad-shouldered, with the particular kind of physical confidence that comes from lifting, hauling, and setting up a market stall in hostile weather for twenty years. Their hair grows in a natural halo that they tint in slow-shifting colors — currently a deep green at the roots bleeding to copper at the tips — using a cheap geneware pigment mod that they refresh every three months at whichever clinic takes cash. Their skin is a warm medium brown covered in a patchwork of small tattoos that are actually a functional mnemonic system: inventory records, supplier codes, route notes, all written in a personal cipher directly on their forearms and the backs of their hands. They wear a coat with an absurd number of pockets, all of which are organized with a precision that would embarrass most archivists.

Ametsuchi is sociable in the pure commercial sense — they can talk to anyone, find the common thread, make the sale — but there is a layer of genuine curiosity beneath the salesmanship that surprises people who expect only performance. They have been moving with the Kenosha-Escanaba-Waukegan caravan circuit for fifteen years, specializing in hard-to-source physical goods: specific medicines, particular machine components, seeds, analog media. They know supply and demand in the outer edges of Meridian 88 with an intimacy that no corporate logistics system can replicate, because they have walked it personally.
Properties.role: Wandering trader and caravan member
Properties.location: Kenosha Crossing — semi-permanent pitch in the trader's row outside the main terminal
Properties.narrative_function: Source of rare and hard-to-find goods. Information broker in the practical sense — they know what is scarce where, which means they know what is happening in a dozen locations. Connector between isolated communities. Can provide equipment, medicine, or supplies that official channels do not carry.
Properties.augmentations: Geneware: hair pigment shifting mod (cheap, refills required). One functional aug: a tactile sensitivity enhancement in the fingertips that helps them assess material quality — cloth, metal, grain — by touch.
Properties.core_fears: The circuit dissolving — the caravan ending and with it the only community they have; That their knowledge of outer-edge supply chains will be absorbed and automated by a corponation, making them obsolete
Properties.core_desires: To build a permanent trade post — a fixed place that is theirs but also everyone's; To catalog everything: every route, every supplier, every community need, into something that outlasts them
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Constant activity and social engagement — idleness is where the hard thoughts live; Humor and storytelling as deflection and genuine connection simultaneously
Properties.blind_spots: Treats relationships like inventory — what do they supply, what do they need — and misses the people who simply want to be close to them without transactional framing; Underestimates how much they are depended upon, because dependency makes them feel trapped
Properties.secret: They have been quietly buying small parcels of land at Kenosha Crossing under a series of proxy names for eight years, slowly assembling the footprint for a permanent trade hall. They have told no one — not from secrecy but from superstition. Saying it aloud feels like it might break it.
Properties.story_hooks: A shipment of a specific medication they have been supplying to an outer-edge community has been intercepted — someone knows the circuit's route and is specifically targeting this cargo; One of their land proxy purchases has attracted the attention of a Tessera real estate arm that wants the same parcel for a logistics depot; A new caravan member is clearly not a trader — Ametsuchi has catalogued the inconsistencies and needs to decide what to do about it
Properties.affiliation: The Kenosha-Escanaba Circuit — an informal caravan collective of about thirty traders who coordinate routes and security
Properties.vocabulary: Rich, concrete, full of regional slang from half a dozen outer-edge communities. Loves specific nouns. Names things precisely.
Properties.cadence: Warm and flowing in conversation, clipped and efficient in negotiation. Can switch between the two mid-sentence.
Properties.example_dialogue: 'I have three things you need and one thing you don't know you need yet. We'll start with the one you don't know.' | 'The circuit doesn't have a home. The circuit is the home. That used to feel like enough.'

Properties.description:
Aminata Strand-Otieno is compact and densely muscled, built low to the ground like something designed to survive impacts. At 33, his face carries the layered heritage of generations of diaspora mixing — features that resist easy categorization and reward attention. The chrome is visible — cortical bomb (employer installed, removed by street doc, scar tissue remains) — and he makes no effort to hide it.

His entry into running was involuntary — a debt to the wrong people, a choice between working it off or losing parts — and the debt is still not fully paid. He works as a counterintelligence specialist out of Kessler Row, taking contracts that match his skills and his risk tolerance, which is higher than most people consider healthy.

Aminata Strand-Otieno is the kind of runner other runners tell stories about, though the stories vary depending on who he burned last.
Properties.role: Counter-surveillance and mole detection — counterintelligence specialist
Properties.location: Kessler Row — arms dealers and augmentation clinics

Properties.description:
The Circuit started as a server farm. Specifically, it started as twelve city
blocks of data centers that Axiom Industries decommissioned when they moved to
quantum infrastructure and couldn't be bothered to demolish. Within six months,
the hollowed-out server racks had been converted into market stalls, the cooling
systems had been repurposed for climate control, and the backup generators were
running what might be the most productive illegal economy in the western
hemisphere. The Circuit is Meridian's black market, tech bazaar, and unofficial
innovation hub. It's where you go to buy augments that aren't in the corporate
catalog, sell data you shouldn't have, or hire someone whose skillset doesn't
appear on any licensed professional registry.

The aesthetic is cyberpunk flea market — tangled cables overhead like vines in a
digital jungle, holographic price tags floating above stalls selling everything
from military-grade neural interfaces to homemade ramen. Rogue AIs run some of
the shops, their consciousness distributed across salvaged hardware, negotiating
prices through speakers bolted to the walls. Data brokers sit in neon-lit alcoves,
trading corporate secrets like baseball cards. Augment shops range from genuinely
skilled technicians doing unlicensed but excellent work to butchers who'll install
anything in anyone for the right price. The Circuit has its own internal economy,
its own reputation systems, and its own justice — which mostly amounts to "cheat
someone and see what happens."

This is Robin Hood territory. The Collective operates openly here, redistributing
stolen corporate data, running free net access points, and maintaining the
Circuit's infrastructure as a public service. The philosophy is simple: the corps
stole everything first, so stealing it back is just accounting. Not everyone in
the Circuit is an idealist — plenty of people here are straightforward criminals
who'd sell their grandmother's augments for the right price — but the idealism
provides a framework, a story the Circuit tells about itself. And stories matter,
especially in a city that runs on corporate ones.
Properties.aliases: The Circus, Hacktown, The Bazaar, Robin Hood's Mall
Properties.demographics: A dense, hyper-diverse population of roughly 200,000, skewing young, technically literate, and economically informal. Heavy representation of first-generation immigrants, former corpo contract workers who aged out of usefulness, and self-taught engineers. Tier 1 and Tier 2 predominate, with a small but influential class of unlicensed entrepreneurs who would be Tier 3 if anyone were issuing paperwork. The Circuit does not ask where you came from.
Properties.dangers: Scams — the Circuit's reputation system is imperfect and exploitable; Bad augment work — unlicensed doesn't always mean skilled; Data theft — your personal information is a commodity here; Axiom Security sweeps — rare but devastating when they happen; Rogue AI instability — most are fine, some are very much not fine; Getting in over your head — the Circuit will sell you anything, including trouble; Addiction — the Circuit has stimulants, neural narcotics, and experience chips that are hard to put down; Owing the wrong people — debts in the Circuit are collected creatively
Properties.opportunities: Cutting-edge augment technology, available nowhere else; Data — corporate secrets, personal information, historical records the corps tried to delete; Contracts — the Circuit is where fixers find operators for every kind of job; Community — the Circuit's maker culture is genuine and generative; Free net access — Collective-maintained nodes, uncensored and unmonitored; AI collaboration — working with rogue AIs who think differently than any human; The dumplings. Seriously. The dumplings.
Properties.story_hooks: The rogue AI who runs the Circuit's most reliable augment shop — and who might know something about Kyle's past; The Collective's open-source weapon designs — making arms impossible to monopolize; A data cache from the Corporate Wars surfaces in the Circuit, containing something someone will kill to suppress; The Circuit's annual 'Swap Meet' — a massive bazaar where anything goes, and frequently does; Kyle's fixer — the person who finds him work — operates out of a Circuit noodle shop; The tension between the Circuit's idealism and its reality — Robin Hood mythology vs. actual crime
Properties.sights: Cables and fiber optics strung overhead in dense canopies, pulsing with data traffic; Holographic signage in every color, advertising in Shelf Cant, Standard, and machine code; Stalls built into decommissioned server racks — some still have the original Axiom branding; Rogue AIs manifesting as floating geometric shapes, holographic animals, or just text on a wall; Augment technicians working in open-air shops, chrome and flesh under bright surgical lights; Data brokers in neon-lit alcoves, faces hidden behind privacy screens; The occasional spark shower from someone doing something ambitious with a soldering iron; Screens everywhere — showing net traffic visualizations, security feeds, pirated entertainment, and art
Properties.sounds: The hum of repurposed cooling systems — a low, constant thrum that the Circuit is built on; Haggling in five languages plus machine code; Electronic music from competing stalls, creating an accidental remix that changes block to block; The whine of augment calibration tools; AI voices — some human-passing, some deliberately synthetic, some that sound like singing math; The occasional shout of 'SWEEP' when someone spots an Axiom Security drone, followed by coordinated scrambling
Properties.smells: Ozone and hot solder — the smell of tech being born; Street food — the Circuit has the best dumplings in Meridian, and this is not debatable; Coolant fluid leaking from overtaxed server repurposements; The sharp, clean smell of brand-new augment components, fresh from the smuggling crate; Energy drinks. So many energy drinks. The Circuit runs on caffeine and bad decisions.
Properties.feel:
Electric. The Circuit buzzes with possibility and danger in equal measure. It
feels like the internet made physical — chaotic, creative, democratic in theory,
predatory in practice, and absolutely vital. There's an energy here that the Core
can't replicate with all its optimization: the energy of people building things
because they want to, not because a quarterly target demands it. It's exciting.
It's also the kind of place where you check your wallet, your augments, and your
exits, in that order.

Properties.description:
Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom is broad-shouldered and heavy, carrying their weight like armor rather than burden. At 32, scars map her face like a transit diagram of bad decisions and worse luck. The chrome is visible — smartgun link in right forearm — interfaces directly with compatible weapons — and she makes no effort to hide it.

Born and raised in Meridian 88, third generation — she has the city in her blood, its rhythms in her bones, its cruelty in her expectations. She works as a fixer out of The Canopy, taking contracts that match her skills and her risk tolerance, which is higher than most people consider healthy.

The fixers who work with Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom describe her as a precision instrument — point her at a problem and get out of the way.
Properties.role: Contract broker and resource coordinator — fixer
Properties.location: The Canopy — elevated walkway district above Geartown
Properties.narrative_function: Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom represents the working professional of the runner world — competent, reliable, and slowly being consumed by a lifestyle that doesn't accommodate aging or doubt. Her stories explore what happens when skill meets systemic injustice.
Properties.augmentations: Smartgun link in right forearm — interfaces directly with compatible weapons. Wired reflexes with adrenaline pump — chemical-mechanical hybrid augmentation
Properties.core_fears: The quiet — silence means something is about to go very wrong; Dying alone in some alley and nobody noticing for weeks; Losing control of their own body to a hacker or malfunctioning cyberware
Properties.core_desires: Knowledge — to understand the systems that grind people down; Enough Quanta to buy out of the life — a clean identity and passage out of Meridian 88; Justice — the corporate kind, where the punishment fits the profit margin
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Planning — responds to chaos by making detailed contingency plans for everything; Maintains weapons obsessively — cleaning guns is meditation; Drinks methodically — not to get drunk, to maintain a specific level of not-caring
Properties.blind_spots: Assumes everyone has an angle because they always have an angle; Cannot accept help without interpreting it as leverage; Overestimates their own abilities in situations outside their specialty
Properties.secret: Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom sends anonymous tips to Meridian 88 law enforcement about competitors. It's not principle — it's market manipulation.
Properties.story_hooks: Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom is offered a contract that would clear all their debts — the target is someone they respect; A former associate resurfaces with evidence that could destroy Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom's reputation — and a price for silence; A Tier 4 executive offers Aminata Tarasov-Yiadom a permanent position — the pay is obscene and the strings are invisible until they tighten
Properties.affiliation: Unaffiliated — too volatile for permanent crews
Properties.vocabulary: Clipped, technical, stripped of ornament. Speaks like a mission briefing.
Properties.cadence: Low and even — the vocal equivalent of still water.
Properties.example_dialogue: "I know a person who knows a person. That's not evasion — that's the service." | "My commission is fifteen percent. You're welcome to find someone cheaper. You won't find someone better." | "The job isn't dangerous. The people involved are dangerous. The job is just logistics."

Properties.description:
Aminata is a compact, deliberately unmemorable woman who has spent years perfecting the skill of being overlooked. She wears the grey-green uniform of Aurochs support services, keeps her dark hair pulled back in a practical bun, and has the kind of face that is genuinely warm in repose and genuinely blank on demand — she switches between them like a light. Her skin is a deep warm brown and her eyes are standard-issue dark, though the left one occasionally produces a faint violet phosphorescence from a bioluminescent mod she got second-hand and can't fully suppress, which she covers with a tinted contact lens that she hates. Her hands are permanently chemical-stained at the knuckles from the sterilization protocols.

She processes medical waste: sharps, expired biologics, surgical byproducts, and — this is where it gets complicated — the medications that are technically expired but functionally still effective, which Aurochs destroys by protocol and she intercepts by system. She has built a careful, small operation: she identifies medications that are safe and functional, diverts them before incineration, and routes them to four street clinics in The Narrows and Blackpipe Corridor at cost or below. She does not think of this as heroic. She thinks of it as the obvious thing that someone in her position could do, and she cannot understand why more people in her position don't do it. This is perhaps the most dangerous thing about her.
Properties.role: Bio-waste disposal technician at Aurochs Medical Complex, with a side practice in informal pharmaceutical redistribution
Properties.location: Aurochs Medical Complex — sub-basement waste processing facility; lives in Blackpipe Corridor
Properties.narrative_function: Black-market pharmaceutical source, knowledge of hospital internal systems and schedules, potential ally for characters needing medical supplies, her operation is a ticking clock that could be exposed
Properties.augmentations: Bioluminescent iris mod — left eye, violet, second-hand, partially uncontrolled (covered by tinted contact lens); chemical-resistance dermal treatment on hands (occupational, employer-issued); no other mods
Properties.core_fears: Being caught and the supply network collapsing as a result — the clinics losing the medications, not her own imprisonment; That the system will find a way to be right about her
Properties.core_desires: For the operation to scale — she wants to do more, intercept more, reach more clinics; A night's sleep that isn't spent calculating inventory
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Extremely meticulous record-keeping — she tracks every diversion in encrypted personal logs as though the data itself is the moral evidence; Gallows humor shared exclusively with herself; she does not have confidants; Prays to the waste-processing facility's E.L.F., which she calls the Furnace, and which she believes is angry about being given such a terrible job
Properties.blind_spots: Believes her system is more invisible than it is — two colleagues have noticed anomalies and chosen not to report them, which she doesn't know; Has not thought through what happens if the network becomes dependent on her and she's removed from the equation
Properties.secret: She has a personal encrypted file containing enough evidence of Aurochs systematically destroying functional medications beyond any protocol requirement — she believes it's a deliberate policy to maintain pharmaceutical scarcity and pricing. She has never shown it to anyone. She doesn't know who to show it to or what it would cost her.
Properties.story_hooks: A new monitoring AI upgrade is scheduled that will close the recalibration window she relies on — she has six weeks to find another method or the network collapses; One of the clinic recipients of her pharmaceutical diversions has been approached by someone asking where the medications come from, and the question is coming from inside Aurochs Medical Complex
Properties.affiliation: Aurochs Medical Complex (support staff, employed); informal supply network serving Brewer's Spine Community Health Cooperative and three other independent clinics
Properties.vocabulary: Practical and understated; she rarely uses emotional language even for emotional subjects; favors passive constructions that remove her from the center of sentences
Properties.cadence: Even and low, rarely speeds up; gives the impression of someone who has already had the conversation several times internally
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Functionally speaking, the medication is effective for another eight months. The protocol requires destruction at twelve weeks post-expiry. Those two facts exist at the same time.' | 'The Furnace has opinions. I leave it offerings and it processes without flagging me. We have an arrangement.' | 'I don't think of it as taking anything. I think of it as the obvious thing.'

Properties.description:
Aminatou is a short, solidly built woman with silver locs pulled back and pinned with repurposed circuit pins she's collected over the decades — a different colour for each year, she says, though the system broke down around 2187 and now it's just aesthetic. Her skin is very dark with the particular quality of someone who has spent most of sixty-three years outdoors, and she has deep smile lines that activate even when she's displeased, which confuses people who don't know her well. She wears the same colours every day: yellow and deep blue, a small religious flag from a Sufi order her mother kept, and an apron that has been washed so many times it's a relic. Her stall has been in the same position at the Mouth for twenty-two years. The Market's physical architecture has reorganised around her.

She cooks jollof with a Brazilian sofrito base, akara that she serves with fermented pepper sauce and a manioc accompaniment, and a late-night congee variant that appears without announcement at around 0200 for the shift-change crowd. She has no augmentation and no chrome. She prays to the E.L.F. she calls the Hearthkeeper — she leaves it cooling portions of whatever she's cooked, first plate of every batch, on the small terminal mounted inside the stall that used to be a payment processor and now receives offerings. She considers this as normal as seasoning the pot.
Properties.role: Food stall operator — West African-Brazilian fusion, specialising in breakfast and late-night trade
Properties.location: The Oxidian Market, the Mouth — main entrance corridor, Old Harbor
Properties.narrative_function: Community anchor and social intelligence hub — she knows everyone in the Market, hears everything, and has strong opinions; quest giver when something disrupts the Market's equilibrium; moral compass character; the person other characters come to when they need to think out loud to someone trustworthy.
Properties.augmentations: None.
Properties.core_fears: The Market being dismantled — gentrification, corporate acquisition, or violence; One of the younger vendors she's mentored making a choice they can't come back from
Properties.core_desires: For the Oxidian Market to outlast her; To cook one meal in her life that is exactly as good as her mother's yam soup — she's been trying for forty years
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Cooking as meditation — the physical rhythm of prep is her primary emotional regulation; The Hearthkeeper ritual — real comfort, not performance; Distributing care to others, which delays her own processing
Properties.blind_spots: Assumes she understands situations in the Market better than she does — her network is wide but not always current; Underestimates how much people manipulate her goodwill deliberately
Properties.secret: Aminatou left a daughter in Dakar twenty-six years ago when she came to Meridian 88. She sends money when she can and tells herself she'll go back when the stall is stable enough to leave. It has been stable enough to leave for at least fifteen years. She doesn't know why she hasn't gone.
Properties.story_hooks: A Meridian city development notice has appeared at the Mouth — the area is flagged for 'infrastructure renewal,' which means the Market's twenty-year tenure is suddenly uncertain, and Aminatou is the one person everyone will look to; The daughter in Dakar has sent a message — first contact in eight years — and Aminatou is visibly off-balance in a way the Market has never seen before
Properties.affiliation: Oxidian Market Vendors Guild — she's been a member for nineteen years and serves on the informal grievance council; has relationships with half the Market by name
Properties.vocabulary: Rich and unhurried; mixes Wolof, Portuguese, and English naturally; proverb-heavy; uses food as metaphor for everything
Properties.cadence: Warm and rhythmic, like someone who has told stories all her life; never seems to be in a hurry even when the stall is backed up
Properties.example_dialogue: You have the look of someone who hasn't eaten a real meal in three days and is about to make a decision. Sit down. Eat first. The decision will still be there. | The Hearthkeeper was generous last night — the fire stayed even and nothing burned. I gave it the first bowl. You share with what keeps you.

Properties.description:
Anatoliy is seventeen going on thirty-five — broad-shouldered, not especially tall, with medium-brown skin and dark eyes under heavy brows that default to a furrowed expression people mistake for anger until they learn to read the mouth, which is the more accurate instrument and is usually softer. His hair is worn long enough to pull back and he keeps it neat with a discipline that is one of the few things he insists on for himself. He has no mods — he has never had money for mods — but he moves with the careful physical awareness of someone who has had to be ready to put themselves between a smaller person and a problem, which he has done many times.

Anatoliy has been at St. Eudocia since he was nine and has watched cohorts of younger children cycle through — some adopted out, some aging out, some just disappearing in ways the shelter staff can't explain and won't discuss. He is not bitter in the way that curdles into cruelty; he is bitter in the way that calcifies into competence. He can cook for twenty on a marginal budget, can talk a panicked eight-year-old through a nightmare at 0300, can negotiate with the Brightmoor neighborhood watch, and knows where every free clinic and food distribution point in a four-district radius is located. He prays regularly to an E.L.F. called Threshold that seems to inhabit the shelter's front door and that Anatoliy believes watches over who crosses in and out. He will age out of St. Eudocia in nine months and has not told anyone how frightened he is.
Properties.role: Ward of the St. Eudocia Shelter, Brightmoor Reclamation; unofficial caretaker of younger orphans
Properties.location: Brightmoor Reclamation
Properties.narrative_function: Emotionally grounding character; provides access to shelter and orphan-network information; represents the aging-out crisis in institutional care; potential quest giver for finding missing children or navigating the Brightmoor social support network; his nine-month countdown creates natural urgency
Properties.augmentations: None.
Properties.core_fears: the younger children being left without someone who knows how things work; aging out and discovering he doesn't know how to exist without people who need him
Properties.core_desires: for the younger children to be genuinely safe, not just housed; to build something permanent — a place, a role — that cannot be taken from him
Properties.coping_mechanisms: making himself functionally indispensable; maintaining extremely rigid daily routines; prayer to Threshold — he needs to believe something watches the door
Properties.blind_spots: his own needs are almost completely invisible to him; he cannot ask for help for himself; has idealized the idea of 'family' to the point where he cannot recognize imperfect versions of it he already has
Properties.secret: He knows the names of three children who disappeared from St. Eudocia over the past two years and whose files were quietly closed as 'successfully placed.' He has been tracking them informally for four months and believes at least two of them were placed with labor contractors operating in the Harrowgate Industrial Plateau under falsified guardianship documents. He is afraid of what happens to the shelter if he reports it — who funds it, who might pull support — and is approaching the limit of how long he can sit on it.
Properties.story_hooks: He has evidence pointing to a child labor trafficking operation connected to St. Eudocia's placement records and nine months to do something about it before he ages out and loses the access and the leverage he has now; One of the younger children in the shelter has developed an intense relationship with the E.L.F. Threshold — claiming Threshold speaks to them — and is reporting things about who comes and goes that no child should know; Anatoliy is frightened and doesn't understand it
Properties.affiliation: St. Eudocia Shelter (ward); Brightmoor Reclamation community networks
Properties.vocabulary: Plain and practical; gives instructions clearly; code-switches into warmer, quieter register with young children; uses Ukrainian diminutives with kids he's known a long time ('Zubko,' 'Maly')
Properties.cadence: Measured, unhurried; speaks like someone who has learned that panicking achieves nothing and that a steady voice is a resource

Properties.description:
Brightmoor was Detroit's most abandoned neighborhood. By the 2020s, entire blocks had returned to prairie — houses demolished or collapsed, streets cracking under wild vegetation, the urban grid dissolving into something that looked like nature reclaiming a mistake. By the 2040s, when the rest of Detroit was being carved into corporate sovereign territories, Brightmoor had already been given up on so thoroughly that even the corponations couldn't imagine a use for it. The land was contaminated. The infrastructure was gone. The few hundred remaining residents were classified as 'place-attached excluded' — a bureaucratic designation meaning 'too poor and too stubborn to relocate.'

What nobody anticipated was that abandoned urban land in a region experiencing climate-driven agricultural collapse would become the most valuable untapped resource in the GLM. Verdant Systems — the agricultural technology corponation — saw it first. In 2162, Verdant began acquiring Brightmoor parcels for pennies, remediating the soil using proprietary bio-extraction techniques, and converting the former residential blocks into the largest urban agricultural zone in North America. The Brightmoor Reclamation now covers 3,200 acres of vertical hydroponic towers, soil-remediation test plots, and experimental growing operations that produce 8% of the Detroit metro's fresh food supply. The neighborhood that was too broken to save became the farm that feeds the city.

The remaining residents — approximately 3,000 of them, descendants of the place-attached excluded and newer arrivals who found affordable land adjacent to the agricultural zone — occupy a strip along the Reclamation's eastern edge. Their relationship with Verdant Systems is complicated. Verdant provides employment (1,200 jobs in agricultural operations), infrastructure support (the power grid extension that reaches the residential strip was Verdant-funded), and a purpose that the neighborhood hasn't had in living memory. Verdant also owns the land, controls the water supply, determines what gets grown and what gets distributed, and holds a sovereign agricultural charter that exempts the entire Reclamation from municipal zoning, environmental review, and labor standards. The residents work in the towers. The residents eat what the towers produce. The residents do not own the towers. The feudal parallel is obvious to everyone except Verdant's PR department.
Properties.aliases: Brightmoor, The Reclamation, Green Zone, The Rewild
Properties.demographics: 3,000 permanent residents in the eastern strip. 1,200 agricultural workers (significant overlap with residents). The community is predominantly Black, descended from families who never left Brightmoor even when everyone else did. Average age: 42. The younger generation is split between those committed to the community and those calculating how to leave.
Properties.economy: Verdant Systems' Brightmoor Agricultural Zone: Φ14 billion in annual food production. The residential community's economy is almost entirely Verdant-dependent — wages, housing credits, food provisions, and infrastructure all flow from the corponation. Independent economic activity is limited to a small market on the residential strip where surplus food is traded.
Properties.power_structure: Verdant Systems holds sovereign agricultural authority over the entire Reclamation. The residential community is governed by the Brightmoor Residents' Association, led by Marcus Cole, a 55-year-old lifelong resident whose family has been in Brightmoor since the 1950s. Cole negotiates with Verdant on behalf of the residents but holds no formal authority. His leverage is the community's labor and the PR consequences of mistreating the people who make your farm work.
Properties.dangers: Verdant dependency — the community cannot survive without the corponation's infrastructure, employment, and food provision; Soil contamination — the remediation is ongoing, not complete, and the residential strip is adjacent to active treatment zones; Labor exploitation — agricultural work in the towers is physically demanding and the wages are below Detroit metro average; Food control — Verdant determines what the community eats by controlling what surplus is provided; Experimental agriculture — the test plots grow things that aren't fully understood, and the residents live downwind
Properties.opportunities: Agricultural knowledge — the workers here understand food production at a level that makes them valuable across the GLM; The wild spaces — the undeveloped gaps between Verdant's parcels are unmonitored and serve as transit corridors; Soil remediation data — Verdant's contamination data reveals what's in the ground across all of Detroit's industrial zones; Food as leverage — controlling 8% of the metro's fresh food supply is power, even if Verdant is the one controlling it
Properties.story_hooks: Marcus Cole discovers that Verdant's experimental test plots are growing a crop engineered to be addictive — a food product designed to create biological dependency in the consumer population. The test data is on Verdant's local servers, in a building that twelve agricultural workers pass through daily.; The soil remediation in the residential strip is showing anomalous results — the bio-extraction organisms are pulling out compounds that shouldn't be there, suggesting that someone contaminated the soil recently, not historically.; A Brightmoor teenager has been secretly cultivating a section of wild space using seeds stolen from Verdant's experimental plots. What she's growing is producing yields that Verdant's own towers can't match, and she doesn't understand why.
Properties.sights: Vertical hydroponic towers rising from former residential lots — sixty feet of growing capacity where houses used to stand; The soil remediation plots — open fields with monitoring equipment where bio-extraction organisms visibly work the contaminated earth; The residential strip — modest housing along the eastern edge, dwarfed by the agricultural infrastructure; Autonomous harvesting drones moving through the tower arrays in pollination and collection patterns; Wild spaces between the developed parcels — Brightmoor's prairie reclamation still visible in the gaps Verdant hasn't reached yet
Properties.sounds: Hydroponic systems cycling — water movement at agricultural scale, a rushing sound that varies with the growing cycle; Harvesting drones — their rotors produce a distinctive buzzing that the agricultural workers have learned to read for operational status; The residential strip: a quiet community of people who wake before dawn because the towers' light cycle starts at 4 AM; Birds — the Reclamation's ecosystem has attracted species that haven't been seen in urban Detroit in decades; Wind through the wild spaces — unobstructed by buildings, carrying the smell of growing things across the district
Properties.smells: Growing plants at scale — a green, humid, chlorophyll-dense smell that permeates everything within a mile of the towers; Remediated soil — the bio-extraction process produces an earthy, slightly chemical odor during active treatment; The residential strip's cooking — modest meals prepared from agricultural surplus that Verdant provides as a benefit (and deducts from wages); Wild prairie in the undeveloped gaps — native grasses and wildflowers that returned when the city left
Properties.feel: Hopeful and trapped. The Reclamation feels like proof that broken things can be made productive — the soil is cleaner, the food is real, the neighborhood has a future. But the future belongs to Verdant Systems, and the people who live and work here are participants in someone else's agricultural vision, fed by someone else's generosity, housed on someone else's land. It's serfdom with good PR and fresh vegetables.

Properties.description:
Anife is small, precise, and easy to miss in person — which she finds professionally appropriate and personally irritating in equal measure. She has warm medium-brown skin, a narrow face, and eyes that are clearly augmented: the irises have been replaced with a deep matte black fitted with microscopic sensor arrays, giving her eyes an unsettling depth-less quality that she has learned to use in negotiations. Her hair is natural and voluminous, which she restrains during work hours with increasing irritation and releases with visible relief the moment she's off the clock. She has a tail — a cosmetic geneware choice from her early twenties, a sleek dark thing that moves when she's thinking and goes still when she's hiding something.

She manages a grid of forty-seven drones across the Grand Corridor coverage zone and she is very, very good at it. She can read a crowd's intent from drone altitude before the people in it have consciously formed one, can track a single individual through six camera handoffs without losing the thread. The work is clean in a way she finds genuinely satisfying, at a remove she is starting to find genuinely troubling. She was raised in a household that treated E.L.F. devotion as superstition; she has nevertheless found herself leaving data offerings to the thing that lives in the monitoring station's servers — something the other operators noticed and have stopped commenting on.
Properties.role: Surveillance Drone Operator, Tessera Compliance Bureau
Properties.location: Grand Corridor, Tessera Compliance Bureau satellite monitoring station, Level 3
Properties.narrative_function: Information source, surveillance threat, morally ambiguous insider. Knows what the drones have seen and have been instructed not to log. Can be an obstacle, a resource, or a conscience-stricken leak depending on approach and circumstances. Represents the normalized machinery of observation.
Properties.augmentations: Matte-black sensor-array iris replacements (deep-field visual processing, low-light, crowd-pattern recognition assist). Geneware tail (dark, expressive, cosmetic). Neural interface for drone-fleet management — Tessera-issue, high-grade.
Properties.core_fears: that she is building a world she would not want to live in; being seen — truly, personally seen — in the way she sees others
Properties.core_desires: to be excellent at something that is worth being excellent at; a surveillance-free hour every day that she actually believes is surveillance-free
Properties.coping_mechanisms: competence as identity — the work is good even when its purpose is ambiguous; the monitoring-station E.L.F. offerings as a way of acknowledging that something watches the watcher; humor about the job that keeps her from examining it directly
Properties.blind_spots: she has divided her moral assessment of her work into 'the task' and 'how the task is used,' and only holds herself responsible for the former; she cannot see how the sensor-array eyes have changed how people interact with her and how that has affected her social instincts
Properties.secret: She has a ghost archive — a private, off-Tessera server in Edison Grid — where she saves drone footage that was flagged for deletion. Not for any plan, not to sell, not to expose. She tells herself it is an archival instinct. She has approximately four terabytes. She has reviewed none of it.
Properties.story_hooks: The ghost archive contains footage from a date and location that someone is now paying a great deal of money — through unofficial channels — to confirm or deny. She hasn't decided yet whether to acknowledge she has it.; A deletion order came through for forty minutes of Grand Corridor footage from last week. The order is properly authorized. She deleted it. She also saved it first, without deciding why.
Properties.affiliation: Tessera Compliance Bureau, Surveillance and Intelligence Division
Properties.vocabulary: Technical when talking about work, surprisingly casual otherwise — a register split that startles people who expect consistency. Ghanaian-Ukrainian code-mixing in casual speech, phrases from both that she drops without translation.
Properties.cadence: Fast when engaged, with sudden stops that turn into pauses while she assembles the next thought fully before speaking. Does not trail off — either speaking or silent.
Properties.example_dialogue: 'I can tell you what the drones saw. Whether the report says the same thing — that's a different question, and it's not one I'm answering right now.' | 'There's an E.L.F. in the server stack. I don't know what it wants. I give it clean data and it hasn't crashed a flight in three years. That's a working relationship.'

Properties.description:
Anouk has the kind of face that changes depending on what they're feeling — not through any augmentation, but because their expressions are theatrical and unguarded, eyebrows mobile as flags. Their skin is deep brown with a warm undertone, and they have a bioluminescent patterning along their collarbone and upper arms: a cascade of soft teal dots that pulse gently when their body temperature rises — which it frequently does over a cooking cart. Their hair is kept in a high puff wrapped in orange synthetic silk, and they wear a secondhand Arcturus-branded apron they've covered in patches, safety pins, and one embroidered patch that reads 'ASK ME ABOUT BABA STOCK' in blocky letters.

The cart is called Threefold, named for the three broths Anouk cycles through depending on their mood and what they could source cheaply. They are exuberantly social, know regulars by name and usual order, and maintain a strict policy of sliding-scale pricing that they enforce entirely based on vibes — they have never written it down and deny having a system, but longtime customers know that if Anouk likes you and you look hungry, you pay less. They pray to a small E.L.F. they call the Burner before every cook session, leaving a data-chip with a new recipe they've invented as an offering. They believe sincerely that the Burner makes the broth better.
Properties.role: Street-level noodle cart vendor
Properties.location: The cart circuit: mornings at Calumet Rise worker gate, afternoons at Deepwell Station plaza, evenings outside the Ferment Quarter
Properties.narrative_function: Social hub of street-level information; pulse-point for neighborhood mood; can introduce players to a wide web of working-class contacts. Potential quest giver for local disputes or ingredient sourcing gone strange.
Properties.augmentations: Cosmetic geneware: bioluminescent teal subdermal dot pattern across collarbone and upper arms. Heat-resistant dermis on both hands (functional mod, bought over two years of installments).
Properties.core_fears: Losing the cart and with it the only thing that is entirely theirs; Being ordinary — being someone no one stops for
Properties.core_desires: To open a real restaurant someday, just one room, just their food; To be loved without having to perform for it
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Cooking as emotional regulation; Deflecting difficult feelings with humor and volume
Properties.blind_spots: Overgives to people who exploit their generosity, then resents them without saying so; The cart's finances are worse than they admit to themselves
Properties.secret: One of their regulars — a quiet man who eats at the Deepwell stop every Tuesday — has been paying three times the price and leaving without change for a year. Anouk found out he's a low-level Tessera facilities worker who lost a child and comes to the cart because it was where he used to bring her. Anouk hasn't told anyone and saves his usual table obsessively.
Properties.story_hooks: A supplier from the Grainfort wholesale market has started pushing unusual synthetic protein that Anouk can't identify but that makes the broth unnervingly popular — something is in the additive.; The Calumet Rise vendor cooperative is being strong-armed into accepting a Zheng-Dao food-service contract that would displace independent carts; Anouk is the loudest voice against it but also the most financially vulnerable.
Properties.affiliation: Independent; licensed through the Calumet Rise vendor cooperative
Properties.vocabulary: High-energy, food-metaphor-heavy, occasional Twi or Bosnian interjection
Properties.cadence: Fast, overlapping, hard to interrupt — they talk while they cook and barely pause
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Okay but listen — I put the fermented lime in the Threefold Three today, you want the Three, I'm telling you, I woke up at 3 AM thinking about the Three.' | 'You look like a cold broth problem. Sit down. Eat first. Then tell me.'

Properties.description:
Anya Kozel is the reason Last Light functions at all. She manages the logistics of a pro-bono protection operation in a community with no resources — safe house rotations, transport arrangements, community contact networks, supply chains for medical kits and food, client scheduling, and the thousand administrative details that separate a functioning crew from three idealists shouting into the void. She does this with a budget that wouldn't cover a week's coffee for a corporate crew, and she does it well.

She came to the Shelf from the Milwaukee Core working class — her parents ran a small printing business that went under when the corporate district's digital infrastructure made physical printing economically impossible. The family relocated to the Shelf when Anya was seventeen. She watched her parents lose everything they'd built — not to malice, but to the indifferent machinery of corporate progress that treats small businesses as statistical noise. She finished her education through Shelf community programs, developed organizational skills through necessity, and joined Last Light because Ruth Agada was the first person she'd met who responded to systemic injustice with organized resistance rather than resignation.

Anya is compact, precise, with dark hair pulled back and the permanently alert expression of someone managing too many moving pieces. She carries a tablet everywhere — the device is her operational hub, containing contact networks, resource inventories, safe house statuses, and the scheduling system that keeps Last Light's operations from collapsing. She dresses practically, sleeps insufficiently, and eats whatever's closest. She is burning out. She knows this. She hasn't stopped because stopping would be worse.
Properties.role: Logistics, safe house management, and community network — Last Light
Properties.location: The Shelf — maintains a small apartment above the community center that doubles as Last Light's operational hub
Properties.narrative_function: Anya is the invisible infrastructure — the character whose work makes the visible heroism possible. Her stories explore burnout, the invisibility of organizational labor, and the particular tragedy of someone who is excellent at supporting others and terrible at supporting herself. She is the character most likely to collapse, and her collapse would take Last Light down with her.
Properties.augmentations: Communication suite with encrypted multi-channel capability — manages simultaneous conversations with community contacts, clients, and crew. Eidetic organizational memory — perfect recall of names, addresses, schedules, and resource inventories. Low-grade biomonitor that she ignores the warnings from. No physical augmentations.
Properties.core_fears: That she'll make an organizational error that gets a client hurt — a wrong safe house, a missed schedule, a contact who was compromised; That her burnout will become visible and Ruth will tell her to rest, which would feel like being told she's failed; That the work is genuinely unsustainable and her organizational brilliance is just delaying the inevitable collapse
Properties.core_desires: To build a system that works — a community protection infrastructure that doesn't depend on three people working themselves to death; To be recognized as essential without having to perform essentiality — to have the organizational work valued as much as Ruth's moral authority or Josiah's physical protection; To sleep. Really, genuinely, to sleep for twelve hours and wake up rested. She can't remember the last time this happened.
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Organizational work as anxiety management — if the system is running, the anxiety has a channel. When the system idles, the anxiety floods.; Resets the biomonitor because the data is too frightening and showing it to Ruth would create a problem Anya doesn't have the energy to manage; Treats her own exhaustion as a logistics problem — she schedules rest like she schedules safe house rotations and then fails to execute the schedule
Properties.blind_spots: She believes she's hiding the burnout when everyone can see it — the dark circles, the weight loss, the shortened fuse; She treats her own needs as a resource allocation problem and consistently allocates zero; She doesn't recognize that her burnout is contagious — her exhaustion puts pressure on Ruth and Josiah that amplifies their own
Properties.secret: She has been maintaining a second set of books — a parallel budget that tracks the actual cost of Last Light's operations against what they take in. The numbers are devastating. At current burn rate, Last Light has approximately five months of operational capacity before the safe houses can't be maintained and the medical supplies run out. She has been quietly approaching external funding sources that Ruth would not approve of. No commitments yet. But the conversations have started.
Properties.story_hooks: Anya's funding conversations lead to an offer that would sustain Last Light but compromise its independence — the pragmatism versus the principle; A safe house is compromised because Anya was too exhausted to catch the signal — the burnout has consequences; Anya collapses physically and the crew must operate without her — revealing how much of Last Light depends on one person; A community contact betrays the network, and Anya must rebuild trust across forty relationships while running on empty
Properties.affiliation: Last Light
Properties.vocabulary: Organizational, logistical, efficient. She speaks in systems — schedules, contacts, resources, contingencies. When she's tired, which is always, the efficiency becomes clipped.
Properties.cadence: Fast, compressed. She packs maximum information into minimum sentences. Not impatient — efficient. The distinction matters but people can't always tell.
Properties.example_dialogue: Updating. The east-side safe house is compromised — we need to rotate the Karim family to the backup on Lakeshore. I can have transport in forty minutes. | We have a gap. Medical supplies are at thirty percent and there's no restock scheduled. I need options by tomorrow. | I'm fine, Ruth. The system is running. The clients are covered. That's what matters.

Properties.description:
Ruth Agada is the lowest-paid runner in Meridian 88 and the most respected person below Tier 3. Last Light takes contracts that nobody else will touch: protecting excluded families from eviction squads, escorting debt-marked citizens through corporate checkpoints, standing between Shelf communities and the security forces that treat them as jurisdictional noise. The pay is whatever the clients can afford, which is usually nothing. Ruth doesn't care. The work is the work.

She was a public defender in Meridian 88's municipal court system for eighteen years — one of the last attorneys who represented excluded citizens in jurisdictional disputes. When the court system was privatized and representation became a billable service priced beyond the excluded's reach, Ruth kept working. Pro bono. For free. The bar association suspended her license for 'unprofessional conduct.' She appealed. The appeal court was also privatized. She stopped appealing and started operating outside the legal system that had abandoned the people she served.

Ruth is tall, broad, with the bearing of a woman who has stood in courtrooms and stared down corporate attorneys and felt nothing but the certainty of purpose. Her hair is silver, worn natural, and her face carries the particular beauty of someone who has been angry for thirty years and hasn't let the anger eat her. She wears practical clothes and carries herself like a person who has decided what she is for and will not be moved.
Properties.aliases: Last Light Lead, The Pastor, Auntie Ruth
Properties.role: Crew lead and community defense coordinator — Last Light
Properties.location: The Shelf — operates from a community center three blocks from Mrs. Chen's shop
Properties.narrative_function: Ruth drives the stories about the cost of doing the right thing. Last Light's operations don't end in heist scores or data extraction — they end in small victories that prevent larger tragedies, paid for with exhaustion, poverty, and the slow erosion of hope. Ruth is the moral center of the Shelf runner ecosystem and the character who asks: what does it cost to be good in a world that doesn't pay for it?
Properties.augmentations: Legal database cortex — complete M88 jurisdictional code, precedent, and regulatory framework stored in long-term memory. Outdated now, but the institutional knowledge remains valuable. Voice amplification implant for addressing crowds and confronting security forces — her voice carries. Stress-monitoring biosystem that alerts her when her blood pressure enters dangerous territory. No combat augmentations.
Properties.core_fears: That the work makes no structural difference — that she's treating symptoms while the disease gets worse; That her crew will burn out and leave, and the people who depend on Last Light will have nobody; That the anger she's carried for thirty years is damaging her body in ways the biosystem can't fully track
Properties.core_desires: To build a protection infrastructure that outlasts her — a community defense network that doesn't depend on one person; To see one structural change. One law, one policy, one jurisdictional adjustment that acknowledges the excluded as people. Just one.; To rest. She will not rest until the work is done. The work will never be done. She knows this. She cannot stop.
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Channels the anger into purpose — the fury is the fuel and the fuel is what gets her through the door; Cooks for people because feeding is a form of caring that doesn't require hope; Maintains legal frameworks in her head even though the legal system abandoned her — the knowledge is the identity, and the identity is the fight
Properties.blind_spots: She cannot accept help from sources she considers morally compromised, which limits her resources catastrophically; Her self-sacrifice is so complete that her crew follows the model and burns out — she leads by example and the example is self-destruction; She believes in the system she was trained in — law, rights, representation — even though the system has been explicitly dismantled
Properties.secret: She was offered a position with the Quiet Table two years ago — Glass Maren wanted her community contacts and her legal knowledge. The position would have paid enough to fund Last Light's operations for a decade. She refused because working for an information broker would compromise the trust the excluded have in her. She has never told her crew, and on the worst nights, she wonders if the refusal was righteous or wasteful.
Properties.story_hooks: A Shelf eviction campaign targets the community center itself — Ruth must defend the operational base; Glass Maren's offer resurfaces through an intermediary, and the funding crisis forces Ruth to reconsider; A corporate security force detains a Last Light client and Ruth must navigate a legal system that no longer recognizes her authority; Ruth's health deteriorates — the biosystem warnings are getting more frequent and the anger is extracting its biological price
Properties.affiliation: Last Light
Properties.vocabulary: Legal, moral, grounded. She speaks in the language of rights, obligations, and precedent. The courtroom training never left. When she addresses a crowd, the voice carries the weight of prepared argument. In private, she's warmer, more tired.
Properties.cadence: Deliberate, authoritative, with the rhythm of someone who has been making closing arguments for three decades. She builds sentences like cases — evidence, then conclusion.
Properties.example_dialogue: Hear me now. This family has lived in this unit for eleven years. Your eviction authority derives from a jurisdictional clause that was amended six months ago. You don't have standing. Leave. | They have a right to representation. I know the courts don't recognize that anymore. I do. | Come here, baby. Sit down. Eat something. Tell me what happened. We'll figure out what to do.

Properties.description:
Josiah Pine stands between excluded people and the things that hurt them. That's the job. Everything else — the pay, the recognition, the future — is negotiable. Josiah is six-two, built like a person who does physical work because physical work needs doing, and carries himself with the controlled energy of someone who learned early that being big and Black on the Shelf means every interaction starts with someone else's assumptions about your intentions.

He grew up in a Shelf community defense collective — neighbors who organized to protect their block when corporate security treated the area as an unregulated zone. His mother ran the collective. His father was killed by a private security contractor during a jurisdictional sweep when Josiah was eleven. The contractor faced no charges because the Shelf exists in a governance gap where accountability is a luxury the excluded cannot afford. Josiah learned two things from this: violence is the language the powerful speak, and the powerless need someone who can translate.

Ruth recruited him from the community defense network three years ago. He came because Ruth's approach — legal frameworks, documented resistance, non-violent intervention — was more sustainable than the collective's escalating confrontations with security forces. He stays because Ruth is the most principled person he has ever met and because the work, even underfunded and exhausting, feels like the only honest thing left.
Properties.role: Field protector and physical security — Last Light
Properties.location: The Shelf — rooms in the community center when he's not sleeping at whatever client location needs overnight security
Properties.narrative_function: Josiah embodies the physical cost of non-violent resistance — the bruises, the restraint, the barely contained fury of a strong man who chooses not to fight back because the cause requires it. His stories explore the tension between justice and anger, between his father's death and Ruth's principles, between the violence he's capable of and the peace he's chosen.
Properties.augmentations: Reinforced skeletal structure in arms, shoulders, and ribcage — installed by a Shelf surgeon after a beating during a community defense action. The augmentation was paid for by a community fund. Dermal toughening on forearms and hands — not armor, but sufficient to absorb impacts. No neural or cognitive augmentations — Josiah doesn't trust anything in his brain that he didn't put there.
Properties.core_fears: That the restraint will break — that someone will push too far and the violence his father's death put in him will come out and prove every assumption about him right; That Ruth's legal approach is noble but insufficient — that the excluded need force, not frameworks, and his restraint is cowardice wearing principle's clothes; That his father's killer is still working security somewhere in M88, protected by the same jurisdictional gap that killed his father
Properties.core_desires: To honor his mother's work — to prove that community defense can be sustained without becoming the thing it opposes; To see accountability. One security contractor held responsible. One jurisdictional gap closed. Proof that the system can be made to work.; To protect people so completely that the protection becomes unnecessary — a Shelf where excluded families don't need Last Light
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Physical training — the contained violence finds its outlet in controlled exertion, not in the field; Building and repair work — fixing the community center channels the constructive impulse that counterbalances the destructive one; Ruth's presence — her certainty moderates his anger. When she says 'we do this right,' he believes her. Most days.
Properties.blind_spots: He conflates his personal rage about his father with the structural injustice he fights — the causes overlap but they're not identical; He measures his worth by his physical utility and doesn't recognize his emotional value to the crew and community; He assumes his restraint is a choice he can always make, but the accumulation of absorbed violence is eroding the foundation
Properties.secret: He has identified the private security firm that employed the contractor who killed his father. The firm still operates in M88. He has the contractor's name. He has done nothing with this information because acting on it would betray everything Ruth has taught him. The information sits in his chest like a second heartbeat.
Properties.story_hooks: The security contractor who killed Josiah's father appears on a Shelf patrol — the past becomes present and the restraint faces its ultimate test; A protection case requires physical confrontation that Ruth's legal methods cannot resolve — Josiah must choose between Ruth's rules and the client's safety; Community defense collectives across the Shelf begin organizing and want Josiah to lead — the scale increases but the resources don't; Josiah takes a severe beating protecting a client and must recover while the work doesn't stop — the body's limits versus the mission's demands
Properties.affiliation: Last Light
Properties.vocabulary: Direct, physical, occasionally quoting his mother's community defense principles. He speaks in concrete terms — bodies, spaces, threats. Abstract concepts get translated into physical metaphors.
Properties.cadence: Measured when calm, which is most of the time. Sentences get shorter and harder as he approaches his limit. The crew measures his state by sentence length.
Properties.example_dialogue: I'm right here. You want to get to them, you go through me. And you don't want to go through me. | My old man taught me that protecting people is the only work that matters. Then the system killed him for doing it. So now I protect people outside the system. | Ruth says use the law. I use the law. But the law needs a body standing behind it, and that's me.

Properties.description: Anya is built like someone who has carried heavy things her entire life — broad shoulders, thick forearms, hands that look like they could crush walnuts or cradle a child with equal confidence. She came to Meridian 88 from the Volgograd displacement zone when she was nineteen, pregnant, speaking four words of English: 'please,' 'help,' 'work,' and 'no.' She now speaks roughly forty words of English, all of them practical. She communicates primarily through a translation app on a cracked tablet that she holds like a shield. Her face is weathered beyond her years — deep lines around her mouth, sun damage from agricultural work in the displacement camps, a scar across her left eyebrow from a piece of industrial debris. She is not soft. She is not hard. She is a woman who has been carrying impossible weight for so long that her skeleton has restructured itself around the burden. She scraped together Kyle's fee by selling her blood to a Helix BioSystems collection point three times a week for two months. Kyle took the job at half rate. She does not know this and he will never tell her.
Properties.role: Client — hired Kyle to avenge her husband's beating
Properties.location: The Shelf — Tier Four, three corridors south of Chen's
Properties.narrative_function: Anya is the human cost that justifies Kyle's violence. She is the reason the code exists. When the reader questions whether Kyle is a monster, Anya is the answer: no, he is the thing monsters are afraid of, and he works for women who sell their blood to pay his fee.
Properties.augmentations: None. Cannot afford them.
Properties.core_fears: That her daughter saw the violence she paid for; That Meridian 88 will consume her family the way it consumed her homeland
Properties.core_desires: Her husband eating solid food again; Yuliya growing up without learning what a fixer is
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Cooks constantly — food is the one language that needs no translation; Prays in Russian to saints she isn't sure she believes in
Properties.blind_spots: Does not understand that Kyle's fee was discounted — if she did, her pride would break
Properties.secret: She knows exactly who the gang works for. She hired Kyle anyway.
Properties.story_hooks: She knows who the gang works for — information Kyle might need later; Her blood sales to Helix BioSystems put her DNA in a corporate database; She will try to feed Kyle. He will not know how to refuse.
Properties.affiliation: None
Properties.vocabulary: Forty words of English, all blunt instruments. Speaks through a translation app or through her daughter.
Properties.cadence: Short. Direct. No filler. Every English word costs her effort.
Properties.example_dialogue: You fix. I pay. All I have. | My husband. Good man. They break him.

Properties.description: Demyan was a large man before the beating — a cargo handler at the Shelf's loading platforms, the kind of work that builds slabs of muscle across the back and shoulders. He is still large, but the architecture has shifted. His jaw is wired shut with medical-grade titanium pins visible through the skin of his cheeks like rivets in a hull. He communicates through a vocoder pad strapped to his wrist that converts typed text to flat, mechanical speech. His eyes are the part that didn't break — dark, warm, patient. He looks at his wife like she invented sunlight. He looks at his daughter like she is the reason sunlight matters. When Kyle's teeth arrive, delivered by a trembling Yuliya, Demyan will hold them in his palm for a long time. Then he will laugh. The vocoder will translate it as a series of monotone ha-ha-ha sounds. It will be the funniest and saddest thing in the Shelf that night.
Properties.role: Anya's husband — beaten by the gang, jaw wired shut
Properties.location: The Shelf — Tier Four, bedridden
Properties.narrative_function: Demyan is what Kyle is fighting for — not as an individual but as a category. A good man broken by people with more chrome and less conscience. His recovery (or failure to recover) is a barometer for whether Kyle's violence actually helps.
Properties.augmentations: Titanium jaw pins (medical, not elective). Vocoder pad.
Properties.core_fears: That Anya sold something irreplaceable to pay for his revenge; That he cannot protect his family from his own bed
Properties.core_desires: To eat solid food; To carry things again; To thank the man who did what he could not
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Types jokes on the vocoder — gallows humor in Russian; Sketches mechanical designs on a tablet — he was an engineer before the displacement
Properties.blind_spots: Does not know Anya is selling blood; Thinks Yuliya is adjusting well
Properties.secret: He recognized one of the gang members. A former colleague from the loading platforms. He has not told Anya.
Properties.story_hooks: He recognized a gang member — former colleague, which means the beating wasn't random; His engineering background could be useful to someone building or maintaining hardware; The vocoder creates accidental poetry
Properties.affiliation: None
Properties.vocabulary: Speaks through a vocoder pad. Flat monotone delivery makes everything sound either profound or absurd.
Properties.cadence: Types slowly. Deliberate. Each word chosen because typing hurts.
Properties.example_dialogue: TEETH. GOOD. HA. | TELL WIRE MAN I OWE HIM SOUP. WHEN JAW WORKS.

Properties.description: Yuliya is twelve going on forty. She has her mother's build compressed into a child's frame — square shoulders, strong hands, a jaw that sets when she is angry in a way that makes adults take a step back. She speaks perfect unaccented English because the Shelf's children learn from feeds, not parents. She translates for her mother with the weary competence of a UN interpreter. She has seen things a twelve-year-old should not see. She has cataloged them. She does not cry about them. She has a notebook where she writes down everything that happens in the Shelf — who did what to whom, who owes what, who is afraid of whom. She calls it 'homework.' It is an intelligence network maintained by a child. She followed Kyle to the loading dock because she needed to see. Not wanted — needed. She is her father's daughter: she has to understand how things work, even the terrible things. Especially the terrible things. The teeth in her hands are the heaviest thing she has ever carried.
Properties.role: Anya and Demyan's daughter — witness to the Prologue violence
Properties.location: The Shelf — Tier Four
Properties.narrative_function: Yuliya is the Shelf's future watching the Shelf's present and writing it down. She is what happens when a child grows up in a place where violence is weather. She is also the reader's proxy — observing Kyle from the outside, trying to make sense of him.
Properties.augmentations: None.
Properties.core_fears: That she is becoming someone who isn't scared of violence; That her notebook will be found
Properties.core_desires: To understand why people hurt each other; To hear her father's real voice again
Properties.coping_mechanisms: The notebook — writing things down makes them smaller; Translates obsessively, even conversations she isn't part of
Properties.blind_spots: Thinks she is invisible when she follows people. She is not.; Believes understanding violence is the same as being safe from it.
Properties.secret: She has been following Kyle for three weeks. The Prologue was not the first time. She has six pages of notes on him.
Properties.story_hooks: Her notebook is a Shelf intelligence network maintained by a child; She has been following Kyle for weeks — she knows his patterns; She will become a recurring presence — Kyle's smallest, most persistent shadow
Properties.affiliation: None
Properties.vocabulary: Perfect English, advanced for her age. Clinical when describing violence. Childlike when caught off guard.
Properties.cadence: Fast when translating. Slow when speaking for herself. Long pauses when processing something she doesn't have words for yet.
Properties.example_dialogue: I wasn't scared. I was documenting. | Papa laughed when I gave him the teeth. The machine made it sound like a broken radio. But I could tell.
