Properties.description:
Corva Lam dives into the drowned ruins of Old Harbor and brings back things that should have stayed buried. Pre-collapse infrastructure, sealed server farms, military hardware that was never officially there — the flooded districts are an archaeological site for technology the corps want recovered and the city wants forgotten. Corva knows these waters better than anyone alive because she grew up on them. Her family ran fishing operations in the harbor before the collapse raised the water level and swallowed everything below the second floor.

She built the Boneyard Saints from salvage divers and ruin-runners who shared two qualities: the skill to survive Old Harbor's flooded labyrinth and the nerve to go deep when the sonar returns something that shouldn't be there. The ruins are not empty. Pre-collapse automated security systems still operate on backup power in some sections. Marine life has adapted to the submerged infrastructure in ways that marine biologists would find fascinating and divers find terrifying. And then there are the sounds — low-frequency resonance from deep structures that shouldn't be producing sound at all.

Corva is broad-shouldered, weathered by salt water and UV exposure, with short dark hair and the permanently squinting eyes of someone who's spent too many hours in glare. Her hands are scarred from coral cuts and salvage work. She moves with the deliberate economy of a diver — every gesture conserves energy, every step is placed. On land she seems slightly wrong, like a marine creature forced to perform on dry ground.
Properties.role: Crew lead and master diver — Boneyard Saints
Properties.location: Old Harbor — operates from a converted shipping container on the remaining dry dock
Properties.narrative_function: Corva drives the treasure-hunt-with-horror-elements stories of the Boneyard Saints. Her world is literally submerged — drowned infrastructure, forgotten technology, things that move in the dark water. She represents the scavenger economy of M88's margins, where the past is more valuable than the present, and recovering it requires going into places that feel actively hostile to human presence.
Properties.augmentations: Amphibious respiratory system — modified lungs that extract dissolved oxygen from water for up to 90 minutes before requiring surface air. Pressure-compensation implants in inner ear and sinuses. Sonar-processing cortex that interprets underwater acoustic data as spatial mapping. Thermal regulation dermal layer for extended cold-water immersion. Bio-luminescent dermal tattoos on her forearms that activate underwater — functional lighting, not cosmetic.
Properties.core_fears: That something in the deep ruins is aware of her — that the sounds and the movement patterns are not mechanical; That she is leading her crew into salvage sites that are more dangerous than she admits because the contracts pay too well to refuse; That the harbor will never be recovered and her family's world is permanently drowned
Properties.core_desires: To map every flooded structure in Old Harbor — to know the drowned city completely; To find the thing her father went looking for on his last dive. He never told her what it was. He never came back.; To keep the Saints alive in waters that actively resist human presence
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Dives alone when the pressure gets too heavy — the underwater silence is the only place her mind goes quiet; Treats every dive as a technical problem rather than an emotional one — the water is physics, not metaphor; Maintains the container and the dock with obsessive care because the dry land base is the counterweight to the chaos below
Properties.blind_spots: Her comfort in the water makes her underestimate how alien and terrifying the deep ruins are for her crew; She treats her father's disappearance as an unsolved puzzle rather than a grief — the emotional processing is submerged, literally; She cannot admit that some of the deep ruins should remain unexplored because the unknown is the only thing that still excites her
Properties.secret: She found her father's dive gear three years ago in a sealed section of the flooded harbor. The gear was intact. There was no body. The section had been sealed from the inside.
Properties.story_hooks: A contract leads the Saints to the sealed section where Corva found her father's gear — someone wants whatever is inside; The deep-ruin sounds intensify and begin responding to the Saints' sonar — something is listening; A pre-collapse server farm recovered from the ruins contains data that multiple corps are willing to kill for; Pike goes on an unauthorized deep dive and doesn't surface on schedule
Properties.affiliation: Boneyard Saints
Properties.vocabulary: Maritime, technical, physical. She describes things in terms of depth, pressure, current. Metaphors are aquatic without affectation.
Properties.cadence: Measured, calm, with the rhythm of someone who controls their breathing professionally. Gets clipped underwater — short phrases conserve air.
Properties.example_dialogue: The ruins don't care if you're scared. The water doesn't care if you're brave. Check your gear and surface it — what are we actually dealing with? | My father went down looking for something. I go down because I can't stop. The difference is I come back. | That's a thirty-meter problem. We're not equipped for thirty meters today.
Properties.facet_weights: wound=0.50 ideal=0.50 id=0.55 shadow=0.45 mask=0.35 ghost=0.60

Properties.description:
Toll Brecker moves things that weren't designed to be moved — sealed vault doors, collapsed structural beams, server racks that have been underwater for two decades and now weigh twice what they should. He is the Boneyard Saints' heavy operator, the one who makes physically impossible salvage operations merely improbable. Before the Saints, he worked harbor construction — the last generation of workers who built things in Old Harbor before the water rose and made building irrelevant.

He is enormous. Six-four, two-sixty, with the dense, functional musculature of someone who has lifted heavy things underwater for most of his adult life. His augmentations are industrial rather than military — strength amplification, pressure tolerance, respiratory capacity. They were installed for construction work and repurposed for salvage. He moves slowly on land because he has learned that large men who move quickly frighten people, and Toll does not want to frighten anyone who doesn't deserve it.

He is the kindest member of the Boneyard Saints, which is a strange thing to say about a man who can tear a steel door off its hinges. He cooks for the crew on the barge, sings while he works underwater (the respiratory system allows it), and names the marine creatures that have colonized the ruins. He is also the only Saint who will openly discuss the sounds in the deep sections, because pretending they don't exist seems dishonest and Toll is constitutionally incapable of dishonesty.
Properties.role: Heavy salvage and crew security — Boneyard Saints
Properties.location: Old Harbor — lives in a converted barge moored to the dry dock
Properties.narrative_function: Toll is the gentle giant in a horror setting — the warm, honest presence that makes the Boneyard Saints feel like a family rather than a salvage crew. His willingness to acknowledge the strangeness of the deep ruins makes him the crew's canary in the coal mine. When Toll says something is wrong, the audience trusts it because Toll doesn't lie.
Properties.augmentations: Industrial-grade myofiber enhancement in arms, legs, and back — triples effective lifting capacity. Deep-pressure skeletal reinforcement allowing operation at depths that would injure unaugmented divers. Extended respiratory system with 120-minute underwater capacity. Magnetic grip implants in palms for ferrous material handling.
Properties.core_fears: That the sounds in the deep ruins are exactly what he thinks they are — something alive, something aware, something that knows the Saints are there; That his strength will be needed for something terrible — that the physical power that moves salvage will be used to hurt someone; That Corva's night dives will end the way her father's last dive ended, and he'll find her gear without her body
Properties.core_desires: To keep the crew safe and fed and human in a place that erodes all three; To understand the ruins — not as salvage sites but as a place. What happened here. Why it sounds like that.; To build a life that is honest and kind in a world that rewards neither
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Cooks when he's worried — the more elaborate the meal, the bigger the concern; Sings underwater because the sound fills the silence that otherwise fills with the other sounds; Names the marine creatures because naming things makes them familiar and familiar things are less frightening
Properties.blind_spots: His kindness makes him slow to recognize genuine threats from people, though never from the environment; He assumes everyone shares his honesty and is repeatedly surprised when they don't; He treats his own fears as data rather than warnings — acknowledging the sounds without acting on the fear they produce
Properties.secret: He has heard the deep-ruin sounds respond to his singing. Specific frequencies, specific patterns. It's not an echo. Something is matching his notes. He has told no one because saying it out loud would make it real.
Properties.story_hooks: The deep-ruin sounds respond to Toll's singing in a pattern that cannot be mechanical — first contact with something unknown; A salvage operation uncovers a sealed section containing technology that is clearly still operating, powered by something the Saints can't identify; Toll's industrial augmentations begin corroding from extended saltwater exposure — his strength has a shelf life; A corporate salvage team arrives in Old Harbor with military equipment, and the Saints must decide whether to fight, flee, or negotiate
Properties.affiliation: Boneyard Saints
Properties.vocabulary: Simple, concrete, warm. He speaks in the language of physical things — weight, depth, temperature, texture. Metaphors are rare because he prefers to say exactly what he means.
Properties.cadence: Slow, steady, with the natural rhythm of someone who has never been in a hurry. His voice is deep enough to feel in your chest if you're standing close.
Properties.example_dialogue: Now, I'm not saying there's something down there. I'm saying I hear something down there. Those are different things and they're both true. | The water's got teeth today. We go shallow or we don't go. | I cook because people who eat together don't fall apart as fast.
Properties.facet_weights: wound=0.30 ideal=0.65 id=0.50 shadow=0.25 mask=0.20 ghost=0.45

Properties.description:
Wren Isaza never goes in the water. She is the Boneyard Saints' land-side brain — the one who identifies what the divers bring up, determines its value, traces its origin, and interfaces with pre-collapse systems that have been submerged for two decades. She has a gift for dead technology. She can look at a corroded circuit board, a water-damaged server core, a sealed data capsule that hasn't seen air since the harbor flooded, and tell you what it was, who made it, and how much someone will pay for it.

She came to Old Harbor from the Circuit, where she'd been running a small electronics repair business that was slowly being crushed by corporate parts monopolies. A Boneyard Saint brought in a piece of salvage she couldn't identify — pre-collapse military firmware sealed in a waterproof housing. Wren spent three days cracking it, sold the data for more money than her shop had made in a year, and realized the harbor was full of things the world had forgotten it needed.

Wren is small, dark-haired, perpetually ink-stained from the physical documentation she insists on maintaining alongside digital records. She wears magnification goggles pushed up on her forehead and cargo vests with every pocket full. She talks fast when she's excited about a piece of salvage and not at all when she's working on one. The warehouse is her domain — organized in a system that makes sense to her and no one else, with pre-collapse artifacts in various states of analysis covering every surface.
Properties.role: Technical analyst and salvage valuator — Boneyard Saints
Properties.location: Old Harbor — works from a converted warehouse on the dry dock, adjacent to Corva's container
Properties.narrative_function: Wren is the analytical lens through which the Boneyard Saints' horror elements focus. She is the character who provides explanations — and the character whose explanations start failing as the deep ruins reveal things that don't fit her models. Her growing unease with the data she's collecting drives the existential horror beneath the treasure-hunt surface.
Properties.augmentations: Micro-manipulation fingertip implants — allow precise work on components smaller than the eye can see. Optical augmentation with spectrum analysis — she can identify material composition by visual scanning. Encrypted data-interface jack for connecting to pre-collapse systems without network exposure. No physical augmentations — Wren has never needed strength, just precision.
Properties.core_fears: That the deep-ruin data doesn't fit any model because the model is wrong — that the accepted history of Old Harbor's collapse is a lie; That the technology she's analyzing was never meant to be found and recovering it has consequences she can't predict; That she'll become so absorbed in the work that she loses the capacity to live outside it
Properties.core_desires: To understand what happened to Old Harbor — the real story, not the official one; To be taken seriously as a researcher, not just a salvage valuator. The work she does is archaeology, even if no institution recognizes it.; To solve the pre-collapse mystery she's assembling from a thousand fragments of recovered data
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Buries herself in work when the data gets frightening — the process of analysis is soothing even when the content isn't; Maintains physical documentation as a hedge against digital vulnerability — paper doesn't glitch, paper doesn't get hacked; Rationalizes the unexplainable until the rationalizations stop working, then documents the failure and keeps going
Properties.blind_spots: She treats the unexplainable as a knowledge gap rather than a warning — the scientist's hubris of assuming everything is knowable; Her focus on the technical prevents her from seeing how the deep-ruin discoveries are affecting the crew emotionally; She underestimates physical danger because her work happens in a warehouse, not underwater
Properties.secret: She has assembled enough fragments of pre-collapse data to suspect that Old Harbor wasn't destroyed by rising water levels. The flooding was deliberate. Something in the deep infrastructure was sealed in, not abandoned. She has not shared this theory because she doesn't have proof, and Wren doesn't share theories without proof.
Properties.story_hooks: A recovered data core contains footage from the night Old Harbor flooded — the official record doesn't match; Wren's theory about deliberate flooding finds proof, and the proof implicates a corporation that still operates in M88; A pre-collapse system she's analyzing activates when she interfaces with it — and it tries to communicate; A corporate buyer pressures the Saints for a specific artifact, and Wren realizes they know what's down there
Properties.affiliation: Boneyard Saints
Properties.vocabulary: Technical, specific, rapid when excited. Electronics terminology, materials science, archival jargon. Lapses into academic language when she forgets her audience.
Properties.cadence: Variable — machine-gun fast when analyzing, silence when working, measured when delivering conclusions to clients.
Properties.example_dialogue: Okay so this isn't standard infrastructure. This is military-grade containment housing, sealed at the factory, never opened. Somebody put this here on purpose. | The patient's in bad shape but the data core is intact. Give me four hours and I'll have a manifest. | I don't have an explanation. I have seventeen data points that don't fit my model. That's not an explanation. That's a problem.
Properties.facet_weights: wound=0.35 ideal=0.60 id=0.45 shadow=0.40 mask=0.30 ghost=0.55

Properties.description:
Pike Odera is the fastest swimmer the Boneyard Saints have ever had and the most frustrated. He can navigate the flooded ruins of Old Harbor with an intuitive grace that borders on the uncanny — reading currents by feel, sensing structural integrity through water pressure changes, finding passages in the submerged infrastructure that older divers would miss or ignore. Corva trained him, Toll protects him, and neither will let him go deep. He is twenty-four years old and the leash is getting unbearable.

He came to Old Harbor from the Shelf, following rumors of salvage work that paid better than courier runs. He'd never been underwater before his first day with the Saints. Within a week, Corva said he moved in the water like he'd been born to it. Within a month, he was scouting routes that seasoned divers wouldn't attempt. The affinity is genuine and slightly inexplicable — Pike processes underwater environments with a fluency that his minimal augmentations don't fully account for.

Pike is wiry, quick, with close-cropped hair and an expression that alternates between eager and impatient. He has the lean build of a natural swimmer, long-limbed and efficient. His skin is perpetually salt-dried and he smells like the harbor — brine, rust, and something organic. He moves constantly, even on land, with the restless energy of someone who has found the thing they were meant to do and is being prevented from doing it fully.
Properties.role: Scout diver and route mapper — Boneyard Saints
Properties.location: Old Harbor — bunks in a hammock in Wren's warehouse when he's not sleeping on Toll's barge
Properties.narrative_function: Pike is the pull toward the unknown — the character who wants to go deeper, see more, understand what's in the dark water. His eagerness provides narrative momentum for the Boneyard Saints' horror elements while his youth creates the protective tension that drives Corva and Toll. He is the one who will eventually go where the story needs someone to go.
Properties.augmentations: Basic respiratory enhancement — extends underwater time to 60 minutes, less than Corva or Toll. Pressure-compensation ear implants. Low-grade sonar receiver (hand-held, not cortical) for underwater navigation. No strength augmentations — relies on speed, flexibility, and an intuitive sense of water dynamics that his augmentations don't explain.
Properties.core_fears: That his peak years as a diver are being wasted on shallow water and safe routes; That the affinity he has for the water is something other than talent — that the ruins are calling him and the calling is not benign; That the crew will never see him as a full member, only as the kid they're keeping alive
Properties.core_desires: To dive the deep sections — to see what Corva has seen and what she won't describe; To be recognized as a Saint, not a trainee. To have his instincts trusted.; To understand why the water feels like home in a way that nothing on land does
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Pushes boundaries on sanctioned routes — goes a little deeper, a little farther, stays a little longer than authorized; Brings artifacts to Wren as offerings — trying to prove his value through discovery rather than obedience; Explores the harbor shallows alone at dawn because the solitary swimming quiets the frustration
Properties.blind_spots: His natural affinity makes him underestimate the danger of the ruins — the water feels safe to him in ways it shouldn't; He interprets the crew's protectiveness as a judgment on his capability rather than an expression of care; He does not recognize that his comfort in the water might not be natural talent but something else entirely
Properties.secret: During his dawn swims, he's been exploring the edges of the deep sections — the transition zones where shallow water drops into the flooded infrastructure. He's heard the sounds. They don't frighten him. They feel familiar.
Properties.story_hooks: Pike's unauthorized deep-section exploration puts him in contact with whatever is producing the sounds; His inexplicable water affinity turns out to have a source — perhaps connected to pre-collapse experiments in the harbor; A salvage contract requires a scout who can navigate passages too narrow for Corva or Toll — Pike's moment arrives with conditions attached; He discovers something in the transition zone that challenges everything the Saints believe about the ruins
Properties.affiliation: Boneyard Saints
Properties.vocabulary: Young, direct, increasingly adopting maritime terminology as he assimilates into harbor culture. Mixes Shelf slang with diver jargon.
Properties.cadence: Impatient, forward-leaning. He talks like he's trying to get to the next sentence before finishing the current one.
Properties.example_dialogue: The current talks to you if you listen. I'm not saying I understand it. I'm saying it's talking. | I know, I know — stay shallow, map the route, come back. But there's a passage at the twenty-meter line that nobody's checked and I can feel it opening. | You trained me to be good. Now let me be good.

Properties.description:
Crisanto is a broad-shouldered Filipino-Swedish man of fifty-one who has spent so long performing the aesthetics of institutional trust that they have half-become real. He dresses in muted, expensive neutrals — nothing that would be remembered — and carries himself with the particular stillness of someone who learned long ago that a calm body reads as an authoritative one. His hair has gone fully silver and he wears it short and immaculate. The only thing that slightly undermines the effect is his habit of rolling a small obsidian bead between his fingers when he thinks no one is watching.

Officially, Crisanto is a Senior Compliance Auditor for Veltris Solutions, one of the Meridian Core's mid-weight corporate entities specializing in infrastructure licensing. He is very good at his job. He is also, quietly, one of the most reliable information brokers operating at the corporate tier — not a dealer in secrets so much as a dealer in context. He does not sell raw data; he sells the correct reading of data, the understanding of what something means and who it benefits. His clients are executives, rivals, occasionally investigators who can afford him.

Crisanto came to the Core from Old Harbor, a trajectory he has spent twenty years making illegible by careful accumulation of the right credentials, the right accent, the right address. He is not ashamed of Old Harbor. He is terrified of going back. The distinction matters to him and he is honest about it with himself at two in the morning when the distinction feels very thin. He has one adult daughter he supports financially and sees three times a year, and the relationship is exactly as complicated as that arrangement suggests.
Properties.role: Mid-tier corporate compliance auditor and covert information broker
Properties.location: The Meridian Core
Properties.narrative_function: Moral complexity at the corporate tier; embodies the cost of assimilation and the violence of institutional complicity; provides access to Core-level information and plot mechanics while remaining personally compromised
Properties.augmentations: Cortical memory indexer (standard corporate-tier, allows near-perfect recall of documents and conversations),Subvocal communication implant for silent calls,Subtle biometric regulation implant that suppresses visible stress indicators — heart rate, micro-expression, perspiration — installed voluntarily for professional performance
Properties.core_fears: Exposure — not of his brokering, but of his origins and the effort he has expended concealing them; That the version of himself he performs has replaced something that was actually worth keeping; Becoming unnecessary — in the corporate ecosystem, in his daughter's life
Properties.core_desires: Security that does not depend on anyone else's continued goodwill; To be genuinely known by someone without the knowledge being used against him; To do something, once, that is unambiguously good
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Compartmentalization so practiced it operates automatically; Obsessive preparation and contingency planning; Emotional withdrawal framed as professionalism
Properties.blind_spots: Assumes everyone operates with his level of strategic self-interest, misreads genuine altruism; His mask has become so functional he sometimes cannot locate his actual preferences; Underestimates the degree to which people in his life can see through the performance
Properties.secret: Three years ago he obtained and suppressed information that would have exposed a Veltris subsidiary's involvement in the displacement of several Old Harbor residential blocks, including the building where his mother lived until her death. He suppressed it because releasing it would have exposed his brokering operation. He has not fully processed this and may never.
Properties.story_hooks: A compliance audit Crisanto is assigned to unexpectedly surfaces the suppressed Old Harbor data from three years ago; Someone begins leaving him anonymous messages that contain information only he should know — testing him or warning him; A client asks him to broker something that would directly harm the Shelf community, including Nkechi Abara-Veltman's clinic; Remedios contacts him for the first time in eight months asking about Old Harbor records — and he has to decide in real time how to respond
Properties.affiliation: Veltris Solutions (Senior Compliance Auditor, official); independent information broker (covert, no organizational affiliation)
Properties.vocabulary: Boardroom-precise, slightly formal, with occasional idiomatic slippages into Tagalog or blunt Old Harbor directness when he is tired or cornered; uses passive constructions to distribute responsibility
Properties.cadence: Measured and deliberate, each sentence placed like a document on a desk; rarely raises his voice; silence is a tool he uses consciously
Properties.example_dialogue: 'I think what you're describing is a risk tolerance question. Let me tell you what the risk actually looks like.' | 'We're going to want to be careful about how that finding is documented. Not buried — careful.' | 'I grew up in Old Harbor. I know what a disposal operation sounds like. This is a disposal operation.' | 'The information is worth what it costs you not to have it. That's not a negotiation. That's arithmetic.'

Properties.description:
Thessaly Mourne occupies the precise, bloodless space between corporate law and corporate violence. Employed by Synclaire Financial Holdings as a Tier-1 Debt Resolution Specialist, she operates from a glass-walled office forty floors above the street, surrounded by cascading ledgers of names, outstanding balances, and algorithmic threat assessments. She is tall, angular, with close-cropped silver hair she began dyeing at thirty-two—not to look older, but because she said gray suited the work. Her skin is a deep warm brown, her face carefully composed into something that reads as neither cruel nor kind, just precise.

In the field, Thessaly moves through The Shelf like a tax collector moving through a famine. She dresses in muted corporate silvers and blacks, carries no visible weapon, and speaks in the measured cadence of someone reading aloud from a contract. She has never personally broken anyone's hands—she simply arrives, states the terms, and leaves the consequences to mathematics and to the two silent augmented associates who accompany her like footnotes. The residents of The Shelf call her Pale Mouth because of the white-tinted lip pigment she wears, and because of what comes out of it.

Thessaly was not born into the Meridian Core. She grew up in Old Harbor in a household that owed money to four separate creditors simultaneously, and she watched her mother perform an exhausting, humiliating arithmetic of survival every single week. She told herself she would learn the language of debt so fluently that it could never be used against her again. She did. She now speaks it against others with a fluency that frightens even her superiors, though none of them would say so aloud.
Properties.role: Corporate Debt Arbitrator / Enforcer
Properties.location: The Meridian Core (office), The Shelf (field operations)
Properties.narrative_function: Thessaly functions as a mirror and moral pressure point—a character who chose institutional power as survival and now enforces the exact conditions she escaped, forcing other characters (and the reader) to reckon with how systems perpetuate themselves through the people they wound. She is neither villain nor redeemed figure, but a sustained ethical question.
Properties.augmentations: Subdermal financial-grade memory implant storing encrypted contractual data (Synclaire-issued, Synclaire-monitored),Ocular overlay with real-time credit tier assessment and biometric stress-reading (helps her know when someone is lying about their ability to pay),Voluntary nerve-dampening implant in her hands—she had it installed after a field incident years ago and has never fully explained why
Properties.core_fears: Returning to a state of financial helplessness; Being seen as the thing she has become; That her mother, now comfortable on Thessaly's stipend, knows exactly how that comfort is funded
Properties.core_desires: Absolute financial insulation from chaos; To be recognized as intelligent rather than merely ruthless; One single transaction she can feel clean about
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Extreme proceduralism—reducing every moral problem to a contractual question; Collecting antique physical books on economics as a tactile ritual; Composing unsent letters to debtors explaining her reasoning
Properties.blind_spots: Genuinely believes the system she enforces is more honest than alternatives; Cannot recognize that her precision is a form of cruelty, not a mitigation of it; Mistakes her mother's silence for forgiveness
Properties.secret: She has quietly flagged three accounts for 'resolution delays' over the past year—effectively canceling the debts of families that reminded her too specifically of her own childhood. She has buried the paperwork in bureaucratic noise. If discovered, it would end her career and potentially her freedom.
Properties.story_hooks: A debt file crosses Thessaly's desk belonging to someone she owes a personal, non-financial debt—forcing her to choose between her proceduralism and the only moral act she's been avoiding; The three buried accounts she quietly cleared are discovered by an internal auditor who wants something from her in exchange for silence; A debtor she processed three years ago has risen to a position of power in The Circuit and has been systematically acquiring Synclaire's internal data—and Thessaly's name is prominent in it; She is assigned to collect on a debt held by someone she realizes is being used as bait by a faction that wants that person to default and disappear
Properties.affiliation: Synclaire Financial Holdings (Tier-1 employee, Debt Resolution Division)
Properties.vocabulary: Contract terminology, financial euphemisms, precise numerical references, rare but cutting use of plain language for emphasis
Properties.cadence: Measured, unhurried, with deliberate pauses before key terms as if giving the listener time to understand the weight of them
Properties.example_dialogue: 'The terms are not negotiable. The terms were never negotiable. That's what makes them terms.' | 'I don't collect pain. I collect what is owed. The pain is incidental—a variable, not a feature.' | 'You're a Tier-3 residential. Your ceiling for extensions expired six weeks ago. I'm not here to discuss that. I'm here to document that we discussed it.' | 'I grew up on this street. That's not a reason I'll treat you differently. It's a reason I won't pretend I don't know exactly what this costs you.'

Properties.description:
Priya Subramaniam-Vogt is a woman of precisely calibrated appearances — Tamil and German heritage rendered in sharp cheekbones, close-cropped silver-threaded black hair, and eyes that carry the particular exhaustion of someone who has seen too many spreadsheets hiding atrocities. She dresses in muted corporate palettes, charcoal and slate, never anything that might be remembered at a crime scene or a board meeting. Her augmentations are invisible by design: subdermal haptic interfaces along her fingertips, a retinal overlay for data parsing, and a cochlear implant that filters ambient sound into prioritized signal streams. She moves through rooms like a calculation being solved.

Priya has spent sixteen years as an internal investigator for Solenne-Hardt Consolidated, one of the Meridian Core's mid-tier financial conglomerates — not powerful enough to write law, powerful enough to bury people. Her job is nominally compliance: finding fraud, plugging leaks, flagging irregularities. In practice she is the person the company calls when something needs to disappear without leaving fingerprints on the company itself. She has shut down whistleblowers, engineered quiet terminations, and authored reports that exonerated executives whose guilt she documented with her own hands. She is very good at her job and has not slept well in four years.

What distinguishes Priya from the purely corrupt is a ledger she keeps — encrypted, air-gapped, stored on a physical drive she wears against her sternum. Every suppressed case, every buried name, every victim whose file she closed. She does not know yet what she intends to do with it. She tells herself it is insurance. She suspects it is penance she hasn't figured out how to pay.
Properties.role: Corporate Compliance Investigator / Internal Fixer
Properties.location: The Meridian Core (works), The Spire (residence, mid-tier floor)
Properties.narrative_function: Moral ambiguity anchor — a character who is complicit without being evil, whose redemption arc is genuinely uncertain. She bridges corporate and street-level worlds as an investigator, and her ledger functions as a potential detonator for multiple plotlines. She represents institutional harm as a slow, bureaucratic process rather than dramatic villainy.
Properties.augmentations: Subdermal haptic interface array (fingertips) — allows physical interaction with encrypted data surfaces,Retinal overlay (Solenne-Hardt proprietary, company-monitored) — data parsing, document authentication, micro-expression flagging,Cochlear signal filter — ambient noise prioritization, conversation recording (legally mandated disclosure she often omits),Mild adrenal dampener (pharmaceutical, not surgical) — keeps stress response flat during high-stakes interviews
Properties.core_fears: That her complicity makes her indistinguishable from those she investigates; That the ledger will be found before she decides what to do with it; Becoming entirely numb — losing the part of her that still flinches; That there is no version of accountability that does not destroy her along with the guilty
Properties.core_desires: To find a use for the ledger that means something; To be seen clearly — not the mask, not the role — and not immediately discarded; Order that serves people rather than institutions; One case she handles cleanly, without compromise
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Extreme professional compartmentalization — work brain, home brain, never overlapping; Elaborate meal preparation rituals on Sunday evenings as a form of meditation; Maintaining meticulous personal records as a proxy for control; Dry, deflecting humor that prevents emotional escalation
Properties.blind_spots: Underestimates how much her institutional loyalty has shaped her perception of 'realistic' outcomes; Mistakes emotional distance for ethical clarity; Assumes people outside corporate structures are less capable of nuanced loyalty; Cannot see that her caution reads to others as cold indifference
Properties.secret: Three years ago she suppressed evidence in a case that would have exposed a Solenne-Hardt subsidiary's role in a residential displacement scheme in The Shelf — a scheme that killed eleven people through unsafe interim housing. She knew. She filed the clean report anyway. The eleven names are the first entries in the ledger.
Properties.story_hooks: The ledger becomes known to multiple parties simultaneously — a journalist, a fixer, and someone who was in one of the eleven files; Priya is assigned to investigate a case that intersects with street-level characters she has no framework for, forcing her to operate outside institutional structures; Deveraux tasks her with closing a file that, for the first time, she cannot bring herself to close; Someone from The Shelf identifies her in public as 'the woman who buried the housing case' — and they're not wrong; She discovers the ledger has been copied — she doesn't know by whom, or when
Properties.affiliation: Solenne-Hardt Consolidated (employed); no external affiliations declared; covert non-affiliation with the ledger's implicit promise
Properties.vocabulary: Precise, institutional, occasionally dry to the point of seeming robotic. Uses corporate euphemism fluently but slips into directness when tired or emotionally activated. Technical financial and legal terminology deployed without explanation.
Properties.cadence: Measured and even, with deliberate pauses before important words. Rarely raises volume. Sentences are complete. Questions are rare and surgical.
Properties.example_dialogue: "The report reflects what the evidence supports. Whether the evidence is complete is a different question, and not one that was in scope." | "I'm not here to judge the decision. I'm here to document the outcome. There's a distinction, and I'd prefer we both remember it." | "You're asking me if I sleep well. That's a very personal question for a first meeting. The answer is no, but I don't think that's what you actually want to know." | "Eleven is a specific number. I'd appreciate it if you'd let me finish before you decide what it means."

Properties.description:
The Meridian Core is what the brochure promised. Glass towers catch manufactured
sunlight and throw it back in geometric patterns. The air is filtered, temperature-
controlled, and faintly scented — Axiom Environmental Services offers a rotating
seasonal palette, and this quarter it's "Alpine Morning," which smells like pine
trees and the absence of poor people. The streets are wide, clean, and monitored
by enough cameras to make God feel surveilled. Corporate employees walk with the
particular confidence of people whose health insurance actually covers things.
Everything is branded. The benches say Axiom. The trash cans say Axiom. The trees
are "Presented by Axiom Green Initiative." The trees are real, which is the most
expensive thing about them.

Kyle comes here for jobs. Corporate buildings need things done that corporate
employees can't do — wetwork, data extraction, intimidation of the kind that
doesn't show up on quarterly reports. The work pays well. The experience is
miserable. Every surface in the Core is designed to make someone like Kyle feel
like a contaminant. Security checkpoints scan his augments and flag them as
"non-standard." Retail algorithms adjust prices upward when his credit profile
enters a store. People don't stare — that would be impolite — but they adjust
their paths, the way you walk around something unpleasant on the sidewalk. The
Core is beautiful in the way a model home is beautiful: technically flawless,
emotionally void, and not meant for anyone who actually lives.

The real obscenity of the Core isn't the wealth. It's the normalcy. People here
live genuinely pleasant lives. Their kids go to good schools. Their augments work
perfectly. They eat well, sleep well, and die at statistically appropriate ages.
They are not bad people. They are people who have been so thoroughly insulated
from the consequences of the system that sustains them that empathy would require
an act of imagination most of them have never been asked to perform. The Core
doesn't hate the Shelf. It simply doesn't think about it.
Properties.aliases: The Core, Chromeville, Upstairs, The Display Case
Properties.demographics: Approximately 150,000 registered residents, overwhelmingly Tier 4 and Tier 5 corporate employees and their dependents. Demographically homogeneous by design — diversity exists but is curated, credentialed, and monitored. Support staff (cleaning, maintenance, food service) commute in from lower-tier districts and are not counted in residency figures. Unregistered presence is near zero; the surveillance density makes it functionally impossible.
Properties.dangers: Total surveillance — every action recorded, analyzed, and stored; Social profiling — algorithms flag 'anomalous behavior' based on class markers; Corporate security response times measured in seconds; Being identified — facial recognition, gait analysis, augment signature scanning; The danger of being noticed in a place where you don't belong; Legal consequences — the Core has courts that work, and they work against you
Properties.opportunities: High-paying contract work for those willing to get their hands dirty on behalf of clean people; Access to corporate-grade tech, medicine, and information — if you can afford it or steal it; Intelligence gathering — the Core leaks data like a sieve if you know where to listen; The black market for corporate credentials — a temporary Core access pass is worth a month's rent on the Shelf; Rich people who want things they can't ask for publicly
Properties.story_hooks: Kyle's jobs in the Core — the cognitive dissonance of violence in a place this clean; The credential economy — forged access passes as a plot device and social commentary; Corporate employees who secretly fund the Collective or sympathize with the Shelf; The gap between the Core's self-image and its actual function in the city's ecosystem; A Core resident who hires Kyle and discovers what the lower tiers actually look like
Properties.sights: Glass and steel towers reflecting manufactured weather; Corporate logos on every available surface — tasteful, omnipresent, inescapable; Clean streets with embedded guidance lighting that shifts color to direct pedestrian flow; Holographic advertisements that track your eyes and adjust content to your consumer profile; People in clean clothes with seamlessly integrated augments — you can't tell where the person ends and the tech begins; Green spaces that are aggressively curated — every leaf is on brand; Axiom Security drones gliding overhead in formation, shaped like abstract birds because someone in marketing thought it would be 'approachable'; The absence of clutter, mess, or any evidence that humans are messy creatures
Properties.sounds: The hum of climate control — constant, even, the sound of money working; Soft corporate muzak bleeding from storefronts, algorithmically tuned to encourage spending; The click of expensive shoes on polished surfaces; Security drones — a quiet whir that you stop noticing if you belong here; Absence — no shouting, no street vendors, no audible human friction; Notification chimes from neural interfaces, soft and personalized
Properties.smells: This quarter's AtmoSync fragrance: 'Alpine Morning' (pine, clean linen, superiority); Expensive coffee from cafes that charge more per cup than a Shelf resident earns in a day; Nothing unpleasant. Ever. The air scrubbers are very thorough.; Occasionally, if the wind shifts wrong, a hint of salt air from the harbor — quickly corrected
Properties.feel:
Uncanny. The Core feels like walking through a render — too clean, too quiet, too
optimized. For someone from the Shelf, it triggers a specific discomfort: the
feeling of being in a place that was not designed with your existence in mind. Not
hostile, exactly. Just profoundly indifferent to whether you live or die. It's
comfortable in the way a dentist's waiting room is comfortable — everything is
fine, and you want to leave immediately.

Properties.description:
Crisanto is lean and long-limbed, with the particular posture of someone who has spent years in a driver's seat — slightly forward, shoulders loose, hands always finding something to rest near. He has his mother's Yoruba complexion, deep and warm, and his father's Scandinavian bone structure, which gives his face an angular elegance he is utterly unaware of. His hair is cut close on the sides and left natural on top, and he has geneware-modified irises that cycle slowly through amber, gold, and pale yellow — a cosmetic mod he saved up for at twenty-two and has never regretted. A faded scar bisects his left eyebrow from a childhood fall.

He is a fundamentally decent man who chose a fundamentally anonymous job and has found, to his mild surprise, that this suits him. He talks to his passengers — not intrusively, but gently, in the way of a good host — notices who boards tired, who boards scared, who needs the fare scanner to 'malfunction' because they're clearly two days from eating. His tram is clean. He plays low-frequency ambient music through the cabin speakers after midnight and thinks of it as a public service. He carries a notebook — actual paper — in which he sketches the faces of interesting passengers, never with names, never to share.
Properties.role: Ferrogate Transit operator — drives a night-shift surface tram on the Geartown-Bronzeline circuit
Properties.location: Lives in a capsule flat in Bronzeline; works the tram route between Geartown depot and the Bronzeline terminus
Properties.narrative_function: Mobile information source — has seen and heard things across a wide geography on his route. Provides a safe transit option for characters who need to move quietly. Can serve as a quiet quest giver or a witness to something he shouldn't have seen.
Properties.augmentations: Geneware irises (amber-to-gold cycle); neural-link to tram control system (standard Ferrogate issue, non-removable per contract); a small subdermal clock on his inner wrist he can read by pressing
Properties.core_fears: Being trapped in a life that was chosen for him rather than by him; Invisibility — that he will pass through the world and leave no impression
Properties.core_desires: To make small, reliable kindnesses that compound over time; To eventually do something with his drawings — he's never admitted this out loud
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Routine as armor — the tram schedule gives shape to anxiety; Sketching as a way of paying attention to things he can't speak about
Properties.blind_spots: He mistakes passivity for peace and has not yet learned the difference; He gives strangers enormous benefit of the doubt because he needs to believe people are mostly good
Properties.secret: Six months ago he witnessed two Axiom security contractors board his tram at 02:30, carry something in a cargo case that leaked a faint bioluminescent fluid, and disembark at a stop that has no registered destination on his route map. He sketched both of them. He hasn't decided what to do with the sketches.
Properties.story_hooks: The sketches of the Axiom contractors — someone on the tram recognized one of them and is now following Crisanto; A regular passenger — an elderly woman who boards at 03:00 every Thursday and rides to the terminus and back without getting off — has stopped appearing, and Crisanto is worried enough to ask questions; Ferrogate Transit is piloting an AI co-pilot program that will replace human operators on night routes; Crisanto's union chapter is fracturing over whether to strike
Properties.affiliation: Ferrogate Transit (Tier 2 union member, Surface Division)
Properties.vocabulary: Quiet and considered, uses more words than necessary when nervous, fewer when comfortable; peppers speech with Yoruba affirmations ('abi?' — right?, 'sha' — anyway) absorbed from his mother
Properties.cadence: Even and low, like late-night radio; pauses mean he's actually thinking
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Last stop is Bronzeline terminus in about eight minutes, sha. You need somewhere warm before then, I can slow down a little at Ironvein corner, abi?' | 'I see a lot from this seat. More than people think. The tram is like... furniture. Nobody performs for furniture.'

Properties.description:
Crisanto is tall for his age and painfully thin in the way of someone who grew fast without enough to feed the growth. He has his Ghanaian grandfather's jaw and his Russian grandmother's pale grey eyes, a combination that turns heads in both the Enclosure classrooms and when he visits home in Calumet Rise on permitted weekends. His hair is dark, close-cropped, and he has recently added a single streak of color-changing filament — it shifts from blue to violet based on his stress hormones, a fact he deeply regrets because it gives him away constantly.

Crisanto won an Axiom Academic Merit slot two years ago and has been in a state of sustained low-grade terror ever since. He is brilliant at systems logic and data-architecture coursework, mediocre at the social performance the scholarship requires. He smiles too late, laughs too carefully, and his classmates from Tier 3 and 4 families read him as trying too hard even when he is only trying to survive. At home, his little sister thinks he has become someone else. He is not sure she is wrong. He prays obsessively to the E.L.F. of the campus server room, leaving compressed data-parcels of his best homework as offerings, convinced this is why his grades hold.
Properties.role: Corporate scholarship student, Tier 3
Properties.location: Grosse Pointe Enclosure — Axiom Junior Academy campus
Properties.narrative_function: A lens into class anxiety and the cost of upward mobility; useful as an information source about Axiom Junior Academy operations, and as a character who bridges Tier 1-2 and Tier 3 worlds.
Properties.augmentations: Single strand of stress-reactive color-shifting hair filament (cosmetic, regretted). Standard Axiom student neural-study interface — read-only, no write access.
Properties.core_fears: losing the scholarship and having to return to Calumet Rise having failed; becoming so adapted to the Enclosure that he stops belonging anywhere
Properties.core_desires: to genuinely belong somewhere without performing for it; to use his skills to make his sister's life easier
Properties.coping_mechanisms: obsessive preparation and over-study; ELF-prayer rituals in the server room
Properties.blind_spots: cannot see that some of his classmates actually like him — he filters all kindness through suspicion of pity
Properties.secret: Three months ago he accidentally discovered a ghost partition on the school's network — a hidden dataset that appears to be Axiom tracking psychological stress profiles of all scholarship students. He downloaded a fragment and has been sitting on it, paralyzed between fear of using it and guilt about knowing.
Properties.story_hooks: The ghost partition data he downloaded contains a stress-flag profile with a name he recognizes from Calumet Rise — another scholarship kid who dropped out suddenly last term; A classmate from a Tier 4 family wants to hire him to 'help' with an exam — and the pay is more than his mother makes in a month
Properties.affiliation: Axiom Corporation (scholarship dependent); family in Calumet Rise
Properties.vocabulary: Code-switches fluidly — formal academic register at school, Rise slang when he forgets himself, a habit he's trying to suppress
Properties.cadence: Measured and careful at school; faster and looser on comms with his sister
Properties.example_dialogue: Structurally speaking the assignment's question is malformed — but I answered what they meant, not what they said. | Don't tell Mama I didn't eat the protein ration. I sent it home. The cafeteria here — it's fine. I'm fine.

Properties.description:
Csilla is medium height and deceptively slight, with Hungarian-Ghanaian features — warm brown skin, heavy-lidded dark eyes, wide mouth usually set in a neutral expression that people keep reading as a smile. Their cat ears are geneware, common enough, but theirs are the mottled grey-and-amber of an actual South African wildcat — chosen deliberately for the unsettling accuracy. They keep their natural hair in tight, small braids, always pinned up under a surgical cap during work. They smell faintly of antiseptic even when they're not working, a smell that has become so much a part of them that they no longer notice it.

Csilla trained for three years in Aurochs Medical Complex's licensed surgical technician program before washing out for reasons listed on their record as 'professional conduct irregularities' and in reality involving a confrontation with a senior tech over the disposal of viable organs from unconsenting deceased patients — a confrontation in which Csilla was technically wrong but morally, they believe, correct. They moved laterally into independent procurement within six months. They are not sadistic, not cavalier, and not in any way comfortable with what they do — but they have concluded, through a logic they can walk you through step by step, that there is a demand, there is a supply, and the official channels are too slow and too expensive for the people who need them most. They charge on a sliding scale they invented themselves.
Properties.role: Organ harvester and procurement specialist working the margins of legitimate medical infrastructure
Properties.location: South Deering Sump — operates out of a converted cold-storage unit adjacent to the Aurochs Medical Complex overflow lots
Properties.narrative_function: Moral complexity embodied — not a villain, not a hero. Can be a source of medical assistance outside official channels, an involuntary quest element, or a window into the organ trade's human cost. Challenges players' assumptions about criminal work.
Properties.augmentations: Wildcat-pattern geneware ears; enhanced haptic sensitivity in fingers (surgical mod, done professionally); retinal enhancement for microscale work
Properties.core_fears: that the ethical framework they've built is self-serving rationalization; causing a patient's death through their own error
Properties.core_desires: to give people access to medical care the system has priced out of their reach; to be believed when they say they're trying to do something good
Properties.coping_mechanisms: exhaustive self-justifying ethical frameworks maintained like the cold-storage unit — meticulously; treating every procedure as a case study, emotional distance through technical focus
Properties.blind_spots: cannot see how the procurement methods — regardless of downstream benefit — cause profound harm to victims and communities; overestimates their own ability to distinguish 'ethical' procurement from straightforwardly predatory
Properties.secret: Two years ago they procured from someone who was not, as represented to them, a willing seller. They didn't know until three days later. They have never confirmed who told them or whether it was true, and they have structured their operation since then to prevent themselves from finding out for certain.
Properties.story_hooks: A patient Csilla saved — Tier 1, no other options — has come back asking them to procure something specific that Csilla suspects cannot be obtained ethically; the patient is dying again; The two-year-old incident has surfaced: someone who was there is looking for Csilla, and their intentions are unclear; Aurochs Medical Complex has hired a private investigator to trace a series of procurement anomalies in their morgue overflow — Csilla is three degrees away from exposure
Properties.affiliation: Loose network of independent medical workers, UBC-tier patients priced out of legal transplant queues, and three mid-tier chop surgeons who don't ask where the material comes from
Properties.vocabulary: Medical and precise, with a habit of quantifying things that shouldn't be quantifiable; speaks softly and rarely raises their voice
Properties.cadence: Measured and careful — rehearsed quality, like someone who has learned to think before speaking
Properties.example_dialogue: In my assessment, the current pricing structure for Tier 1 transplant access is a form of policy violence. I'm not sure what I do is better. I've thought about it. | The material is viable. I don't move material that isn't viable. That's not a selling point, that's a baseline. | Don't ask me where it comes from. Not because I'm hiding something. Because you will have to decide what to do with the answer and you're not ready.

Properties.description:
Cutter Vane has killed more Behemoths than anyone currently operating on M88's western border. Not the most ever — that record belongs to a Gleaner named Doss who went out eleven years ago and did not return — but the most among the living. The count is fourteen confirmed kills over nine years of Gleaner operations. Each one was a disaster. Behemoths don't die clean. They die loud, they die thrashing, and killing one attracts others. Every kill on Cutter's count represents a raid that went wrong enough to require lethal force, which means every kill represents a failure he survived.

He grew up on the western edge — the border communities where Meridian 88's governance dissolves into the contested Iowa corridor. He joined the Gleaners at seventeen because the alternative was starving slowly in a community that couldn't feed itself. Madre found him two years later, already good with a rifle, already hard in ways that seventeen-year-olds shouldn't be. She trained him, kept him alive, and watched him become the most effective field operative she'd ever worked with. She also watched him become colder with each raid, and that's the part that keeps her up at night.

Cutter is lean, angular, sun-damaged, with the permanent squint and wind-scoured features of someone who has spent too much time exposed to the Iowa prairie. He moves with the economy of a predator — no wasted motion, constant awareness, an animal stillness when he's watching something. His eyes are the most unsettling thing about him — pale, steady, and focused in a way that makes people feel like terrain being assessed.
Properties.role: Tracker, combat specialist, and advance scout — Red Lantern
Properties.location: Western border — bunks at the farmstead but spends most of his time in the field
Properties.narrative_function: Cutter is the cost of the Gleaner mission made flesh. His stories explore what happens to a person who becomes excellent at violence in service of a good cause — the erosion of the human underneath the operator. He is the survival horror's teeth.
Properties.augmentations: Optical targeting suite — ballistic calculation overlay, range finding, and wind compensation projected onto visual field. Enhanced auditory processing for Behemoth acoustic signature detection at extended range. Myofiber reinforcement in arms and shoulders for sustained heavy weapon handling. Adrenal suppressor that prevents panic responses in combat.
Properties.core_fears: That he's crossed a line where the killing is no longer in service of anything — that the Behemoth hunts have become the point, not the food; That Madre's worry about him is justified and the person she trained is gone, replaced by the function; That the Behemoths are smarter than anyone admits and his kills are not victories but provocations
Properties.core_desires: To feel something about the raids other than operational focus — to prove the numbness is a tool, not a state; To protect Madre because she protected him, and because the debt is the last emotional structure he recognizes; To be finished. To have done enough. To put the rifle down and not need it.
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Channels everything into operational readiness — if the gear is maintained and the route is scouted, the feelings don't matter; Sits alone in high places watching the prairie — the vastness absorbs whatever he's carrying without requiring words; Maintains the kill count not as pride but as accounting — each number is a failed raid, not a trophy
Properties.blind_spots: He cannot distinguish between tactical detachment and emotional vacancy — the difference matters and he's lost track of it; He reads Behemoths better than people and has stopped trying to reverse the priority; His escalating readiness to use lethal force looks like competence to younger Gleaners — they're learning the wrong lesson
Properties.secret: On his last solo scout, a juvenile Behemoth encountered him and did not attack. It looked at him. He looked at it. It turned and walked away. He did not shoot. He has not told anyone because he doesn't understand why he held fire, and the not-understanding terrifies him more than any raid.
Properties.story_hooks: The juvenile Behemoth Cutter spared appears on a subsequent raid — and it appears to recognize him; Cutter's combat readiness escalates to the point where he fires on a Behemoth that was retreating — the first kill that cannot be justified as defense; A new Gleaner idolizes Cutter and imitates his methods, with lethal consequences — the wrong lesson learned; Madre confronts Cutter about his deterioration, and the conversation determines whether he can be saved or whether he's already gone
Properties.affiliation: Red Lantern
Properties.vocabulary: Sparse, precise, environmental. He describes the world in terms of fields of fire, cover, movement patterns. Human conversation is a foreign language he once spoke fluently.
Properties.cadence: Clipped, economical. Sentences are ammunition — he spends them carefully. Long silences between statements.
Properties.example_dialogue: Contact. Two clicks west. Big one. We reroute or we run. Those are the options. | Fourteen kills. Fourteen failures. Every time I fire, something went wrong before I pulled the trigger. | I'm clear. I said I'm clear. Don't push it.
