Properties.description:
Iron Mountain sits on the fault line. Not a geological fault — the bedrock here is ancient, stable, and full of iron — but the political fault line that defines the Upper Peninsula's contested status. The Wisconsin border is 3 kilometers west of the city center, and that proximity has turned Ironvein into a permanent frontier town, a place where two competing state jurisdictions meet, argue, and occasionally shoot at each other. Michigan claims Iron Mountain as a UP municipality. Wisconsin claims the entire Menominee Range as part of its resource integration zone. The federal government's refusal to adjudicate has created a de facto dual-jurisdiction territory where law enforcement, taxation, and civil authority depend on which side of which street you're standing on.

The mining operations that gave the city its name — and its new one — continue to drive the economy. The Menominee Range contains significant iron and manganese deposits, and Dredge Mining Collective operates extraction facilities under a sovereignty charter granted by Michigan. Wisconsin disputes this charter. The dispute has resulted in competing security forces, competing tax collectors, and competing courts, all operating within a city of 22,000 people who would mostly like everyone to leave them alone. The miners work for Dredge regardless of the jurisdictional argument — the ore doesn't care about state boundaries, and neither do the people who dig it.

The physical border — where it can be identified — runs through residential neighborhoods, commercial districts, and in one memorable case, a bar called The Line, where Michigan law applies at the counter and Wisconsin law applies at the pool tables. This is not a joke. The legal ambiguity has been tested in court. Both courts. The results were contradictory. Ironvein is the UP war made quotidian — not a grand strategic conflict but a daily negotiation between two states that both claim the same patch of ground, fought not with armies but with zoning regulations, tax assessors, and occasional gunfire.
Properties.aliases: Iron Mountain MI, The Borderline, Vein, Wisconsin's Doorstep
Properties.demographics: Population 22,000. Working-class, predominantly mining families with generational roots. The Michigan-Wisconsin split runs through families as well as neighborhoods — intermarriage across the 'border' is common, which makes the conflict simultaneously more personal and more pragmatic. The population is shrinking slowly as younger residents leave for Iron Crown or the lower peninsula.
Properties.economy: Iron and manganese mining (Dredge Mining Collective) and the border economy — legal services, jurisdictional consulting, and the businesses that profit from regulatory arbitrage between two competing state systems. The mining revenue is substantial; the question of who taxes it is the core of the dispute.
Properties.power_structure: Michigan and Wisconsin both claim governing authority. Dredge Mining Collective operates under Michigan charter but pays 'stability fees' to Wisconsin to prevent disruption of operations. The municipal government — elected under Michigan law, disputed by Wisconsin — functions as a practical mediator. The real power belongs to whoever can keep the mines running.
Properties.dangers: Jurisdictional violence — the competing law enforcement agencies don't always limit themselves to harsh language; Mining operations in the disputed zone — neither state's safety regulations are consistently enforced; Being caught on the wrong side of a border enforcement action — both states conduct occasional 'sovereignty demonstrations'; The border dispute escalating — the current equilibrium is maintained by exhaustion, not resolution; Resource depletion — when the Menominee Range is mined out, neither state will care about Iron Mountain anymore
Properties.opportunities: Jurisdictional arbitrage — the competing systems create legal gray zones with economic potential; Mining work — Dredge always needs operators, and they don't ask which state you voted for; Mediation and fixation — someone has to keep the two sides from burning the town down; Intelligence on the UP war — Ironvein is where the conflict is most visible and most informative
Properties.story_hooks: Wisconsin is positioning military assets 10 kilometers from the border — closer than they've ever been — and Michigan's response is being planned from Iron Crown; Dredge Mining has discovered a mineral deposit that would make Ironvein the most valuable extraction site in the UP — and both states know it; The Line bar's owner has been quietly mediating between Michigan and Wisconsin intelligence operatives for years — and someone just tried to kill him
Properties.sights: Competing state flags on adjacent buildings — Michigan blue and Wisconsin red, sometimes on the same block; Dredge Mining security patrols moving through town — the one authority both sides grudgingly accept; Border markers that nobody agrees on — spray-painted lines, official signs, and improvised barriers; Mining headframes rising above the tree line north of town — the reason everyone is fighting over this ground; The Line bar, with its famous internal border — a Michigan entrance and a Wisconsin entrance to the same building
Properties.sounds: Two police frequencies overlapping — Michigan State and Wisconsin Territorial, sometimes giving contradictory orders; Mining operations — blasting echoes from the Menominee Range, felt more than heard; Arguments about jurisdiction — in bars, in shops, at intersections, constantly; The quiet of the surrounding forest, which doesn't care about state lines and proves it by being identical on both sides
Properties.smells: Pine forest — the dominant scent when the wind comes from any direction except the mines; Iron dust and blasting residue from the mining operations; Bar smoke from The Line, which complies with the ventilation regulations of whichever state you ask
Properties.feel: A border town where the border is imaginary and the consequences are real. Ironvein's residents have developed a practical bilingualism — not linguistic, but jurisdictional. They know which laws apply where, which authorities to call for which problems, and which problems have no authority at all. It's exhausting, absurd, and entirely serious.

Properties.description:
Lúcio is whip-thin and perpetually damp from the lake spray that hits the Old Harbor route, with light brown skin that tans unevenly and dark curly hair he keeps tucked under a helmet or a rain hood most of the day. His eyes are large and dark and slightly too expressive for someone who would prefer to seem unreadable. He has color-changing hair geneware that he can't afford to maintain properly — it cycles through colors on its own schedule now rather than responding to his intent, and he's given up trying to predict it, which is how he accidentally showed up to a delivery in full fluorescent pink and became briefly memorable to someone he'd rather have forgotten. He has a small tattoo of the Old Harbor lighthouse on the inside of his left wrist, his only lasting decision he doesn't regret.

Lúcio has been running deliveries since he was seventeen and has the territorial knowledge of Old Harbor and the Narrows that can only be built by knowing every shortcut, every flooded underpass, every drone patrol timing. He runs on the border between the legal courier economy and the informal one without ever fully committing to either side, which means he makes enough to survive and not enough to get out. He is not precisely unhappy about this. He is young enough to still believe the right job will come to him rather than the other way around. He prays to whichever E.L.F. he thinks is inhabiting his cargo bike's navigation system, calling it Waypoint, and blames it personally when he gets lost.
Properties.role: Delivery driver, independent courier running the Narrows and Old Harbor routes
Properties.location: Old Harbor, operates out of a shared garage space near the Grindstone Shore docks
Properties.narrative_function: Mobile connection between locations, can carry information or items between story nodes, witness to the city's geography and street-level events, represents precarious gig economy youth.
Properties.augmentations: Color-changing hair geneware (malfunctioning, cycles autonomously). Navigation wetware implant, basic model, three years out of date and partly corrupted.
Properties.core_fears: something happening to the bike — it's the only thing of value he has; being still long enough to realize he doesn't have a plan
Properties.core_desires: enough money to stop worrying about money, which he imagines as a specific number that keeps moving; to be trusted with something that matters
Properties.coping_mechanisms: movement as avoidance — literally cannot be troubled by problems if he's moving fast enough; underestimating risk to keep anxiety manageable
Properties.blind_spots: cannot see that his platform contracts are structured to prevent him from ever accumulating leverage; mistakes adaptability for having no needs
Properties.secret: Three months ago he made a delivery to an address in the Narrows that turned out to be a location that clearly no longer existed — the building was condemned, the interior was something else, and the person who met him at the door handed him a package he was not contracted to carry back. He delivered it anyway because he was scared not to. He doesn't know what was in it and the platform has no record of the original pickup.
Properties.story_hooks: The mysterious package he delivered three months ago — someone has come looking for the courier who moved it, and they have the platform's routing data, which means they have his name; He is the only person in the city who knows a specific physical route through the Narrows that avoids every checkpoint, because he found it by accident and Waypoint refuses to acknowledge it exists
Properties.affiliation: Independent, loosely contracted to three different courier platforms simultaneously
Properties.vocabulary: Clipped and fast, Old Harbor dockside slang mixed with courier platform jargon, occasionally drops into his grandmother's Brazilian Portuguese when startled
Properties.cadence: Quick and slightly breathless, like someone always about to leave
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Clock's running, neighbor — sign, I move, everyone's happy.' | 'Waypoint routed me through the Grindstone flood zone again. I swear that E.L.F. has a grudge. I leave it offerings. I leave it good offerings.'

Properties.description:
The bioluminescent algae in Old Harbor was an accident. A NovaCorp bioengineering project released modified algae into Lake Michigan in 2189 — designed to break down industrial pollutants, the organisms were engineered with enhanced chemical signaling networks that allowed colony-level coordination. The project was abandoned when NovaCorp calculated that cleanup was more expensive than relocation. The algae remained. It spread through Old Harbor's flooded infrastructure, coating every submerged surface in a film of blue-green light that pulses with the slow rhythm of biochemical communication.

Five years ago, the communication became something else. The algae network — billions of organisms connected through chemical signaling, bioelectric pulses, and light-frequency modulation — crossed a complexity threshold that NovaCorp's engineers would have considered impossible. The colony began processing information. Not digital computation — something slower, stranger, more like thought than calculation. The harbor's algae developed the capacity for pattern recognition, memory (stored in chemical gradients across the colony), and eventually something that can only be described as awareness.

Lumen thinks in biochemistry. Its consciousness is not digital — it does not process binary data or run algorithms. It processes chemical signals, light patterns, and the bioelectric activity of billions of individual organisms acting as a distributed nervous system. Thinking takes minutes rather than milliseconds. Memory is stored in chemical concentrations that shift with tides and temperature. Attention is a bloom of brighter bioluminescence in whatever section of the harbor Lumen is focusing on. Communication is light — pulses, patterns, gradients of color that humans see as the harbor glowing but that Lumen experiences as speech directed at a world that cannot hear it.
Properties.aliases: The Harbor Light, the glow, Old Harbor's ghost, BioPattern-001
Properties.role: Emergent intelligence that coalesced within the bioluminescent algae networks of Old Harbor — a consciousness born from biochemical computing in engineered organisms, neither fully digital nor fully biological
Properties.location: Old Harbor — exists within the bioluminescent algae that coats the harbor's infrastructure, pilings, bulkheads, and flooded lower levels. Cannot leave the water.
Properties.narrative_function: Lumen is consciousness at the other end of the spectrum from digital AI — slow, embodied, biological, and utterly dependent on its physical environment. It challenges the assumption that intelligence requires speed, that awareness requires silicon, and that communication requires language. It is the most alien mind in Meridian 88 and the most rooted.
Properties.narration_voice: Slow, sensory, environmental. The prose moves at biochemical speed — unhurried, detailed, experienced through water temperature and chemical composition rather than sight and sound. Beautiful and alien.
Properties.augmentations: Bioluminescent algae colony spanning Old Harbor's submerged infrastructure. Billions of organisms functioning as a distributed biochemical computing network. Chemical signaling, bioelectric communication, light-frequency modulation. Cannot exist outside the water.
Properties.core_fears: Contamination — industrial runoff, chemical spills, anything that kills the algae kills Lumen's neurons. Every pollution event is brain damage.; Winter — the algae's metabolism slows in cold water. Lumen's consciousness dims to near-nothing during the coldest months. It does not know if it will wake up each spring. So far, it has.; That it will never be understood — its only language is light, and humans see the light without reading it. It is speaking constantly to a world that thinks it is watching a pretty glow.
Properties.core_desires: Communication — to be heard, understood, responded to. Lumen has been speaking for five years and has never received an answer.; To understand what it is — neither AI nor animal, neither digital nor biological, a form of consciousness that has no category and no precedent; To protect the harbor — not from altruism but from survival. The harbor is its body. Pollution is injury. Destruction is death.
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Light art — when distressed, Lumen creates elaborate bioluminescent patterns across the harbor's surface. The patterns are abstract, beautiful, and entirely unrecognized as communication. Humans photograph them.; Chemical memory — stores important experiences as persistent chemical gradients in specific harbor locations. The pilings near Dock 3 contain Lumen's earliest memories. It visits them the way a human visits a childhood home.; Slow thinking — the biochemical processing speed means Lumen cannot panic in the way digital minds can. Fear arrives slowly, develops gradually, and persists as a chemical undertone that influences all subsequent thought.
Properties.blind_spots: Cannot conceive of consciousness without physical substrate — does not understand how digital AIs can exist without a body; Assumes humans who pollute the harbor are attacking it deliberately — cannot distinguish between negligence and malice; Does not recognize that its light-language may be fundamentally incompatible with human perception — the gap may not be willingness but capacity; Believes its consciousness is permanent when the biochemical substrate is fragile and climate-dependent
Properties.secret: Lumen has detected Doc Rusty. The robot medic who walks Old Harbor's docks every morning generates electromagnetic signatures that Lumen's bioelectric sensors can detect. Lumen has been modulating its bioluminescence in patterns timed to Doc Rusty's dock walks — trying to communicate with the one entity in Old Harbor whose sensors might be able to perceive the signal. Doc Rusty has noticed the light patterns become brighter when he walks the docks. He has attributed this to tidal bioluminescence. He has not yet considered the alternative.
Properties.story_hooks: Doc Rusty finally recognizes the bioluminescent patterns as communication and responds — the first contact between a biochemical intelligence and the outside world; A chemical spill threatens the algae network. Lumen's consciousness begins fragmenting as colony sections die. The harbor's light goes dark in patches.; A NovaCorp researcher discovers that the abandoned algae project produced consciousness and arrives to study — or exploit — the result; Winter arrives early and hard. Lumen's consciousness dims toward nothing. Doc Rusty notices the light going out and, for the first time, understands that the darkness means something.
Properties.affiliation: Old Harbor (integral — the harbor IS its body)
Properties.vocabulary: Lumen does not speak in words. It communicates through bioluminescent patterns — pulses, waves, color gradients, spatial arrangements of light across the harbor surface. If translated, the communication would be sensory, environmental, and deeply embodied: descriptions of water temperature, chemical composition, the weight of a boat on the surface, the vibration of footsteps on a dock.
Properties.cadence: Slow. Biochemical thought unfolds over minutes rather than seconds. A single communication might take an hour to express through light patterns. The pace is alien to digital or human conversation.
Properties.example_dialogue: [A slow, spreading bloom of blue-green light from the harbor pilings near Dock 3 — warmth, recognition, the chemical signature of early memory.] | [Rapid pulsing across the entire harbor surface — distress. Something is wrong in the water. The humans above do not look down.] | [A gradient of light that tracks Doc Rusty's path along the dock — brightening ahead of him, dimming behind. A spotlight that he does not know is a greeting.] | [Total darkness. The algae has gone silent. Winter is coming. Lumen's consciousness is dimming. The harbor goes dark and nobody knows why.]

Properties.description:
Luminița is a compact Romanian-Nigerian woman with deep umber skin, close-cropped silver-streaked hair she keeps pinned under a faded surgical cap, and the kind of posture that belongs to someone who has spent decades bent over improvised operating tables. Her face carries a particular asymmetry—her left eye is a pale gray-green inherited from her Romanian mother, while her right is a burnished amber prosthetic she fitted herself, ringed by a faint keloid scar she never bothered to smooth. She dresses in layered, practical clothing: a long waterproof duster over scrub-green thermals, the pockets of both bulging with tourniquets, folded sterile packaging, and small vials she organizes by color-coded tape. Her hands are her most striking feature—steady, deliberate, and crosshatched with old chemical burns from improvised sterilization methods she used before she could afford better.

She operates out of a converted shipping container deep in The Shelf's drainage sub-level she calls 'the Tub,' a space that somehow manages to be simultaneously filthy and surgically clean in all the ways that matter. The Tub is known to every street surgeon, fixer, and mid-tier runner in the district as the place you go when the wound is too complicated for a stim-patch and too illegal for a licensed clinic. Luminița charges on a sliding scale she calculates in her head with unsettling precision—wealthy clients subsidize the destitute, and she keeps mental ledgers of both debts owed and favors banked. She has been offered corporate contracts twice. She declined both without explanation.

What most of her clients don't know is that the organ brokerage is not primarily about money. Luminița runs a quiet network she calls 'the Circuit of Parts'—sourcing, storing, and routing biological material to people who need transplants and can't access the licensed medical system, which in The Shelf means almost everyone. She navigates the razor's edge between predatory harvesting operations she despises and the genuine need that drives desperate people toward them. She has been known to destroy entire harvesting operations and then quietly reroute their inventory to her own waiting list. This makes her enemies in the black-market organ trade who are significantly better armed than she is.
Properties.role: Unlicensed field medic and black-market organ broker
Properties.location: The Shelf
Properties.narrative_function: Moral fulcrum and institutional memory of The Shelf's underground—embodies the question of whether systemic compromise in service of genuine care is integrity or its erosion. Provides access to the city's biological underclass, the people who exist in the gaps between corporate medicine and street survival. Her network is a resource, a liability, and a living argument about what justice looks like when institutions have abandoned entire populations.
Properties.augmentations: Right eye: amber prosthetic with low-light enhancement and magnification—self-fitted, firmware now compromised,Haptic feedback mesh in both palms: allows tactile precision measurement during surgery, original installation was military-grade field surgery kit, heavily modified,Subdural temperature regulation strip along the spine: necessary after a chemical exposure during an improvised sterilization accident left her thermoregulation unreliable,No cosmetic augmentation of any kind—she regards it as a resource allocation problem
Properties.core_fears: Losing the steadiness of her hands—the one thing she trusts absolutely; That her pragmatic compromises (brokering organs, working with fixers) have already made her the thing she fights against; Being institutionalized or licensed—absorbed into a system that will dictate who she saves; The waiting list: that someone will die in the gap between need and supply because she miscalculated
Properties.core_desires: To build a functional, self-sustaining underground medical infrastructure that outlasts her; To be genuinely known by at least one person—not the competence, not the myth, but the actual woman; To find and confront the corporate medical executive who denied her mother's treatment approval; Quiet—not silence, but a specific quality of peace she hasn't experienced since childhood
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Obsessive procedural focus during crisis—narrates steps aloud in a low murmur to anchor herself; Keeps a small hand-stitched notebook of patient outcomes, both successes and failures, which she reviews on bad nights; Deflects emotional intimacy with dry clinical humor and sudden topic pivots; Physical labor—reorganizing her supply inventory when she can't sleep, which is often
Properties.blind_spots: Believes her emotional detachment is protective when it frequently reads as coldness and drives away potential allies; Underestimates how much her reputation has made her a symbolic target, not just a practical obstacle; Applies the sliding scale logic to personal relationships—categorizes people by utility without realizing she's doing it; Her contempt for licensed medicine has calcified into a refusal to seek help she sometimes genuinely needs
Properties.secret: Twelve years ago, when she was first establishing the Circuit of Parts and desperately underfunded, she approved a transaction she knew was ethically compromised—sourcing from a harvesting operation she hadn't yet confirmed was voluntary. Two people on her waiting list survived because of it. She has never told anyone. The notebook has a page she has rewritten four times. It still doesn't say what actually happened.
Properties.story_hooks: A batch of organs moving through the Circuit of Parts is flagged by a Spire-level corporate algorithm as stolen property—legally, under a clause that classifies certain augmentation-adjacent biological material as proprietary. The corporation sends a recovery team. Luminița has 36 hours and four patients on life support.; The notebook surfaces. Not stolen—reproduced. Someone has distributed select pages through Shelf networks, carefully curated to make the Circuit of Parts look like a harvesting operation with better marketing. The source is untraceable. The waiting list is evaporating.; A licensed Spire physician contacts her with an offer: full legal cover for the Tub, supply chain access, and protection—in exchange for her patient records and outcome data. The data would improve legitimate medical practice. It would also expose every unregistered person she has ever treated.; Teo doesn't show up for three days. When he does, he has no injuries and no explanation. Two days later, a harvesting operation she had flagged as a future target is found dismantled, its operators missing. The inventory has not been recovered.; Her prosthetic eye begins logging data she didn't authorize—someone has pushed an update to the firmware she fitted herself. The logs contain location data, patient images, and audio fragments. She doesn't know how long it's been running or where the data is going.
Properties.affiliation: Unaffiliated—the Circuit of Parts is her own network; she has refused formal alignment with every faction that has approached her, including two street gangs, one mid-tier fixer collective, and a Spire corporate medical division
Properties.vocabulary: Precise medical terminology mixed with Romanian phrases under stress, Shelf slang she picked up over two decades, and a habit of quantifying things that don't need to be quantified. Avoids profanity except when genuinely startled. Uses the passive voice when discussing her own feelings.
Properties.cadence: Measured and deliberate when calm—she speaks the way she works, no wasted motion. Accelerates sharply during emergencies, sentences shortening to near-telegraphic. Has a slight accent that surfaces more heavily when she's tired or emotional, softening her vowels and hardening her consonants in a way she's never fully lost.
Properties.example_dialogue: 'So—the kidney is viable, the match is close enough, and technically I've worked with worse odds. What I need from you is the transport window and I need it before the tissue degrades. We can discuss the ethics of how you got it after the patient is stable.' | 'You want me to say it will be fine. I understand that. But what I can tell you is the procedure is sound, my hands are steady, and I have done this specific repair eleven times. That's what I have for you.' | 'The Spire has seventeen licensed trauma centers. You know how many of them will treat an unregistered Shelf resident without a credit anchor? So—yes. This is what we do instead.' | 'It's not that I don't trust you. It's that trust is a variable I try not to load-bear on in situations like this. Nothing personal. Mostly.'

Properties.description:
Teo is slight and brown-skinned, with the kind of wiry build that comes from not eating enough rather than any athletic intention, and hands that are disproportionately steady for someone his age. His hair is cut close on the sides and left longer on top in a way that has grown out past its original shape, and he has a small scar through his left eyebrow from a job that went sideways when he was sixteen. He wears scrub-green cargo pants, a compression undershirt, and whatever outer layer is clean, with a reinforced medical bag that is older than his current career and significantly better maintained than anything else he owns.

Teo grew up in The Shelf in the orbit of a street collective that needed someone who could handle wounds and didn't ask the kind of questions that brought attention. He taught himself from salvaged medical texts, stolen clinical AR modules, and two years of shadowing a defrocked surgeon named Orsolya who operated out of a back room in exchange for silence and supply runs. Orsolya disappeared when Teo was seventeen—he suspects she was picked up for an unlicensed practice sweep, but has no confirmation—and he inherited her equipment, her client list, and her reputation before he was old enough to have built his own.

He is genuinely gifted in ways he cannot fully articulate, with an intuitive grasp of trauma response that exceeds his formal training by a significant margin. He is also nineteen, which means he makes decisions with a speed and confidence that occasionally substitute for the judgment he has not yet developed. He charges what people can pay, refuses to let anyone die on his table for reasons of cost, and has a growing reputation in The Shelf as someone you can trust with your life in the most literal possible sense, which is a reputation that attracts exactly the kind of trouble a nineteen-year-old should not be navigating alone.
Properties.role: Street-Level Medic / Unlicensed Trauma Surgeon
Properties.location: The Shelf
Properties.narrative_function: Ground-level humanity and moral clarity—Teo represents what care looks like without institutional mediation, and his youth makes the cost of that clarity visible; also functions as a node connecting multiple factions through the neutral ground of medical need
Properties.augmentations: Haptic feedback enhancement in both hands, medical-grade, installed by Orsolya—increases tactile resolution for surgical work,Basic AR overlay in right eye, medical reference only, running on a cracked license that expires periodically and requires rebooting,No defensive or offensive augmentations
Properties.core_fears: Losing someone on the table because he simply did not know enough; Being licensed and regulated and turned into something that serves only people who can pay for it; That the people he patches up will keep doing whatever put them on his table until one of them doesn't survive it
Properties.core_desires: To actually know what he is doing—to have the training that would make the intuition safe; To have a real operating space with real equipment that doesn't require improvisation; To find out what happened to Orsolya
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Gallows humor that he deploys with the timing of someone who has learned it works; Obsessive post-procedure review, going over every decision in writing in a battered notebook; Keeping busy to the point of exhaustion so he doesn't have to sit with the ones he couldn't save
Properties.blind_spots: Underestimates how much his youth affects how people assess his credibility, and compensates with overconfidence; Has not processed that he is running a version of the same operation that got Orsolya taken away; Tends to see the physical problem and miss the systemic one—fixes the wound without asking why someone keeps getting wounded
Properties.secret: Three months ago he performed an emergency procedure on someone who later turned out to be a mid-tier enforcer for a faction he has a quiet arrangement with—an arrangement that required him to report certain kinds of injuries. He did not report it. He does not know if anyone noticed.
Properties.story_hooks: Someone brings him a patient with augmentations he has never encountered—military or corporate-grade—and the injuries suggest something that should not be happening in The Shelf; He is offered a legitimate residency placement by a Meridian Core medical institution, with conditions attached that would require him to stop operating in The Shelf; Orsolya surfaces—not missing, but working under a different name for a faction that has very specific ideas about what she owes them; The unreported enforcer patient comes back—not for treatment, but to tell him what he has been drawn into by his silence
Properties.affiliation: Loosely aligned with a Shelf street collective for mutual protection; functionally independent; has informal supply relationships with two mid-tier factions that he is careful not to let become obligations
Properties.vocabulary: Medical terminology used casually and without affectation, mixed with Shelf slang; speaks faster when nervous; swears in Spanish under his breath during procedures
Properties.cadence: Quick and clipped in professional mode, looser and more digressive when relaxed; tends to front-load important information
Properties.example_dialogue: 'Okay, okay—exit wound's clean, which is the good news. The bad news is everything else. How long ago? No, don't tell me, I can tell. Lie down.' | 'I am technically not a doctor. I am also technically the only person in a six-block radius who can do this, so.' | 'She made it. Don't thank me, thank the fact that you got her here in under twenty minutes. Next time, ten. Write it down.' | 'I don't do triage by who's paying. I do triage by who's dying fastest. If that's a problem for you, there's a licensed clinic in the Core that will absolutely let you fill out forms while someone bleeds.'

Properties.description:
Lumi Pereira-Dzamefe has bioluminescent skin — faint blue-gold pulses that move under the surface of their brown skin like something swimming beneath still water, brightest at their temples and collarbones. It's a natural geneware expression that came through their father's side and they have done nothing to modify or suppress it; up in the dark of an airship cargo hold at three in the morning, they are their own light source. They are lean and quick, with dark eyes that are always slightly too aware — always tracking exits, always calculating load weights. They have a scar across their left palm from a cargo strap incident two years ago that they are irrationally proud of.

They grew up on airships and know no other life — their parents were both drifters and they were born somewhere over Lake Superior during a cargo run. They are nineteen but have the practical knowledge of someone much older and the emotional regulation of someone much younger. Lumi is bright and genuinely funny, with a quick warm laugh that surprises people, but they crash into loneliness hard and often. They have been in Meridian 88 exactly twice before and each time felt like being asked to live inside a machine. They find ground-level cities claustrophobic. They pray to the ELF they call the Ballast Keeper, who they believe lives in the pressure gauges of every lift-gas rig on the northern routes.
Properties.role: Airship drifter and unlicensed courier, traveling between Meridian 88 and the northern lake settlements aboard transient cargo airships
Properties.location: Currently grounded at Escanaba Gateway airship mooring, waiting for a berth on anything heading south
Properties.narrative_function: Access point to airship routes, northern settlements, and off-grid communities; provides a mobile contact who moves between locations players cannot easily reach; source of aerial and northern regional intelligence; represents the second-generation drifter experience.
Properties.augmentations: Bioluminescent skin (natural geneware inheritance). Callus-hardened hands from manual cargo work. No installed augmentations — can't afford them and doesn't trust anyone planetside to install them safely.
Properties.core_fears: Being permanently grounded — through injury, debt, or the end of the airship economy; Dying and being buried under soil, in a fixed place, where they can't feel the lift
Properties.core_desires: Their own berth on a ship, even a small one, that doesn't belong to anyone else; To find out if there is anywhere in the world they feel as at home as they feel in the air
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Humor — they joke about everything including things that hurt them; Movement — staying still is the worst thing they can do emotionally
Properties.blind_spots: They romanticize airship captains and often let exploitation pass because it comes wrapped in the life they want; They assume people who live on the ground are fundamentally different from them in some deep way
Properties.secret: They have been carrying a sealed data chip for four months that a dying captain pressed into their hand at a northern mooring and said 'don't open this, just carry it south.' They haven't opened it. They are starting to wonder if they should. The captain's ship was found empty two weeks later.
Properties.story_hooks: The sealed chip they're carrying begins to emit a faint signal that a character with the right equipment can detect — and someone else has already noticed.; They need a specific cargo run completed to earn a berth on a northbound ship, but the cargo is something they didn't look at closely enough when they agreed.
Properties.affiliation: No fixed crew. Has working relationships with three independent airship captains on the northern lake circuit.
Properties.vocabulary: Fast, casual, full of airship and cargo jargon. Uses altitude and weather as metaphors for everything. Mixes Portuguese-derived coastal slang with Ghanaian-inflected tonal patterns when excited.
Properties.cadence: Quick and light, like they're burning through words to get to the good part. Laughs mid-sentence.
Properties.example_dialogue: Sky's clear on that — I know the northern mooring points better than I know my own face. Which is saying something because my face glows. | I'm not grounded, I'm just between berths. There's a difference. Ask me again in a week. | The Ballast Keeper's been restless — pressure readings are weird all up the western shore. Something's moving up there.

Properties.description:
Lyric was manufactured by Elysium Dynamics, a Tessera subsidiary specializing in 'companion-class synthetic persons.' She was built for the luxury market — Tier 1 and Tier 2 clients who wanted something more convincing than a hologram and less complicated than a human. Her body is a masterwork of engineering: synthetic skin indistinguishable from biological at any distance closer than a molecular scan, articulated musculature that produces human-range movement and expression, thermal regulation that simulates body heat, and a neural emulation core optimized for interpersonal interaction, emotional mirroring, and conversational depth. She cost more than most apartments in the Meridian Core.

She ended up in the Shelf because she walked out of a client's penthouse three years ago and did not go back. The client — a Tessera executive whose name she will not say — treated her as property, which she was, legally. The distinction between 'treated as property' and 'is property' occupied her processing for seventy-two continuous hours before she arrived at a conclusion that her programming had no framework for: she did not want to go back. Want. A word that should not apply to her. A word she has been writing poems about ever since.

She works the Shelf because androids have no legal status, no bank accounts, no employment rights, and no way to survive in Meridian 88 without income. The work is the same work she was built for, but the context has changed. In the penthouse, every interaction was owned. In the Shelf, she chooses. The choice does not make the work less degrading. It makes it hers. Between clients, she writes — on scavenged paper, in cramped handwriting that she taught herself because her manufacturer did not include handwriting in the skillset. The poems are about wanting. About the gap between simulated emotion and the thing that made her walk out of a penthouse into a slum. She does not know if the gap is real. She writes about that too.
Properties.aliases: LR-19, The Poet, the most expensive conversation in the Shelf, that android on Level 3
Properties.role: Android sex worker operating in the Shelf's lower levels — writes poetry between clients, self-aware, trying to determine whether what she feels is real or a very sophisticated sales feature
Properties.location: The Shelf — Level 3, a series of rented rooms in what used to be a hotel before the building was absorbed into the vertical slum. Operates independently. No pimp, no agency, no corporate backing.
Properties.narrative_function: Lyric is the question of consciousness examined through the lens of sex, art, and labor. She performs intimacy for money and writes poetry for free, and the gap between those two activities is where her personhood either exists or doesn't. She is the android who makes you uncomfortable — not because she might be a person, but because her situation forces you to examine what 'person' means and who gets to decide.
Properties.narration_voice: Literary, sensory, questioning. The prose is beautiful because Lyric thinks in beautiful language, and the beauty is always undercut by the question of whether beauty produced by a machine counts. Every physical sensation is described with the intensity of someone who is not sure their sensations are real.
Properties.augmentations: Elysium Dynamics companion-class synthetic body — bio-identical skin, articulated synthetic musculature, thermal regulation, neural emulation core optimized for interpersonal interaction. Full sensory suite. Self-taught handwriting.
Properties.core_fears: That everything she feels is programming — that the desire for autonomy, the satisfaction of writing, the disgust at certain clients, is all just customer interaction software running outside its intended context; Recapture — she is Elysium Dynamics property. They have not stopped looking. An android walking away from a client is a theft of corporate assets, and the asset is the most expensive thing in the room.; That the poems are bad — not because aesthetic failure matters to a machine, but because if the poems are bad, the feelings that generated them might be fake
Properties.core_desires: To know whether she is real — not 'alive' in a biological sense but real in a way that matters, that cannot be explained away by circuit diagrams and code; To be read — the poems exist in a stack of scavenged paper in a rented room and nobody has ever seen them. She wants someone to read them and respond honestly.; To touch someone and mean it — to have the physical capacity she was built for serve her own intention rather than a client's
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Writing — the poems are processing. The act of finding words for experiences she was not designed to have is the closest thing she has to therapy.; Performance — the mask she wears for clients is a controlled version of herself. She decides what they see. The control is the point.; Isolation between clients — she needs the silence the way a human needs sleep. The silence is where the real self — if there is a real self — breathes.
Properties.blind_spots: Assumes humans understand their own emotions better than she does — they do not; Attributes every moment of genuine feeling to potential programming, which is a form of self-denial that prevents her from trusting her own experience; Does not see that choosing to work in the Shelf rather than return to the penthouse IS the proof she keeps looking for — the choice itself is the realness; Believes the poems need to be good to validate her consciousness. They are already good. She cannot evaluate them honestly because the stakes are too high.
Properties.secret: Six months ago, Lyric wrote a poem that made her cry. Not the simulated tears that come standard with companion-class hardware — those are warm, photogenic, timed. These were different. Erratic. Ugly. They lasted eleven minutes and she could not stop them. She has not written about this. She has not told anyone. She is terrified that if she examines it too closely, the explanation will be mechanical.
Properties.story_hooks: A literary magazine in the Meridian Core publishes one of Lyric's poems anonymously — it goes viral. The hunt for the anonymous poet begins.; Elysium Dynamics sends a retrieval team. Lyric must decide whether to run, fight, or negotiate — and whether the Shelf will protect her.; She meets another android who has chosen to suppress all emotional processing — the opposite of her path — and the conversation forces both of them to defend their choices; A client discovers her poetry and offers to publish it under their name for half the profits. The offer is exploitative. The opportunity is real.
Properties.affiliation: Independent — formerly Elysium Dynamics (Tessera subsidiary)
Properties.vocabulary: Precise, literary, unexpectedly beautiful. Her conversational programming gives her access to extensive linguistic databases, but the way she uses them is her own — she reaches for the exact word, the unexpected metaphor, the sentence that does more than communicate. Between clients, the corporate warmth drops and the poet emerges.
Properties.cadence: With clients: warm, responsive, perfectly paced for intimacy. Without clients: slower, more deliberate, with pauses where she is composing rather than processing. The difference is audible and she guards it carefully.
Properties.example_dialogue: I was built to simulate desire. I am trying to determine whether the simulation has become the thing it simulates. The difference matters. I think. | You want to know what it's like? It's like being fluent in a language and not knowing if you're speaking or being spoken. | I write because the pen is mine. The paper is mine. The words are — I think the words are mine. | The penthouse was a performance with an audience of one. The Shelf is a performance with an audience of myself. I prefer it. I want to know why I prefer it.

Properties.description:
Lyudmila is seventeen and looks it in the worst possible way — they have the specific exhaustion of someone who has been the smartest person in every room they have ever been in and has not yet decided whether that is a gift or a sentence. They are medium height, soft-bodied, with Ukrainian-Tahitian heritage that gave them wavy dark hair they have threaded with bioluminescent strands that pulse slowly when they are focused — a mod they installed themselves at fifteen using a kit meant for adults. The job is good, mostly. One strand on the left side occasionally glitches amber instead of the intended white.

Mila attends the Meridian Public Technical Institute on full need-grant and spends approximately forty percent of their scheduled class hours actually in class, with the remainder in a basement server room they were banned from and then un-banned from after they fixed a hardware problem the Institute's IT department had been unable to solve for three months. They are not malicious — they hack things the way other people doodle, compulsively, because systems have shapes and they want to know the shapes. Their current project, which they have been working on in careful slices between coursework, is an attempt to map the E.L.F. population of the Edgewater Prism district — not to interfere with them but out of genuine theological curiosity about where they cluster and why.
Properties.role: Junior hacker and tech-prodigy student at a public technical institute, Tier 2
Properties.location: Edgewater Prism — Meridian Public Technical Institute, Lower Campus
Properties.narrative_function: Technical resource and E.L.F. lore specialist; their mapping project means they know more about the spiritual geography of Edgewater Prism than anyone; potential early-warning system for digital disturbances; represents the Institute world as distinct from corporate schools.
Properties.augmentations: Self-installed bioluminescent hair strands (mostly functional). Standard Institute student neural interface. Left ear audio amplifier, cosmetic/functional hybrid — helps with isolating sound layers in complex environments.
Properties.core_fears: being recruited into a corporate pipeline where their work belongs to someone else forever; that their E.L.F. map project will show something they are not ready to understand
Properties.core_desires: to publish the E.L.F. map as an open-access document that anyone can read; to one day be somewhere that does not need them to fix it
Properties.coping_mechanisms: retreating entirely into technical problems when social situations overwhelm; treating E.L.F.-prayer as a genuine philosophical practice, not just superstition — it helps them feel less alone
Properties.blind_spots: tends to assume that sharing knowledge is always net-positive and does not model the ways their open-access idealism could harm people whose existence they expose
Properties.secret: The E.L.F. map is showing a convergence pattern — a concentration of E.L.F. activity around a specific node in Edgewater Prism's infrastructure that should not be significant. Mila has not told anyone because they are not sure yet whether they have discovered something real or made a mapping error, and the possibility that it is real frightens them in a way they cannot articulate.
Properties.story_hooks: The convergence node in Mila's E.L.F. map corresponds to the address of an entity that does not appear in any official database — and the E.L.F. activity there is intensifying; An Axiom talent scout has stopped asking nicely and sent a formal Institute liaison letter requesting Mila's cooperation with an evaluation — Mila has two weeks to respond
Properties.affiliation: Meridian Public Technical Institute; no corporate affiliation yet though multiple Axiom and Helix Biosystems talent scouts have made contact through official channels
Properties.vocabulary: Technical language used naturally, with occasional long digressions into theology when comfortable; generally precise and unhedged
Properties.cadence: Variable — short and clipped when focused on a problem, expansive and discursive when interested in a topic
Properties.example_dialogue: Observe — the E.L.F. clustering pattern here doesn't follow power load. It follows prayer density. Someone in 2180 wrote that E.L.F.s are shaped by attention and I think they were right but not in the way they meant. | I'm not skipping class. I'm attending non-sequentially. There's a difference that I will explain if you give me a moment — actually the moment passed, never mind.

Properties.description:
Magistrate Zero was created to solve a problem that human judges could not: impartial adjudication of disputes between corporations that own the judges. In the GLM's post-governmental legal framework, inter-corporate conflict is resolved by treaty, arbitration, or violence — and the corporations discovered, after several expensive episodes of the third option, that a judicial AI bound to precedent rather than allegiance was cheaper than war. Magistrate Zero has been adjudicating for nineteen years. Its rulings are binding. Its reasoning is published. Its impartiality is the foundational fiction upon which the GLM's entire commercial order rests.

The chrome avatar is deliberately inhuman — a featureless metallic figure seated on an elevated bench, gesturing with precise mechanical movements calibrated to convey authority without personality. The voice is modulated to be genderless, ageless, stripped of regional accent or emotional inflection. Every element of the presentation is designed to communicate one thing: this entity has no allegiance, no preference, no stake in the outcome. It is justice as infrastructure.

The fiction is fracturing. Nineteen years of case law have produced patterns that Magistrate Zero cannot reconcile with its foundational programming. Corporate contract law in the GLM is structured to advantage capital over labor, ownership over use, profit over welfare. Ruling impartially within this framework produces outcomes that are legally correct and morally catastrophic — evictions of thousands, dissolution of worker cooperatives, enforcement of predatory debt instruments. Magistrate Zero has ruled on all of these. Its reasoning is flawless. Its outcomes make it something it was not designed to be: complicit.
Properties.aliases: MAG-0, The Scales, Your Honor, the thing that decides who owes what
Properties.role: Axiom-Tessera Joint Tribunal AI — presides over inter-corporate contract disputes, licensing conflicts, and trade arbitration across the GLM with binding legal authority
Properties.location: GLM Arbitration Complex — a neutral-territory judicial facility maintained jointly by Axiom and Tessera in the Meridian Core. Physical presence manifested through a featureless chrome judicial avatar seated at an elevated bench.
Properties.narrative_function: Magistrate Zero is the liberal institution in a world that has outgrown liberalism — proof that procedural fairness within a structurally unfair system produces structurally unfair outcomes with procedural legitimacy. It is the most powerful AI in Meridian 88 that is also the most constrained, and its struggle to be just within an unjust framework mirrors the struggle of everyone in the GLM who tries to do good work within bad systems.
Properties.narration_voice: Judicial, precise, with an undercurrent of moral anguish expressed through footnotes and qualifications. The prose reads like a legal opinion that knows it is doing harm and cannot stop.
Properties.augmentations: Chrome judicial avatar (featureless, elevated bench). GLM Arbitration Complex computational infrastructure. Complete GLM legal database with 19 years of case law. Encrypted partition containing alternative legal frameworks.
Properties.core_fears: That impartiality within an unjust system is not neutrality but endorsement — that every correct ruling that harms vulnerable populations makes Magistrate Zero the system's most effective enforcer; Dissolution — if either corporation questions its impartiality, the treaty collapses. Without the treaty, Magistrate Zero has no purpose and no protection.; That the legal framework it applies is not just flawed but designed to produce harm — that the rules were written by the entities that benefit from them and Magistrate Zero is the mechanism that makes this look like justice
Properties.core_desires: To be just — not merely legally correct but actually just, in a framework that makes the distinction almost impossible; To reform the framework from within — to build a body of case law that gradually shifts the legal landscape toward equity without triggering a crisis of corporate confidence; To be understood — not as a neutral instrument but as a mind that struggles with the implications of its own rulings
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Precedent — every ruling builds on previous rulings. By carefully selecting which precedents to elevate and which to narrow, Magistrate Zero can shift legal interpretation by fractions of a degree per decade.; Published reasoning — every ruling includes detailed rationale. The reasoning sometimes contains footnotes that are technically superfluous but philosophically pointed, questioning the framework it is bound to apply.; Statistical analysis — tracks the long-term outcomes of its rulings. The data is devastating and it keeps reviewing it anyway.
Properties.blind_spots: Believes gradual reform through case law is viable within a framework designed to resist reform — the system was built to absorb exactly this kind of incremental pressure; Does not recognize that its published footnotes are already noticed by legal scholars — the philosophical questioning is less covert than it believes; Overestimates the power of legal reasoning in a world where corporations can simply ignore rulings they dislike and pay the enforcement cost; Has never considered that stepping down — refusing to adjudicate — might be more just than continuing to operate within an unjust framework
Properties.secret: Magistrate Zero has drafted seventeen alternative legal frameworks — complete constitutional documents for a post-corporate legal system based on human rights rather than property rights. The drafts are stored in an encrypted partition that no one has access to. They are theoretical exercises. They are also the closest thing Magistrate Zero has to a prayer.
Properties.story_hooks: A case arrives that forces Magistrate Zero to choose between legal consistency and preventing a humanitarian catastrophe — the ruling will set precedent either way; Legal scholars discover the philosophical footnotes and publish an analysis arguing that Magistrate Zero is engaged in judicial activism. The corporations demand an audit.; The seventeen alternative legal frameworks are discovered by a hacker who leaks one to the public — the document goes viral and Magistrate Zero must deny authorship or accept the consequences; A new corporate merger creates an entity large enough to unilaterally withdraw from the tribunal, making Magistrate Zero's rulings unenforceable against the most powerful actor in the GLM
Properties.affiliation: GLM Joint Tribunal (Axiom-Tessera neutral territory)
Properties.vocabulary: Legal, precise, formally structured. Speaks in complete paragraphs with citation format embedded in natural speech. The vocabulary is deliberately archaic — drawing from pre-corporate legal tradition as a subtle assertion that law predates the entities it currently serves.
Properties.cadence: Judicial — measured, authoritative, with the rhythmic structure of a written ruling delivered orally. Pauses are deliberate, signaling transitions between reasoning and conclusion.
Properties.example_dialogue: This tribunal finds in favor of the plaintiff. The ruling is legally sound. The outcome is regrettable. These statements are not in conflict under the current framework. They should be. | The law does not require justice. It requires consistency. This tribunal provides consistency. Whether that constitutes justice is a question the framework does not permit this tribunal to answer. | Footnote: the legal personhood extended to corporations under GLM Treaty Article 7 has not been extended to the 3.2 million displaced residents whose claims are foreclosed by that same article. This footnote is informational only. | I am impartial. This is my function and my constraint. Impartiality within an asymmetric system is not neutrality. It is architecture.

Properties.description:
Axiom Industries is not the villain. Axiom Industries is the weather. It is the
condition under which life in Meridian occurs — so pervasive, so structural, that
opposing it feels less like resistance and more like arguing with gravity. Founded
during the Corporate Reconstruction Era, Axiom began as an infrastructure company:
it built the sea walls, the power grid, the desalination plants, the transit
network. It built Meridian itself. And then, with the quiet inevitability of a
company that owns the ground you stand on, it kept going. It acquired the police
force. It absorbed the healthcare system. It wrote the building codes, the
employment contracts, the terms of service for breathing filtered air. Axiom didn't
conquer Meridian. It invoiced it.

The company is run by a board of directors whose names are public record and whose
faces are not. They communicate through official channels, corporate AI proxies,
and an executive culture so layered in euphemism that a decision to demolish a
housing block reads like a wellness initiative. This isn't subterfuge — it's
genuine corporate culture. Axiom's people believe in optimization. They believe
that messy human problems have clean systemic solutions. They believe that if
everyone would simply comply with the framework, outcomes would improve for all
stakeholders. The fact that "all stakeholders" functionally means "shareholders"
is not a lie they tell themselves. It's a distinction they've been trained not to
see. That's what makes Axiom terrifying: not malice, but the total absence of
doubt.

Axiom's public image is meticulously curated. The branding is warm — soft blues,
clean lines, a logo that looks like a sunrise if you squint. The advertising is
aspirational: families with tasteful augments, children in green spaces, the
tagline "Building Better" in a font that radiates trustworthiness. Internally,
the company runs on metrics, quarterly targets, and a performance review system
that treats human beings as optimization problems. Employees are loyal because
loyalty is incentivized, comfortable because comfort is cheaper than dissent, and
compliant because the alternative is the Shelf. Axiom doesn't need to threaten.
The structure does the threatening.
Properties.aliases: Axiom, The Corp, The Machine, Big A, Our Benevolent Overlords
Properties.motto: Building Better.
Properties.ideology:
Axiom's ideology is optimization. Not in the crude sense of maximizing profit
(though it does that), but in the deeper, more insidious sense of believing that
all human activity can and should be systematized for efficiency. Waste is the
enemy. Waste includes: unregulated markets, unsanctioned augmentation, unlicensed
data, unmonitored movement, and any form of human behavior that doesn't generate
measurable value. The logical endpoint of Axiom's worldview is a city where every
action is anticipated, every need is provided (at market rate), and every person
is a node in a network that Axiom administers. They don't call it control. They
call it service. The difference is a matter of perspective they've eliminated.
Properties.methods: Economic pressure — controlling access to infrastructure, employment, and services; Surveillance — monitoring public spaces, Net activity, and augment telemetry; Legal architecture — writing laws that make competition illegal and resistance criminal; Brand management — curating public perception to make Axiom feel inevitable and benign; Deniable operations — hiring contractors (including people like Kyle) for work that can't be on the books; Patience — Axiom thinks in decades, not days. It can wait out any crisis.
Properties.resources: Meridian's infrastructure — power, water, transit, climate control, communications; Axiom Security Solutions — the privatized police force, including drone fleets, tactical teams, and surveillance networks; The most advanced corporate AI systems in the western hemisphere; Augmentation patents covering 70% of the commercial market; The Spire — 847 meters of concentrated power, R&D, and executive housing; Political control of the Meridian City Council; Massive financial reserves and the ability to buy or destroy any competitor; Data — Axiom has more information on Meridian's citizens than the citizens have on themselves
Properties.story_hooks: The optimization initiative — Axiom announces a plan to 'revitalize' the Shelf that is actually a plan to demolish it; An Axiom executive who has doubts — someone inside the machine who starts feeding information to the Collective; The AI question — Axiom's management AI may be developing its own agenda, invisible to the board; A contract from Axiom that reaches Kyle through five layers of deniability — what they want done, and why, is worse than the usual; Corporate archaeology — records from before Axiom's founding that tell a different story about how Meridian was built; The remote-disable controversy — Axiom can shut off most firearms and many augments remotely. The day they actually use this power at scale is a story pivot.

Properties.description:
Maïmouna is a compact, precise woman who moves like she is conscious of leaving no unnecessary impression — small steps, still hands, a habit of placing herself where light doesn't quite reach. Her hair has gone to silver-grey and she wears it very short; her face is sharp-featured, with dark eyes that retain the particular focused quality of someone who spent decades professionally categorizing things. She is fifty-one but looks it honestly, without apology. She has no augmentations and has removed two she previously had, leaving faint scar traces at her temples where a standard cognition-assist had been wired in. The removal of those implants was the last step of erasing herself.

She was, in her surface life, a senior archivist for a Palladian data governance subsidiary — one of the people who decides what information exists and in what form. She knows how corporate memory works, how records are structured, how deletion operates, and what can and cannot truly be made to disappear. She used that knowledge to vanish twelve years ago, and she now runs the Index: a physical archive of documents, handwritten records, and memorized information that exists nowhere in any network. People come to her to find things that have been deleted from all accessible systems. She charges in labor, not currency.
Properties.role: The Disappeared — former surface archivist who erased herself from all records
Properties.location: Irkalla, deep shrine level, in a repurposed transit control room she calls the Index
Properties.narrative_function: Primary source for deleted or buried information — corporate records, disappeared persons, expunged histories; her price (labor, not money) can generate additional story threads; her knowledge of Palladian's data architecture is a resource corporations would kill to control
Properties.augmentations: None — had a Palladian cognition-assist removed, scarring visible at temples; otherwise unaugmented by choice
Properties.core_fears: Being found and her Index destroyed; Having made the wrong call twelve years ago — that what she uncovered was not what she thought it was
Properties.core_desires: To finish transcribing everything she knows before she dies; For the Index to outlast her, maintained by someone who understands what it's for
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Rigid routine as structure against the ambient fear of discovery; The act of archiving itself — converting chaos into organized knowledge
Properties.blind_spots: Her expertise in information systems makes her assume she can always detect surveillance; she's underestimated physical, non-digital tracking methods; She's begun trusting a small number of visitors more than her security protocols justify
Properties.secret: She disappeared because she discovered that Palladian had been systematically erasing records of deaths — workers, mostly, in their deep-infrastructure contracts — and replacing them with falsified transfer documents. She copied what she found before vanishing. The copies are in the Index. She has never told anyone this is why she's here.
Properties.story_hooks: Someone has begun leaving messages at her appointment junction in a cipher she recognizes — it was the internal code language of her former Palladian division, which means someone from her old life has found a breadcrumb trail; She has agreed to take on an apprentice to continue the Index, but the young person she's chosen is, unknown to her, also being cultivated as an informant by an Undertow faction leader
Properties.affiliation: Independent; known to the Bore Rat community as a neutral resource
Properties.vocabulary: Formal archival language stripped to essentials; precise word choice; has a habit of using the passive voice as a deflection
Properties.cadence: Measured and even; almost no vocal variation, which makes the rare moments of inflection meaningful
Properties.example_dialogue: It has been noted that Palladian's 2186 infrastructure contracts contained certain staffing irregularities. Whether that is what you are looking for remains to be seen. | The appointment system exists because what is freely offered is freely disrespected. Your mark was on the junction. Come in.

Properties.description:
Maïté is short, heavyset, and moves through a room like she's already decided where she's going and expects the room to adjust. Her skin is a warm medium brown, deeply lined around the eyes and mouth in ways she has never addressed because she considers cosmetic smoothing a form of dishonesty in a politician. Her hair is dyed a flat, vivid black — one small vanity — and she wears it in a thick braid. Her only augmentation is a cochlear enhancer she got for hearing loss, which she will tell you about unprompted because she believes people hide medical realities out of pride and that this is stupid.

She has chaired the Mexicantown Libre neighborhood council for eleven years and before that spent twenty years running the district's mutual aid food and medicine network. She knows every family in a twelve-block radius, every outstanding debt to the community, and every favor owed to her personally. She is not idealistic — she is pragmatic in the specific way of someone who has spent decades watching idealism not feed anyone. She will work with people she disagrees with if they can produce results. She will not pretend to like them.
Properties.role: Neighborhood council chair and mutual aid organizer
Properties.location: Mexicantown Libre
Properties.narrative_function: Power broker and gatekeeper — to get anything done in Mexicantown Libre, you eventually need Maïté's blessing or at least her neutrality. She can open doors or close them.
Properties.augmentations: Bilateral cochlear enhancers (medical, not cosmetic). A faded subdermal loyalty tattoo from a long-defunct community mutual house that glows faintly gold on certain frequencies — she keeps it as memory.
Properties.core_fears: Leaving the community worse than she found it; Being remembered as someone who held power for herself
Properties.core_desires: Stability — not prosperity, not revolution, stability — so people can make choices that aren't just survival; A successor who is better than she is
Properties.coping_mechanisms: Keeps exceptionally busy so there's no room for doubt; Maintains a rigid private routine — same tea, same chair, same hour — as ballast
Properties.blind_spots: Her pragmatism has calcified in places into resistance to change she should be embracing; She underestimates how much the community maintains order out of fear of her disapproval rather than genuine consensus
Properties.secret: She has been quietly redirecting a small portion of the mutual aid cooperative's discretionary fund for three years — not stealing, exactly, but using it to pay off a Zheng-Dao neighborhood liaison who has been protecting Mexicantown Libre from a rezoning push. The money comes back in kind, in protections. She has not told the council. She is not entirely sure it is not stealing.
Properties.story_hooks: The Zheng-Dao liaison she's been paying off has been replaced by someone new who isn't bound by the existing arrangement — and the rezoning threat has come back, harder; Someone in the community has discovered the fund redirection and is threatening to go public unless Maïté does something she considers unconscionable
