Properties.story_hooks: Dredge Mining's automated tunnel network has intersected with something beneath the city that predates human habitation — the mining AI flagged it, and Dredge corporate sealed the data; A university researcher has developed a cold-weather augmentation that would transform UP habitability — and both Michigan and Wisconsin want exclusive access; The UP Administrative Authority is quietly preparing for a sovereignty declaration independent of both Michigan and Wisconsin — and they need external support to survive the aftermath
Properties.sights: The ore docks extending into Lake Superior like industrial fingers — automated loading systems running day and night; Northern Michigan University campus, its buildings a mix of pre-corporate stone and modern research facilities; Sandstone cliffs along the lakefront, red-brown against Superior's grey-blue — beauty that nobody has managed to monetize; Mining transport vehicles moving through the city center — the underground economy surfacing for resupply; Michigan state flags flying from government buildings alongside UP independence banners — a political identity still forming
Properties.sounds: Ore loading operations on the docks — the deep metallic groan of tonnage moving from land to ship; University activity — the sounds of a campus that hasn't given up on public education; Lake Superior weather — wind off the lake that carries cold and context; Mining transport convoys — heavy vehicles on roads not designed for them, a grinding complaint from the infrastructure
Properties.smells: Iron ore dust — the city's signature scent, red-brown and metallic, coating every surface; Lake Superior air — the cleanest air in the GLM, when the wind comes off the water; Pine forests north of the city, carried on north winds; University cafeteria food — bad, but the smell of an institution that still feeds people rather than charging for nutrient optimization
Properties.feel: A city that is trying to be something more than a mine with addresses. Iron Crown has ambition beyond extraction — the university, the lakefront, the administrative infrastructure — but the iron is what pays for it, and everyone knows it. The tension between resource colony and actual community defines the place.

Nodes.Name: Keweenaw Peninsula wilderness — effectively uncharted corporate-free territory

Properties.description: Houghton-Hancock's 200-year-old connection — upgraded, automated, and the oldest continuously operating bridge in the GLM
Michigan Tech's underground research facilities — repurposed copper mine shafts housing the GLM's premier extreme-environment engineering programs
Deep-mine data centers using natural cooling — some of the most physically secure data storage in the world

A decommissioned Metra transit hub buried forty meters beneath the Old Harbor district, its vaulted ceilings still wearing the oxidized copper cladding that gave it its name — great sweeping arches of verdigris green and rust-brown that catch the light of jury-rigged sodium strips in ways that feel almost religious. The station was sealed in 2087 after a Ferrogate Security crackdown on a synthetic labor strike, and the official record lists it as a flooded maintenance corridor. It is neither flooded nor a corridor.

Over the decades since, Copperveil has become one of the most reliable underground transit exchanges in the southern Meridian corridor. Four unofficial rail lines — none operated by any corponation — thread through its platforms, running reconditioned cargo cars between Shelf communities, the Stockyard underbelly, and the eastern Slagshore. Tickets are traded in favors, Φ, and contraband data chips, enforced loosely by a coalition of former transit workers who call themselves the Lamplighters.

The station's commercial layer occupies the old ticketing concourse: a dense sprawl of stalls selling salvaged BCI hardware, gene-edited street food, bootleg Diaspora access nodes, and medical services that don't ask for identity verification. It smells like copper and cooking fat and the particular ozone tang of overtaxed rail systems.
Properties.aliases: The Veil, Copper Bottom, Downgate Hub, The Tarnish
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 3 and Tier 4 residents who depend on off-grid transit, with a significant synthetic population using the station as a safe waypoint between hostile surface zones. Lamplighter personnel skew older, many former transit union members from pre-crackdown labor cohorts.
Properties.economy: The station runs on a barter-and-cash economy; the Lamplighters levy a small transit tax on all rail traffic and a stall-license fee on vendors, generating enough revenue to maintain the rail infrastructure and pay their own modest wages.
Properties.power_structure: The Lamplighter coalition governs through a council of seven senior members, each responsible for a station zone; they hold a fragile but functional monopoly on violence and dispute resolution within the station's bounds.
Properties.dangers: Ferrogate Security runs periodic tunnel sweeps from the surface, forcing rapid station lockdowns that can trap travelers for hours.; The unofficial rail lines share aging track with unmapped maintenance drones that do not yield to passenger cars.; Rival courier syndicates occasionally use the station's crowds to settle debts violently when they believe the Lamplighters are occupied elsewhere.; Bootleg BCI hardware from the concourse stalls has a documented failure rate that can cause neural bleed events in vulnerable users.
Properties.opportunities: The Lamplighters quietly hire outside contractors for tunnel reconnaissance ahead of Ferrogate sweep cycles.; The station's medical corridor is one of the few places in the southern corridor where synthetic injury can be treated without identity logging.; Off-grid rail access to three separate Shelf communities makes Copperveil an irreplaceable logistics node for anyone needing to move people or goods without a paper trail.
Properties.story_hooks: A Lamplighter council member has gone missing between a routine tunnel inspection and her scheduled return — her colleagues are quietly desperate, unwilling to surface the matter publicly because her route passed through a section of tunnel they officially claim is impassable.; A cargo car arrived on Platform 3 two nights ago with no crew, no manifest, and seventeen crates of Arcturus Defense Solutions hardware that nobody ordered. The Lamplighters want it gone before Ferrogate's next sweep, and they're not particular about how.; A synthetic traveler named Oswin has been sleeping on a concourse bench for eleven days, claiming she cannot leave because something in the station's old copper wiring is broadcasting a signal she describes as her name being called. She is lucid, calm, and terrified.
Properties.sights: Arched copper ceilings patched with mismatched alloy panels glow amber and green under flickering sodium strips.; Crowds press through narrow platform lanes between rail cars spray-painted with route glyphs no official map acknowledges.; A Lamplighter checkpoint — two heavyset figures in orange high-vis with non-Ferrogate sidearms — watches every train arrival from a repurposed ticket booth.; Stall tarps hang from old departure boards, still occasionally cycling ghost schedules from 2087.
Properties.sounds: The low harmonic groan of approaching rail cars echoes through the tunnels seconds before their lights appear.; A dozen competing languages blend into a single ambient roar from the concourse market.; Somewhere deeper in the maintenance shafts, something large and mechanical operates in irregular, patient rhythms.
Properties.smells: Hot copper oxidation mixes with frying synthetic protein from the food stalls.; Ozone and rail grease hang in layers, thicker near the active platforms.; Unwashed bodies and cheap disinfectant dominate the medical corridor on the east concourse.
Properties.feel: Copperveil exists in a state of deliberate illegibility — it is busy and functional and completely invisible to official infrastructure. The Lamplighters maintain just enough order that violence is rare but never impossible. First-timers feel the weight of the ceiling and the weight of being somewhere they are not supposed to know about.

Properties.description: The deepest and least-trafficked platform, used for cargo runs and known among regulars as the place where things arrive that weren't meant to.
A six-bed medical operation run by a former Helix Biosystems surgeon who lost her license after treating synthetic patients without corponation authorization.

The Rouge Furnace takes its name from the River Rouge industrial complex — once the largest integrated factory in the world, where Henry Ford turned iron ore into finished automobiles in a single facility. The complex is still there. It is still enormous. It no longer makes cars. What it makes now depends on who you ask and what level of security clearance they hold. The official designation is the Rouge Autonomous Manufacturing Campus, operated by a joint venture between Ford Meridian and Arcturus Defense Solutions. The campus produces autonomous vehicle chassis, military drone components, and — according to the workers who live in the surrounding blocks — things that arrive in sealed containers and leave in different sealed containers and nobody is encouraged to ask questions.

Southwest Detroit around the Rouge complex is a working district in the oldest sense: people here make things with their hands, maintain things that break, and go home tired. The population is predominantly Latino and Middle Eastern, communities that have lived in this area for over a century and survived every economic cycle the city threw at them. The housing stock is dense, practical, and aging. The air quality is managed by an Ouroboros Energy atmospheric processing station on Zug Island that does a reasonable job of filtering industrial particulates and an unreasonable job of charging residents for the privilege of breathing air that the factory contaminated in the first place.

The district's relationship with the Rouge campus is parasitic and mutual. The factory provides employment — roughly 6,000 jobs, mostly Tier 1 and Tier 2 maintenance and logistics positions. The neighborhood provides labor, proximity, and the kind of community infrastructure that keeps workers functional without the factory having to provide it. Schools, clinics, groceries, bars — the neighborhood handles the human maintenance so the factory doesn't have to. The arrangement has worked for a hundred and fifty years. It has never been fair for a single one of them.
Properties.aliases: Southwest Detroit, The Furnace, Rouge Country
Properties.demographics: Approximately 52,000 residents. Predominantly Latino (60%) and Middle Eastern (25%) communities with deep generational roots. Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers make up 85% of the population. Income inequality within the district is low because everyone is equally underpaid.
Properties.economy: The Rouge campus dominates — 6,000 direct jobs and approximately 18,000 in the supply chain and service economy that supports it. Average household income: Φ34,000. The informal economy adds roughly 30% to household income through unlicensed repair work, gray-market parts trading, and the kind of side jobs that keep families above the survival line.
Properties.power_structure: Ford Meridian and Arcturus Defense Solutions jointly govern the Rouge campus through the Industrial Zone Authority. The surrounding neighborhood falls under nominal municipal governance, which in practice means Ford Meridian's community relations office handles disputes, approves construction permits, and funds the two schools. Labor organizing is technically legal and practically career-ending.
Properties.dangers: Industrial exposure — the atmospheric processor handles most airborne contamination but soil and water exposure are cumulative; Arcturus military production — the sealed container operations create security risks for anyone who gets curious; Economic dependency — the Rouge campus is the single employer, and layoffs ripple through every household; River contamination — the chemical sheen is monitored but the monitoring reports are not public; Exoskeleton addiction — workers who spend shifts in load-bearing rigs develop dependency on the enhanced strength, and withdrawal is physical
Properties.opportunities: Industrial skills — the workers here can build, repair, and maintain anything mechanical or autonomous; Parts access — the gray-market parts economy moves military-grade components through neighborhood repair shops; The sealed container operations present intelligence-gathering opportunities for the right buyer; Labor organizing — the workforce is sympathetic to collective action if someone can navigate the risks
Properties.story_hooks: A Rouge worker opens a sealed container that was mis-routed to a civilian maintenance bay. What's inside is not a vehicle component. The worker has twelve hours before the inventory system flags the discrepancy.; Zug Island's atmospheric processor is scheduled for a firmware update that will reduce its filtration capacity by 15% — Ouroboros Energy calls it optimization, the neighborhood calls it a death sentence; An exoskeleton repair tech in the neighborhood has been modifying military-grade rigs for civilian use. Arcturus has noticed.
Properties.sights: The Rouge complex's silhouette against the sky — massive, geometric, lit from within at all hours; Zug Island's atmospheric processor stacks venting filtered air in white plumes that look clean and might be; Workers in industrial exoskeletons walking home along Fort Street, still wearing their load-bearing rigs; Dense residential blocks where every third house has a rooftop garden and every fifth has a FOR SALE sign; The Detroit River curving past the complex, its surface carrying an iridescent chemical sheen on warm days
Properties.sounds: The Rouge complex — a low, continuous industrial chord that the neighborhood has absorbed into its definition of silence; Shift-change traffic — thousands of workers moving in synchronized waves, three times daily; The atmospheric processor's rhythmic cycling, a mechanical breathing that the neighborhood unconsciously synchronizes with; Music from the bars on Fort Street — where three shifts' worth of exhaustion gets processed nightly; River barges moving materials upstream to the factory docks, their navigation horns echoing off the complex walls
Properties.smells: Industrial process exhaust — filtered but present, a metallic tang that coats the back of your throat; Cooking from the residential blocks — the food is better here than in the Axis because it's made by people, not algorithms; The river — petroleum undertones near the factory, cleaner downstream, never fully clean
Properties.feel: Hardworking and resigned. The Rouge Furnace feels like a place that has been making things for other people's benefit for 150 years and has internalized the arrangement. There's pride here — in the work, in the community, in the survival — but it comes with the particular exhaustion of people who know they're essential and disposable at the same time.

Properties.description: Twelve square miles of sovereign corporate territory — where the autonomous vehicle industry's future is designed, tested, and deployed
Two miles of Arab-American businesses — a century of community continuity, measured in storefronts and stubbornness
The relocated Islamic center — beautiful, state-of-the-art, and a reminder of what was taken to make room for a parking algorithm

Freestone is the first and largest of the Great Lakes seacrete cities — a sovereign free nation grown from the body of Lake Michigan itself. It began in 2161, when a coalition of climate refugees, displaced academics, anarchist engineers, and people who had simply run out of continent built a wire-mesh framework twelve nautical miles off the Wisconsin shore, dropped it into the lake, and ran electrical current through it. The principle is electrodeposition: pass low-voltage direct current through a submerged conductive framework in mineral-rich water, and dissolved calcium and magnesium carbonates precipitate onto the mesh, building up layer by layer into a material harder than concrete. The pioneers called the process seacrete — mineral accretion, the same chemistry that builds coral reefs, accelerated by human engineering. Marshall T. Savage described it in 'The Millennial Project' as a way to colonize the oceans. The Freestone founders used it to escape the corponations.

The city grew the way coral grows: slowly, organically, and in every direction. The original framework was a flat platform roughly the size of a city block. Within five years, it had accreted into a multi-level structure with subsurface foundations reaching thirty meters down to the lakebed. New frameworks were attached to the edges and submerged; the current was extended; the reef expanded. Solar arrays and wave-energy converters powered the electrodeposition continuously. By 2180, Freestone was a floating reef-city of 340,000 people, roughly two kilometers in diameter, with docking platforms, desalination systems, hydroponic farms, workshop districts, and residential warrens grown directly from the lake's own minerals. The structures are rough-textured, organic, vaguely biological — walls that curve like bone, archways that look grown rather than built, surfaces encrusted with the mineral patterns of their own creation. It looks like someone taught a coral reef to be a city.

Freestone's sovereignty is a legal accident that became a political fact. The original platform was anchored in water deep enough to be outside any state or corponation's territorial claim — the Great Lakes sovereignty framework, written by corporate lawyers for corporate purposes, never anticipated that anyone would build a nation in the middle of the lake. By the time M88's legal apparatus noticed Freestone, it had 50,000 residents, its own desalination infrastructure, a functional economy, and enough defensive capability to make forced removal expensive. The Corridor Council issued seventeen non-recognition declarations between 2168 and 2175. Freestone ignored all of them. The corponations tried economic blockade; Freestone traded with the other lake cities instead. They tried diplomatic pressure; Freestone's elected council responded with a one-sentence communique: 'We grew this from water. Come take it.' Nobody did.

Governance is direct democracy mediated by rotating councils. There are no corporations on Freestone — the founding charter prohibits sovereign corporate entities within its waters. The economy runs on a labor-credit system internally and trades in Q externally, primarily exporting seacrete construction expertise, desalinated water, aquaculture products, and a fierce independence that the shore-based population finds either inspiring or irritating depending on their tier. Freestone is not utopia. The housing is cramped, the infrastructure is perpetually strained, the mineral-accretion walls sometimes grow in directions nobody planned, and the democratic process is exactly as slow and frustrating as democracy always is. But nobody here answers to a board of directors, and that fact is worth more than comfort.
Properties.aliases: The First Reef, Freestone Republic, The Raft, Michigan Free City
Properties.demographics: Approximately 340,000 permanent residents. Ethnically and nationally diverse — the founding population was climate refugees, academics, and political dissidents from across the Great Lakes region and beyond. No tier system — Freestone rejected M88's citizenship framework entirely. Literacy rate: 97%. Average age skews young; people come to Freestone to build something.
Properties.economy: Internal: labor-credit system where contribution to city infrastructure, food production, or public services earns credits exchangeable for housing, goods, and leisure. External: Freestone trades seacrete engineering expertise, desalinated water, aquaculture products (lake perch, engineered kelp, freshwater crustaceans), and artisanal goods. Imports include electronics, medical equipment, and raw metal stock for new accretion frameworks. Annual external trade volume estimated at Φ8.2 billion.
Properties.power_structure: Direct democracy with rotating councils. The Reef Council — twelve members, term-limited to two years, selected by sortition — handles day-to-day governance. Major decisions go to general assembly vote. No corporate entities permitted. The military defense cooperative, the Breakwater, operates under civilian oversight and cannot initiate offensive action without assembly approval.
Properties.dangers: Storm damage — Lake Michigan storms can be brutal, and seacrete structures, while strong, are not invulnerable; Cormorant Naval Systems patrols — Freestone exists in a legal grey zone and Cormorant occasionally tests boundaries; Infrastructure strain — 340,000 people on a structure that grows slowly; capacity is always being chased; Political tension with M88 — the Corridor Council has never formally recognized Freestone's sovereignty; Internal democratic gridlock — direct democracy means every major decision is a fight
Properties.opportunities: Seacrete construction expertise — Freestone's engineers are the best in the world at mineral accretion building; A genuine alternative to corporate life — Freestone proves it's possible to live outside the tier system; Trade connections with all seven lake cities and several shore communities; The Breakwater's intelligence network — they know what moves on the lake
Properties.story_hooks: Freestone's Reef Council offers Kyle asylum — a life outside the tier system, if he can get there and if he's willing to leave everything on shore behind; A Cormorant Naval Systems operation targets Freestone's water supply infrastructure. The city needs someone shore-side to disrupt the operation before it launches.; Freestone's founding charter is being challenged from within — a faction argues that prohibiting corporate entities is holding the city back. The debate threatens to split the republic.
Properties.sights: Mineral-accretion architecture — walls and archways grown from the lake itself, rough-textured, organic, faintly luminescent where phosphorescent algae has colonized the surfaces; Solar arrays and wave-energy converters ringing the city's outer platforms like a mechanical reef; Hydroponic farms in transparent-roofed growing halls, green against the grey lake water; Fishing boats and trade vessels docked along the organic harbor formations — coral-like piers that grew into their current shape; The Anchor Stone — the original wire-mesh framework, now encrusted in decades of mineral growth, preserved as a monument at the city's center
Properties.sounds: Water — everywhere, always. The lap of waves against accreted walls, the rush through channel passages, the drip in lower-level corridors; The low electrical hum of the accretion current — the sound of the city growing; Market noise from the harbor platforms — trade in four languages plus the lakeside pidgin; Wind through the upper-level structures, which are more porous than planned and sing in storms
Properties.smells: Clean lake water — Freestone sits far enough from shore that the toxicity is manageable; Mineral deposits — a faintly chalky, calcium-rich scent that clings to everything; Hydroponic growth medium and fresh produce — the smell of food that wasn't synthesized; Salt-free brine from the desalination returns
Properties.feel: Alive. Freestone feels alive in a way that Meridian's steel-and-glass corridors do not. The walls are textured, irregular, warm to the touch where the accretion current runs. The city shifts subtly with the lake's movement. Nothing is straight, nothing is polished, nothing was designed in a boardroom. It feels handmade — because it was, molecule by molecule, pulled from the water by people who decided to build something that belonged to them. It also feels precarious. The lake is not gentle, and Freestone is a human settlement balanced on a reef that humans tricked into existence. The precariousness is part of the identity.

Properties.description:
The Vagrant is a city that refuses to stay put. A mobile seacrete-and-steel platform approximately 800 meters long and 400 meters wide, the Vagrant moves between the Great Lakes via the canal and lock systems that connect them — the Welland Canal between Erie and Ontario, the Soo Locks between Huron and Superior, the Straits of Mackinac between Huron and Michigan, and the Chicago Sanitary Canal connecting Michigan to the Mississippi watershed (though the Vagrant has only used this route twice, both times under circumstances its captain describes as 'interesting'). It is, depending on your perspective, a nomadic free city, a floating trade bazaar, a diplomatic headache, or the most creative interpretation of maritime law since someone first nailed a flag to a boat.

The Vagrant started as a conventional barge platform — a decommissioned Great Lakes ore carrier called the SS Edmund Reborn (the name was deliberate and nobody aboard apologizes for it) — purchased in 2176 by a collective of traders, smugglers, and maritime engineers who wanted access to every lake city without belonging to any of them. Over two decades, the original hull has been expanded, reinforced, and encrusted with seacrete growth that the collective encourages along the waterline and hull, creating an organic armor layer that makes the Vagrant look like a ship that a reef is slowly eating. Which is accurate. The seacrete accretion is continuous — every lake the Vagrant visits adds minerals to its hull in different chemical signatures, and marine geologists can read the Vagrant's travel history in cross-sections of its encrustation the way dendrochronologists read tree rings.

The Vagrant's legal status is its masterpiece. Because it moves between lakes, it is simultaneously in and out of every jurisdiction. When it's on Lake Michigan, it's outside M88's territorial waters. When it's on Erie, Cormorant Naval Systems classifies it as a 'transient vessel.' When it's on Ontario, the remnant Canadian government lists it as an 'unincorporated maritime entity.' The Vagrant's captain — elected by the resident population every three years, currently a former Cormorant Naval Systems deserter named Idris Achebe — maintains that the Vagrant is a sovereign vessel under maritime common law and that its residents are citizens of the Vagrant and nowhere else. Every legal authority on the Great Lakes has a different opinion about this claim's validity. None of them can agree on whose jurisdiction it falls under, which is exactly the point.

The Vagrant serves as a mobile marketplace, connecting the lake cities' economies in ways that fixed trade routes cannot. It carries goods, passengers, mail, and information between all seven settlements, plus shore communities that the corponations would prefer remained unconnected. It is the circulatory system of the free lake city network — the moving platform that turns isolated settlements into a connected civilization. Population: 12,000 permanent residents, plus a transient population of traders, passengers, and stowaways that varies between 3,000 and 8,000 depending on the season and which lake the Vagrant is currently on.
Properties.aliases: The Wanderer, The Moving City, Nomad Platform, That Damn Barge
Properties.demographics: 12,000 permanent residents, plus 3,000-8,000 transient population. Permanent residents are a self-selected community of traders, mechanics, sailors, and people who cannot or will not stay in one place. Demographically diverse — the Vagrant draws from every lake city and every shore community. Children born aboard are 'wave-born' — citizens of the Vagrant from birth, which means citizens of nowhere that any shore-based authority recognizes.
Properties.economy: Trade arbitrage — buying where goods are cheap and selling where they're expensive, which is the oldest economic model and still the most effective. The Vagrant's mobility gives it access to every market on the Great Lakes, and its cargo holds are a rotating inventory of whatever the lake cities need from each other. Annual trade volume: approximately Φ5.7 billion, most of it in physical goods that can't be transmitted digitally. The Vagrant charges transit fees, docking fees, and a percentage on all transactions conducted aboard. Captain Achebe calls this 'the motion tax.' The residents call it rent.
Properties.power_structure: The Captain — elected every three years by permanent residents — holds executive authority over navigation, defense, and external relations. A Ship's Council of eight elected members manages internal affairs, trade regulation, and dispute resolution. The Vagrant's security force, the Hull Watch, is a volunteer militia of 600 armed residents trained in shipboard combat and canal defense. Governance is pragmatic: the Captain decides where the ship goes, the Council decides what happens aboard, and the residents decide both by vote when they disagree strongly enough.
Properties.dangers: Canal transit — the Vagrant is large enough that lock passage is a complex, vulnerable operation. Ambush during canal transit is the city's nightmare scenario.; Jurisdictional hostility — every authority on the Great Lakes has a reason to impound the Vagrant. None can agree on who has the right to, which is protection, but it's not permanent.; Mechanical failure — the Vagrant is a twenty-five-year-old converted ore carrier. Things break.; Smuggling — the Vagrant's cargo holds contain legitimate trade and things that are very much not. The line between the two is the Captain's judgment call.; Weather — a mobile platform cannot anchor and hunker like a fixed city. The Vagrant must navigate storms, not endure them.
Properties.opportunities: Access to every lake city market — the Vagrant is the only entity that trades with all seven settlements; Information flow — the Vagrant carries news, intelligence, and rumors between isolated communities; Jurisdictional immunity — the Vagrant's legal ambiguity protects people and goods that need protecting; The Captain's network — Idris Achebe knows everyone on the Great Lakes, and everyone knows him. His introductions open doors.
Properties.story_hooks: The Vagrant is transiting the Welland Canal when Cormorant Naval Systems attempts to board, citing a new sovereignty enforcement order. Captain Achebe needs someone on shore to challenge the order's legality before the Hull Watch has to fight.; A sealed cargo container loaded at Tidebreak turns out to contain something alive. The Vagrant is mid-lake with no port for 200 kilometers, and the container is making sounds.; Kyle needs to get from Meridian 88 to a lake city without any corponation knowing. The Vagrant is his only option — but passage requires a favor that the Captain will collect at the worst possible time.
Properties.sights: A massive barge-platform encrusted in multi-colored seacrete layers — each lake's mineral signature visible in the hull like geological strata; Market stalls lining the main deck, their goods changing completely depending on which lake the Vagrant is currently transiting; The navigation tower — the original Edmund Reborn's bridge, now elevated on seacrete-grown pylons, flying the Vagrant's flag (a compass rose on black); Docking clamps and gangway systems designed to interface with every lake city's unique harbor architecture; The wake — the Vagrant displaces enough water that its passage is visible from shore, a moving V-shape that announces its arrival hours before docking
Properties.sounds: Engines — the Vagrant runs on a hybrid system of converted diesel, wave energy, and a single Charnel Propulsion plasma-electric drive (acquired through channels the captain declines to discuss); Trade — the constant negotiation of a floating bazaar, in every language spoken on the Great Lakes; The hull groaning as seacrete layers shift with temperature changes between lakes — the Vagrant complains audibly about weather; Lock mechanisms when transiting canals — the grinding, rushing, mechanical symphony of water levels changing
Properties.smells: Every lake simultaneously — the Vagrant carries the mineral signatures of all five Great Lakes in its seacrete layers, and they off-gas differently in different temperatures; Market goods — whatever's being traded this week, from Shallowgrave algae compounds to Deepwell ore samples to Tidebreak artwork; Engine exhaust from the hybrid drive system — cleaner than diesel, dirtier than plasma, distinctively Vagrant; The particular smell of a ship that has been lived on continuously for twenty-five years and has developed its own microbiome
Properties.feel: Freedom as a vehicle. The Vagrant feels like what it is — a city that decided the best way to avoid being controlled was to never stop moving. There's an energy aboard that's different from any fixed settlement: the transience, the constant change of scenery and trading partners, the knowledge that tomorrow you'll be on a different lake surrounded by different water. It's exciting and unstable in equal measure. The permanent residents have a particular looseness — people who've chosen motion over roots, who define home as a heading rather than a location. The Vagrant doesn't belong anywhere. That's the whole idea.

Properties.description:
Before the incorporation, Dunning was known for two things: being far from everything, and the former state mental hospital that had been converted into a forest preserve. The hospital closed in 1970. The ghosts didn't. When the corps carved up the city, Dunning's remote northwest location and its unsettling history made it unattractive for development. Axiom Environmental Services acquired the forest preserve land for carbon credit accounting purposes — trees on paper, value on balance sheets — and the residential blocks around it were left ungoverned. What happened next was either a miracle or a horror, depending on your relationship with the natural world.

The forest grew back. Not the manicured, corporate-approved green space of the Core. Real forest. Unmanaged, unfiltered, fed by decades of Chicago's buried topsoil and whatever the old hospital had put into the ground. The trees in Dunning Preserve are wrong in ways that botanists from the Core's research divisions have tried and failed to categorize. They grow too fast. Their root systems interface with buried infrastructure in ways that suggest intentionality. In Year 22, a survey team found fungal networks connecting the preserve's trees to decommissioned fiber optic cables, creating what one researcher described as 'a biological internet running on mycelium and dead copper' before her report was classified and she was reassigned to atmospheric monitoring on the lakefront.

The people who live in and around the Preserve have adapted. The old residential blocks on the perimeter house a community of roughly 12,000 who have developed a symbiotic relationship with the forest that corporate science does not have a framework to explain. They call themselves the Wardens, and their knowledge of the Preserve's ecology is practical, generational, and deliberately undigitized — nothing written down, nothing stored on any network, everything taught person to person. They harvest the forest's pharmaceutical products — compounds that no lab has synthesized, painkillers and nootropics that grow on bark and in root systems — and trade them through the Souk and the Circuit. The Preserve is Dunning's economy, its pharmacy, its religion, and its weapon.

The old hospital's foundations are still down there, under the roots. The Wardens say the forest grew from it. They say this without metaphor.
Properties.aliases: Dunning, The Asylum Grounds, The Preserve, The Warded Forest
Properties.demographics: Approximately 12,000 Wardens and affiliated residents on the forest perimeter. Untier-ed by choice — the community rejected the tier system in Year 6 and has maintained autonomy through the Preserve's pharmaceutical value and its genuine inaccessibility. Ethnically diverse but culturally unified around the Warden tradition.
Properties.dangers: The forest itself — navigation without a Warden guide is genuinely dangerous; Pharmaceutical compounds that are beneficial in correct doses and lethal in incorrect ones; The root network — Wardens claim it can detect intruders, and evidence supports this; Corporate extraction attempts — Axiom has sent teams into the Preserve before, and not all returned; The old hospital foundations — structurally unstable and psychologically disturbing; Getting lost — GPS does not function reliably under the canopy, and the paths change
Properties.opportunities: Pharmaceutical compounds unavailable anywhere else — the Preserve's primary trade goods; Warden knowledge of biological systems that corporate science hasn't cracked; Complete surveillance invisibility under the canopy; The hospital foundations may contain pre-collapse records sealed when the institution closed; Alliance with the Wardens provides access to the most defensible position in the northwest districts
Properties.story_hooks: Axiom Environmental Services has discovered the mycelium-fiber optic network and wants to weaponize it — the Wardens need help stopping an extraction team; A pharmaceutical compound from the Preserve is the only treatment for a condition affecting someone Kyle cares about, and the Wardens don't trade with strangers; The hospital foundations contain patient records from before the closure — records that include the names of people who became very powerful during the incorporation
Properties.sights: Canopy so dense it blocks the Meridian haze — actual sky visible in gaps between branches; Trees growing through and around pre-collapse structures, absorbing brick and steel into living wood; Bioluminescent fungi along forest paths that pulse in patterns the Wardens can read like signage; The hospital foundations visible in places — concrete and tile emerging from root systems like bones from skin; Warden settlements built into the canopy and forest edge, structures that look grown rather than constructed
Properties.sounds: Wind through real leaves — a sound so rare in Meridian 88 that visitors sometimes cry; Bird and insect life that exists nowhere else in the Corridor — an ecosystem in a bottle; The forest's own sounds — creaking, settling, the deep subsonic hum of root systems moving; Silence that is actually silence, not the corporate simulation of it; Warden communication — subtle percussive signals against tree trunks that carry through the root network
Properties.smells: Earth. Real, living soil — the single rarest smell in Meridian 88; The pharmaceutical compounds — sweet, resinous, faintly metallic, growing on bark and fungus; Decay and growth simultaneously — the forest recycling itself in real time; Rain captured by canopy, released slowly — petrichor that lasts for hours
Properties.feel: Sacred. Whether you believe in anything or not, the Preserve triggers something primal — the recognition that this is older than the city, older than the corps, older than the tier system. It feels like standing in the one place that the incorporation couldn't reach. The Wardens say the forest is watching. Spending any time under the canopy, you start to believe them.

Properties.description:
Montclare barely existed before the incorporation. A small, quiet, far-northwest neighborhood of single-family homes — the kind of place that didn't make the news because nothing happened there. After the incorporation, nothing continued to happen, and this became its defining characteristic. Montclare Quiet is the single least surveilled, least noticed, least anything district in Meridian 88. Corporate cartography systems list it as 'residential — low priority.' The population registers are out of date by at least a decade. Axiom Security's coverage map shows a gap here that nobody has been assigned to fill, because filling it would require acknowledging it exists, and acknowledging it exists would require explaining why it was ignored, and explaining requires meetings.

The houses are still standing. That's the strange part. In a city where every square meter of space has been fought over, developed, flooded, or burned, the bungalows of Montclare Quiet simply persist. They've been modified — solar arrays on roofs, water recyclers in basements, communication blackout mesh over windows — but they're recognizably houses, recognizably suburban, recognizably the kind of place where someone once parked a station wagon and argued with their spouse about the lawn. The current residents maintain this appearance with deliberate precision, because looking boring is Montclare Quiet's primary defense mechanism.

What actually happens behind those bungalow walls is another matter entirely. Montclare Quiet is the northwest corridor's premier safe house district. Every faction, fixer, and freelance operator in the outer districts knows that if you need a place to hold someone, hide someone, store something, or plan something, Montclare has a house for rent and a community that will not ask a single question. The residents aren't criminals. They're simply people who discovered that invisibility is the most valuable commodity in a surveillance economy, and they are very good at selling it. The community operates on a single rule: nothing that happens here draws attention. Violate that rule, and you don't get a second warning. You get an address that no longer exists.

There are no notable landmarks in Montclare Quiet. That is the point.
Properties.aliases: Montclare, The Quiet, The Blank Spot, Dead Channel
Properties.demographics: Population unknown, estimated at 5,000-8,000. Tier status mixed and deliberately obscured. The community's demographic profile is, by design, the least documented in Meridian 88. Census attempts return incomplete data. The residents prefer it this way.
Properties.dangers: Drawing attention — the community enforces its invisibility with absolute commitment; Unknowingly renting a safe house adjacent to a faction that considers you an enemy; The community's rules are unwritten and violations are handled without appeal; Not knowing the protocols — Montclare looks like an ordinary neighborhood, and treating it as one is a mistake; The things stored in those basements — proximity to other people's problems
Properties.opportunities: Safe houses of unparalleled quality — invisible to surveillance, maintained to residential standards; A communications dead zone useful for meetings that cannot be recorded; Community contacts who know how to make people, objects, and information disappear; Staging ground for operations in the northwest corridor; Rest — Montclare is one of the only places in the outer districts where you can sleep without listening
Properties.story_hooks: Kyle needs a safe house for a client extraction, and the Montclare contact gives him a house next door to an operation run by people who would kill him on sight; Someone has violated the attention rule — a firefight in a Montclare bungalow, and the community's response mechanism reveals how organized they actually are; The reason Montclare stays off corporate maps isn't community effort alone — someone inside Axiom's cartography division is protecting it, and they want payment
Properties.sights: Bungalows that look exactly like bungalows should — maintained, unremarkable, identical in their ordinariness; Empty streets with working streetlights — a surreal luxury in the outer districts; Communication blackout mesh visible on windows if you know what to look for; The occasional delivery van that arrives at odd hours and leaves lighter than it came; No corporate signage. No advertisements. No branding. Nothing to look at.
Properties.sounds: Quiet. Genuine, deliberate, maintained quiet.; The hum of signal-dampening equipment running in basements — audible only to augmented hearing; Doors closing. Carefully, without slamming.; The absence of drone traffic — Montclare's airspace is somehow always deprioritized in the routing algorithms
Properties.smells: Cut grass — someone maintains the lawns, and the smell is aggressively normal; Nothing distinctive. Nothing memorable. Nothing that would make you describe this place to someone.; Cleaning products — the houses are maintained with the kind of thoroughness that suggests evidence management
Properties.feel: Uncanny in the opposite direction from the Core. Where the Core is too perfect, Montclare Quiet is too normal. It feels like a neighborhood that has been held in amber since before the collapse — preserved not by corporate investment but by collective will. Standing on a Montclare street at night, under working streetlights, with the sound of nothing at all, you experience a specific vertigo: the sense that the world ended everywhere except here, and the people who live here would prefer you didn't mention it.

Properties.description: A sprawling industrial neighborhood built atop the skeletal remains of a 20th-century garment district, The Laceworks has been repurposed layer by layer into one of Meridian 88's most densely inhabited residential warrens. Converted textile factories now house thousands of mid-to-low income residents in stacked micro-apartments, their facades draped in a permanent tangle of laundry lines, fiber-optic cables, and handmade signage that gives the district its name. The original brick architecture survives beneath decades of patchwork renovation, visible in archways and loading docks now serving as storefronts, shrines, and impromptu community spaces.
Properties.aliases: The Lace, Threadtown, The Old Stitching
Properties.demographics: Predominantly first- and second-generation migrant workers, service-sector laborers, and aging legacy residents who survived the district's earlier incarnations. A significant population of undocumented individuals with no official city registration. Mixed ages, heavily family-oriented.
Properties.economy: Informal micro-economies dominate: street food, repair work, unlicensed clinics, textile recycling, and small-batch fabrication. Remittance transfers to outside the corridor are a major financial artery. Some residents work shifts in the adjacent corporate manufacturing zones but spend their wages locally.
Properties.power_structure: No single entity controls The Laceworks. Block-level councils negotiate resource allocation and settle disputes. The Needle — a loose confederation of older residents and community organizers — holds informal authority, but enforcement depends on persuasion and reputation. Corporate security rarely enters without cause, which is considered a fragile blessing.
Properties.dangers: Structural failures in poorly maintained converted buildings; Predatory lenders and organ-debt collectors operating openly; Occasional violent incursions by fringe gangs from bordering districts; City utilities are unreliable — power brownouts and water rationing are cyclical; Unlicensed chip clinics with substandard sterilization practices
Properties.opportunities: Access to a dense, tight-knit information network — locals know everything about their neighbors; Black-market fabrication services that ask no questions; Recruitment of skilled but desperate individuals with reason to stay off-grid; The Needle's community archives contain decades of unofficial city history; Safe houses available through trust-based networks for those who earn goodwill
Properties.story_hooks: A community elder has gone missing days before she was scheduled to testify before a city zoning tribunal about corporate encroachment; A series of fires in the district follow an unusual pattern — always near buildings whose residents recently refused buyout offers; A child found wandering the Laceworks speaks no known language and carries a neural implant of unidentified manufacture; The pirate radio signal that has broadcast for twenty years suddenly begins transmitting encrypted data packets no one can decode; A new lender has arrived offering impossibly favorable terms — and residents who accept begin behaving differently within weeks
Properties.sights: Cascading laundry lines strung between buildings like low-tech prayer flags; Neon signs in a dozen languages advertising tailors, noodle shops, and black-market chip clinics; Exposed brick faces tagged with hyperlocal gang markers and community murals; Residents leaning from narrow windows watching the street below; Repair drones weaving between fire escapes
Properties.sounds: Overlapping music from competing storefronts; Children shouting in Tagalog, Yoruba, and Mandarin; The distant mechanical thrum of legacy HVAC systems; Street vendors hawking printed food and counterfeit skins; Occasional bursts of feedback from illicit pirate radio broadcasts
Properties.smells: Frying oil and synthetic spices; Damp concrete and mildew from overcrowded plumbing; Cheap solvent from nearby repair shops; Incense burning at street-level shrines; Ozone from overloaded electrical conduits
Properties.feel: Claustrophobic and alive, a pressure-cooker community where everyone knows everyone and strangers are noted immediately. There is warmth here, but also exhaustion — people working too hard for too little, holding onto dignity through ritual and solidarity.

Properties.description:
Edison Grid is the neighborhood that polices itself and doesn't apologize for it. The far northwest corner of Meridian 88, Edison Park was always Chicago's most suburban enclave — tidy bungalows, neat lawns, families where both parents worked for the city. Police officers, firefighters, paramedics, public works employees. When the corporations privatized everything, Edison Park's residents found themselves in a unique position: they were the people who'd kept the old city running, and the new city needed their skills even if it didn't want their independence. Axiom Security Solutions absorbed the police force. Corporate emergency services absorbed the fire department. The old public servants became corporate contractors with better salaries and fewer rights. But they kept living in Edison Park, kept raising their families on the same blocks, and kept the one thing the corps couldn't privatize: the institutional knowledge of how a city actually works, passed down through families like a genetic trait.

The Grid earned its name from the power infrastructure. When Meridian 88's energy grid was being built, Edison Park's residents — many of them electrical workers and engineers by trade — negotiated a deal that no other neighborhood managed: a dedicated power substation feeding the district directly, bypassing the corporate metering system. It was supposed to be temporary. That was thirty years ago. The Grid still has the most reliable electricity in Meridian's outlying districts, and the substation has been quietly expanded, modified, and hardened by residents who understand power systems the way other people understand cooking. The electricity is technically corporate property. The Grid's position is that they built the system, they maintain the system, and anyone who wants to renegotiate can discuss it with the electricians' union, which is also the neighborhood militia.

The culture of Edison Grid is cop culture — for better and worse. The streets are orderly. Crime is low. Community standards are enforced by social pressure and, when necessary, by retired Axiom Security contractors who still have their training and most of their augments. There's a code: you look out for your neighbors, you maintain your property, you don't bring trouble home. It's effective and stifling in equal measure. The Grid's children grow up safe and grow up to leave, because safety and predictability are not the same as freedom. The ones who stay become cops or electricians or both, and the cycle continues.

The Grid's relationship with Axiom Security is the district's defining tension. Many residents work for the corporation. Many residents distrust the corporation. These are often the same people. An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer follows corporate orders during shift and comes home to a neighborhood that views corporate authority with the skeptical eye of people who remember when authority was public and accountable. This cognitive dissonance produces a population that is simultaneously Axiom's most competent workforce and its most quietly resistant. The Grid doesn't rebel. It doesn't protest. It maintains its power substation, trains its children in skills the corporation needs, and waits — with the patience of people who understand infrastructure — for the system to need them more than they need it.
Properties.aliases: Edison Park, The Grid, Blue Line's End, Coptown
Properties.demographics: Approximately 10,000 residents, predominantly Tier 2 and Tier 3. Multigenerational families with backgrounds in public safety, infrastructure maintenance, and emergency services. Racially and ethnically mixed but culturally uniform — the shared identity is occupational, not ethnic. The most stable population in Meridian's northwest.
Properties.economy: Skilled labor export — Edison Grid's residents work throughout Meridian's infrastructure and security sectors. The power substation generates surplus electricity that's traded to neighboring districts. Small-scale commercial services support the residential population. The economy is wages, not entrepreneurship.
Properties.power_structure: The Grid Council — elected from resident families, heavily weighted toward senior infrastructure and security workers. The electricians' union holds veto power over energy-related decisions. Axiom has no direct governance role but exercises influence through the employment relationship with most working-age residents.
Properties.dangers: Social conformity enforcement — deviance from community standards is punished by isolation and ostracism; The Axiom loyalty question — residents who are seen as too corporate or too resistant to corporate authority face suspicion from both sides; Power substation dependency — the Grid's independence is built on infrastructure that could be targeted; Insularity — outsiders are tolerated but not trusted, and the Grid's closed culture limits information exchange; The militia's competence — Edison Grid's residents are trained, equipped, and organized enough to be dangerous if the wrong situation triggers a response
Properties.opportunities: Reliable power — the Grid's electricity supply is a strategic resource in a city of rolling blackouts; Skilled labor connections — the Grid's workers have access to every level of Meridian's infrastructure; Institutional knowledge — these families know how the city works in ways that blueprints don't capture; Security expertise — retired Axiom personnel with training and augments, available for contract work if the cause is right; The Blue Line terminal — the last transit connection to the northwestern suburbs, a smuggling route that the Grid quietly tolerates
Properties.story_hooks: An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer discovers that the corporation is planning to bypass the neighborhood's power substation — routing the Grid into the metered system. The Grid Council prepares for a confrontation that could turn the district's quiet resistance into open conflict.; Kyle needs information that only an active Axiom Security officer can access. The officer is Edison Grid — loyal to the community first, the corporation second. The price of the information is a favor that puts Kyle on the wrong side of people he'd rather not cross.; A Grid family's child returns from a stint in the Shelf with augments, ideas, and associations that violate everything the community stands for. The family is torn between protecting their own and maintaining the social contract that keeps the Grid functioning.
Properties.sights: Neat residential blocks — bungalows maintained to standards that would have been normal in the old city and are remarkable now; The power substation at the district's center, expanded and reinforced over decades, humming with dedicated electricity; Retired security contractors walking patrol routes out of habit, augmented eyes scanning without urgency; Family gardens in every yard — practical vegetables, not decorative landscaping; The Blue Line terminal at the district's edge — the last stop, literally and figuratively, before the suburban wastelands begin; Memorial plaques on homes — names of officers and firefighters who died in service, maintained by families who remember
Properties.sounds: The hum of the power substation — louder than you'd expect, a low throb that residents stop hearing after a week; Children playing in actual yards — one of the few districts where outdoor play space exists; Scanner chatter from homes where off-duty security personnel keep a radio on — old habit, professional compulsion; The Blue Line train arriving and departing — a schedule so reliable it functions as a neighborhood clock; Quiet — but a different quiet than the Palisade. This is the quiet of a place where trouble knows better than to make noise.
Properties.smells: Grilled food from backyard cookouts — the Grid maintains a cookout culture that is part social tradition and part defiant normalcy; Ozone from the power substation, strongest in humid weather; Cut grass — real grass, maintained by hand, a point of pride; Coffee from kitchens in the morning — the Grid wakes up early because shift work starts early
Properties.feel: Controlled. Edison Grid feels like a place where everything works because someone made it work and continues to make it work through daily effort and communal will. It's reassuring and claustrophobic — the safety is real, the order is real, and the social pressure to conform is equally real. The Grid is what a neighborhood looks like when the people who run the city's systems build a place for themselves. It's functional. It's dependable. It's not a place that welcomes questions about whether there might be a better way.

Properties.description:
Norwood Quiet is the neighborhood that decided the best response to the end of the world was to pretend it hadn't happened. The old Norwood Park — Chicago's historic bungalow district, with its arts-and-crafts homes and tree-lined streets — has achieved something that shouldn't be possible in Meridian 88: it looks almost exactly the same as it did before the Corporate Reconstruction. The bungalows are still standing. The trees are still growing, maintained by a community arborist program that's been running for forty years. The streets are still quiet. And the residents — predominantly elderly, predominantly long-tenured, predominantly determined — maintain their neighborhood with the kind of stubborn attention to detail that makes reality bend around willpower.

The trick is simple and brilliant: Norwood Quiet is boring. Strategically, intentionally, aggressively boring. There's nothing here for the corporations to want. No commercial potential, no strategic infrastructure, no exploitable population. The residential stock is pre-collapse bungalows that are historically protected under a designation the old city government issued before it ceased to exist — a designation that Axiom has never formally recognized but has also never formally challenged, because challenging it would require acknowledging that pre-corporate law has standing, which opens legal doors that Axiom's attorneys would rather keep sealed. So the bungalows persist, legally ambiguous and physically immaculate, a quiet act of civil disobedience expressed through maintained gutters and painted trim.

Beneath the suburban surface, Norwood Quiet serves a function that its residents would never publicly acknowledge: it's a safe house district. The combination of minimal surveillance, boring optics, and a community that minds its own business while maintaining total awareness of who enters and leaves makes the Quiet an ideal location for people who need to disappear temporarily. Not criminals — or not exclusively criminals. Whistleblowers, corporate defectors, witnesses under threat, families fleeing Iron Lotus debts. They arrive quietly, stay in guest rooms that several bungalow owners maintain for exactly this purpose, and leave when it's safe. No records. No questions. The neighborhood watch knows who belongs and who's visiting. They don't share that information with anyone outside the community.

The Quiet's greatest vulnerability is time. The population is old and getting older. The bungalows are maintained but cannot be maintained forever. The historic protection designation exists in a legal limbo that could be resolved at any moment by a corporate attorney with a motive. The trees, real trees in real soil, are irreplaceable if they die. Norwood Quiet is a time capsule with a slowly expiring seal, and its residents know it. They maintain the houses, tend the trees, and shelter the people who need sheltering, because that's what they've always done. When the last bungalow finally falls, they want it to fall clean.
Properties.aliases: Norwood Park, The Quiet, Bungalow Belt, The Sleep
Properties.demographics: Approximately 6,000 residents, the majority over sixty. Long-tenured families, many in the same bungalows for three generations. Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2. The youngest demographic in the district is the rotating population of temporary residents in the safe-house rooms, who skew younger and more desperate.
Properties.economy: Minimal — residential maintenance, small-scale gardening, and the invisible safe-house economy. The Quiet's residents are mostly retired or working in neighboring districts. The community is self-sustaining but not productive in any way that registers on economic metrics, which is part of the strategy.
Properties.power_structure: The Norwood Homeowners Association — the oldest continuously operating civic organization in Meridian's northwest. Authority is exercised through consensus, social norms, and the quiet understanding that the community's survival depends on collective discipline. No one person is in charge. Everyone is in charge of their own house.
Properties.dangers: Legal challenge to the historic protection designation — if Axiom decides the bungalows are worth more as rubble, the legal defense is thin; Aging infrastructure — the bungalows and community systems need maintenance that gets harder every year; Safe-house discovery — if corporate intelligence identifies the Quiet's shelter function, the consequences would be severe; Demographic collapse — the community is aging out with insufficient replacement, and the bungalows may outlast their owners; Complacency — the Quiet's strategy of being boring only works as long as no one decides boring is interesting
Properties.opportunities: Disappearance — the Quiet's safe-house network is one of the most discreet in Meridian; Real nature — trees, soil, birdsong, seasonal change. Therapeutic for people who've forgotten what the outdoors used to feel like; Historical knowledge — the Quiet's elderly residents remember the old city and maintain oral histories that have been lost elsewhere; Social camouflage — no one looks for anything in Norwood Quiet, which makes it ideal for hiding things in plain sight; Community model — the Homeowners Association's governance structure is studied by people interested in alternatives to corporate control
Properties.story_hooks: A corporate defector with critical information about Axiom's plans for the northern districts is sheltered in the Quiet — but the corporation's search is getting closer, and the community must decide whether to protect one stranger at the risk of exposing the entire safe-house network; One of the Quiet's oldest residents dies, and the contents of her bungalow reveal a hidden archive of pre-corporate city records — including documents that prove Axiom's original incorporation was built on forged municipal approvals; Kyle needs a place to recover after a job goes wrong. The Quiet takes him in — but the community's rules require him to contribute, which means helping with the mundane maintenance that keeps the bungalows standing. It's the most human work he's done in years.
Properties.sights: Pre-collapse bungalows in maintained condition — painted, repaired, landscaped, impossible; Real trees lining real streets, their canopy creating shade that feels like a memory of the old city; Elderly residents on porches, watching the street with the calm attention of people who notice everything; No corporate signage — none. Not a single Axiom logo, holographic ad, or branded surface; Garden plots in every yard — flowers in front, vegetables in back, a pattern that hasn't changed in decades; The neighborhood watch — not visible as a patrol, but visible in the way every window has a line of sight to the street
Properties.sounds: Birdsong — real birds in real trees, a sound that most of Meridian has forgotten; Wind through leaves — actual rustling, not atmospheric simulation; The near-total absence of electronic noise — no drone hum, no holographic buzz, no ambient corporate audio; Lawnmowers — hand-powered, maintained like heirlooms, used on Saturday mornings as a communal ritual; Screen doors closing — the most domestic sound in Meridian, preserved here like an artifact
Properties.smells: Cut grass and garden soil — the authentic versions, not the engineered scents of the Palisade; Baked goods from kitchens — the Quiet's residents bake, and the smells carry on the quiet air; Old wood and paint — the bungalows have their own scent profile, preserved materials breathing in the sun; Seasonal change — Norwood Quiet is one of the few places in Meridian where you can smell autumn arriving
Properties.feel: Ghostly. Norwood Quiet feels like visiting a place that time forgot, or more accurately, a place that time remembers and the present has abandoned. The peace is genuine — this is a calm, safe, beautiful neighborhood. But there's an unreality to it, the sense that you've stepped out of Meridian and into a memory. The residents' determination to maintain normalcy is admirable and heartbreaking in equal measure, because normalcy is exactly what the world they live in is no longer capable of providing.

Properties.description:
Jefferson Switch is the place where Meridian's circulatory system comes to the surface. The old Jefferson Park was Chicago's northwest transportation hub — the intersection of the CTA Blue Line and the Metra commuter rail, a transit center that connected the city to its suburbs and the suburbs to the world. When the Corporate Reconstruction replaced public transit with the corporate MeriRail system, Jefferson Park's transit infrastructure was too extensive to rebuild and too useful to abandon. So it was absorbed, upgraded, and expanded into what is now Meridian 88's northwest interchange: Jefferson Switch, the point where maglev lines, legacy rail, freight logistics, and human traffic converge in a permanent state of organized chaos.

The Switch is not a neighborhood in any traditional sense. It's a machine — a transit machine with 40,000 people living inside it. The old residential blocks around the transit center have been consumed by the infrastructure, their buildings converted to maintenance bays, worker housing, logistics staging areas, and the peculiar commercial ecosystem that grows around any place where large numbers of people wait for things. The transit center itself has expanded vertically — six levels of platforms, concourses, and transfer halls, handling an estimated 200,000 passenger movements per day. Freight traffic moves through sub-levels that the public never sees, automated cargo pods delivering goods from the suburban production zones to Meridian's interior. The whole thing runs on a schedule that Axiom's logistics AI manages with a precision that borders on the beautiful, if you can appreciate the beauty of a system that treats human beings as throughput.

The Switch's population is defined by transit. Everyone here is going somewhere else — or they were, once, and then the transit center became their life. The permanent residents are transit workers, maintenance crews, logistics handlers, and the service workers who feed and house them. The transient population is everyone else: commuters, travelers, freight brokers, smugglers using the cargo sub-levels, and the untier-ed who discovered that a transit center with 200,000 daily users is the easiest place in Meridian to disappear into a crowd. The Switch has its own internal economy — platform-level food stalls, information brokers who sell schedule data and cargo manifests, mechanics who repair personal transit vehicles in alcoves between the maintenance bays. It's a city within a transit center within a city, and it never stops moving.

For Kyle, the Switch is infrastructure — a tool, not a destination. Every operator in Meridian knows the Switch's schedule, its blind spots, its maintenance windows. The cargo sub-levels are the northwest's primary smuggling route, used by everyone from Collective data runners to Iron Lotus arms dealers. The platform crowds provide cover for meetings, handoffs, and the kind of conversations that can't happen in quieter places. The Switch doesn't care who you are or what you're carrying. It only cares that you keep moving, because the next train is in four minutes and the platform needs to clear.
Properties.aliases: Jefferson Park, The Switch, Transit Central, The Junction
Properties.demographics: Approximately 40,000 permanent residents, predominantly transit workers and logistics handlers, Tier 1 and Tier 2. The transient population — 200,000 daily movements — is the most demographically diverse cross-section of Meridian, from Tier 5 executives in private transit pods to untier-ed migrants riding the cargo sub-levels without tickets.
Properties.economy: Transit operations, freight logistics, platform-level commerce, and the gray-market information and smuggling economy that piggybacks on the cargo infrastructure. Axiom's transit division is the primary employer. The informal economy runs on schedule knowledge, cargo manifest data, and access to the sub-levels.
Properties.power_structure: Axiom Transit Division manages the infrastructure directly. The Transit Workers Union — one of the few recognized labor organizations in Meridian — holds limited negotiating power through the threat of slowdowns. Platform-level commerce is self-governing. The cargo sub-levels are a jurisdiction gap — nominally Axiom territory, practically no-man's-land.
Properties.dangers: Getting caught in the cargo sub-levels without authorization — Axiom's automated security is lethal below platform level; Crowd crush during peak transit hours — the platforms are overcapacity and safety margins are theoretical; Pickpockets and data-skimmers working the crowds — the Switch is prime territory for petty predators; Schedule disruptions — when the system breaks down, 200,000 people are stranded in a space designed for movement, not habitation; Corporate surveillance — the Switch's security cameras are dense and the facial recognition is current-generation
Properties.opportunities: Smuggling routes through the cargo sub-levels — the northwest's primary gray-market logistics pipeline; Information — schedule data, cargo manifests, and passenger movement patterns are all tradeable commodities; Crowd anonymity — 200,000 daily faces means yours disappears into the noise; Transit connections — the Switch links northwest Meridian to everywhere else in the corridor; The Transit Workers Union — one of the few organizations that can pressure Axiom through labor action
Properties.story_hooks: A cargo pod arrives in the sub-levels with contents that don't match its manifest — something alive, something valuable, something that multiple parties are converging on the Switch to claim; The Transit Workers Union calls a slowdown that paralyzes northwest Meridian's logistics — behind the labor dispute is a demand that has nothing to do with wages and everything to do with something the workers found in the sub-levels during a maintenance shift; Kyle uses the Switch for a handoff that goes wrong when the recipient doesn't show. The package is time-sensitive, the platform cameras have his face, and the next train out is in four minutes.
Properties.sights: Six levels of transit platforms stacked vertically, maglev trains arriving and departing in synchronized precision; Holographic schedule displays in every sightline, updating in real-time with delays, reroutes, and security advisories; Platform-level food stalls and service kiosks squeezed into every available space between structural supports; The cargo sub-levels visible through grated floors — automated pods moving in silent, choreographed patterns below; Crowds — constant, dense, moving. The Switch never empties.; Transit workers in Axiom-branded uniforms maintaining equipment, changing shifts, eating at platform stalls between trains
Properties.sounds: Maglev arrival tones — a musical scale that plays through the station, each note corresponding to a different line; The subsonic rumble of cargo pods in the sub-levels, felt more than heard; PA announcements in three languages and machine code — schedule updates, security warnings, corporate wellness reminders; The white noise of 200,000 daily movements — footsteps, conversations, luggage, life; Train doors closing — a pneumatic hiss that happens every ninety seconds on the main platform
Properties.smells: Platform food — fried noodles, nutrient wraps, stimulant coffee, all competing for aromatic dominance; Ozone from the maglev systems, strongest on the upper platforms; Human density — the Switch smells like people, a lot of people, in a space that manages airflow but can't manage biology; Lubricant and metal from the maintenance bays, leaking into the concourse levels through inadequate sealing; Rain — the Switch's upper levels are partially open, and wet weather brings the smell of real air into the transit cocoon
Properties.feel: Kinetic. Jefferson Switch feels like standing inside a clock — every element in motion, every motion serving a purpose, every purpose serving a schedule. It's overwhelming for the first visit and invisible by the tenth. The Switch doesn't invite you to linger. It processes you, routes you, and sends you on your way. For the people who live here, home is the pause between transits — a meal eaten on a platform, a conversation held in a maintenance alcove, sleep taken in shifts in worker housing that vibrates with every passing train.

Properties.description:
Escanaba occupies the UP's southern shore, facing Lake Michigan across Little Bay de Noc, and its function is exactly what the name suggests: it is the gateway. The port handles the ore, timber, and manufactured goods that flow south from the UP's interior to the markets and mills of the lower Great Lakes. Kelpline Logistics operates the port facilities under a sovereignty charter, and the automated cargo handling systems move tonnage 24 hours a day through a facility that was built for ten times the human workforce it currently employs. The port is efficient, profitable, and nearly empty of people — the automation revolution hit Escanaba harder than anywhere else in the UP, replacing dock workers with systems that don't take breaks, don't form unions, and don't spend money in local bars.

The result is a city that processes enormous wealth and retains almost none of it. The ore comes down from Marquette and Iron Mountain. The timber comes down from the northern forests. The finished materials come from Copperhead's fabrication facilities. All of it passes through Escanaba's port, loaded onto lake barges bound for Meridian 88, The Lattice, and points south. The city takes its cut — port fees, maintenance contracts, fuel sales — but the cut is thin and getting thinner as automation reduces the human infrastructure required to move cargo. The residential population has been declining for two decades, and the downtown district has the particular emptiness of a place that was built for more people than currently inhabit it.

Escanaba's strategic value in the UP war lies in its position. Control the southern port and you control the UP's economic output. Michigan holds it. Wisconsin wants it. The Mackinac Bridge — 150 kilometers east — is the only other route south from the UP, and it's a chokepoint, not a port. Whoever holds Escanaba can starve the UP or feed it, which makes the city's small population disproportionately important and disproportionately nervous.
Properties.aliases: Escanaba MI, The Gate, South Port, UP's Back Door
Properties.demographics: Population 18,000, down from 35,000 two decades ago. The decline tracks automation adoption almost exactly. The remaining population is predominantly port support workers, Kelpline employees, and the businesses that serve them. Median age is rising. Young people leave for Iron Crown or the lower peninsula. The ones who stay have reasons.
Properties.economy: Port operations (Kelpline Logistics) and cargo transit. Escanaba is a throughput economy — value passes through without accumulating. The city's GDP per capita is technically high; the city's livability is technically declining. The automation dividend goes to Kelpline shareholders, not to Escanaba residents.
Properties.power_structure: Kelpline Logistics holds port sovereignty. Michigan municipal government holds residential jurisdiction. The practical power balance is determined by employment — Kelpline employs 40% of the remaining workforce directly, and another 30% indirectly. The mayor governs at Kelpline's convenience.
Properties.dangers: Economic obsolescence — automation is reducing the human workforce required, and the trend has no floor; Strategic vulnerability — the port is a high-value target in the UP war, and the population is too small to defend it; Kelpline workforce reductions — each round of automation eliminates jobs that don't come back; Wisconsin-aligned sabotage of port operations — disrupting southern shipping to weaken Michigan's economic position; The psychological toll of living in a shrinking city — Escanaba's mental health infrastructure is as understaffed as everything else
Properties.opportunities: Port access — Escanaba is the gateway to southern markets, and access has value; Automation systems expertise — the port's technology is state-of-the-art, and technicians who maintain it are employable everywhere; Strategic intelligence — shipping manifests from Escanaba reveal the UP's economic activity in real time; Real estate — the depopulation has made property cheap, which attracts certain kinds of operations that prefer low visibility
Properties.story_hooks: Kelpline Logistics is negotiating a 'security partnership' with Wisconsin that would effectively surrender the port without Michigan's consent; Automated cargo containers are being loaded with unmanifested materials at night — the port's own systems are being used to smuggle something south; A Wisconsin military force is staging 80 kilometers west, and the only thing between them and Escanaba is forest and a population too small to matter
