Properties.sights: Automated cargo cranes operating on the port — massive, precise, and eerily unmanned; Empty storefronts on Ludington Street — the downtown built for a population that left; Lake Michigan visible from everywhere — blue-grey and busy with cargo barge traffic; Kelpline Logistics sovereign territory markers along the waterfront — corporate authority over public shore; The ore trains arriving from the interior, loaded cars stretching to the horizon
Properties.sounds: Automated port operations — the whir and clank of machines handling cargo without human direction; Wind off Lake Michigan — steady, cold, and carrying the sound of barge traffic; The absence of crowds — Escanaba's streets are quiet in a way that feels like a warning; Ore trains arriving and departing — the rhythm of extraction moving through the city like a pulse
Properties.smells: Lake Michigan air — cleaner than Superior, warmer, carrying a different mineral profile; Iron ore dust from the transit operations — the UP's export made visible and breathable; Diesel and electric motor exhaust from the cargo handling systems
Properties.feel: A city that serves a function and wonders if the function will continue to need a city. Escanaba works, but it works the way a machine works — efficiently, impersonally, and without any particular attachment to the people who live alongside it. The emptiness is not desolate. It is procedural.

Properties.description:
The Mackinac Bridge spans 8 kilometers across the Straits of Mackinac, connecting Michigan's lower peninsula to the Upper Peninsula, and in 2200 it is the single most strategically contested piece of infrastructure in the state. The bridge was built in 1957 to unify Michigan's two halves. It now separates them. The UP's contested status — the war between Michigan and Wisconsin over territory and resources — has turned the bridge from a transportation link into a military chokepoint, a jurisdictional boundary, and the physical manifestation of a political crisis that nobody can resolve.

The bridge itself has been reinforced, widened, and enclosed against weather — the original open-deck design could not survive Superior storms with modern traffic loads. Ferrogate Transit operates the crossing under a dual charter from Michigan state authority and federal critical infrastructure designation. Six lanes of traffic — four automated cargo, two passenger — move across the straits in conditions that include 150 km/h winds, ice loading, and the occasional Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempt. The toll is the highest per-kilometer rate on any road in the GLM, justified by the crossing's irreplaceability: there is no alternative route between the peninsulas that doesn't involve a 500-kilometer detour through Wisconsin, which Michigan will not permit and Wisconsin will not facilitate.

The bridge's southern approach is controlled by a Ferrogate waystation complex. The northern approach is controlled by a joint Michigan-federal military installation that serves as the de facto entry checkpoint for the contested UP. Every vehicle, every passenger, and every cargo container crossing north is scanned, assessed, and logged by systems that report to Michigan state intelligence, federal military command, and Ferrogate's traffic management simultaneously. The bridge is the UP's umbilical cord to the lower peninsula — the supply line, the communication link, and the escape route. Cutting it would isolate 300,000 people in contested territory with no reliable alternative connection. Both sides of the UP war understand this. The bridge is defended like what it is: the only thing holding Michigan together.
Properties.aliases: The Bridge, Mighty Mac, The Crossing, Peninsula Gate
Properties.demographics: No permanent residential population on the bridge itself. The waystation complexes at each approach house approximately 2,000 personnel — Ferrogate operators, military staff, security contractors, and the service workers who support them. Transient crossing population averages 15,000 per day, with significant variation based on UP conditions, weather, and the current state of the territorial dispute.
Properties.economy: Toll revenue (Ferrogate Transit) and military logistics. The bridge generates approximately 850 million Q annually in toll revenue, making it one of the most profitable single pieces of infrastructure in the GLM. The military installation at the northern approach is federally funded. The economics are simple: the bridge is irreplaceable, so it charges accordingly.
Properties.power_structure: Ferrogate Transit operating charter, Michigan state authority, and federal military designation — three jurisdictions layered on 8 kilometers of bridge deck. Ferrogate handles traffic and maintenance. Michigan handles civil authority. The military handles security. Conflicts between the three are resolved by whoever has the most immediate operational necessity, which is usually the military.
Properties.dangers: Weather — Straits storms can close the bridge, isolating the UP from its supply line; Structural vulnerability — the bridge is reinforced but irreplaceable, and its destruction would be catastrophic for 300,000 UP residents; Military escalation — the northern checkpoint's rules of engagement are classified, and crossing incidents are adjudicated by military tribunal; Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempts — the bridge has been targeted multiple times, and the attempts are growing more sophisticated; Toll economics as population control — Ferrogate's pricing determines who can afford to cross, which determines who can access the UP
Properties.opportunities: Bridge crossing intelligence — the checkpoint data reveals everything about UP supply, personnel movement, and military readiness; Ferrogate transit contracts — the bridge needs maintenance, and the contracts are valuable; The straits beneath the bridge — unmonitored water routes between the lakes that bypass the checkpoint entirely; Military liaison — the bridge's federal designation creates opportunities for operators with the right clearances
Properties.story_hooks: Structural sensors on the bridge have detected anomalies that don't match weather stress or traffic loading — something is affecting the bridge's integrity from below; A Wisconsin-aligned team has developed a plan to close the bridge for 30 days — long enough to starve the UP of supplies and force Michigan to the negotiating table; Ferrogate Transit has been selectively allowing unscanned cargo across the bridge on a schedule that correlates with Wisconsin intelligence deliveries — the bridge operator is playing both sides
Properties.sights: The bridge spanning the Straits — 8 kilometers of enclosed highway suspended above grey-green water, lit by navigation arrays; The northern approach military installation — concrete, steel, and the architecture of controlled access; The Straits below, churning with Lake Michigan and Lake Huron's currents meeting — visible through the bridge's lower observation panels; Ghostbridge Island visible 5 kilometers to the east — the analog anomaly, watching the hypermodern crossing from its disconnected shore; Automated cargo convoys crossing in formation — the UP's supply line made visible as a procession of identical vehicles
Properties.sounds: Wind — the bridge is 60 meters above the water, and the Straits funnel weather into a permanent gale; Structural stress sounds — the bridge groans, creaks, and flexes, and the sounds are monitored by sensors that detect danger before humans can; Military checkpoint operations at the northern approach — automated processing, authorization announcements, the controlled tempo of access; The water below — audible from the bridge deck on calm days, a reminder of the distance between the vehicle and the surface
Properties.smells: Strait air — the meeting point of Lake Michigan and Lake Huron, carrying the mineral signatures of both; Enclosed bridge atmosphere — filtered, recycled, and carrying the faint ozone of the scanning systems; Military installation fuel and equipment at the northern approach — the smell of preparedness
Properties.feel: Crossing the Mackinac Bridge is an act of commitment. You are leaving one jurisdiction, one economic reality, one set of rules, and entering another. The bridge takes 8 minutes at highway speed, and in those 8 minutes you are suspended between two worlds — literally, above the water, between the peninsulas, in transit between the stable south and the contested north. The bridge does not feel safe. The bridge feels necessary.

Properties.description:
Meridian 88 is the official corporate-administrative designation for the continuous urban sprawl covering the entire western shore of Lake Michigan, extending north through Lake Superior's southern coast and into Canadian territory. The name derives from the 88th meridian west, the longitudinal line that roughly bisects the urban mass at its widest point near old Chicago. Nobody who lives here calls it that. To the corps it is Meridian 88, a regulated economic zone. To everyone else it is the Corridor, the Spine, or just the city — singular, because after two centuries of unchecked growth, the distinction between Chicago, Milwaukee, Green Bay, and the Fox Cities dissolved into one continuous concrete nervous system stretching over 500 kilometers from the Indiana border to the Canadian frontier.

The sprawl is not uniform. The dense urban core — old Chicago, the Shelf, the Spire, the Circuit — is the heart, where 60 million people stack vertically in arcology towers and cling to the sea wall over Lake Michigan. North of the core, the density thins but never stops: Milwaukee's thirteen districts bleed into Sheboygan's industrial lakeshore, which bleeds into the Fox Cities Nexus and its 200 data centers, which bleeds into Green Bay's Lambeau Terminus, which bleeds into the contested Upper Peninsula frontier. Even the spaces between are not empty — they are filled with maglev corridors, troll bridges, ungoverned zones, and the infrastructure arteries that keep 80 million people fed, powered, and surveilled.

The population is estimated at 80 million registered citizens across all tiers. The excluded and undocumented push the real number past 100 million. Meridian 88 contains hundreds of named districts, neighborhoods, and zones — from the Spire's corporate apex to the Shelf's unlicensed construction jutting over the lake, from the flooded ruins of Old Harbor to the contested mining towns of the Upper Peninsula. Between and beneath them lie the ungoverned corridors — the gaps in jurisdiction where corporate sovereignty ends and nothing replaces it. The western shore of Lake Michigan is not a city that grew. It is a civilization that metastasized.
Properties.aliases: M88, The Corridor, The Western Shore, The Spine
Properties.demographics: 80 million registered across all tiers, 100+ million actual when the excluded and undocumented are counted. The densest concentration is the old Chicago core (60 million in the vertical stack), thinning northward through Milwaukee (8 million), the Fox Cities (3 million), and the frontier settlements. Tiered citizenship from Tier 5 (corporate elite) down to Tier 1 (street-level) and the excluded (no tier, no rights, no record). Climate refugees, coastal collapse survivors, and economic migrants from the fallen cities make up roughly 20% of the lower-tier population.
Properties.economy: Corporate sovereign territories generate 80% of GDP across the entire western shore. The excluded economy — barter, dead drops, analog currency, gray market, troll bridges — sustains the other 40+ million who exist outside corporate systems. The gap between the two economies is not a gap. It is a wall that runs the entire length of the Corridor.
Properties.power_structure: The Big 20 corponations hold sovereign authority over their respective territories. Municipal government exists as a rubber stamp. Law enforcement is privatized above Tier 2. Below Tier 2, there is no law — only jurisdiction gaps and the people who fill them.
Properties.dangers: Corporate jurisdiction boundaries — cross the wrong line and your rights change; Surveillance saturation in upper tiers, surveillance absence in lower tiers; Climate infrastructure failure — flooding, heat events, air quality collapses; The Community Integration Initiative — corporate-funded population management disguised as social services
Properties.opportunities: The jurisdiction gaps are where freelancers like Kyle operate; The excluded economy runs on trust and reputation — valuable currencies; Information flows downward through the tiers faster than the corps can contain it; Every corponation has enemies, and enemies pay well
Properties.story_hooks: Meridian 88 is applying for UN Economic Zone redesignation — which would give the Big 20 even more sovereign authority; The flooded lower districts are slowly being reclaimed by automated construction drones — but who is paying for it and why?; A second maglev network is being built beneath the existing one. The official explanation does not explain the military-grade shielding.
Properties.sights: Arcology towers punching through permanent haze layers; Maglev lines threading between buildings like steel tendons; Corporate logos projected onto cloud cover — advertising you cannot escape; Lake Michigan visible from the upper tiers, a grey expanse choked with automated cargo platforms
Properties.sounds: The low hum of the maglev network — constant, omnipresent; Drone swarms overhead, navigation pings overlapping into white noise; Emergency sirens from districts you will never visit; The silence of the ungoverned corridors, which is not silence at all
Properties.smells: Ozone from the maglev rails; Recycled air with chemical undertones in the enclosed tiers; Lake rot from the flooded lower districts when the wind shifts; Synth-food vendors and nutrient paste — the smell of 40 million people eating
Properties.feel: A city that was never designed, only accumulated. Every layer built on top of the last, infrastructure decaying beneath the weight of what was added. The higher you go, the cleaner the air. The lower you go, the more honest the people.

Properties.description: The primary cargo handling facility — the UP's economic outlet, operated by machines and overseen by a skeleton crew
The old downtown commercial district — half-occupied, architecturally intact, and waiting for a population that isn't coming back
The cargo barge staging area in Little Bay de Noc — where the UP's resources wait to become someone else's profit

Fenwick Float is a semi-permanent flotilla of linked barges, decommissioned ferry hulls, and modular platform sections anchored roughly two kilometers off the Chicago Lakeshore, accessible by water-taxi, private skiff, or the one functional mag-cable gondola that runs from a crumbling pier near the old Adler site. The Float began as an emergency housing overflow measure during the 2161 Shelf flooding crisis and was never formally dissolved — it simply accumulated residents, commerce, and eventually its own internal logic, drifting slightly with seasonal anchor adjustments but always remaining within the same rough coordinates.

Because the Float sits in jurisdictionally ambiguous water — technically under Meridian 88 municipal charter but practically unreachable by standard Ferrogate ground patrols — it has become a preferred location for operations that require distance from civic scrutiny. Legitimate floating restaurants and water-purification co-ops share deck space with unlicensed medical clinics, data brokerage nodes, and at least two competing smuggling operations that have achieved a workable truce. The lake wind is constant and the horizon is always visible, which residents cite with surprising frequency as reasons they stay.
Properties.aliases: The Float, Fenwick's, The Raft Quarter, Lake Fenwick
Properties.demographics: A genuinely mixed population ranging from Tier 1 laborers who could not secure Shelf housing to deliberate off-grid professionals (data brokers, unlicensed medics, gray-market logistics coordinators) to a small number of Tier 3 residents who maintain secondary residences here for privacy reasons.
Properties.economy: Tourism and food service from the restaurant barges, water purification co-op revenues, and a substantial gray-market economy centered on data brokerage, unlicensed medical services, and logistics coordination for contraband moving in and out of the Lakeshore Corridor.
Properties.power_structure: The Float has no formal governance; a rotating Harbor Committee handles platform maintenance and inter-operator disputes, but real authority is exercised by the two dominant smuggling operations — Carrion Logistics' unofficial lake division and an independent crew known as the Meridian Drift — who maintain their truce through mutual dependency.
Properties.dangers: Platform connection joints fail periodically, separating sections of the Float during storm conditions and stranding residents until emergency lashing can be rigged.; The jurisdictional ambiguity that protects the Float also means emergency services response times from the shore average forty-seven minutes — effectively nonexistent.; The Meridian Drift crew is volatile; their truce with Carrion Logistics has collapsed twice in six years, and both incidents produced casualties among uninvolved Float residents.; Arcturus Defense Solutions operates an intermittent aerial surveillance drone pattern over the lake, and the Float is logged in their tracking database as a 'person of interest aggregation site.'
Properties.opportunities: The Float's unlicensed medical clinic operates with equipment and pharmaceutical access that rivals some legitimate Tier 3 facilities, at a fraction of the cost and with no identity verification.; The data brokerage nodes on the Float maintain Diaspora connections routed through lake-bed relay buoys that are effectively invisible to standard municipal traffic monitoring.; Carrion Logistics' lake division offers reliable, quiet transport of persons and cargo to points along the entire Great Lakes coastline, no manifest required.
Properties.story_hooks: A Palladian Group corporate attorney arrived on the Float three weeks ago and has not left — she is not using her credentials, not contacting her firm, and the one Float resident who tried to speak with her says she seemed genuinely terrified. Someone from the Spire is now offering Φ15,000 for her safe return, and someone else is offering Φ20,000 for confirmation that she never makes it back.; The mag-cable gondola broke down mid-crossing yesterday with six passengers aboard, and when the maintenance crew finally reached it, four of the six were dead from apparent BCI-induced cardiac arrest — the other two have no memory of the crossing at all.; The water purification co-op has quietly discovered that the lake-bed relay buoys routing the Float's Diaspora connections are also carrying an encrypted secondary signal of unknown origin — one of the co-op's engineers believes it is an E.L.F. using the Float's infrastructure as a refuge node.
Properties.sights: The Float's connected platforms undulate gently in a slow, breathing rhythm, making every structure on it appear subtly, perpetually in motion.; String lights and bioluminescent algae panels illuminate the inter-platform walkways at night, reflecting in broken columns across the black lake surface.; Laundry, solar collection film, and signal-mesh antennae all compete for vertical space on every mast and railing, giving the Float a festive, cluttered skyline.; The mag-cable gondola arrives every forty minutes, its single cabin lit warm amber against the dark water, trailing a thin wake of spray.
Properties.sounds: The constant low percussion of lake swells against hull metal creates a rhythm that residents stop consciously hearing within days of arrival.; Competing music from the floating restaurant barges bleeds together across the walkways into a layered, accidental ambience.; The gondola cable hums a descending note as it approaches the Float's main dock, serving as the closest thing to a public clock the community has.
Properties.smells: Lake air dominates — clean and cold with an algal mineral edge that sharpens in the morning and softens at dusk.; Cooking smells from a dozen different culinary traditions drift and combine across the platform walkways, strongest near the central barge cluster.; Below the waterline access hatches, a persistent smell of treated bilge water and hull sealant rises whenever they are opened.
Properties.feel: There is a looseness to Fenwick Float that the city proper cannot replicate — the sense that the rules apply differently here, or not at all, or only the ones that residents have agreed to among themselves. The constant motion underfoot is disorienting for newcomers and becomes, for long-timers, a physical reassurance. The lake horizon provides a psychological expanse that the corridor's vertical density forecloses entirely.

Properties.description:
South Haven was a resort town built on sunsets. The kind of place where the entire economy ran on people driving three hours to watch the sun go down over Lake Michigan and then buying fudge. It was charming. It was seasonal. It was exactly the kind of economy that does not survive climate destabilization, lake-level rise, and the collapse of the middle class that used to fund weekend getaways.

What South Haven became is harder to categorize. The old downtown -- what's left above water -- has been repurposed as an offshore recreation zone for mid-tier corporate workers from the Meridian 88 corridor. Tessera Leisure Holdings operates the beachfront, offering 'authentic lakeside experiences' to employees who earn enough to afford a weekend pass but not enough to access the elite resorts further north. The experience is manufactured nostalgia: reconstructed beach cottages, artisanal ice cream that costs more per scoop than the original shops charged per gallon, and sunset viewing decks with augmented reality overlays that filter out the cargo platform traffic on the horizon. It is a theme park version of a place that used to be real.

Below the tourist layer, the Undertow earns its name. The lake has risen nearly two meters since South Haven's resort heyday, and the lower sections of the old town are permanently flooded. This submerged district -- locally called the Undertow -- is where the people who actually live here year-round have settled. Houseboats, converted marina structures, and floating platform homes connected by walkways and rope bridges. The Undertow community is small, insular, and deeply suspicious of outsiders. They fish the lake, maintain their own power grid from wave-energy converters, and operate one of the most effective smuggling networks on the eastern shore. Cargo that enters the lake from offshore and needs to reach the inland corridor without passing through any checkpoint goes through the Undertow. The residents don't advertise this. They don't need to. Everyone who needs to know already does.
Properties.aliases: South Haven, Undertow Beach, The Drowning
Properties.demographics: Surface tourist district serves approximately 15,000 visitors per week during high season. Year-round Undertow population is roughly 1,200 -- tight-knit, multi-generational fishing and maritime families, predominantly Tier 1-2 with a handful of former Tier 3 residents who chose this life deliberately.
Properties.economy: Surface economy is Tessera Leisure Holdings tourism revenue -- significant but entirely extracted. Undertow economy is fishing, wave-energy generation, boat repair, and smuggling. The smuggling income alone is estimated at Φ40 million annually, distributed across the community through a share system that ensures nobody starves and nobody gets rich enough to attract attention.
Properties.power_structure: Tessera Leisure Holdings controls the surface tourist infrastructure. The Undertow is governed by a harbor council of senior residents who operate by consensus and enforce decisions through social pressure and the ultimate sanction: exile from the community, which in a place this isolated is effectively a death sentence for your livelihood.
Properties.dangers: Lake storms -- the Undertow's floating structures are resilient but not invincible, and rescue services don't extend below the boardwalk; Tessera security occasionally sweeps the waterline district, looking for smuggling infrastructure they know exists but can't map; Drowning -- the flooded lower town has currents, submerged structures, and no lifeguards; Getting caught in a smuggling run -- the penalties are corporate jurisdiction, which means Tessera decides your sentence; Trust -- the Undertow doesn't forgive outsiders who betray their confidence
Properties.opportunities: The smuggling network moves anything that fits on a boat -- cargo, people, data stored on physical media; The Undertow's wave-energy tech is innovative and could be scaled if someone provided capital without strings; Clean lake water is increasingly rare and increasingly valuable -- South Haven has it; Information passes through the Undertow from offshore sources that the inland surveillance networks can't monitor
Properties.story_hooks: A Tessera Leisure executive discovers the Undertow and sees not a community to displace but a 'lifestyle brand' to monetize -- and the harbor council is divided on whether to negotiate or fight; Something is surfacing from the flooded lower town -- artifacts from before the rise, including sealed data storage that predates the corporate era and might contain records someone deleted; A smuggling run goes wrong and the cargo turns out to be a person who multiple corponations are looking for
Properties.sights: The Tessera beachfront above -- neon-lit boardwalk, holographic sunset enhancement, tourists in branded leisure wear; Below, the Undertow -- houseboats and floating platforms connected by rope bridges, lit by salvaged LEDs and bioluminescent panels; Flooded storefronts visible through clear water on calm days, the old town preserved like a museum nobody curates; Wave-energy converters bobbing offshore, their rhythmic motion the Undertow's heartbeat; The lighthouse at the harbor mouth, still functional, now serving as both navigation aid and Undertow community meeting point
Properties.sounds: Water everywhere -- lapping, dripping, the constant conversation between the lake and the structures built on it; Tourist noise from the upper boardwalk -- filtered, distant, another world; Boat engines at odd hours -- the smuggling runs happen between 2 and 5 AM; Wave-energy converters churning -- a rhythmic mechanical pulse; The creak of floating structures adjusting to swell -- the Undertow is never still
Properties.smells: Clean lake water -- South Haven is far enough from the industrial zones that the lake actually smells like a lake here; Fish, fresh and smoked -- the Undertow eats what it catches; Salt-treated wood and marine sealant from constant structural maintenance; Manufactured nostalgia scents pumped onto the Tessera boardwalk -- cotton candy and sunscreen, algorithmically optimized
Properties.feel: Two places occupying the same coordinates. The surface is a corporate vacation simulation, pleasant and hollow. Below the waterline is something older and more honest -- a community that lives with the lake rather than on top of it. The Undertow has the specific energy of a place that has decided the official world is irrelevant and built its own. It's peaceful in a way that the upper boardwalk can only simulate.

Properties.description: The Float's largest restaurant barge, serving a rotating menu sourced entirely from lake-harvested and vertical-farm stock — the best meal available outside the Spire, if you can get a reservation and find a way out here.

The below-waterline access corridor connecting the Float's oldest hull sections, used officially for maintenance and unofficially as the primary meeting space for dealings neither party wants conducted in open air.

Forest Hollow is the district that Meridian forgot, and that's exactly how its residents like it. The old Forest Glen was always Chicago's least densely populated community area — winding streets, large lots, a suburban feel that made no sense inside city limits. When the Corporate Reconstruction mapped Meridian 88's zones, Forest Glen's low population density, minimal commercial value, and confusing street layout caused it to fall through the cracks of multiple corporate planning algorithms. It was assigned to no sovereign territory. It appeared on no development plan. It was, in the language of corporate logistics, a null zone — a place that existed in geographic space but not in administrative space. By the time anyone noticed the oversight, the residents had adapted to their invisible status and had no intention of being noticed.

The Hollow's winding streets — originally a product of the neighborhood following the contours of the North Branch river and the forest preserves — now serve as a natural labyrinth. Drone navigation struggles with the irregular grid. Surveillance coverage is patchy because the camera placement algorithms were designed for Meridian's standard block structure, not Forest Glen's organic curves. The tree canopy — maintained by residents who understand that overhead cover defeats satellite imaging — creates a green ceiling that makes the Hollow invisible from above. The forest preserve land, never developed and never formally acquired by any corporation, has grown wild, its paths known only to the Hollow's residents and the animals that have moved in as Meridian's development pushed wildlife to the margins.

What Forest Hollow does with its invisibility is a matter of some speculation among the few outsiders who know it exists. The truth is less dramatic than the rumors suggest: the Hollow is a community of roughly 3,000 people who live off the grid in the most literal sense. Power comes from solar panels hidden under tree cover. Water comes from wells tapping the old aquifer. Communication uses mesh networks that don't route through Axiom's infrastructure. The residents grow food, maintain their homes, educate their children, and ignore Meridian with the comprehensive commitment of people who've decided that the city's problems are not their problems. It's not paradise — the medical resources are primitive, the winters are brutal without corporate climate control, and the isolation can eat at you. But it's free, in a way that nowhere else in Meridian can claim to be.

The Hollow's relationship with the outside world is managed through a single controlled point of contact: a resident designated as the Interface, who handles all necessary interactions with neighboring districts and ensures that nothing about Forest Hollow enters any database, manifest, or conversation that corporate systems might parse. The current Interface is a woman in her fifties who worked for Axiom's surveillance division before she disappeared — officially dead, actually living in a bungalow surrounded by oak trees, making sure that the community that took her in stays invisible. She is very good at her job.
Properties.aliases: Forest Glen, The Hollow, The Blind Spot, Ghost Grid
Properties.demographics: Approximately 3,000 residents, officially zero. No tier assignments — the Hollow doesn't exist in Axiom's population databases. A mix of original Forest Glen families, corporate defectors, off-grid idealists, and people who needed to stop existing on paper. All ages, but skewing toward adults who made a deliberate choice to disappear.
Properties.economy: Subsistence — the Hollow grows its own food, generates its own power, and maintains its own infrastructure. Trade with the outside world is minimal and conducted through the Interface. The Hollow's only export is invisibility, offered selectively to people who need it.
Properties.power_structure: Consensus governance among household heads. The Interface holds unique authority over external relations. No formal hierarchy — the community is small enough for direct negotiation. Disagreements are resolved face-to-face because there's nowhere to hide from your neighbors in a community of 3,000.
Properties.dangers: Discovery — if Axiom's planning systems correct the null-zone oversight, the Hollow's independence ends; Medical emergencies — the Hollow's healthcare is pre-corporate level, and serious injuries or illnesses require breaking cover to access outside facilities; Internal conflict — in a community this small and isolated, personal disputes can become existential threats; Winter — without corporate climate control, the Great Lakes winter is a survival challenge that claims lives in bad years; The forest itself — the wild preserve contains animals, terrain, and weather that an urbanized population isn't always prepared for
Properties.opportunities: Total invisibility — Forest Hollow is the only place in Meridian that genuinely doesn't exist in any database; The Interface — a former Axiom surveillance specialist whose knowledge of corporate monitoring systems is invaluable; Off-grid infrastructure knowledge — the Hollow's residents know how to build and maintain systems without corporate supply chains; Forest preserve resources — medicinal plants, clean water, building materials, and wildlife that the rest of Meridian has lost access to; Perspective — time in the Hollow reminds you what human life looked like before the optimization
Properties.story_hooks: The Interface intercepts a corporate survey drone that's been programmed with Forest Hollow's coordinates — someone inside Axiom has noticed the null zone, and the Hollow has weeks, maybe days, before a planning team arrives to fill the gap on the map; A critically injured person is brought to the Hollow's border by someone who shouldn't know the community exists. The injury requires medical resources the Hollow doesn't have. Saving this person means exposing the community to outside contact. Not saving them means letting someone die.; Kyle discovers that Forest Hollow exists during a job that takes him through the northwest. The community's existence — proof that opting out of Meridian is possible — changes his understanding of what his life could be. The Interface offers him a choice he's not ready to make.
Properties.sights: Winding streets under a full tree canopy — green overhead, dappled light, the visual signature of a place that hides; Solar panels concealed beneath leaf cover, visible only from the right angle; Wild forest preserve land — overgrown paths, animal tracks, the unmanaged beauty of nature left alone; Homes that blend into the landscape — maintained but not conspicuous, designed to not be seen from any distance; The absence of corporate signage, surveillance cameras, or any evidence that Meridian 88 exists here; Deer. Actual deer, standing in yards, unbothered by human presence.
Properties.sounds: Forest sounds — rustling leaves, birdsong, animal movement in the underbrush. Sounds Meridian has forgotten.; Wind through the tree canopy — a continuous, layered sound that masks other noise naturally; The absence of electronic ambient noise — no drone hum, no maglev whine, no corporate audio. Profound silence by Meridian standards.; Children's voices from somewhere in the trees — the Hollow's kids play in the forest like children from another century; Well pumps and hand tools — the analog sounds of a community that maintains itself manually
Properties.smells: Forest floor — decomposing leaves, damp earth, mushrooms, the rich biological smell of land that hasn't been paved; Woodsmoke from heating fires in winter — the Hollow doesn't have corporate climate control; Growing things — vegetable gardens, fruit trees, herbs. The smell of food being produced, not manufactured.; Clean air — genuinely clean, not filtered or processed, just air that's been through a forest and nothing else
Properties.feel: Hidden. Forest Hollow feels like stepping through a door in a wall you didn't know had a door. The transition from Meridian's constant electronic presence to the Hollow's analog silence is physically disorienting — your neural interface gets quieter, your augments find fewer signals to process, and your senses recalibrate to an environment that hasn't been optimized for human comfort but hasn't been stripped of natural comfort either. It feels like trespassing in a place that chose to leave the world, which is exactly what it is.

Properties.description:
Nordpark Sanctuary is the district that traded its future for its library. When the Corporate Reconstruction swept through Meridian 88's northern districts, North Park University — the small Christian college that had anchored this quiet neighborhood for over a century — made a deal that its founders would have found either pragmatic or damning, depending on their theology. The university surrendered its accreditation, its degree-granting authority, and its right to operate as an independent educational institution. In exchange, Axiom agreed to leave the campus and its surrounding residential blocks alone, designated as a Cultural Preservation Zone — a status that grants no political power but provides legal protection from development, demolition, and corporate acquisition. The university kept its buildings, its library, and its community. It lost everything else.

What remains is not a university in any functional sense but something harder to define: a sanctuary. The campus buildings — modest brick structures along the North Branch of the river — house a library collection that has become one of the most valuable information resources in northern Meridian. Not because the books are rare (though some are) but because they're physical. In a city where digital information is controlled, curated, and deletable by corporate systems, a building full of paper books that no one can remotely edit or erase is a strategic asset. The library's collection includes pre-corporate history texts, unredacted news archives, theological and philosophical works that challenge corporate ideology, and — most valuably — a complete set of Chicago municipal records from the decades before the Reconstruction, donated by a city clerk who saw what was coming and wanted someone to remember what was lost.

The residential blocks around the campus have taken on the character of the institution they surround. Quiet, scholarly, maintained with modest care. The population is small — mostly former faculty, students who never left, and families who value the Sanctuary's peace above the amenities that other districts offer. The North Branch river flows through the district, less channelized here than in the Commons, almost natural in places. A small seminary operates informally on campus — not granting degrees, just teaching theology, philosophy, and ethics to anyone who shows up. The students are a mix of genuine seekers and people who've discovered that a campus setting is a safe place to think dangerous thoughts.

The Sanctuary's value to Meridian's underground information economy cannot be overstated. The Collective maintains an unofficial relationship with the library, sending researchers to access the municipal archives and physical texts that can't be found on any network. Data brokers from the Circuit make pilgrimages to verify information against print sources. Corporate historians — the ones who work off the record — use the library to cross-reference official narratives against pre-Reconstruction documentation. The library staff are aware of all this and permit it with the understanding that the library serves everyone and belongs to no faction. It's the last neutral ground in a city of territories, and its neutrality is protected by the one thing that even Axiom respects: the fact that destroying a library looks bad, even for a corporation that doesn't care about looking bad.
Properties.aliases: North Park, The Sanctuary, Seminary Row, The Quiet College
Properties.demographics: Approximately 4,000 residents, predominantly former academic community — retired faculty, long-term students, families with university connections. Tier 1 and Tier 2. Older than average but not as elderly as Norwood Quiet — the seminary attracts younger residents who choose scholarship over employment. The most educated population per capita in Meridian's northern districts.
Properties.economy: The library — information services, research access, and archival preservation. The seminary's informal education program. Small-scale residential economy. The Sanctuary doesn't produce goods; it preserves knowledge, and in Meridian 88, that's an economy unto itself.
Properties.power_structure: The Library Council — former faculty and senior staff who manage the campus and make community decisions. The head librarian holds outsized influence as the custodian of the collection. No corporate governance, no militia. The Sanctuary's protection is cultural — it survives because destroying it would mean destroying a library, and nobody wants to be the person who orders that.
Properties.dangers: Corporate reclassification — the Cultural Preservation Zone designation could be revoked if Axiom finds sufficient reason; Information theft — the library's physical archives are irreplaceable, making them targets for anyone who wants to control the narrative; Dependency on neutrality — the Sanctuary's survival strategy requires all factions to respect its non-aligned status, and that respect could erode; Resource scarcity — the campus needs maintenance, and the community has limited means; Infiltration — the open-door policy makes the Sanctuary vulnerable to agents seeking to identify who accesses which records
Properties.opportunities: The library — physical documentation of pre-corporate history, unredacted and uneditable; The seminary — ethics and philosophy education in a city that has abandoned both; Neutral ground — the Sanctuary is one of the few places where representatives of different factions can meet without territorial implications; Research access — the municipal archives contain information that could challenge corporate legitimacy; Community — a small, educated, thoughtful population that values discourse and preserves knowledge as a moral obligation
Properties.story_hooks: A researcher from the Collective discovers that the library's municipal archives contain documentation of the original corporate charter that established Axiom's sovereignty — and the documentation reveals a legal flaw that, if publicized, could unravel the corporation's authority. The Library Council must decide whether to allow the information to leave the Sanctuary.; Someone is systematically removing pages from the library's pre-Reconstruction news archives — physical pages, cut from physical books, the only copies in existence. The head librarian hires Kyle to find the thief before the historical record is permanently damaged.; The seminary's newest student is a former Axiom executive who claims to have experienced a crisis of conscience. She wants to teach ethics. The community is divided between those who see redemption and those who see infiltration.
Properties.sights: The university campus — modest brick buildings, a bell tower, paths worn smooth by generations of students who no longer attend; The library's reading rooms — natural light through old windows, physical books on wooden shelves, readers working in analog silence; The North Branch river flowing through the district, less channelized here, almost remembering what it used to be; Seminary students debating on campus benches — young people discussing ethics in a city that considers ethics an inefficiency; The residential blocks' maintained modesty — clean, cared-for homes that don't draw attention or envy; Handwritten signs on campus: READING ROOM OPEN, THEOLOGY SEMINAR TUESDAY, ALL WELCOME
Properties.sounds: Pages turning — the library's reading rooms are the quietest inhabited spaces in Meridian, and the sound of paper is the soundtrack; The river — audible here in a way it isn't in the Commons, flowing over rocks that haven't been removed; Seminary discussions — earnest, sometimes heated, occasionally brilliant arguments about what it means to be human in a city that's stopped asking; The bell tower — rung manually, marking the hours with a sound that predates everything Meridian has become; Wind through campus trees — smaller than the Hollow's forest but real, living, and cherished
Properties.smells: Old books — paper, binding glue, aged ink. The specific, irreplaceable smell of physical knowledge.; River water — cleaner here than downstream, with a mineral freshness that smells like the old geography; Campus grounds — cut grass, garden plots, the faint mustiness of old brick buildings breathing; Candle wax from the chapel — still lit, still used, still serving a purpose that can't be quantified
Properties.feel: Sacred. Not in a religious sense — or not only in a religious sense — but in the older meaning: set apart, protected, important beyond its material value. The Sanctuary feels like a place that has been deliberately preserved against the current of history, maintained by people who understand that some things matter more than efficiency. It's calm in a way that the Quiet mimics but the Sanctuary genuinely achieves, because the Sanctuary's calm comes from purpose, not avoidance.

Nodes.Name: The forest preserves and ungoverned wilderness

Properties.description:
Waukegan was an industrial city before the word 'industrial' became a euphemism for 'expendable.' The lakefront that once hosted a naval training station and a pharmaceutical campus now hosts the northern terminus of M88's automated cargo logistics network — a sprawl of container yards, drone maintenance hangars, and processing facilities where Lake Michigan's cargo platforms offload goods that will be distributed throughout the Corridor. The work that remains for human hands is the work machines can't do cheaply enough yet, which is a category that shrinks every fiscal quarter.

The old naval station — Great Lakes Naval Training Center, decommissioned by the remnant federal government in 2158 — was acquired by Ringo Defense Solutions in the sovereignty charter fire sale of 2161. Ringo converted it into a regional security operations base, which means the northern edge of Waukegan is a walled compound where private military contractors train, refit, and stage for operations throughout the upper GLM. The base employs 12,000 people and contributes exactly nothing to the surrounding community except a perimeter wall, a no-fly zone, and the occasional sound of live-fire exercises at 3 AM.

Between the cargo yards and the Ringo wall, the residential district survives the way organisms survive in extreme environments: by adapting to conditions that would kill anything designed for comfort. The housing stock is a mix of 20th-century bungalows — some of them literally a hundred and fifty years old, patched with whatever was available — and modular refugee housing units dropped by the GLM Metropolitan Authority during the Gulf Coast Displacement crisis of the 2070s. The modulars were supposed to be temporary. Temporary, in municipal planning, means 'until someone allocates a budget that will never be allocated.' They're still here. The people inside them have made them home, which is what people do.

The lakefront itself is poisoned. A century of industrial runoff, compounded by the cargo platform chemical discharge that nobody regulates because the platforms operate in federal — now corporate — waters, has made the shoreline a dead zone. The water is technically Lake Michigan. The color is not.
Properties.aliases: Waukegan, The Rust Shelf, WaukeGone, North Shore Docks
Properties.demographics: Approximately 140,000 residents. Heavily working class, Tier 1-2. Significant Gulf Coast displacement population (roughly 30%). Large Latino community predating the displacement era. Ringo base personnel technically reside in Waukegan but exist in a separate jurisdiction and economy. Median age skews young — people leave when they can afford to, which means the ones who stay can't.
Properties.economy: Logistics labor — the cargo yards employ approximately 15,000 people in roles that automation hasn't eliminated yet. Ringo base support services. Informal economy is substantial: repair work, food service, unlicensed medical care. The nearest licensed medical facility is in The Threshold, twenty minutes south by Purple Line.
Properties.power_structure: No single authority. Ringo controls the northern perimeter. Axiom Logistics controls the cargo yards. The residential district falls into a jurisdiction gap — nominally under GLM Metropolitan Authority, which maintains a single administrative office staffed by two people who process complaints they cannot act on. Real authority is community-based: block captains, mutual aid networks, and the occasional intervention by whoever is currently running the local gray market.
Properties.dangers: Ringo perimeter enforcement — the compound's automated defense systems have a documented shoot-first protocol for the buffer zone; Cargo yard accidents — automation failures kill roughly twenty workers per year, classified as 'operational incidents'; Environmental exposure — the lakefront contamination causes elevated cancer rates that nobody is studying because nobody is funding the study; Jurisdiction void — no reliable law enforcement means disputes are settled by whatever means are available; Displacement violence — resource competition between established residents and newer refugee populations
Properties.opportunities: Cargo theft — the logistics network moves Q billions in goods through a district with no effective security; Ringo intelligence — the base leaks information through its support staff, who live in the community and talk; Mutual aid networks — the community infrastructure here is among the strongest in the upper Corridor; Labor organizing — the cargo yard workforce is large, angry, and increasingly coordinated
Properties.story_hooks: A cargo container from the Ringo base was accidentally routed to the civilian yard — and its contents don't match any known Ringo inventory; The lakefront contamination is getting worse, and a community health worker has data suggesting it's not just industrial runoff — someone is actively dumping; A Ringo contractor has gone AWOL into the residential district, carrying information worth enough to change jurisdictions
Properties.sights: Cargo platform drones descending in formation over the container yards, navigation lights blinking in synchronized patterns; The Ringo compound wall — three meters of reinforced concrete topped with sensor arrays, visible from most of the district; Modular housing units stacked two and three high, connected by improvised walkways and exterior staircases; The dead lakefront — grey-brown water, no vegetation, automated warning buoys marking chemical discharge zones; Old bungalow neighborhoods where century-old architecture meets salvaged solar panels and jury-rigged power taps
Properties.sounds: Container yard automation — the grinding of cargo cranes, the hiss of pneumatic seals, running 24 hours; Ringo live-fire exercises — distant but unmistakable, a sound the residents have learned to sleep through; Wind off the lake carrying a faint chemical whistle through gaps in the modular housing stacks; Children playing in the spaces between housing units, their games adapted to the narrow corridors available; The low thrum of the cargo maglev running containers south toward M88's distribution centers
Properties.smells: Chemical lake — an acrid, metallic smell that residents stop noticing after a few months and visitors never forget; Diesel exhaust from the backup generators that keep the modular units running when the grid fails, which is often; Cooking smells from the housing corridors — a dense mix of Gulf Coast, Central American, and Southeast Asian cuisines, the smell of every displacement crisis blended together; Ozone and machine lubricant from the cargo yards
Properties.feel: A place that works hard and gets nothing for it. The cargo moves through Waukegan at enormous volume and none of it stops here. The wealth generated by the logistics network is measured in billions of Q and accrues to companies headquartered in buildings the residents of Waukegan will never enter. The community is real, the mutual aid is genuine, and the anger is justified. This is what a company town looks like when the company doesn't even bother to pretend it's a town.

Properties.description:
Delray has been dying for a century and nobody has had the decency to let it finish. The neighborhood sits at the confluence of the Detroit River and the River Rouge, wedged between the Marathon petroleum refinery (now Ouroboros Energy's Great Lakes Processing Hub), the Rouge industrial complex, and the international freight crossing to Canada. In the 20th century, Delray was a working-class immigrant neighborhood — Hungarian, then Mexican, then whoever was willing to live next to a refinery. In the 22nd century, the human population has dwindled to approximately 1,100 residents who are too rooted, too poor, or too sick to leave, occupying a landscape so contaminated that the soil itself is classified as industrial waste.

Ouroboros Energy's Great Lakes Processing Hub dominates the district — a chemical refinery and energy processing complex that no longer refines petroleum but converts industrial waste streams, biomass, and recycled materials into the synthetic fuel and chemical feedstocks that the GLM's manufacturing sector requires. The process is cleaner than oil refining was. The residual contamination from a century of petroleum processing is not clean. The ground is saturated with heavy metals, volatile organic compounds, and substances that environmental scientists identify by number rather than name because naming them would require acknowledging what they do to human tissue. Ouroboros maintains an air quality monitoring station in the district. The station's readings are technically within legal limits. The legal limits were set by a panel that included three Ouroboros consultants.

The 1,100 remaining residents live in what environmental justice researchers call a sacrifice zone — a geographic area where the cost of industrial activity is borne by the people who can least afford to leave. They are predominantly elderly. They are predominantly sick. The cancer cluster data is robust enough for an epidemiological study but not for a lawsuit, because Ouroboros's sovereign industrial charter exempts the Processing Hub from external environmental litigation. The residents have a community center, a volunteer health clinic, and a priest who holds services in a building where the paint peels in patterns that trace the groundwater contamination plume. They also have something the corponations didn't expect: a comprehensive archive of environmental monitoring data going back to the 1970s, maintained by three generations of residents who understood that the only defense against institutional denial is institutional documentation.
Properties.aliases: Delray, The Sacrifice, Dead Zone, Marathon Country
Properties.demographics: Approximately 1,100 residents. Predominantly elderly (median age: 67), predominantly Hispanic and Black, predominantly affected by chronic respiratory, neurological, and oncological conditions linked to environmental contamination. The population decreases by approximately 60 people per year. No one is moving in.
Properties.economy: Ouroboros Energy's Processing Hub: Φ180 billion annual output. The residential community's economy is effectively zero — the remaining residents survive on disability payments, community aid, and the stubborn math of owning homes that are worth nothing on the market but cost nothing to live in.
Properties.power_structure: Ouroboros Energy holds sovereign industrial authority. The Delray Community Association, led by Father Miguel Santos and the three-member environmental archive committee, has no formal power but maintains the documentation that Ouroboros spends significant legal resources trying to discredit. The dynamic is David and Goliath, except David is 67 years old and has stage 3 lymphoma.
Properties.dangers: Environmental contamination — the soil, water, and air carry toxic loads that affect anyone who spends time in the district; The Processing Hub — industrial accidents are infrequent but catastrophic when they occur, and the blast radius includes the residential blocks; Health deterioration — extended exposure to Delray's environment causes cumulative biological damage; Corporate legal aggression — Ouroboros's legal team actively works to discredit the community archive and its maintainers; Psychological toll — living in a sacrifice zone requires a particular kind of endurance that has consequences
Properties.opportunities: The environmental archive — 50 years of monitoring data that documents corporate contamination across Detroit's entire industrial corridor; Father Santos's network — the priest has connections to environmental justice organizations, legal advocates, and media contacts across the GLM; The Processing Hub's proximity — the industrial complex's perimeter security is designed for corporate espionage, not for the elderly neighbors who have been watching its operations for decades; Moral leverage — Delray's story is powerful enough to damage any corponation associated with it, if the story reaches the right audience
Properties.story_hooks: The environmental archive contains data from the 2050s that shows Ouroboros deliberately routed contaminated groundwater toward the residential blocks to avoid processing costs. The data is authentic. Father Santos is dying. The archive needs a custodian who can use it before it becomes a historical curiosity.; Ouroboros is planning to expand the Processing Hub into the residential blocks. The relocation offer is generous. The residents are split. Father Santos believes the expansion would also destroy the archive, which is stored in the community center's basement — and he believes that's the point.; A Delray resident's grandchild — who left the district twenty years ago and now works in corporate pharmaceuticals — returns with a treatment protocol that could help the community's health conditions. The treatment is Ouroboros-patented. Using it would require accepting Ouroboros's medical sovereignty.
Properties.sights: The Ouroboros Processing Hub — pipes, tanks, stacks, and vapor plumes dominating the skyline like a mechanical forest; Residential blocks where half the houses are occupied and the other half are slowly returning to the contaminated earth; Soil discoloration visible from ground level — patches of ground that are wrong colors for reasons that require chemistry to explain; The international freight crossing — autonomous cargo vehicles passing through the district without stopping, their routing algorithms having long since deprioritized Delray's existence; The community center's environmental monitoring station — a resident-maintained sensor array that contradicts the official readings
Properties.sounds: The Processing Hub — a continuous industrial roar that the residents have absorbed into their definition of background noise; Freight crossing traffic — heavy autonomous vehicles shaking the remaining houses as they pass; The health clinic — coughing, medical equipment, the sounds of chronic illness managed with inadequate resources; Wind through empty houses — the particular sound of structures decomposing at the pace of residential abandonment; The river — audible from anywhere in Delray, carrying the chemical signature of everything upstream
Properties.smells: Chemical processing — the Hub's output is filtered but the smell permeates, a petroleum-derivative scent that coats the tongue; Contaminated soil — a metallic, organic wrongness that is strongest after rain when the ground releases stored compounds; The river at Delray — industrial, biological, and chemical notes combining into an olfactory experience that environmental scientists call 'mixed-source anthropogenic'
Properties.feel: Poisoned and persistent. Delray feels like a place that has been told to die and refused, not out of hope but out of the particular stubbornness of people who know that leaving would mean admitting the thing that was done to them was acceptable. The contamination is real. The illness is real. The community's refusal to disappear is the most aggressive act of resistance in Detroit, and nobody frames it that way because the people doing it are old and sick and poor.

Properties.description: The restored train station, now Ford Meridian's AV fleet command center — 18 million vehicles tracked as points of light in a vaulted cathedral
Six-block restricted testing zone where experimental autonomous platforms run continuous loops
The maintenance facility where military-grade platforms are serviced — the most restricted civilian space in Detroit

Mackinac Island banned automobiles in 1898. In 2200, it has banned everything else. The island sits in the Straits of Mackinac, 5 kilometers from the bridge that connects Michigan's two peninsulas, and it has leveraged its historical no-motor ordinance into something unprecedented in the GLM: a technology restriction zone. No motorized vehicles. No neural interface connectivity. No augmentation uplinks. No corporate sovereign territory. No surveillance infrastructure. The island operates under a municipal charter that predates corporate sovereignty law, and the charter's technology restrictions have been upheld by every court that's reviewed them — not because the courts agree with the principle, but because the precedent of overturning a 200-year-old municipal ordinance terrifies the legal establishment.

The result is an island of 600 permanent residents and up to 5,000 visitors at any time, living in conditions that most GLM inhabitants would consider medieval. Horse-drawn transport. Paper documents. Face-to-face communication. No data trail. No surveillance record. No jurisdictional tracking. The implications have not been lost on anyone. Ghostbridge Island is the GLM's premiere dead-drop location, negotiation venue, and disappearance destination. If you need to have a conversation that no system can record, you have it here. If you need to meet someone without creating a data point, you meet here. If you need to vanish, the island's analog infrastructure means you were never digitally here in the first place.

The Grand Hotel — a Victorian-era structure maintained in deliberately anachronistic condition — serves as the island's primary venue for the negotiations, deals, and betrayals that require total surveillance absence. The hotel's guest list is not recorded digitally. The rooms are not monitored. The staff are hired for discretion, paid in physical currency, and trained in the art of not seeing things. Ghostbridge Island is a loophole in the GLM's total information architecture — a place where the panopticon blinks — and every powerful interest in the Great Lakes knows it, uses it, and fears what happens when someone else uses it.
Properties.aliases: Mackinac Island MI, The Island, No-Motor Zone, The Anomaly
Properties.demographics: 600 permanent residents. Self-selected for analog life, multi-generational island families mixed with people who chose disconnection deliberately. Up to 5,000 transient visitors — a rotating population of fixers, negotiators, fugitives, diplomats, and tourists who want to know what silence feels like.
Properties.economy: Hospitality, dead-drop services, and the anonymity premium. The island charges for what the rest of the GLM cannot provide: unrecorded space. The Grand Hotel's rates are astronomical. The smaller inns and boarding houses serve the same function at lower price points. The economy is entirely analog — physical currency, paper ledgers, handshake agreements. GDP is unmeasurable by design.
Properties.power_structure: Municipal charter authority, enforced by the island's own constabulary and the legal precedent that protects the technology restriction zone. No corporate sovereign territory. No state jurisdiction beyond what the charter permits. The island's governance is the closest thing to genuine self-determination in the GLM, sustained not by power but by legal precedent and the useful fiction that the island is too small to matter.
Properties.dangers: The lack of surveillance means the lack of emergency response infrastructure — violence here is private and unreported; Dead-drop operations gone wrong — the island's anonymity attracts people with things to hide, and some of those things are dangerous; The legal precedent protecting the technology restriction zone is always one court challenge away from collapse; Being recognized in a place designed for anonymity — some visitors take the unrecorded status very seriously; The ferry crossing — the 5-kilometer strait is the only access, and it can be watched even if the island cannot
Properties.opportunities: Unrecorded meetings — the island's primary commodity is surveillance absence; Dead-drop facilitation — serving as intermediary for information exchanges that cannot happen on the grid; Disappearance infrastructure — the island's analog systems can absorb identities that need to stop existing; The Grand Hotel's network of contacts — the staff know everyone who matters and remember nothing officially
Properties.story_hooks: A negotiation at the Grand Hotel between two corporate sovereigns has gone wrong, and both parties are trapped on an island with no communications and no way to call for backup; The technology restriction zone's legal challenge has reached a court that might actually rule against it — and the island's permanent residents are preparing for a siege; Someone has been leaving analog messages at dead-drop sites across the island — written in a code that predates digital encryption — and the messages describe events that haven't happened yet
Properties.sights: Horse-drawn carriages on streets with no power lines, no signal towers, no surveillance cameras; The Grand Hotel's 200-meter porch, overlooking the Straits, populated by people whose faces you are not supposed to remember; The Mackinac Bridge visible from the east shore — the hypermodern world, close enough to see, far enough to deny; Victorian architecture maintained with deliberate precision — not nostalgia, but infrastructure for anonymity; Visitors unconsciously reaching for neural interfaces that don't connect — the phantom limb of a disconnected world
Properties.sounds: Horse hooves on pavement — the island's primary transportation sound; Human conversation without the overlay of augmented reality — raw, unfiltered, and strangely intimate; Lake water on the shoreline — the sound of a place where nature is louder than technology; The absence of electronic noise — no hums, no pings, no background data traffic — a silence most visitors have never experienced
Properties.smells: Horse, hay, and leather — the organic infrastructure of pre-motor transportation; Mackinac Island fudge — still produced, still sold, still the island's most innocent tradition; Lake Huron air, unprocessed and unfiltered — what air smelled like before the cities
Properties.feel: Uncanny. Ghostbridge Island feels like a glitch in the timeline — a place where 2200 forgot to arrive. The sensation of disconnection is physical for augmented visitors. Neural interfaces go silent. Uplinks drop. You are alone with your unaugmented senses, and for most GLM residents, that is the most disorienting experience available. It is also, for some, the most honest.

Properties.description:
Every ton of iron ore, grain, limestone, and manufactured goods moving between Lake Superior and the lower Great Lakes passes through the Soo Locks, and the Soo Locks sit on the American side of the St. Marys River, which makes Lockhaven South the most strategically valuable small city in the Great Lakes Metropolitan Area. The locks were built by the Army Corps of Engineers in the nineteenth century. They are now operated by a rotating consortium of corporate sovereigns — currently led by Stonepath Logistics and Ferrogate Transit — who maintain the infrastructure in exchange for tariff revenue on every vessel that transits. The arrangement makes the consortium very rich and makes Lockhaven South very tense, because everyone involved understands that controlling the locks means controlling the GLM's arterial commerce.

The city wraps around the lock complex like a parasite around its host. The waterfront is entirely corporate sovereign territory — lock operations, vessel staging areas, cargo inspection facilities, and the security infrastructure required to protect the most important chokepoint in the interior of the continent. Behind the waterfront, the city proper is a contested zone in a different sense: Lockhaven South sits in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, which is the subject of an ongoing territorial dispute between the states of Michigan and Wisconsin. Michigan claims historical sovereignty. Wisconsin claims the UP was economically abandoned by Michigan's lower peninsula government and that Wisconsin's integration of the UP into its economic sphere constitutes de facto jurisdiction. The federal government, such as it remains, has declined to adjudicate. The result is a city with three competing authority structures — corporate (the lock consortium), state (Michigan and Wisconsin both), and federal (the military presence that guards the locks as critical infrastructure).

The residential population lives in this jurisdictional overlap and has developed the particular cynicism of people governed by everyone and represented by no one. The Upper Peninsula's war — Wisconsin versus Michigan — plays out here in competing propaganda, dueling law enforcement agencies, and occasional violence that both sides blame on the other. The locks don't care. The ships keep coming.
Properties.aliases: Sault Ste. Marie MI, The American Soo, South Lock, The Chokepoint
Properties.demographics: Population 45,000 permanent residents, plus an estimated 8,000 transient military, corporate, and shipping personnel. The permanent population is predominantly Tier 2, with deep roots — families that have lived here for generations, through every jurisdictional change. Michigan loyalists and Wisconsin partisans split the city roughly 60-40.
Properties.economy: Lock operations and shipping services. The consortium's tariff revenue flows through the city's economy like blood through a body — when shipping volumes drop, everything drops. The military presence provides a stable secondary income stream. The contested jurisdiction makes formal business difficult, which makes informal business thrive.
Properties.power_structure: The lock consortium (Stonepath Logistics, Ferrogate Transit, and rotating members) controls the waterfront. Federal military authority controls the security perimeter. Michigan claims civil jurisdiction. Wisconsin claims economic jurisdiction. The four authorities maintain an uneasy coexistence that functions only because the locks must function, and nobody is willing to be the one who breaks them.
Properties.dangers: Jurisdictional paralysis — four competing authorities means emergency response is a negotiation; The UP territorial war — Michigan-Wisconsin tensions erupt into violence here more than anywhere else in the peninsula; Lock infrastructure sabotage — the highest-consequence target in the interior GLM; Espionage density — the intelligence presence per capita is the highest in the Great Lakes; Federal military authority operating with wartime rules of engagement around the lock perimeter
Properties.opportunities: Shipping intelligence — same as the Canadian side, but with better access to the primary locks; Jurisdictional arbitrage — the competing authorities create gaps that operators can exploit; The UP war creates demand for intermediaries, fixers, and people who can move between Michigan and Wisconsin networks; Federal contracts for lock security — lucrative, stable, and available to those with the right clearances
Properties.story_hooks: The lock consortium's next rotation is contested — two corponations claim the seat, and both are willing to shut down shipping to prove their point; A vessel carrying Wisconsin military hardware was detained in the locks by Michigan-aligned corporate security — the UP war's first naval engagement; The federal military has been quietly expanding the lock security perimeter into the residential city, and nobody is sure if it's infrastructure protection or occupation
Properties.sights: The Soo Locks in operation — massive vessels rising 6 meters as Lake Superior becomes Lake Huron; Corporate sovereign territory signs on the waterfront, overlapping with Michigan state markers and Wisconsin claim notices; Military checkpoint infrastructure around the lock perimeter — federal authority made visible in concrete and steel; The International Bridge to the Canadian side, a thin line of lights over dark water; Competing Michigan and Wisconsin flags on residential buildings — a territory war fought in fabric
Properties.sounds: Lock gates cycling — the sound of continental commerce being physically moved; Ship-to-shore communications on public frequencies — automated traffic management speaking to itself; Michigan State Police and Wisconsin Territorial Authority drones competing for airspace; The water — the St. Marys River moving with purpose, funneled through infrastructure into utility
Properties.smells: Iron ore dust from the cargo vessels — red-brown and gritty, the UP's primary export made airborne; River water processed through lock mechanisms — a clean, hydraulic smell; Military vehicle exhaust from the federal security perimeter
Properties.feel: A city that matters more than it should and knows it. Lockhaven South's 45,000 residents live at the intersection of four competing jurisdictions, and the locks are the reason all four care. The city doesn't belong to anyone, which means everyone is trying to take it.

Properties.description: Victorian-era negotiation venue — 200 meters of porch, zero meters of surveillance coverage, and a guest list that exists only in the concierge's memory
A system of physical information exchange points maintained across the island — the analog internet, operated by hand
The historical military fortification, now serving as the island constabulary's headquarters and the physical symbol of the charter's authority

University Circle was Cleveland's cultural and intellectual center — home to Case Western Reserve University, the Cleveland Clinic, the Cleveland Museum of Art, and a concentration of educational and medical institutions that made the neighborhood one of the most institutionally dense square miles in America. All of those institutions still exist, technically. What they have become is something their founders would not recognize.

Case Western Reserve University was acquired by Tessera CorpoNation in 2158 as part of a broader strategy to secure academic research pipelines for neural interface development. The university's name was preserved — Tessera understands the value of institutional branding — but its research agenda is now entirely aligned with Tessera's product roadmap. The Cleveland Clinic underwent a parallel transformation, absorbed into Helix Biosystems' medical services division in 2163. The Clinic's famous research campus is now a Helix sovereign medical zone where experimental procedures are conducted under proprietary jurisdiction, exempt from whatever remains of medical ethics oversight. The Cleveland Museum of Art, unable to compete with neural-direct experience galleries, was converted into a Vantablack Media production facility in 2171, its permanent collection digitized, archived, and reportedly sold to private collectors whose identities Vantablack declines to disclose.

What connects these institutions is the Spine — a climate-controlled elevated walkway system that links every major building in the district, creating a continuous interior environment that Tessera, Helix, and Vantablack employees can traverse without ever touching the ground-level streets. The Spine is the district's real architecture. Below it, the original streets serve as loading docks, maintenance access, and housing for the service workers who keep the elevated institutions running. The vertical segregation is literal: the people who work in the Spine look down at the people who work beneath it, and the sightline goes only one way because the Spine's windows are one-way smart glass.
Properties.aliases: University Circle, The Spine, Case District, Clinic Row
Properties.demographics: Above the Spine: approximately 8,000 Tessera, Helix, and Vantablack employees, predominantly Tier 3-4, universally augmented. Below the Spine: approximately 20,000 service workers, maintenance staff, and their families, predominantly Tier 1-2. The two populations share physical space and inhabit different worlds.
Properties.economy: Neural interface R&D (Tessera), experimental medicine and biotech (Helix Biosystems), media production (Vantablack). The above-Spine economy is entirely corporate. The below-Spine economy is service-based — food preparation, cleaning, maintenance, delivery — compensated at rates that keep workers functional but never mobile. The three corponations maintain a joint economic zone agreement that standardizes wages below the Spine at levels that are, by pure coincidence, identical across all three employers.
Properties.power_structure: Tripartite corporate sovereignty. Tessera controls the university campus. Helix controls the medical campus. Vantablack controls the cultural campus. The Spine itself is jointly administered under a shared governance protocol called the Circle Compact. Ground-level territory is technically under Tollgate infrastructure sovereignty, but Tollgate's presence is minimal — they collect fees and maintain systems, but the three resident corponations effectively control everything.
Properties.dangers: Corporate jurisdiction complexity — three overlapping sovereignties create legal ambiguities that are dangerous for anyone without a corporate attorney; Helix medical testing — the sovereign medical zone operates without external oversight, and the below-Spine population is a convenient source of test subjects who have limited legal recourse; Tessera neural research proximity — experimental BCI signals occasionally leak from the research campus, causing interface glitches in anyone within range; Surveillance density — above the Spine is one of the most monitored environments in the corridor, with three corporate security systems operating simultaneously; Below-Spine exploitation — the wage-fixing arrangement keeps service workers in permanent economic stasis with no pathway to above-Spine employment
