Properties.opportunities: Disappearance services — for the right reason or the right price, Wautoma Null can make someone cease to exist in every database that matters; Route intelligence — knowledge of safe passage through ungoverned territory is extraordinarily valuable to anyone operating outside corporate zones; Off-grid staging — the Null is an ideal base for operations that require complete signal darkness and zero corporate surveillance; Analog living — skills, knowledge, and social structures that predate corporate dependency, preserved here and increasingly rare everywhere else
Properties.story_hooks: A runner arrives in Wautoma Null carrying something that multiple corponations want badly enough to break the town's obscurity — and the town council must decide whether to hand it over, hide it, or use it; Saltmarsh Telecom announces plans to extend its signal grid through Wautoma Null, which would connect the town to the corridor's communications infrastructure and simultaneously end its invisibility — the council is split between those who want connection and those who understand that connection means control; Something is killing livestock and occasionally people in the wildlands north of town — not wildlife behavior, something deliberate, and the tracks suggest a biotech origin that points back toward one of the corporate zones to the east
Properties.sights: The old courthouse, limestone and fern, its clock tower stopped at 3:47 — the moment the power grid was disconnected in 2143; Hand-painted signs replacing the holographic advertisements that exist everywhere else — directions, warnings, and community notices in actual paint on actual wood; Solar arrays and wind turbines cobbled together from salvaged components, the town's independent power grid visible on every rooftop; The darkness at night — real darkness, no light pollution, stars visible in a way that corridor residents have never experienced; Runners' vehicles parked at the provisioning depot, modified for off-grid travel with extra fuel cells and signal-dampening armor
Properties.sounds: Wind — unobstructed, unfiltered, carrying sounds from the surrounding wildlands that urban ears can't identify; The absence of machine hum — no server farms, no data conduits, no climate control. The silence is physical, a pressure on the eardrums; Town council debates echoing from the courthouse, audible through broken windows — democracy conducted at speaking volume; Generator startup sounds at dusk as the town's patchwork power grid comes online; Coyote packs in the surrounding territory, closer to town than they should be, recolonizing the spaces humans abandoned
Properties.smells: Wood smoke — Wautoma Null heats with actual fire, a smell that has become as exotic as perfume; Pine and earth from the encroaching forest, which has advanced three kilometers toward town since 2160; Cooking — real food, not synthetic, grown in community gardens and hunted from the wildlands; The particular clean emptiness of air that hasn't been processed, filtered, or scented by corporate AtmoSync systems
Properties.feel: Quiet in a way that frightens corridor visitors and soothes everyone else. Wautoma Null feels like the world used to feel, or at least like people imagine it did — slower, smaller, governed by weather and daylight instead of shift schedules and tier access. It is not a utopia. The winters are brutal, the medical resources are primitive, and the isolation is occasionally lethal. But it is free in a sense that the word has almost lost, and the people who live here carry themselves with the particular self-possession of those who've chosen difficulty over dependence.

Properties.description: The Windsor-Detroit Tunnel — 1.6 kilometers of jurisdictional void where neither Canadian nor corporate law applies, and everyone moves fast
The manufacturing enclave strip along the riverfront — corporate sovereign territory technically in Canada, practically in nowhere
Climate-refugee housing district — 80,000 people in prefab towers, building a community out of displacement
A cluster of interconnected rooftops that serves as Old Harbor's closest thing to a town square — market stalls, a clinic, and the community's only working comm relay
Three drowned churches whose spires still break the waterline — the upper galleries are used as meeting halls and the underwater naves are sacred diving sites
Engineered bioluminescent algae farms that provide both light and a meager food source — tended by families who treat the cultivation as an art form

O'Hare Sovereign is the hole in the map. When corporate sovereignty claims carved Meridian 88 into jurisdictional territories, the airport was the first piece claimed and the most completely transformed. It is no longer an airport in any traditional sense — it is a sovereign logistics zone, a corporate free port, and the single most important physical node in Meridian 88's connection to the outside world. Three corponations share sovereignty over O'Hare's territory in a rare joint-governance arrangement: Helion controls passenger processing and data, Vantage Meridian controls cargo and logistics, and Axiom Industrial controls the aerospace infrastructure itself. The three-way governance creates jurisdictional complexity that would be bureaucratic nightmare if it were not, in fact, the point — the complexity is the product, because complexity creates gaps, and gaps create opportunities for the kind of commerce that thrives in the spaces between rules.

The physical footprint is immense — O'Hare Sovereign occupies more land area than any other single jurisdiction in Meridian 88. The original airport's footprint has expanded outward, consuming the surrounding neighborhoods and replacing residential blocks with logistics infrastructure: automated cargo handling systems, drone launch platforms, VTOL pads, fuel processing facilities, and the Runway — an eight-kilometer strip that can accommodate the suborbital freight carriers that connect Meridian 88 to the global supply chain. The scale is inhuman, designed for machines and cargo rather than people, and the human population that exists within the zone reflects this: workers are temporary, badged, tracked, and discarded when their contracts expire.

The Terminal is where humans interface with the machine. A vast, multi-level processing facility that handles the passengers, refugees, diplomats, corporate transfers, and undocumented travelers who move through O'Hare's gates daily. The upper levels are corporate transit — clean, efficient, surveilled, and expensive. The lower levels are general processing — crowded, slow, invasive, and designed to extract maximum data from every person who passes through. Below general processing, there are levels that do not appear on any public directory — the transit detention facilities where people whose documentation does not satisfy the three-way jurisdictional requirements are held in a legal limbo that can last days, weeks, or indefinitely.

The free-port economy is O'Hare Sovereign's true purpose. Cargo that enters the zone is subject to the governance of whichever corponation processes it, which means that by routing goods through the right jurisdictional channel, importers can subject their cargo to whichever regulatory framework is most permissive. Weapons that are prohibited in Helion territory can be processed through Axiom's jurisdiction. Data that Vantage restricts can be routed through Helion's processing. Biological materials that all three nominally prohibit somehow find their way through the gaps between their overlapping authorities. The free port is not lawless — it is over-lawed, with three competing legal systems creating a regulatory labyrinth that only specialists can navigate, and navigating it is one of the most lucrative professions in Meridian 88.
Properties.aliases: O'Hare, The Port, O'Hare Free Zone, The Runway
Properties.demographics: Transient worker population of approximately 40,000-60,000, badge-tracked and jurisdiction-assigned. Permanent residents effectively zero — the zone is not designed for habitation. Transit population varies between 100,000-200,000 on any given day. The detention levels hold an undisclosed number of people in jurisdictional limbo.
Properties.economy: The free-port economy is Meridian 88's primary interface with the global supply chain. Revenue is split between the three sovereign corponations according to processing jurisdiction. The regulatory arbitrage industry — specialists who route cargo and people through optimal jurisdictional channels — generates billions annually. The underground economy within the zone focuses on transit services, document fabrication, and the movement of goods and people through jurisdictional gaps.
Properties.power_structure: Three-way corporate sovereignty: Helion (passenger and data), Vantage Meridian (cargo and logistics), Axiom Industrial (aerospace infrastructure). A joint coordination body called the Triad Commission manages inter-jurisdictional disputes, but in practice each corponation governs its domain independently. Security is provided by each corponation within its jurisdiction, creating overlapping patrols with different rules of engagement. The gaps between jurisdictions are where the real power operates — the fixers, brokers, and regulatory arbitrage specialists who know how to move through the seams.
Properties.dangers: Three overlapping security jurisdictions with different rules of engagement — crossing the wrong line can trigger an incident with no clear resolution authority; Transit detention — being flagged by any of the three jurisdictions can result in indefinite holding without recourse; The free-port economy attracts the full spectrum of organized criminal enterprise, operating behind regulatory arbitrage cover; Badge tracking means total surveillance within the zone — every movement logged by at least one jurisdiction; Suborbital freight operations create physical danger zones where ground-level humans are not expected to survive; Document seizure — the three jurisdictions do not share data, which means travel documents valid in one zone may be flagged in another
Properties.opportunities: O'Hare Sovereign is the only way in or out of Meridian 88 for most people — controlling access to transit is enormously valuable; Regulatory arbitrage skills are among the most lucrative in the corridor — knowing the three jurisdictions is a career; The jurisdictional gaps create space for moving goods and people that cannot be moved through any single corporate system; The transit population includes people from everywhere — O'Hare is the best place in Meridian 88 for global intelligence; The Triad Commission's inter-jurisdictional disputes create leverage opportunities for anyone with information about corporate wrongdoing in the zone
Properties.story_hooks: A person is being held in transit detention who should not exist — their biometric data matches someone who died in corporate records three years ago, and all three jurisdictions are claiming authority over the case while secretly trying to acquire the detainee for different reasons. Someone needs to extract them before any of the three corponations succeeds.; A cargo container routed through Axiom's jurisdiction has been flagged by Helion's data systems as containing biological material that violates all three sovereignty codes. The container is sitting on a processing pad, and the clock is ticking before Axiom's automated systems route it to its destination. The contents could be evidence of corporate bioweapons research — or it could be a Helion false-flag operation designed to trigger a Triad Commission investigation that weakens Axiom's position.; A regulatory arbitrage specialist has disappeared inside the zone — last badged entering Vantage's cargo jurisdiction and never badged out. Their client list includes some of the most sensitive operations in the free port. Whoever finds them first controls a significant amount of leverage over multiple powerful interests.
Properties.sights: The Runway — eight kilometers of landing strip lit by approach lighting that is visible from orbit; Automated cargo systems moving containers with inhuman precision, twenty-four hours without pause; The Terminal's layered architecture — corporate transit gleaming above, general processing grinding below; Suborbital freight carriers descending on approach — massive, loud, trailing heat signatures visible for kilometers; Badge-tracked workers moving in shift patterns, color-coded by corponation jurisdiction; VTOL pads launching in sequence, the staccato rhythm of logistics in motion
Properties.sounds: Engine noise — constant, layered, ranging from the deep rumble of freight carriers to the high whine of VTOL systems; The Terminal's public address system announcing in twelve languages, the same information in different jurisdictional contexts; Automated cargo handling — the mechanical percussion of containers being sorted, scanned, and routed; The particular silence of the transit detention levels, insulated by design; Security checkpoint tones — badge verification, access granted, access denied, repeated thousands of times per hour
Properties.smells: Aviation fuel — the chemical baseline of every breath in the zone; Recycled air in the Terminal, processed to different quality standards by level; Cargo holds opened in processing — the mixed scents of goods from every origin point on the planet; Ozone and overheated electronics from the automated systems; The detention levels smell like disinfectant and fear — a combination that is universal across holding facilities
Properties.feel: Overwhelming and dehumanizing. O'Hare Sovereign operates at a scale that reduces people to cargo — processed, sorted, routed, and valued by throughput rather than identity. The three-way jurisdiction creates a permanent sense of uncertainty about which rules apply, which makes the zone simultaneously the freest and most controlled space in Meridian 88. Power here is not about authority — it is about knowing which authority to invoke.

Properties.description:
Tidebreak was not planned. It was panicked. In 2169, when the New York Coastal Inundation Events — a sanitized term for the systematic drowning of a city that had been told for fifty years it was going to drown — displaced 4.2 million people in eighteen months, the refugee wave crashed westward along the old I-90 corridor toward the Great Lakes like water finding its own level. Most ended up in M88's lower tiers, absorbed into the Shelf's excluded population. But a contingent of roughly 40,000 — organized by a coalition of displaced NYC community leaders, union organizers, and one profoundly stubborn marine engineer named Rosa Espinoza — refused to become someone else's underclass. They had seen what happened when you trusted institutions to house you. They had seen the refugee camps. They chose the water instead.

Espinoza had studied the seacrete cities. She'd corresponded with Freestone's Reef Council. She understood the electrodeposition process — low-voltage current through submerged wire mesh, mineral accretion from dissolved lake carbonates, structures that grow from the water itself. She also understood that Lake Ontario, the easternmost Great Lake, was the closest to the displaced New York population and the least claimed by existing corponation interests. The first frameworks went into the water in the winter of 2169, powered by generators salvaged from flooded Con Edison substations. The accretion was slow in Ontario's cold water. People lived on rafts and barges lashed together while the reef grew beneath them. They called the settlement Tidebreak — a name that referenced both the lake's currents and what they were trying to do to the tide of displacement that had swept them here.

Tidebreak grew unevenly, desperately, and beautifully. Unlike Freestone's organic expansion or Deepwell's engineered precision, Tidebreak's architecture reflects the chaos of its founding: platforms at different heights, structures that lean, walkways that zigzag around obstacles that were living spaces before they were obstacles. The city looks improvised because it was improvised, and the improvisation became an aesthetic — layered, dense, human-scaled, full of the kind of detail that emerges when forty thousand people are all building at once without a master plan. New Yorkers brought New York with them: the density, the vertical ambition, the stubborn belief that a city is defined by its people rather than its infrastructure. Tidebreak is the most culturally vibrant of the lake cities — music, art, food, theater, argument. It is also the poorest, the most crowded, and the most in need of everything from medical supplies to structural engineers.

Governance is a borough system adapted from New York's old structure — five boroughs, each with an elected borough council, overseen by a General Council that manages inter-borough affairs and external relations. The system is chaotic, loud, and functional in the way that democracy is functional when the alternative is drowning. Population: 210,000 — the second-largest lake city, and growing, because refugees keep coming and Tidebreak keeps saying yes.
Properties.aliases: The Refugee Reef, Ontario Free City, New Hope, The Raft of the Displaced
Properties.demographics: 210,000 permanent residents, predominantly descended from the New York Coastal Displacement wave of 2169-2172. Ethnically and culturally diverse — Tidebreak reflects New York's demographics compressed onto a seacrete reef. Significant communities of Caribbean, East Asian, Latin American, and Eastern European heritage. The city continues to accept refugees from shore-based displacement events and has never turned anyone away.
Properties.economy: The poorest lake city in per-capita terms. Economy is service-based, cultural, and aid-dependent. Primary exports: artisanal goods, cultural products (music recordings, art, handcrafted items), and labor — Tidebreak residents hire out as construction workers, seacrete engineers, and translators to the other lake cities. Imports: almost everything. Annual external trade: approximately Φ3.1 billion, supplemented by Φ1.8 billion in mutual aid from Freestone and Threshold. The economy is precarious and everyone knows it.
Properties.power_structure: Borough council system. Five boroughs — Midtown, Battery, Heights, the Yards, and Newtown — each elect a borough council of five. The General Council of twenty-five manages external affairs and resource allocation. Decision-making is slow, contentious, and broadly legitimate. No corporate entities permitted under the founding charter. The Harbor Guard — 1,400 volunteers with converted civilian vessels — provides defense.
Properties.dangers: Structural instability — Tidebreak's improvised construction means that some sections are genuinely unsafe; Resource scarcity — the city doesn't produce enough food, medicine, or building materials internally; Proximity to old New York ruins — salvage expeditions into the flooded city are lucrative and frequently fatal; Population pressure — Tidebreak keeps accepting refugees without the infrastructure to support them; Political exploitation — shore-based factions see Tidebreak's poverty as leverage
Properties.opportunities: Cultural capital — Tidebreak's art, music, and cuisine are valued across the Great Lakes; New York salvage — the flooded ruins of the old city contain technology, data, and materials worth fortunes; Labor force — Tidebreak's people are resourceful, multilingual, and willing to work; Moral authority — Tidebreak's refugee-founded identity gives it a rhetorical power that richer cities lack
Properties.story_hooks: A salvage team returns from the flooded New York ruins with a sealed data archive from a pre-collapse financial institution. The contents could shift the balance of power among the corponations. Multiple factions converge on Tidebreak to acquire it.; Tidebreak's General Council votes to accept 30,000 new refugees from a Gulf Coast displacement event. The city's infrastructure can't handle the influx. Freestone offers help — with conditions.; Kyle is hired to escort a cargo shipment to Tidebreak. The cargo is medical supplies. The client who hired him is Lazarus Pharmaceuticals. Something doesn't add up.
Properties.sights: Layered, uneven seacrete architecture — platforms at different heights, structures leaning into each other, a vertical density that echoes old Manhattan; Murals everywhere — Tidebreak's artists have covered every available surface with color, memory, and defiance; Refugee arrival platforms on the eastern edge, where boats from shore still bring new residents regularly; Laundry lines strung between structures, flags and banners from a hundred communities of origin; The Espinoza Monument — a seacrete statue of the founder, grown organically from the city's first accretion framework, perpetually being added to by residents
Properties.sounds: Music — constantly, from everywhere. Tidebreak's musicians play on platforms, in corridors, on boats. The city has more live music per capita than any settlement on the Great Lakes.; Argument — Tidebreak is loud, opinionated, and never not having a political discussion; Construction — the city is always building, always expanding, always accreting; Languages — English, Spanish, Mandarin, Haitian Creole, and a dozen others. Tidebreak's linguistic diversity exceeds M88's.
Properties.smells: Cooking from a hundred culinary traditions — Tidebreak's food scene is legendary among the lake cities; Fresh seacrete — the mineral-chalk smell of new growth, a constant presence in a city that never stops building; Lake Ontario — cleaner than Erie, warmer than Superior, carrying the faint organic scent of the St. Lawrence outflow; Paint and adhesive from the mural artists — Tidebreak smells like art being made
Properties.feel: Alive and desperate and beautiful. Tidebreak has the energy of a place that was built by people who had no other option and decided to make it extraordinary anyway. It's crowded, chaotic, structurally questionable, and more culturally alive than anything on shore. Walking through Tidebreak feels like walking through a city that is simultaneously falling apart and being born. The people here have already lost one home. They will fight for this one with everything they have.

Properties.description: The half-submerged Ringo Industries hull whose flooded lower decks now house the settlement's primary food production — a bioluminescent algae farm that also serves as the community's most surreal social space.
The central pleasure craft that houses the Ship Council chamber, the community radio station, and the settlement's only functioning med-bay with shore-grade diagnostic equipment.

The Catalytic Mile is Detroit's cultural preservation district — a roughly one-mile stretch of Woodward Avenue anchored by the Detroit Institute of Arts on one end and the Wayne State University Cognitive Sciences Campus on the other. The name is corporate marketing, coined by the Palladian Construction subsidiary that rebuilt the district in the 2060s, referencing both the catalytic converter (automotive heritage) and the idea of cultural catalysis. Locals just call it Midtown, because they called it that before the corps arrived and they'll call it that after the corps leave, assuming the corps ever leave.

The DIA survived the collapse years because someone — the historical record is deliberately vague about who — negotiated a cultural preservation easement with Cinderblock AI in exchange for data rights to every visitor's neural interface. The museum still stands, its Diego Rivera murals intact behind climate-controlled glass, and every person who looks at them has their aesthetic response recorded, analyzed, and sold on the Tessera Behavioral Exchange. Rivera would have appreciated the irony. Wayne State University was absorbed into the Tessera Academic Partnership Network in 2158, its cognitive sciences department becoming one of Tessera's primary research feeders. The campus is technically independent. The funding is not.

The district between these two anchors is a curated bohemia — galleries, performance spaces, restaurants, and residential blocks designed to feel organic while being entirely corporate-planned. Artists live here on subsidized leases, producing work that makes the district attractive to the Tier 3 residents whose rents actually pay for things. It's a terrarium. The art is real, the community is real, the subsidies create a dependency structure that means the entire cultural ecosystem exists at the pleasure of the corporate landlords. Pull the subsidies and the Mile dies in six months. Everyone knows this. Nobody says it at gallery openings.
Properties.demographics: Approximately 45,000 residents. A mix of subsidized artists (Tier 1-2), university students and faculty (Tier 2-3), and the Tier 3-4 professionals whose market-rate rents cross-subsidize the entire district. The demographic balance is carefully managed by Palladian's district algorithms.
Properties.economy: Cultural tourism, university research funding, gallery sales, and the invisible economy of neural data harvested from every aesthetic experience in the district. The DIA alone generates Φ2.1 billion annually in behavioral data licensing.
Properties.power_structure: Palladian Construction owns the land and manages the district through an AI-driven property management system called the Curator. Wayne State's administration answers to the Tessera Academic Partnership Board. The artists' cooperative has a seat at district planning meetings but no vote.
Properties.dangers: Subsidy dependency — cross the wrong corporate sponsor and lose your housing in 30 days; Neural data harvesting — every aesthetic experience in the district is recorded and monetized; Academic surveillance — Wayne State research is monitored for commercially exploitable discoveries; Gentrification pressure — the district's success constantly pushes outward, consuming adjacent neighborhoods; The Curator algorithm — Palladian's district AI makes residency decisions that no human reviews
Properties.opportunities: Access to Wayne State's cognitive sciences research — cutting-edge BCI work with less security than a corporate lab; The artist community is a network of people who see things differently — valuable for intelligence and perspective; Gallery openings are where corporate executives drop their guard and talk to people they consider harmless
Properties.story_hooks: A Wayne State researcher discovers that the DIA's neural harvesting system has been modified to do more than record — it's been inserting cognitive suggestions into visitors for years; The Curator algorithm is about to terminate subsidies for an entire block of artist housing. The residents have 30 days to find Φ4 million or become homeless.; A student collective has been using Wayne State's cognitive lab after hours to develop open-source BCI firmware — Tessera has noticed
Properties.sights: The DIA's Beaux-Arts facade preserved in amber — literally encased in transparent protective shielding; Street murals refreshed by AR overlay, the original paint preserved beneath digital augmentation layers; Wayne State's cognitive sciences tower, its upper floors glowing with Tessera branding after dark; Gallery windows displaying art that your neural interface automatically prices and attributes; Students and artists mixing on Woodward, distinguishable by the age of their augments
Properties.sounds: Live music from subsidized venues — jazz, electronic, neo-Motown, all of it genuine, all of it funded; The murmur of gallery crowds, punctuated by the soft chime of neural interface art-purchase confirmations; University lecture broadcasts leaking from open windows — cognitive science terminology in excited voices; Street performers who are actually good, because the bad ones get algorithmically de-prioritized by the district management AI; The 5 PM autonomous transit chime, when the subsidized artist shuttles run to cheaper districts
Properties.smells: Coffee and paint thinner — the two fuels of the creative class; Restaurant row along Cass Avenue, where the food is excellent and the prices exclude anyone below Tier 2; Old building materials — the district preserved some original structures, and they smell like history slowly losing to chemistry
Properties.feel: Beautiful and compromised. The Catalytic Mile feels like a place where genuine creativity happens inside a corporate terrarium. The art is real. The music is real. The community is real. The fact that all of it exists because a construction corponation decided cultural districts increase adjacent property values by 23% does not make the art less real. It makes everything else less honest.

Properties.description: 296 acres of urban green space, maintained by the cooperative's environmental systems — the neighborhood's lungs and its most valuable non-technical asset
Ground-floor workshops along Woodward — where cooperative members build things that corporate R&D labs wish they'd thought of first
A converted apartment building that houses the cooperative's central computing infrastructure — where four-second democracy runs on hardware maintained by volunteers

Pelican Drift is Meridian 88's largest permanent floating settlement, a loose confederation of barges, decommissioned platform rigs, and engineered pontoon structures moored approximately four kilometers off the western shore of Lake Michigan. It began in the 2150s as a squatter settlement on a pair of abandoned Arcturus Defense Solutions test platforms — Arcturus had used the lake for weapons systems trials and walked away when the contracts ended, leaving the infrastructure behind. Squatters arrived within months. By 2200, Pelican Drift has grown to a population of roughly twelve thousand people spread across sixty-plus connected structures ranging from a repurposed Carrion Logistics freight barge to handbuilt pontoon cabins barely large enough for two.

The settlement is technically outside Meridian 88's jurisdictional boundary, which is drawn at the shoreline. This legal ambiguity is the foundation of Pelican Drift's entire identity. No corponation has formal claim. No Tier system officially applies. Taxes don't reach here. Neither does most enforcement. The Drift operates its own water reclamation, its own power grid (a patchwork of wave energy converters, solar film, and a single aging micro-fission cell that everyone agrees is probably fine), and its own adjudication system built around something its founders called the Compact — a simple document that has been amended forty-seven times and argues about as often.

The lake around Pelican Drift is not safe. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric runs power cables along the lakebed that occasionally fault and electrify surface water in localized patches. There are E.L.F. signal clusters in the deep water that mess with navigation systems. And every few months, a Tessera Corporation drone passes overhead performing what Tessera calls 'environmental monitoring' and what the Drift calls 'harassment.' But the people of Pelican Drift are lake people now, defined by distance from shore, and most of them would not go back for anything.
Properties.aliases: The Float, Drift City, Lake Town, The Pelican
Properties.demographics: Extraordinarily diverse. Pelican Drift draws from every Tier and background — Tier 1 refugees who couldn't afford shore life, Tier 3 idealists who chose the Drift deliberately, former corponation employees who burned their contracts and ran, fisherfolk who predate the settlement's formal structure, and a growing second generation born on the water who have never lived on shore. Synthetic persons constitute roughly 8% of the population and have full Compact rights, making the Drift one of the few places in Meridian 88 where synthetic personhood is not debated.
Properties.economy: Fishing remains the foundational economy — the Drift runs serious commercial operations that supply protein to Lakeshore Corridor markets. Secondary income comes from lakebed salvage (both the Arcturus-era test equipment and older wreckage), Diaspora signal relay services (the Drift's elevated antenna structures make it a useful relay point despite the weaker signal), and grey-market services that benefit from being four kilometers outside any jurisdiction. The Drift also runs a small but profitable tourism operation for shore-dwellers who want to experience lake life without committing.
Properties.power_structure: The Compact Council is elected annually from among registered residents — registration requires one continuous year of residency. Executive decisions require a simple majority; changes to the Compact itself require two-thirds. Enforcement is handled by the Drift Watch, a rotating volunteer constabulary that carries non-lethal equipment and has a reputation for genuine impartiality. Corponation influence is minimal but not zero — Carrion Logistics, which owns the largest barge in the Drift's core, has never formally relinquished its claim to that vessel, a legal shadow that comes up in Compact discussions every few years.
Properties.dangers: Zheng-Dao Bioelectric lakebed cable faults, which electrify surface water with lethal unpredictability; Storm events — the Drift is engineered for lake weather but a bad November storm tests every connection point; The micro-fission cell on the Arcturus rig, which is older than anyone is comfortable with and serviced by a single engineer who refuses to share her maintenance logs; E.L.F. signal clusters in the deep water, which interfere with navigation systems and occasionally produce stranger effects; Tessera Corporation's escalating 'environmental monitoring' — there is credible intelligence that Tessera wants the platform location for a lakeborne data center
Properties.opportunities: Lakebed salvage from Arcturus Defense Solutions test equipment — weapons systems, navigation hardware, and classified prototype components; Jurisdiction-free services: contracts, meetings, and transactions that need to happen outside Meridian 88's legal framework; Deep-water E.L.F. signal clusters have been partially mapped by a Drift resident — the map is for sale, the price is negotiable
Properties.story_hooks: The micro-fission cell on the Arcturus rig has begun producing anomalous readings that the Drift's sole engineer is refusing to disclose to the Compact Council. Three people who live nearest the rig have independently reported the same dream — a woman in an Arcturus uniform standing on the bottom of the lake, looking up. The engineer's name is the same as the woman in the dream. The Compact Council needs someone external to find out what's happening before they have to make a decision they can't take back.; Tessera Corporation has quietly purchased Carrion Logistics' legal claim to the core barge through a chain of shell entities — a fact that a Diaspora investigator has just uncovered and brought to the Drift Watch. Tessera's claim, if pressed, would give them legal standing to demand access to the Drift's most central structure and potentially the Arcturus rig beneath it. The Compact Council needs people who can move fast and off-book to either invalidate the purchase or find out what Tessera actually wants, before Tessera realizes the Drift knows.
Properties.sights: A skyline of mismatched structures — barge hulls, lattice towers, pontoon cabins — connected by rope bridges and gangplanks; Solar film stretched across every available horizontal surface, iridescent in the lake light; Children fishing from the edges of platforms with homemade rods, dropping lines into dark water; The old Arcturus test rig at the Drift's center, its military architecture unmistakable beneath decades of paint and habitation; Fog rolling in off the lake at dawn, reducing visibility to ten meters and making the Drift feel like the only place in the world
Properties.sounds: The creak and slap of structures moving with the lake — constant, rhythmic, almost meditative; Arguments and music carrying clearly across open water, no walls to absorb them; The deep throb of the aging micro-fission cell from the Arcturus rig's lower deck; Foghorns — actual physical foghorns — the Drift maintains them out of tradition and genuine navigational necessity
Properties.smells: Lake water and rust and diesel — the base note of everything; Cooking fish, smoked and fresh, from the eastern food platforms; Ozone from the wave converters and solar film; Wet rope and treated wood
Properties.feel:
Pelican Drift moves. Not dramatically — a meter or two in heavy weather, a gentle sway in calm — but constantly, and this fact shapes everything about life here. Residents develop their sea legs within weeks of arrival and lose their tolerance for perfectly still floors. Visitors often feel mildly nauseated for the first day; residents often feel mildly nauseated on their first night back on shore.

There is a freedom here that is not simply political. The lake surrounds you. The shore is visible but not close. The Diaspora signal is weaker four kilometers out — not absent, but degraded enough that BCI users report a quieter, less crowded mental space. People talk to each other more. The Compact, for all its arguments, actually works, because the alternative is falling in the lake.

Properties.description: The Drift's oldest and largest structure, a decommissioned military test platform that now serves as the Compact Council chamber, the Drift Watch headquarters, and housing for the micro-fission cell
A massive Carrion Logistics freight barge that functions as the Drift's commercial center — market stalls, workshops, and the main Diaspora relay antenna
The outermost floating platforms, where new arrivals typically begin and the fishing lines run deepest, closest to the E.L.F. signal clusters

Peregrine Deck is a rooftop settlement spanning seventeen contiguous building crowns in the Old Harbor mid-tier zone, connected by a web of tensioned cable bridges, pressurized tube corridors, and open-air market platforms bolted to former HVAC infrastructure. It began as a squatter encampment when a Palladian Group development stalled mid-construction forty years ago, leaving three rooftops capped with unfinished structural plating. Enterprising residents welded the gaps, and the settlement grew outward one rooftop at a time until it became something too large and too useful to evict.

The Deck operates at approximately forty stories above street level, above most of the smog band, and benefits from genuine lake wind and unfiltered daylight — luxuries that make it more desirable than its Tier 3 paperwork would suggest. A thriving informal economy has grown around this: rooftop cafes with actual views, solar-capture cooperatives, and a well-regarded open-air clinic run by a Helix Biosystems-trained surgeon who left the corporate track under circumstances she declines to specify. The Palladian Group has never formally abandoned its development claim on the underlying structures, which means Peregrine Deck exists in perpetual legal limbo — one board vote away from demolition, and aware of it.
Properties.aliases: The Deck, High Peregrine, The Roost, Falconplate
Properties.demographics: Tier 2-3 residents with a meaningful population of downwardly mobile former Tier 1 professionals — architects, medics, engineers — who chose community over corporate track. Significant synthetic personhood activist presence; the Deck's legal ambiguity makes it a natural gathering point for those whose own status is similarly unresolved.
Properties.economy: Solar energy cooperatives sell surplus power back into the Old Harbor grid at competitive rates. The open-air market hosts specialty food, BCI repair, and fabrication services. The clinic operates on a sliding-scale payment system that somehow stays solvent, to everyone's mild surprise.
Properties.power_structure: A Residents' Assembly meets weekly and governs by rough consensus, but the clinic's director, Dr. Amara Osei-Bonsu, holds extraordinary informal authority — she has treated nearly every resident and knows things about the community that no one else does.
Properties.dangers: Palladian Group's development claim is active and has been assigned to a new acquisitions team known for aggressive timeline compression — eviction could come with as little as seventy-two hours' legal notice.; The cable bridge connecting Decks 9 and 10 has a stress fracture in its primary tension anchor that the Assembly has been debating how to fund-repair for six months.; Ferrogate Security does not formally patrol the Deck but occasionally sends contractors to 'assess structural safety,' which is understood to be intelligence gathering for Palladian.; The altitude and open exposure make Peregrine Deck visible and vulnerable to precision drone surveillance in ways that street-level communities are not.
Properties.opportunities: The Deck's solar cooperative is looking for someone to negotiate a better grid-sale rate with the Old Harbor energy brokers — the current contract was written by someone who didn't understand leverage.; Dr. Osei-Bonsu has a patient whose BCI implant is transmitting medical data to an unknown third party; she needs someone to trace the signal without alerting whoever is listening.; The Palladian Group's development files on the underlying buildings contain structural surveys that would also reveal every hidden passage and unlisted room in the seventeen structures below — worth considerable money to the right buyer.
Properties.story_hooks: Palladian Group's new acquisitions lead has offered the Residents' Assembly a buyout figure — generous by any measure — but three Assembly members who were leaning toward acceptance have each quietly reversed position within the last week, and no one will say why. Someone is applying pressure, and the Assembly's leadership wants to know the source before the next vote.; A former Sterling-Nakamura data architect arrived on the Deck two months ago with no BCI implants — had them surgically removed, which is both expensive and painful — and has been living quietly under a new name. Someone from off the Deck is asking around about a person matching his description, and the community is divided on whether to protect him or find out what he did first.; The Deck's youngest solar cooperative members have been intercepting a fragmented Diaspora transmission that originates from somewhere within the seventeen buildings below street level — below the Deck, below Old Harbor, somewhere in flooded infrastructure. The signal contains what appears to be a distress call in a language that predates the Diaspora's current architecture.
Properties.sights: Cable bridges sway gently between rooftops, pedestrians gripping the guide rails as lake wind pushes through the open spans.; Solar capture arrays spread across every flat surface like geometric gardens, their tracking mirrors pivoting slowly to follow the sun.; The Lake Michigan horizon is visible on clear days — an unbroken grey-blue line that residents treat as a kind of communal landmark.; Palladian Group survey drones circle at a respectful distance, their camera arms extended, logging everything without ever quite landing.
Properties.sounds: Wind is constant and present here, a low sustained note that underlies every conversation and transaction.; The creak and tension-ping of cable bridges under foot traffic, harmonic and slightly musical.; Laughter and argument from the open-air market platforms, voices carrying further than expected in the clean upper air.
Properties.smells: Genuine fresh air above the smog band, carrying lake salt and cold mineral clarity that feels almost medicinal.; Coffee — real roasted coffee from the Deck's most famous stall, the smell spreading across three rooftops on a good wind.; Hot solder and polymer insulation from the repair workshops clustered near the western bridge terminals.
Properties.feel: Peregrine Deck has the specific energy of a place that knows it is beautiful and knows it might not last. Residents are warm but slightly vigilant — every stranger is assessed for Palladian affiliations before being fully welcomed. The altitude gives everything a quality of remove from the city below, as though the ordinary rules are slightly suspended up here, which they both are and aren't.

Properties.description:
Erie, Pennsylvania was always a port city — defined by Presque Isle, the sandy peninsula that curves into Lake Erie and creates the natural harbor that gave the city its economic reason for existing. In the corridor era, that harbor has become one of the most contested pieces of geography on the lake. Presque Isle itself was designated a restricted sovereign zone in 2154, claimed simultaneously by Cormorant Naval Systems (which wanted it as a forward operating base), the remnant Pennsylvania state government (which wanted to preserve it as a park), and Dredge Sovereign Mining (which discovered that the peninsula's subsurface sediment contained commercially significant mineral deposits). The resulting three-way legal dispute has been in arbitration for forty-six years. In the meantime, all three parties maintain a presence on the peninsula, and none has full control.

The civilian city of Erie occupies the mainland south of the harbor, a mid-sized industrial-residential zone that has maintained a degree of independence unusual for the corridor. The explanation is geographic: Erie sits between the Meridian 88 corridor's western concentration (Cleveland-Toledo) and its eastern terminus (Buffalo), connected to both by the I-90 highway and Ferrogate rail but far enough from either to avoid full economic integration. The result is a city that functions as a transit point and neutral meeting ground — a place where corponation representatives, independent operators, and excluded-economy brokers can conduct business without being in anyone's sovereign territory.

The harbor itself is the city's economic heart. Commercial fishing operations — depleted but persistent — share dock space with cargo handling facilities, a small Kelpline waystation, and the independent boat-repair operations that serve the lake's non-corporate maritime traffic. The fishing fleet is a fraction of what it was, but Lake Erie's fish populations have partially recovered from their 20th-century collapse thanks to the unintentional environmental benefits of industrial lakebed disturbance pushing nutrients upward. The fishers sell to the civilian economy, not to the corponations. This is a point of pride that borders on ideology.
Properties.aliases: Erie PA, The Anchorage, Peninsula City
Properties.demographics: Approximately 55,000 residents. Mixed population reflecting Erie's transit-point function — established families, transient workers, independent operators, and a significant community of fishers whose families have worked the harbor for generations. Tier 1-2 predominantly, with a small Tier 3 professional class. The population's diversity is economic rather than planned.
Properties.economy: Transit services, harbor operations, and neutral-ground commerce. Ferrogate rail transit generates the largest revenue stream. The harbor's fishing and cargo operations employ approximately 4,000 workers. Erie's real economic function is as a meeting place — the neutral-ground commerce generated by corponation negotiations, operator contracts, and gray-market brokerage is difficult to quantify but essential to the eastern corridor's functioning.
Properties.power_structure: No dominant sovereignty. The Presque Isle dispute prevents any single entity from claiming the city. Ferrogate holds transit corridor sovereignty along the rail line. Kelpline maintains waystation authority at the harbor. The Erie Municipal Council — a functioning remnant of the pre-corridor city government — manages civilian affairs with surprising effectiveness, leveraging the sovereignty dispute to maintain autonomous governance.
Properties.dangers: Sovereignty dispute escalation — the Presque Isle arbitration has been peaceful for decades, but the peninsula's strategic value increases as the corridor grows, and all three parties have military capability; Transit vulnerability — Erie's position on the I-90 corridor makes it a chokepoint that Ferrogate could weaponize by restricting service; Cormorant patrols — the fishing fleet operates under constant surveillance and risks interception if it strays beyond the harbor's recognized fishing zones; Neutral-ground risk — a city where everyone does business is also a city where everyone's enemies know where to find them; The peninsula's mineral deposits — if Dredge wins the arbitration, mining operations would fundamentally alter the harbor's ecology and economics
Properties.opportunities: Neutral ground — Erie's sovereignty stalemate makes it the eastern corridor's most reliable location for cross-faction meetings and negotiations; Harbor independence — the fishing fleet and boat-repair operations represent one of the few non-corporate maritime economies on the lake; Transit intelligence — Ferrogate's Erie station processes every shipment moving between Cleveland and Buffalo, and information about that traffic is valuable; The Presque Isle installations — three competing sovereign entities maintain personnel and equipment on the peninsula, and the overlapping security gaps between them create exploitable access points
Properties.story_hooks: The Presque Isle arbitration is about to conclude — after forty-six years, a ruling is expected, and every faction in the corridor is positioning for the outcome; An Erie fisher has pulled something from the lake that none of the three Presque Isle parties want made public — an object that suggests the mineral deposits under the peninsula are not the most valuable thing buried there; A neutral-ground meeting between two corponation representatives has gone wrong — one is dead, the other is missing, and the Erie Municipal Council is under pressure to resolve it before the situation destabilizes the city's carefully maintained neutrality
Properties.sights: Presque Isle curving into the lake — its sandy beaches now divided by jurisdictional markers from three competing sovereignties, each maintaining visible installations; The harbor — a working waterfront where fishing boats, cargo haulers, and the occasional Cormorant patrol vessel share space in uneasy proximity; The civilian city rising from the harbor in layers of mixed-era architecture — 19th-century commercial buildings alongside Palladian residential blocks; Ferrogate's Erie transit station — a fortified hub where the I-90 rail corridor pauses before continuing east toward Buffalo; Lake Erie's horizon line, visible from the harbor without the industrial obstruction that characterizes most of the shore — one of the few places where the lake looks like a lake
Properties.sounds: Harbor sounds — diesel engines, hull impacts, the creak of dock infrastructure, and fishers calling in a mix of languages; The Ferrogate transit station — rail activity producing the district's eastern-corridor pulse, trains arriving and departing on schedules that structure the city's rhythm; Presque Isle — the sound of sand and water, audible from the harbor when the industrial noise pauses, a reminder that the peninsula was a beach before it was a contested zone; Negotiation — Erie's neutral-ground status means people are always talking, always dealing, and the city's cafes and harbor bars carry a constant murmur of business being conducted; Cormorant patrol vessels — their engines distinctive, their presence a reminder that the lake's surface belongs to someone even if the city doesn't
Properties.smells: Fish — fresh catch and processing, the smell that has defined Erie's harbor for three centuries; Lake water — cleaner here than in the industrial zones, carrying the cold mineral scent of deep freshwater; Diesel and dock materials — creosote, rope, the particular smell of a working harbor that hasn't been fully automated
Properties.feel: Presque Anchorage feels like a city that has survived by being useful to everyone and owned by no one. The three-way sovereignty dispute on the peninsula has paradoxically protected the mainland by making Erie too legally complicated for any single corponation to absorb. The result is a rare thing in the corridor: a place with genuine autonomy, purchased not through self-sufficiency or resistance but through the strategic exploitation of stalemate. Erie is neutral ground because neutrality is its product.

Pullman Works is the cruelest district in Meridian 88, not because of what was done to it but because of how perfectly it predicted everything that came after. George Pullman built his company town in the 1880s with a simple proposition: the company provides everything — housing, shops, utilities, recreation — and the worker provides labor. The town was beautiful, planned, and totally controlled. When the workers struck in 1894 because Pullman cut wages without cutting rents, the federal government sent troops. The lesson was clear then and remains clear now: a company town is a company town, and the aesthetics are irrelevant.

When the tier system was implemented, a mid-level Axiom executive with a sense of irony — or perhaps no sense of irony at all — designated Pullman as a model corporate residential zone. The original row houses, designated a National Monument in the old United States, were restored to their 1880s specifications with modern infrastructure hidden behind the period facades. New residential units were built in the same architectural style, extending the original grid. The result is a district that looks like a museum and functions like a labor camp. Tier 2 workers are assigned housing in Pullman Works through their employment contracts — live here, work at the assigned facility, shop at the company store (rebranded as an Axiom Essentials outlet), and maintain your tier status through continued employment. Leave the job, lose the house. The parallels to the original Pullman are exact, and Axiom's promotional materials describe this as heritage preservation.

The residents live in genuine architectural beauty. The row houses have real brick facades, restored ornamental ironwork, and interior spaces designed with a proportion and care that modern construction doesn't attempt. The Hotel Florence — George Pullman's showcase guesthouse — has been restored as an Axiom executive retreat, its bar serving drinks to visiting managers who admire the craftsmanship while reviewing workforce productivity reports. The Greenstone Church still stands, its green serpentine stone exterior cleaned and lit, holding services that are technically nondenominational and practically company-sponsored. The clock tower keeps perfect time, which is appropriate for a district where time belongs to someone else.

But Pullman has always produced resistance proportional to its control, and the current iteration is no different. The workers here understand their situation with a clarity that comes from living inside a metaphor — they know they are the 21st-century version of the Pullman porters, and they know how that story ended. Underground organizing happens in the spaces between the heritage surveillance cameras, in the row houses whose restored walls hide conversations that Axiom's microphones can't reach because the original brickwork is too dense for standard audio penetration. The organizers study the 1894 strike not as history but as a playbook, noting what worked, what failed, and what's different now. What's different now is the neural interface network, which allows communication that doesn't require physical meetings. What's the same is everything else.
Properties.aliases: Pullman, The Works, The Model, Company Town
Properties.demographics: Approximately 8,000 residents, all Tier 2, all housed through Axiom employment contracts. Workforce composition reflects Axiom's hiring patterns — diverse in origin, uniform in status. Turnover is low because leaving employment means leaving housing, and the housing is better than anything Tier 2 can access elsewhere.
Properties.economy: Fully corporate. Employment, housing, retail, and services are all provided through Axiom's integrated residential-labor system. There is no independent economy — by design. Workers receive wages that are sufficient to cover company-store prices with a small remainder, a ratio that George Pullman himself would recognize.
Properties.power_structure: Axiom Industries holds total sovereign authority. The district manager reports directly to Axiom's workforce optimization division. Resident input is solicited through a heritage council that has advisory status and no decision-making power. Underground organizing exists but has not yet produced a visible structure.
Properties.dangers: Employment termination results in immediate housing loss and tier demotion — the ultimate leverage; Heritage surveillance is comprehensive — cameras, audio, neural interface monitoring in public spaces; The planned grid offers no hiding places — every sightline was designed for observation; Corporate social engineering includes managed recreation, managed socialization, and managed discontent — Axiom studies Pullman's mistakes and tries not to repeat them; Organizers face the same risk the 1894 strikers faced: overwhelming institutional response; The beauty of the environment creates psychological dependency — leaving means losing the best living conditions most Tier 2 workers will ever have
Properties.opportunities: The original brickwork blocks standard audio surveillance — a material advantage the organizers use; Neural interface communication allows organizing without physical meetings; Axiom's commitment to heritage aesthetics creates maintenance requirements that provide cover for unauthorized activities; Workers with inside access to Axiom's workforce systems have data that labor organizers across Meridian would value; The Hotel Florence hosts Axiom executives who discuss things they shouldn't in a building they feel safe in — the walls have ears that Axiom didn't install
Properties.story_hooks: The underground organizers have identified a date for action — the anniversary of the 1894 Pullman Strike. The symbolism is deliberate. The plan requires disabling the heritage surveillance network for forty-five minutes, and they need outside technical support.; An Axiom executive staying at the Hotel Florence has been overheard discussing a workforce optimization initiative called Project Renewal that involves Pullman Works. The details suggest something worse than the current system. A worker in the hotel's service staff has partial recordings.; A row house renovation uncovered a sealed room behind the original brickwork containing documents from the 1894 strike — personal letters, organizing plans, names. The historical value is immense. So is the contemporary relevance, because some of the organizing tactics described have no modern countermeasure.
Properties.sights: Restored 1880s row houses in perfect condition — red brick, ornamental iron, a beauty that is also a cage; The Pullman clock tower keeping time for a workforce that doesn't own its own hours; The Hotel Florence glowing with warm light, its windows showing Axiom executives at leisure in a building built by a man who crushed a strike; Workers walking the planned grid in company-issued clothing, the uniformity deliberate and enforced; Heritage surveillance cameras mounted in period-appropriate housings — the aesthetic commitment extends to the panopticon; The Greenstone Church, lit green at night, its beauty so precise it feels like a threat
Properties.sounds: The clock tower marking each hour — a sound that structures every day and belongs to the company; Company announcements through period-styled speakers, their brass housings containing modern surveillance equipment; The quiet of a planned community where noise is a deviation from the plan; Workers' boots on original paving stones, a rhythm that hasn't changed in 140 years; Neural interface whispers — subvocalized conversations in the spaces where audio surveillance can't reach
Properties.smells: Restored brick and mortar — the smell of heritage preservation applied to a labor system; Axiom Essentials outlets — the standardized scent of corporate retail, identical in every company store; The Hotel Florence's kitchen, preparing meals for executives that the workers can smell from the row houses; Old wood and iron from the original structures, a material honesty that the corporate overlay can't quite suppress
Properties.feel: Pullman Works feels like living inside a museum exhibit about your own exploitation. The beauty is real — the architecture is genuinely magnificent — and the control is real, and the combination produces a cognitive dissonance that is the district's defining emotional texture. You can admire the brickwork and resent the system simultaneously, and in Pullman, everyone does.

Properties.description:
South Deering Sump is where Meridian 88 keeps its worst secrets, sealed under contaminated water and abandoned industrial infrastructure. The original South Deering was already haunted before the collapse — the Wisconsin Steel plant closure in 1980 was one of the most brutal in American industrial history, three thousand workers losing their jobs in a single day with no warning and no severance, their pension fund looted by management. The land the plant stood on was so contaminated that remediation estimates exceeded the property value by a factor of ten. Nobody cleaned it up. Nobody ever does.

When the Calumet River's water levels rose, the contaminated industrial sites along its banks didn't just flood — they dissolved. Decades of industrial waste that had been sitting in soil and slag heaps entered the water column, creating a toxic soup that now fills the low-lying areas of the former industrial zone. The Sump, as locals call it, is a landscape of half-submerged factory ruins standing in water that changes color depending on what the current is stirring up. Orange means iron compounds. Green means copper salts. Black means don't ask. The water is warm in places where underground chemical reactions are still running, steam rising from the surface on cold mornings like breath from a sleeping industrial corpse.

Axiom classified South Deering Sump as an exclusion zone — corporate territory in name, abandoned in practice, maintained at the minimum level required to prevent contamination from spreading to adjacent districts. This means a perimeter fence, monitoring stations that are checked quarterly, and a total absence of residential services. But people live here anyway, because people live everywhere that institutions abandon. The Sump's population consists of the truly excluded — those whose tier status is so far below the floor that even the Shelf won't have them. They live in the upper floors of factory ruins, above the waterline, in conditions that no one with options would accept. They fish the contaminated water for mutated species that they eat because the alternative is not eating.

The Sump's value, such as it is, lies in its toxicity. Nobody comes here willingly, which makes it an effective hiding place for things that need hiding. Smugglers use the flooded factory complexes as warehouses — the contamination keeps casual intruders out and the Axiom exclusion zone classification keeps corporate security from patrolling beyond the perimeter. The Calumet River provides water access to South Calumet, Old Harbor, and eventually Lake Michigan. And beneath the water, in the sealed vaults of the old Wisconsin Steel administrative complex, there are records — personnel files, financial documents, corporate communications — that were never digitized because the company died before the digital transition and nobody thought paper records at the bottom of a toxic lake were worth recovering. Someone might think differently now.
Properties.aliases: South Deering, The Sump, Slag Beach, Wisconsin Grave
Properties.demographics: Population estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, though no census has been attempted. Entirely untier-ed or functionally Tier 0. The most marginalized population in Meridian 88 — those with nowhere else to go. Mixed origins, united by exclusion.
Properties.economy: Subsistence fishing in contaminated water. Smuggling infrastructure — warehouse space in the flooded factories, water route access via the Calumet River. Salvage operations in the industrial ruins, extracting metals and materials that retain value despite contamination. No formal economy exists.
Properties.power_structure: No governance. Axiom's exclusion zone classification means the district exists on paper as corporate territory with no corporate presence. Informal authority belongs to whoever controls the most functional factory shelter and the best water access points. Smuggling operations bring external power dynamics into the Sump on a transactional basis.
Properties.dangers: Toxic exposure — the water, the air, the soil are all contaminated, and the health effects are cumulative and severe; Structural collapse — flooded factory ruins are structurally unpredictable and fail without warning; Isolation — the Sump is far from medical care, mutual aid networks, and emergency response of any kind; The things in the water — mutated aquatic life that has adapted to the contamination and doesn't always avoid humans; Smuggling operations attract attention that the Sump's vulnerable population cannot defend against; The contamination itself is not stable — chemical reactions continue underground, and sudden toxic releases have occurred
Properties.opportunities: The flooded factory complexes provide unmonitored warehouse space accessible by water; Calumet River access connects to the broader southern waterway network; The Wisconsin Steel administrative vault contains undigitized records that may have significant intelligence value; The Sump's exclusion zone status means Axiom security does not patrol inside the perimeter — an increasingly rare condition in Meridian; Environmental contamination data, properly documented, could support legal action against Axiom or its predecessor entities
Properties.story_hooks: A salvage diver working the Wisconsin Steel ruins has found the sealed administrative vault and realized the paper records inside are intact. She can't read them — they're in 20th-century corporate accounting notation — but she knows someone who can, if she can get the documents out without them dissolving in the contaminated water.; The warm zones in the Sump are getting warmer. Underground chemical reactions are accelerating, and the excluded population is reporting new symptoms — neurological, not just respiratory. Something has changed in the chemistry, and no one with the expertise to diagnose it is willing to enter the exclusion zone.; A smuggling operation has established a major waypoint in the Sump, and the traffic has attracted attention from a competing faction. The excluded population is caught in the middle, and the only person who's offered to help them is asking for something in return that they don't understand.
Properties.sights: Half-submerged factory ruins rising from discolored water — industrial cathedrals slowly being consumed; Water that shifts color by the hour: orange, green, iridescent black, depending on subsurface chemistry; Steam rising from warm spots where underground chemical reactions continue decades after operations ceased; The perimeter fence, more symbolic than functional, its warning signs faded to illegibility; Improvised shelters in factory upper floors, lights visible through broken industrial windows after dark; Mutated aquatic life visible in the shallows — oversized, discolored, moving in ways that suggest adaptation to something
Properties.sounds: Water moving through industrial ruins — a gurgling, echoing sound unique to flooded structures; Chemical reactions bubbling to the surface in the warm zones, a low persistent fizz; The creak of metal structures under water stress, factory skeletons shifting on their foundations; Quiet — the Sump is one of the quietest places in Meridian because almost no one is here; Occasionally, the sound of a hull moving through water — smugglers navigating the flooded channels
Properties.smells: Chemical contamination — sharp, metallic, with an organic undertone that suggests biological processes nobody wants to study; Rust and decay — the smell of industrial infrastructure returning to its constituent elements; Steam from the warm zones carrying a sulfurous edge; Nothing clean — the Sump has no clean smell. Every breath carries a reminder of what was done here.
Properties.feel: South Deering Sump feels like guilt made physical. This is what happens when industry takes everything from a place and then leaves the corpse for someone else to deal with. The contamination is not an accident or a tragedy — it's a ledger entry, a cost that was calculated, accepted, and externalized onto people who couldn't refuse it. Living here means breathing that calculation every day.

Properties.description:
Rogers Reef is what happens when the lake decides to take back what the city borrowed. The northernmost edge of Meridian 88's lakefront, once a haven of affordable diversity where Jamaican patties shared a block with Ethiopian injera and Polish pierogi, now exists in a state of permanent negotiation with Lake Michigan. The old sea walls here were never corporate-grade — they were municipal leftovers, patched and re-patched by a city government that stopped existing before it could finish the job. The result is a district that floods on a schedule, a twice-monthly tidal incursion the residents call the Rinse. The water comes in knee-deep, fills the ground floors, and recedes twelve hours later, leaving behind silt, debris, and the particular resignation of people who've learned to keep their valuables above waist height.

The multicultural character of old Rogers Park didn't die — it adapted. The Devon corridor food stalls became amphibious, their owners building elevated serving platforms and waterproof storage beneath. The old loyola campus, half-submerged, was claimed by a loose collective of unlicensed educators who run classes in the upper floors during dry periods and distribute lesson packets on waterproof tablets when the Rinse is in. The lakefront itself has become a reef in the literal sense: decades of flooded infrastructure have created an artificial ecosystem where engineered coral clings to rusted CTA rail supports and fish schools navigate the submerged remains of Sheridan Road. Divers harvest the reef for biotech compounds that the pharmaceutical corps will pay handsomely for, no questions asked.

What makes Rogers Reef unique in Meridian is its stubborn cosmopolitanism. In a city that sorts people by tier and function, the Reef sorts by nothing. Tier 1 climate refugees from the Gulf share walkways with Tier 2 biotech harvesters and untier-ed families who've been here since before the floods. Six languages are spoken on any given block. Three different religious communities maintain temples on the upper floors of the same building, sharing a single generator and arguing about the electricity schedule with the kind of intensity that only neighbors who actually depend on each other can muster. The Reef doesn't have diversity as an aspiration. It has diversity as a survival strategy.

Axiom has designated Rogers Reef as a Managed Decline Zone, which means they've stopped maintaining infrastructure but haven't bothered to formally abandon it. This limbo status gives the Reef a peculiar freedom: corporate security doesn't patrol here because there's nothing to protect, but the district isn't lawless enough to attract the kind of attention that triggers a crackdown. It exists in the gap — too flooded to gentrify, too alive to demolish, too complicated to categorize. Kyle passes through occasionally, buying reef-harvested biotech for his medical kit and eating jerk chicken from a woman named Mrs. Adebayo who remembers when Sheridan Road had cars on it.
Properties.aliases: Rogers Park, The Reef, Roj-Par, The Drowning Mosaic
Properties.demographics: Approximately 25,000 residents in a rotating population that swells during dry periods. Predominantly Tier 1 and untier-ed, with a significant population of climate refugees and first-generation immigrants. The most ethnically diverse district in northern Meridian — over forty languages documented in the last informal census.
Properties.economy: Reef biotech harvesting, informal food economy, unlicensed education services, and salvage diving. Mrs. Adebayo's jerk chicken alone probably constitutes a measurable percentage of the local GDP.
Properties.power_structure: No single authority. A loose council of community elders from the major ethnic groups meets irregularly to resolve disputes and coordinate flood response. The Reef Divers Guild controls access to the most profitable harvesting sites and functions as the closest thing to an organized power bloc.
Properties.dangers: The Rinse — twice-monthly flooding that can trap the unprepared in lower floors; Structural collapse from water damage — buildings here have been soaking for decades; Reef predators — the artificial ecosystem includes things with teeth that weren't in the original design; Contaminated water during heavy floods — industrial runoff from upshore mixing with lake water; Isolation during storms — the Reef can become unreachable when weather overwhelms the makeshift infrastructure; Biotech poachers from corporate labs who don't ask permission and don't leave witnesses
Properties.opportunities: Reef-harvested biotech compounds — pharmaceutical corps pay premium prices, no questions asked; Cultural exchange — the Reef's diversity means access to knowledge, skills, and networks from across the globe; Anonymity — Axiom's Managed Decline designation means minimal surveillance; The Loyola collective's education services — free, unlicensed, and genuinely excellent; A community that actually functions as a community — trust networks that money can't buy
Properties.story_hooks: A reef diver discovers something growing in the submerged infrastructure that isn't coral and isn't natural — it responds to neural interface signals; The Loyola collective intercepts a corporate communication suggesting the Managed Decline designation is about to be upgraded to Active Reclamation — which means eviction for 25,000 people; Mrs. Adebayo's food stall is a dead drop for information moving between Old Harbor and the northern districts — she's been doing it for twenty years and nobody knows
Properties.sights: Ground floors filled with murky lake water during the Rinse, residents wading through on elevated walkway planks; Engineered coral formations growing on rusted CTA rail supports, visible through translucent shallows; Food stalls on elevated platforms — hand-painted signs in Amharic, Spanish, Urdu, Polish, and Shelf Cant; The half-submerged Loyola campus, upper windows glowing with makeshift classroom light; Fishing nets strung between buildings, drying in the lake wind; Bioluminescent algae creeping north from Old Harbor, painting the waterline in pale green during floods
Properties.sounds: Water — always water. Lapping against foundations, dripping from eaves, sloshing under foot traffic; Multilingual haggling at the elevated market stalls, three conversations overlapping in different languages; The groan of waterlogged building foundations settling after the Rinse recedes; Call to prayer from the third-floor mosque mixing with hymns from the fourth-floor church next door; Dive boats putting out at dawn, small electric motors humming across the flooded streets; Children splashing — they treat the Rinse as a swimming pool, which terrifies their parents
Properties.smells: Lake brine and wet concrete — the permanent base note; Spices from six continents drifting from the elevated food stalls; The chemical-sweet smell of engineered coral when the tide is low; Mildew in the lower floors, a smell the Reef's residents have stopped noticing; Fresh fish being gutted and cleaned on rooftop platforms
Properties.feel: Exhausting and beautiful. Rogers Reef demands constant adaptation — you have to time your movements to the flood schedule, keep your gear elevated, maintain relationships with neighbors who speak different languages and worship different gods. But there's a warmth to it that comes from mutual dependence. The Reef is a community that floods together and dries out together, and that shared rhythm creates something that the perfectly climate-controlled tiers above can never replicate.

Properties.description:
Riverbottom is the lowest point in Meridian 88 that isn't underwater. That distinction matters here more than anywhere else, because the water is always coming. The district sits at the absolute southern terminus of the megacity, where the engineered drainage systems that protect the Meridian Core and the Shelf thin out to nothing. When the lake surges or the spring melt overwhelms the pumping stations, Riverbottom floods first and drains last. The old Altgeld Gardens public housing blocks -- themselves a monument to decades of environmental racism in pre-Meridian Chicago -- were rebuilt as Meridian Residential Block South-9, a name so deliberately forgettable it amounts to erasure. The new blocks are identical modular stacks, six stories of poured composite with neural-compatible wiring and nothing else. No common spaces. No green areas. No pretense.

The environmental justice concerns that defined old Riverdale didn't go away when the neighborhood got a new name. They got a corporate rebrand. Three waste processing facilities ring the district, handling chemical reclamation for the southern industrial zone. The air quality index in Riverbottom regularly exceeds Meridian safety thresholds by 200%, but the thresholds are advisory, not mandatory, and advisories don't apply below Tier 3. Residents have filed 14,000 environmental complaints through the Meridian civic interface in the past decade. The system logs them, categorizes them, and routes them to a processing queue that has never, in its operational history, produced a response.

But Riverbottom endures, the way things endure at the bottom of gravity wells -- not by climbing out but by becoming so dense that nothing can compress them further. The community organizing tradition that existed in Altgeld Gardens survived the transition to Meridian, adapted, and hardened. Block councils operate with military discipline, coordinating flood response, air filtration maintenance, and the distribution of smuggled medical supplies for the respiratory conditions the waste plants cause and the corporate health system doesn't cover. There is a saying in Riverbottom: the water rises, and so do we. It's painted on the side of Block South-9 in letters three stories tall. Nobody has tried to remove it.
Properties.aliases: Riverdale, The Pit, Altgeld, Ground Floor
Properties.demographics: Overwhelmingly Tier 1 and untier-ed residents. The legacy Black community from Altgeld Gardens persists alongside environmental refugees and workers displaced from shuttered southern industrial operations.
