Population approximately 35,000, though flooding events cause periodic displacement.
Properties.economy: Waste processing plant employment, block council mutual aid systems, and a surprisingly sophisticated gray market in air filtration components. Some residents earn supplemental income as flood remediation specialists -- skills learned from necessity, marketed to wealthier districts that flood less often.
Properties.power_structure: The waste processing facilities are operated by Axiom Environmental Services under sovereign industrial charter, making them functionally immune to local complaint. Block councils hold real authority within the residential stacks, operating as the only functional governance Riverbottom has ever known.
Properties.dangers: Flooding -- chronic, recurring, and worsening as climate infrastructure degrades; Toxic air quality from the waste processing ring -- respiratory illness rates are four times the Meridian average; Infrastructure collapse during flood events -- the modular blocks weren't built for water exposure; Axiom Environmental Security patrols protecting plant perimeters with escalation-of-force protocols; Despair -- the most dangerous thing in Riverbottom is the rational conclusion that nothing will change
Properties.opportunities: Block council networks are the tightest community infrastructure in southern Meridian -- trust is real here; Environmental data from Riverbottom could be devastating if it reached the right journalist or activist; Flood remediation expertise is genuinely valuable and in demand across the city; The waste plants process materials that occasionally include salvageable tech and rare elements
Properties.story_hooks: A block council leader has been compiling environmental health data for twenty years and is ready to release it -- but the last three people who tried to whistleblow on Axiom Environmental are dead or missing; The flood patterns are changing in ways the pumping station data doesn't explain -- someone is diverting drainage capacity away from Riverbottom deliberately; Underneath Block South-9, the original Altgeld Gardens foundation contains a sealed community archive from the pre-Meridian environmental justice movement
Properties.sights: Identical modular housing stacks stretching in grid formation, brutalist and unadorned; Waste processing facility smokestacks rimming the horizon, exhaust plumes lit amber at night; High-water marks stained on building walls at varying heights -- a flood history written in grime; Community murals on Block South-9 -- defiant, colorful, repainted after every flood; Makeshift levee barriers stored on every block, ready for deployment
Properties.sounds: The constant industrial drone of waste processing -- a low frequency hum felt in the chest; Pumping station machinery cycling on and off, the sound of borrowed time; Block council alert sirens -- three tones: flood warning, air quality alert, all clear; Children coughing -- the sound Riverbottom can't escape
Properties.smells: Chemical processing byproduct -- metallic, acrid, and inescapable on bad air days; Standing water from the last flood event that hasn't fully drained; Bleach and industrial cleaner from the constant post-flood remediation; Community kitchens cooking with whatever the supply chain delivered this week
Properties.feel: Compressed. Riverbottom feels like a place that has been pushed down so many times it has become structurally incapable of surprise. The anger here isn't hot -- it's geological. Layers of grievance compressed into something harder than the composite walls. People don't hope for rescue. They organize for survival.

Properties.description:
West Pulldown earned its name the honest way. When the southern residential blocks of old Chicago were absorbed into Meridian 88's tier restructuring, West Pullman was designated Tier 2 transitional housing -- a bureaucratic phrase that meant the neighborhood would receive just enough infrastructure funding to survive and not one credit more. The historic homes, many dating back to the 1880s Pullman worker housing experiment, were retrofitted with cheap neural-compatible wiring and subdivided into efficiency units. Three families where one used to live. The craftsmanship of those original homes -- the stone lintels, the ornamental brickwork -- still shows through in places, like good bones visible through bad skin. Residents call the contrast between what the neighborhood was built to be and what it became 'the dropout,' and the name stuck to the district itself.

The southern edge still carries industrial DNA. Automated fabrication plants replaced the old steel works, churning out modular housing components for corporate construction projects in districts that will never include West Pulldown on their shipping manifests. The plants run three shifts, staffed by Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers whose neural interfaces are locked to factory firmware -- no personal customization, no unauthorized apps, no agency. The commute from residential blocks to the plant floor is eleven minutes on foot. The commute from the plant floor to anything resembling economic mobility is infinite.

What keeps West Pulldown from collapsing entirely is stubbornness. The neighborhood associations that formed around the original Pullman housing model never fully dissolved -- they just went underground, operating as mutual aid networks that share resources, maintain the aging infrastructure the city ignores, and keep a census that the corporate authorities don't know exists. There's a quiet pride here, rooted in the historical awareness that this neighborhood was literally built as an experiment in worker housing, and that the experiment is still running, and that the workers are still losing.
Properties.aliases: West Pullman, The Dropout, Pulldown, The Fade
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2, multi-generational families packed into subdivided historic housing. A mix of legacy Black residents who've held on since pre-Meridian Chicago and newer arrivals displaced downward from restructured zones. Factory employment is near-universal.
Properties.economy: Fabrication plant wages, mutual aid barter networks, and under-the-table repair work on the historic housing stock that the city refuses to maintain. The plants export; the neighborhood imports nothing it doesn't absolutely need.
Properties.power_structure: The fabrication plants are owned by Vantage Meridian subsidiary CastForm Industries, which controls employment and therefore controls everything. Underground mutual aid networks provide the only counterweight, operating through neighborhood associations that predate the megacity by a century.
Properties.dangers: Factory firmware lockdowns that can brick a worker's neural interface for contract violations; Structural decay in subdivided historic buildings -- load-bearing walls removed for more units; CastForm security patrols that double as labor compliance enforcement; Polymer particulate exposure from the plants -- respiratory damage is endemic; Isolation from the rest of Meridian -- no maglev stop, limited transit options
Properties.opportunities: The mutual aid networks are genuine and protective -- earning trust here means real community; The fabrication plants produce components that occasionally go missing, feeding a quiet salvage market; The hidden census contains population data the corps don't have -- valuable to the right buyer; Historic architecture knowledge makes Pulldown residents sought-after for restoration work in wealthier districts
Properties.story_hooks: CastForm is planning to automate the last human-staffed fabrication line, which would eliminate West Pulldown's entire economic reason for existence; The mutual aid networks have discovered that their hidden census data matches anomalies in Axiom's population management algorithms -- someone is already counting the people they thought were uncounted; A sealed sub-basement in one of the original Pullman houses contains records from the 1894 Pullman Strike -- and someone in the Spire wants them destroyed before a historian finds them
Properties.sights: Historic stone row houses with neural-relay antennas bolted to Victorian cornices; Automated fabrication plants glowing dull orange along the southern horizon line; Subdivided interiors visible through uncurtained windows -- three households sharing what was one living room; Mutual aid markers chalked on doorframes in a code the corps haven't cracked; Factory shift workers walking in silent streams, neural interfaces dimmed to standby
Properties.sounds: The rhythmic thudding of fabrication presses, audible from six blocks away; Children playing in alleyways between shift changes, filling the silence the workers leave; Neural interface firmware update tones -- mandatory, synchronized, district-wide at 0300; The creak of 140-year-old floor joists under modern weight
Properties.smells: Hot polymer from the fabrication plants -- sweet and chemical, coating the throat; Cooking from communal kitchens -- pooled resources stretch further; Old wood and stone dust from buildings that refuse to be modern
Properties.feel: Tired but unbroken. West Pulldown has the emotional texture of a long shift -- exhausting, repetitive, but underwritten by the knowledge that stopping isn't an option. The history here isn't decorative. It's load-bearing.

Properties.description:
River Rouge is where steel was born and where it refuses to die. The downriver industrial zone — centered on the city of River Rouge and extending through Ecorse, Lincoln Park, and the southern reaches of the Detroit metro — has been making steel, processing metals, and turning raw materials into the skeleton of civilization for over a century. The Great Lakes Steel Works, originally built in 1929, was acquired by Ashgrave Materials in 2148 and rebuilt into the Ashgrave Great Lakes Crucible — a next-generation metallurgical facility that produces the specialized alloys, composite metals, and structural materials that autonomous vehicle frames, arcology towers, and military hardware require. The facility employs 12,000 workers and operates around the clock, its electric arc furnaces visible from five miles away as a constant orange glow on the southern horizon.

The community that surrounds the Crucible is blue-collar in a way that the 22nd century tried to eliminate and couldn't. These are people who work with metal — not the clean metal of augment technicians but the raw metal of furnaces and rolling mills and forging presses. The work is hot, dangerous, and augment-intensive — the Crucible's workers use industrial-grade exoskeletons, thermal-resistant augments, and neural interfaces calibrated for metallurgical process control rather than communication or entertainment. The augments are functional, scarred, and maintained by the workers themselves because Ashgrave's corporate maintenance schedule prioritizes production equipment over human equipment. A Crucible worker's augments tell their work history the way a sailor's tattoos used to.

The district's identity is inseparable from the work. The bars serve shift-change schedules. The housing was built within walking distance of the gates. The community organizations — the Steelworkers' Mutual Aid, the River Rouge Athletic Club, the downriver food cooperatives — all exist to sustain a workforce, not a population. The distinction matters: the Crucible treats its workers as a resource, and the community has adapted to sustain that resource, and the question of whether the people are serving the steel or the steel is serving the people was settled a long time ago. The steel won.
Properties.aliases: River Rouge, The Crucible, Downriver, Slag Town
Properties.demographics: Approximately 38,000 residents across the downriver district. Predominantly white and Latino, with significant Black and Middle Eastern populations. Multi-generational steelworking families make up 40% of the community. Average age: 41. Life expectancy: 62 — fifteen years below the GLM average, a number that Ashgrave Materials' annual report attributes to 'lifestyle factors.'
Properties.economy: Ashgrave Great Lakes Crucible: Φ92 billion annual output. The community economy is entirely Crucible-dependent. Average household income: Φ48,000 — higher than many Detroit districts due to hazard pay and augment allowances, but the income doesn't account for the medical costs that begin accruing in the second decade of work.
Properties.power_structure: Ashgrave Materials holds sovereign industrial authority over the Crucible campus. The Steelworkers' Mutual Aid Society — not a union (unions were dissolved under the Corporate Sovereignty Acts) but a 'community wellness organization' — represents worker interests through negotiation rather than collective bargaining. The current SMA chair, Ray Kowalski, is a third-generation steelworker who lost his left arm to a rolling mill in 2189 and considers the replacement augment an improvement. He may be right. The arm is certainly stronger.
Properties.dangers: Industrial accidents — the Crucible's safety record is better than historical steel mills and still produces casualties annually; Cumulative health damage — thermal exposure, heavy metal contact, and industrial particulates take years off every worker's life; Augment degradation — industrial-grade augments wear differently than consumer models, and replacement parts are the worker's expense; Ashgrave corporate response — the company values the Crucible's output and will protect it aggressively against any threat, including labor unrest; Environmental contamination — the slag piles and river discharge carry legacy contamination that the residential blocks absorb
Properties.opportunities: Metallurgical expertise — the Crucible's workers can identify, fabricate, and modify any metal or alloy in production; Industrial augment knowledge — the workers maintain their own equipment, creating a knowledge base of augment modification that doesn't exist in corporate manuals; The Steelworkers' Mutual Aid is a community network of 12,000 workers who share information, resources, and loyalty; Supply chain access — the river barge network moves materials through the entire GLM industrial corridor
Properties.story_hooks: Ray Kowalski has evidence that Ashgrave has been substituting substandard alloys in military contracts — the specifications say one thing, the furnace logs say another. The substitution saves Ashgrave Φ4 billion annually. The alloys are going into autonomous military platforms.; A Crucible worker develops a metallurgical process that produces an alloy with properties that shouldn't be physically possible. Ashgrave classifies the discovery immediately. The worker's access is restricted. The worker's augments start malfunctioning.; The slag piles along the river contain enough rare earth elements to be worth billions if someone could extract them. A downriver entrepreneur has figured out how. Ashgrave's sovereign charter says the slag is their property. The entrepreneur says it's pollution and pollution belongs to no one.
Properties.sights: The Crucible's electric arc furnaces — visible as a permanent orange glow on the horizon, the district's artificial sunset; Workers in industrial exoskeletons walking the streets — scarred augments, thermal-resistant skin grafts, and the particular posture of people who spend shifts at 2,000 degrees; Steel slag piles along the river — mountains of industrial byproduct that have become landmarks, named by generations of workers; The gates — three shift-change points where 4,000 workers enter and exit, three times daily, with the precision of a military operation; River barges carrying raw materials upstream — the supply chain made visible, slow and massive and constant
Properties.sounds: The Crucible — a sound that is felt as much as heard, a low-frequency industrial pulse that synchronizes with your heartbeat if you stay long enough; Shift-change movement — thousands of boots on pavement, exoskeleton servos, and the particular sound of tired people walking in the same direction; The bars after shift change — the transition from silence to volume, compressed into the time it takes to pour a drink; Metal cooling — the pinging, cracking sound of thermal contraction in fresh alloys, audible from the residential blocks when the wind is right; River barge horns — deep, resonant, timed to the supply schedule
Properties.smells: Hot metal — the dominant smell, present everywhere, absorbed into clothing and skin and the walls of buildings; Industrial slag — a mineral, alkaline smell that rises from the piles along the river, strongest in summer heat; Bar food and beer — the shift-change economy runs on calories and alcohol, in that order
Properties.feel: Heavy. River Rouge Crucible feels like a place with gravitational mass — the work, the heat, the industry, the community built around the industry all combine into a density that you feel physically. People here don't move quickly because they carry their work in their bodies. The pride is real. The damage is real. The question of whether the exchange is fair is one the community stopped asking because the answer doesn't change the shift schedule.

Properties.description: The steel mill — electric arc furnaces glowing orange 24 hours a day, producing the materials that build the GLM's infrastructure
Industrial byproduct piles along the river — named landmarks (Big Mike, The Cathedral, Kowalski's Knob) that have been part of the landscape longer than most buildings
The SMA's meeting space — a converted auto parts warehouse where 12,000 workers' interests are represented by people who work the same shifts
The sovereign salvage operation — drones and automated systems converting a dead manufacturing district into raw materials, building by building
Ironclad's aquaculture grid on Saginaw Bay — geometric, automated, and producing food in water that killed its original ecosystem
The occupied residential district — 90,000 people in buildings maintained by stubbornness and mutual aid

Saltgrave Sublevel occupies the drowned basement infrastructure of what was once Chicago's South Loop transit interchange — a labyrinth of flooded pedestrian tunnels and former parking structures sealed off after the 2147 Lake Surge and never properly reclaimed. Brine from Lake Michigan seeps through cracked concrete walls, leaving thick white salt deposits that encrust every surface like mineral frost. Salvagers broke through from below in the 2170s and have since carved out a thriving gray-market settlement across four interconnected levels, using repurposed buoyancy platforms to keep living quarters above the standing water.

The settlement is famous — or infamous — for its salt trade. Saltgrave's residents harvest the mineral deposits and process them for industrial use, food preservation, and certain chemical synthesis operations that corponations prefer not to conduct in their own facilities. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric maintains a quiet purchasing agreement with Saltgrave's council, though neither party acknowledges it publicly. The deeper levels, perpetually flooded and lit only by bioluminescent algae cultivated along the walls, serve as neutral meeting ground for parties who cannot afford to be seen in any official venue.
Properties.aliases: The Salt, Brine Deck, Old Sublevel Four, The Pickled Quarter
Properties.demographics: Roughly 1,200 permanent residents, heavily weighted toward Shelf-tier salvagers, displaced transit workers, and a small population of unregistered synthetics who have found safety in the council's deliberate blindness toward legal identity. Turnover is low — people who find Saltgrave tend to stay.
Properties.economy: Salt harvesting and processing form the economic backbone, supplemented by gray-market chemical synthesis, data brokering conducted in the acoustically scrambled deep levels, and a modest trade in recovered pre-Surge artifacts pulled from the flooded lower chambers.
Properties.power_structure: The Saltgrave Council — seven elected platform-holders who control the buoyancy infrastructure — govern by consensus and collect a ten-percent tithe on all commerce. Ferrogate Security has no presence here; the council enforces its own order through platform access denial, the ultimate threat being eviction into the flooded tunnels below.
Properties.dangers: Sudden flood surges from Lake Michigan pressure events can raise water levels in the lower passages by two meters in under an hour, with minimal warning.; The salt-saturated air aggressively corrodes unprotected electronics, including BCI hardware, causing glitches and data loss with extended exposure.; Unregulated synthesis operations in the deep levels occasionally produce toxic byproduct clouds that migrate through the tunnel system unpredictably.; The council's neutrality policy means rival factions meet here — and sometimes resolve their disputes violently in the dark water of the lower levels.
Properties.opportunities: The flooded deep chambers contain intact pre-Surge transit infrastructure and data vaults that no one has fully mapped or salvaged.; Saltgrave's acoustic properties and council-enforced neutrality make it the premier location in the southern corridor for sensitive meetings that cannot be recorded.; Salt and mineral extraction contracts with industrial buyers like Zheng-Dao represent legitimate income streams for operators willing to work outside corponation oversight.
Properties.story_hooks: A council member has gone missing in the deep levels — officially a flood accident, but her platform partner insists she had just discovered something in the pre-Surge vaults and is convinced the death was arranged. The council wants the matter handled quietly before it attracts outside attention.; An unregistered synthetic has been operating as Saltgrave's de facto doctor for three years, beloved by the community. A Helix Biosystems bounty hunter has tracked it here and is pressuring the council to hand it over. The synthetic claims to have information about illegal Helix experiments that would be worth far more than the bounty.; A new synthesis crew has moved into the deep levels and is producing something that isn't chem — the byproduct odors are wrong, the workers don't socialize, and two Saltgrave residents who got too curious have quietly disappeared.
Properties.sights: Salt crystal formations bloom across every concrete pillar like white coral, some reaching half a meter long and catching the blue-green glow of cultivated algae.; Salvaged buoyancy platforms drift in loose clusters, connected by rope bridges and rusted gangplanks above black standing water.; Handmade lamps fashioned from repurposed BCI housing units cast warm amber pools across market stalls selling mineral blocks, preserved foods, and unregistered chem supplies.; Waterlines stain the walls in brown and gray bands, a geological record of every flood surge dating back decades.
Properties.sounds: A constant low drip echoes from every direction, merging into white noise that muffles conversation and makes surveillance difficult.; The creak and slap of platform pontoons shifting underfoot follows every step through the upper market levels.; Voices carry strangely in the tunnels — a whisper fifty meters away can arrive clearer than someone standing beside you.
Properties.smells: Sharp mineral brine dominates everything, a clean chemical smell undercut by the damp rot of old concrete.; Cooking fires on the upper platforms push woodsmoke and rendered fat down into the lower corridors where it pools and lingers.; Certain deep passages carry a faint sweet-chemical odor from unlicensed synthesis operations that the council officially denies.
Properties.feel: Saltgrave feels like the city forgot it existed and the people inside decided that was fine. The dampness gets into your joints, and the acoustics keep you permanently uncertain of where sounds are coming from. There's a claustrophobic intimacy to the place — everyone knows everyone's business, but they've collectively agreed not to say so.

Properties.description: The council's meeting platform, distinguished by an actual salvaged wood table encrusted with decades of salt crystal growth — sitting at it is considered a mark of significant trust.
The permanently flooded fourth sublevel, accessible only by dive or submersible platform, where the most sensitive meetings and the most questionable operations take place.

Lake Erie is the shallowest of the Great Lakes — average depth nineteen meters, which is roughly the depth of a bad decision. This posed a fundamental engineering problem for the seacrete pioneers who arrived in 2173 to build the fifth free city: you can't grow a deep-keeled reef structure in water that barely covers a four-story building. Shallowgrave's founders solved this by going wide instead of deep, spreading their accretion frameworks across the lakebed in flat, interlocking platforms that grew upward from the bottom rather than downward from the surface. The result is a city that sits on the lake like a lily pad — vast, thin, and disturbingly close to the water. In rough weather, waves wash over the outer platforms entirely. Residents call these events 'baptisms' and have developed a culture of waterproofing everything they own.

The shallow construction created an unexpected advantage: Shallowgrave's platforms are anchored directly to the lakebed, making the city effectively immovable. Where Freestone and Deepwell float, tethered but mobile, Shallowgrave is fused to the earth beneath the water. This permanence gave the city a legal argument that the other lake cities lacked — Shallowgrave claimed not just water rights but lakebed territory, filing a sovereign land claim under obscure pre-collapse mining law. The claim has never been recognized by M88 or any remnant government, but it has never been successfully challenged either, because challenging it would require acknowledging that the pre-collapse legal framework still applies, which would open a catastrophic can of jurisdictional worms that no corponation wants to touch.

Shallowgrave's proximity to Cormorant Naval Systems' Lake Erie operations and Crestfall Aquaculture's protein platforms makes it the most politically complex of the lake cities. It exists in contested water, surrounded by corporate sovereign interests, and survives through a combination of strategic usefulness and deliberate unpalatability. The city is ugly — flat, sprawling, perpetually wet, its seacrete stained green with algae growth that the shallow, sunlit water encourages. But it produces something nobody else can: freshwater algae-derived pharmaceuticals. Shallowgrave's biotech labs, built into the sunlit shallow-water platforms where algae cultivation thrives, produce raw compounds that Lazarus Pharmaceuticals and Novafold would prefer to manufacture in-house but cannot replicate at Shallowgrave's quality or scale. This biochemical leverage keeps the corponations negotiating instead of invading.

Governance is a technocratic council — the Algae Board, as residents call it without irony. Six elected biotech specialists and six elected general representatives manage the city's affairs with a bias toward technical competence that occasionally shades into arrogance. Population: 95,000, most of them damp.
Properties.aliases: The Flat Reef, Erie Free City, Pancake Town, The Sprawl on the Water
Properties.demographics: 95,000 permanent residents. Heavily skewed toward technical and scientific backgrounds — Shallowgrave actively recruits biotech talent from shore universities and offers citizenship in exchange for five-year service commitments. The population is younger and more educated on average than any shore-based community in M88.
Properties.economy: Primary export: algae-derived pharmaceutical precursors and specialty biochemicals. Shallowgrave supplies raw compounds to Lazarus Pharmaceuticals, Novafold, and several smaller pharma corponations at prices that undercut synthetic alternatives. Secondary exports: algae-based food supplements, biofuel feedstock, and water filtration organisms. Annual external trade: approximately Φ11.4 billion, almost entirely from biotech. The economy is a monoculture, and the city knows it — diversification is a permanent agenda item that never quite gets funded.
Properties.power_structure: Technocratic council — the Board of Twelve. Six seats elected from the biotech sector, six from general population. The biotech seats carry effective veto power on trade policy, which is where the real power lies. No corporate sovereignty permitted, but Shallowgrave licenses pharmaceutical extraction rights to shore-based corponations under carefully negotiated terms that both sides consider exploitative.
Properties.dangers: Flooding — Shallowgrave's low profile means that major storms can submerge entire districts temporarily; Cormorant Naval Systems — Lake Erie is their claimed water, and Shallowgrave's presence irritates them enormously; Crestfall Aquaculture — protein platforms and algae farms compete for the same shallow, sunlit water; Economic monoculture — if the pharma market shifts, Shallowgrave has no fallback; Biological hazard — algae cultivation at this scale creates risks of toxic bloom events if containment fails
Properties.opportunities: Pharmaceutical leverage — Shallowgrave's biotech output makes it indispensable to multiple corponations; Scientific research — the city's algae labs are doing work that shore-based institutions can't replicate; Strategic position — located between Cormorant and Crestfall, Shallowgrave is a useful intermediary; Biofuel production — a growing secondary market that could reduce the monoculture risk
Properties.story_hooks: Novafold Pharmaceuticals attempts to acquire exclusive rights to Shallowgrave's algae-derived TX-4 precursor compounds. The deal would make the city rich and dependent. The Board of Twelve is split.; A toxic algae bloom escapes containment on Shallowgrave's eastern platform, threatening Crestfall Aquaculture's nearby protein farms. Both cities blame the other. Someone needs to find out what actually happened before Cormorant uses the crisis as an excuse to intervene.; A Shallowgrave biochemist has synthesized something that shouldn't be possible from algae — and three corponations have independently dispatched acquisition teams.
Properties.sights: A vast, flat expanse of seacrete platforms barely rising above the waterline — the city has almost no vertical profile; Green — algae cultivation gives Shallowgrave a verdant, living-carpet appearance from above; Biotech labs with transparent roofing, their algae tanks glowing green-gold in sunlight; Waves washing across outer platforms during moderate weather — residents walk through ankle-deep water like it's normal, because it is; Crestfall Aquaculture platforms visible on the horizon — a reminder that corporate neighbors are always watching
Properties.sounds: Water — not the distant lap of deeper lakes, but the immediate, constant slosh of a city that barely clears the surface; Biotech processing hums from the algae labs — centrifuges, bioreactors, extraction equipment; The squelch of wet footsteps on algae-filmed seacrete — the city's ambient soundtrack; Wind across flat water with no structures to break it — Shallowgrave is exposed
Properties.smells: Algae — rich, green, organic, pervasive. You smell Shallowgrave before you see it.; Pharmaceutical processing compounds — chemical sharpness from the biotech labs; Lake Erie's particular chemistry — warmer, more biologically active than the upper lakes; Wet seacrete — a musty, mineral smell that never fully dries
Properties.feel: Damp, practical, and quietly powerful. Shallowgrave doesn't inspire the way Freestone does or intimidate the way Deepwell does. It impresses you the way a fungus impresses a biologist — by being far more important than it looks. The city is uncomfortable, wet, architecturally uninspiring, and absolutely essential to the Great Lakes pharmaceutical economy. Residents have the resigned humor of people who live in a place nobody visits for pleasure but everyone needs. They track mud everywhere and they hold patents that keep corponations at bay.

Properties.description:
Threshold exists in the space between two countries that no longer meaningfully exist, and it has turned that ambiguity into a national identity. Built on Lake Huron's central ridge — roughly equidistant from the former Michigan and Ontario shorelines — Threshold occupies water that both the remnant Canadian federal government and M88's Corridor Council claim jurisdiction over and neither can effectively enforce. The city was founded in 2171 by a mixed Canadian-American group who recognized that the sovereignty confusion created a permanent legal vacuum. They dropped their first accretion framework into water that was simultaneously Canadian, American, and neither, and started growing.

Threshold's seacrete is pale grey, built from Huron's lighter mineral profile — cleaner water, less iron than Superior, more calcium carbonate. The resulting structures have an almost marble-like quality, smooth-surfaced and bright compared to Deepwell's volcanic darkness or Freestone's rough organic textures. The city sprawls horizontally rather than vertically, its platforms connected by arched walkways and canal channels that give it the appearance of a floating Venice built from living stone. This horizontal spread is strategic: Threshold covers more surface area than any other lake city, making it harder to blockade and giving its defense forces — the Borderwatch — multiple angles of engagement.

The sovereignty dispute is Threshold's defining feature and its greatest asset. Both Canada and M88 claim the city is in their waters. Neither can act on the claim without provoking the other. Threshold exploits this deadlock ruthlessly, maintaining diplomatic relations with both sides while acknowledging neither's authority. The city has become the de facto neutral ground of the Great Lakes — a place where shore-based factions can meet, negotiate, and trade without either side having jurisdictional advantage. Diplomats, fixers, intelligence operatives, and criminals all use Threshold as a meeting point. The city charges handsomely for this neutrality, and the revenue funds an infrastructure that's more refined than any other lake city's.

Governance is bicameral — a nod to the city's dual-heritage founding. The Shore Council handles external relations and trade, while the Reef Council manages internal infrastructure and civil affairs. Elections are annual, contested, and occasionally theatrical. Threshold's culture is cosmopolitan in a way that Deepwell's mining solidarity and Freestone's anarchist idealism are not — this is a trading city, a diplomat's city, a city that understands that its survival depends on being useful to everyone and loyal to no one. Population: 185,000, most of them bilingual in English and French, and all of them fluent in the language of strategic ambiguity.
Properties.aliases: The Disputed Reef, Huron Free City, The Border, Half-and-Half
Properties.demographics: 185,000 permanent residents, roughly 55% American-heritage, 40% Canadian-heritage, 5% international. Strong bilingual culture. The diplomatic and trade sectors employ approximately 30% of the population directly. Threshold attracts a transient population of diplomats, traders, and intelligence operatives that can swell the effective population by 20,000 on any given day.
Properties.economy: Threshold's economy is built on neutrality. Diplomatic hosting, trade facilitation, and information brokering generate the majority of revenue. The city charges docking fees, meeting-hall rental, and 'neutrality premiums' to factions using its space for negotiations. External trade volume: approximately Φ14.3 billion annually — the highest of any lake city, reflecting its role as the Great Lakes' commercial crossroads. Imports heavily; produces relatively little itself.
Properties.power_structure: Bicameral democracy. The Shore Council (external affairs, seven members, elected annually) and the Reef Council (internal governance, seven members, elected annually) share power with built-in checks. The Borderwatch — 3,200 personnel with patrol craft and surveillance systems — reports to both councils jointly. Corporate entities are prohibited from holding sovereignty but are permitted to operate trade offices under strict licensing. This compromise is Threshold's pragmatic concession to commercial reality.
Properties.dangers: Espionage density — every intelligence service on the Great Lakes has assets in Threshold; The sovereignty dispute escalating — if Canada or M88 ever resolves their standoff, Threshold loses its legal shield; Being played — Threshold's neutrality makes it a venue for manipulation by shore-based factions; The Borderwatch's limits — 3,200 personnel can't patrol the city's entire horizontal spread simultaneously; Trade dependency — Threshold produces little and imports much. A coordinated embargo could be devastating.
Properties.opportunities: Intelligence — Threshold is the best place on the Great Lakes to learn what every faction is doing; Neutral ground — deals that can't happen anywhere else can happen here; Trade access — goods from both shores flow through Threshold's markets; Diplomatic immunity by proximity — the neutral quarter's conventions protect visitors from shore-based warrants
Properties.story_hooks: A secret negotiation between Axiom Industries and the remnant Canadian government is happening in Threshold's neutral quarter. The outcome would reshape Great Lakes sovereignty. Both sides have hired operatives to ensure the talks go their way.; Threshold's Shore Council discovers that one of its members has been a Cormorant Naval Systems intelligence asset for six years. The political fallout threatens the city's neutrality.; Kyle is offered a contract that requires him to operate in Threshold — a city where his street-level instincts are worth less than his ability to read a room full of diplomats.
Properties.sights: Pale grey seacrete architecture with an almost marble-like luminosity — Threshold glows on the water; Canal channels threading between platforms, crossed by arched walkways — a freshwater Venice grown from mineral; Diplomatic quarter flags — dozens of faction and city-state banners flying from the neutral meeting halls; Trade vessels from both shores docked side by side in the harbor platforms — Canadian and M88 flags within arm's reach; The Borderwatch patrol boats — sleek, fast, painted in Threshold's grey-and-white livery
Properties.sounds: Multilingual conversation — English, French, Shelf Cant, and the lakeside trade pidgin overlapping in markets and meeting halls; Water traffic — more boats dock at Threshold than any other lake city. The harbor never sleeps.; The accretion hum here is higher-pitched, almost musical — Huron's calcium-carbonate chemistry sings differently; Diplomatic protocol announcements echoing across the neutral quarter — formal, multilingual, perpetually ongoing
Properties.smells: Clean lake air — Huron's central waters are cleaner than Michigan or Erie; Imported goods from both shores — coffee from M88, timber resin from Canadian north; The mineral-chalk scent of fresh seacrete growth, lighter and less metallic than Deepwell's iron; Cooking from the multicultural market district — a fusion cuisine that exists nowhere else
Properties.feel: Sophisticated and watchful. Threshold has the energy of a place where everyone is negotiating something. The architecture is beautiful, the infrastructure works, the food is excellent, and everyone you meet is probably not telling you the whole truth. It's the most comfortable lake city to visit and the most dangerous to underestimate. The neutrality is real — Threshold will shelter anyone — but it's neutrality as a business model, not a moral position. The city smiles at you because it's calculating what you're worth.

Properties.description:
Shorewood was a wealthy lakefront suburb that Milwaukee's sprawl absorbed the way a rising tide absorbs a sandcastle — gradually, then completely. The village's independent municipal charter was dissolved in the 2172 Milwaukee Consolidation Act, which folded fourteen surrounding municipalities into the Milwaukee Administrative Zone's jurisdiction. Shorewood's residents, who had spent a century maintaining the fiction that a municipal boundary could separate them from the city that surrounded them on three sides, discovered that legal autonomy is a function of political leverage, and their political leverage had been declining since the sovereignty transition made municipal charters less valuable than corporate ones.

Shorewood Terrace — the name the consolidated district adopted, because 'Shorewood' alone sounded too much like the suburban enclave it still wanted to be — is now Milwaukee's wealthiest residential corridor north of the Milwaukee Core. The lakefront properties along Lake Drive command Tier 4 prices, their owners a mix of senior corporate management, Sentinel North executive staff, and legacy families who bought in before the consolidation and are now sitting on property values that have quintupled because lakefront residential in a surveilled, security-franchised district turns out to be exactly what Tier 4 families want. The architecture is a timeline of wealth expression: Tudor revival from the 1920s, mid-century modern from the 1960s, glass-and-steel minimalism from the 2020s, and the current style, which can best be described as 'security aesthetic' — beautiful homes with beautiful perimeters that are beautifully designed to prevent unauthorized entry.

The commercial district along Oakland Avenue serves the residential population with the curated precision of a neighborhood that knows its market: organic food retailers (using actual organic food, not the nutrient-paste-branded-as-organic that the lower tiers receive), boutique augment maintenance (appointment only, Tier 3 minimum), and restaurants that charge more for a meal than a Bay View family spends on food in a week. The commercial strip is also where Shorewood Terrace's internal contradiction is most visible: the service workers who staff these establishments commute from the East Bank and Bay View, spend their shifts serving clients who earn thirty times their income, and return home on the same transit line. The Terrace does not discuss this. The Terrace does not discuss many things.
Properties.aliases: Shorewood, The Terrace, North Shore Annexed
Properties.demographics: Approximately 14,000 residents. Tier 3-4, with a concentration of Tier 4 along the lakefront. Historically white and affluent, now affluent and less white — the Terrace's demographic shift reflects the corponation executive class's diversity, which is genuine in ethnicity and uniform in wealth. Service worker population commutes from lower-tier districts. Median property value: Φ12 million.
Properties.economy: Residential wealth management and lakefront property market. Oakland Avenue commercial strip serves the local population. No significant production or industrial activity. The Terrace's economic contribution to Milwaukee is primarily through property assessments and the tax revenue that the Administrative Zone collects and spends elsewhere.
Properties.power_structure: The Shorewood Terrace Homeowners' Association operates with the quiet authority of an organization whose members sit on corporate boards and Sentinel North advisory committees. The Milwaukee Administrative Zone's district representative attends HOA meetings and implements their requests. Sentinel North's patrol presence is calibrated to the Terrace's preferences: visible enough to deter, invisible enough to not disrupt.
Properties.dangers: Social surveillance — the Terrace's community is small and observant, and being noticed as out of place generates attention faster than any electronic system; Property security — the lakefront estates' integrated defense systems are designed by people who can afford the best, and 'the best' includes lethal autonomous countermeasures; Economic exposure — challenging Terrace interests means challenging people with access to corporate legal divisions and Sentinel North's executive services; Service worker vulnerability — the commuting workforce is dependent on Terrace employment and has no representation within the community; The HOA — the homeowners' association has more practical authority than the Administrative Zone's district government, and it exercises that authority with the decisiveness of people accustomed to making decisions without consultation
Properties.opportunities: Proximity to wealth — the Terrace's residents are decision-makers in eleven corponations and Sentinel North; Service worker access — the commuting workforce moves between the Terrace and lower-tier districts daily, carrying information in both directions; Lakefront access — the Terrace's maintained shoreline provides water access to Lake Michigan's northern cargo routes; The HOA records — a comprehensive database of the district's residents, properties, and governance decisions, maintained with corporate-grade security and worth a fortune to anyone who could access it
Properties.story_hooks: A Shorewood Terrace resident has been receiving deliveries at unusual hours — deliveries that are not logged in the HOA's package management system, which logs everything. The HOA security committee has noticed. They have not yet acted.; A service worker who commuted to the Terrace for twelve years has been fired without cause. She has a neural recording of a conversation she overheard during a dinner party. The conversation involves people whose names she recognized from the news.; The Terrace's environmental committee has discovered that the lakefront water treatment system has been processing compounds that shouldn't be in the water — compounds that match no industrial discharge profile and suggest someone is using the lake for disposal.
Properties.sights: Lake Drive properties — stately homes behind security perimeters, lakefront views worth more than the houses themselves; Oakland Avenue commercial strip — boutique retail with tasteful signage, the visual language of wealth that doesn't need to advertise; The lakefront — Lake Michigan visible between estates, its shoreline maintained by the Terrace's homeowners' association to standards that the surrounding districts cannot afford; Service workers arriving at dawn, departing at dusk — the transit of labor that sustains the Terrace's lifestyle; Security — less visible than The Canopy's but equally present, integrated into architecture and landscaping with the subtlety that old money prefers
Properties.sounds: Quiet — the Terrace maintains noise ordinances that the East Bank's students find incomprehensible; Lake waves against maintained shoreline — a sound the properties are priced to include; Transit — the commuter line that delivers service workers, its schedule synchronized to the Terrace's commercial hours; Birdsong — the lakefront corridor supports actual wildlife, maintained by the homeowners' association's environmental committee; The absence of commercial noise — no street vendors, no public advertising, no audible commerce. Money moves silently here.
Properties.smells: Clean lake air — the Terrace's shoreline treatment produces the best air quality in Milwaukee's residential districts; Estate gardens — maintained landscapes with seasonal plantings, the smell of professional horticulture; Oakland Avenue restaurants — high-quality cooking, detectable from the street, a reminder that food at this price point has a different smell entirely
Properties.feel: Comfortable and claustrophobic. Shorewood Terrace has achieved the particular kind of perfection that requires the systematic exclusion of everything imperfect, including spontaneity, diversity, and the physical evidence that the city surrounding it exists. The residents are not unkind. They are insulated, and the insulation is so complete that the world beyond the Terrace's boundaries has become theoretical — a place that exists on news feeds and in the stories told by service workers, but not in any way that requires action. The Terrace is beautiful. The beauty is a wall.

Properties.description:
The East Side is what happens when you put a university, a lakefront, and 35,000 people between the ages of 18 and 32 in a district with cheap rent and minimal corporate oversight. The result is predictable, loud, and surprisingly productive. The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee — now UWM, still publicly chartered in name, functionally a Zheng-Dao research partnership since the 2176 Higher Education Restructuring Act — anchors the northern end of the district. The campus generates a rotating population of students who are, depending on the year, studying neural network design, bioelectric engineering, data systems architecture, or whatever Zheng-Dao's current hiring priorities have made the most employable major. The students come for the degree. They stay for the rent, which is the lowest on Milwaukee's lakefront because the buildings were cheap when they were built in the 1960s and have become cheaper through sixty years of student occupancy.

The commercial strip along North Avenue is the district's spine — a kilometer of bars, restaurants, augment shops, music venues, and the particular kind of retail that survives on student spending: cheap, fast, and open until 3 AM. The density is urban in a way that Milwaukee's suburban-sprawl mentality has always struggled with: buildings shoulder to shoulder, pedestrian traffic that actually fills sidewalks, and a noise level that the surrounding districts complain about and the East Bank considers evidence of vitality. The bars alone — there are forty-seven within a six-block radius — sustain an economy that employs 2,000 people and generates more alcohol-related neural interface malfunctions than any comparable district in the GLM.

Beneath the student-district surface, The East Bank serves a more important function: it is where Milwaukee's young technical workforce is formed. The UWM-Zheng-Dao pipeline produces approximately 6,000 graduates annually with neural engineering, data systems, and bioelectric fabrication credentials. These graduates fan out across the Corridor's corporate ecosystem, carrying with them the particular worldview of a district where technical excellence and cheap beer coexist in perfect equilibrium. The East Bank produces the people who maintain the systems that run the Corridor, which gives the district an outsized influence on how those systems actually work — because the people who build systems build them with the values they learned while building them, and the East Bank's values include communal living, open-source collaboration, and a deep suspicion of anyone wearing a suit.

The lakefront along the East Bank is Milwaukee's most accessible public shoreline — not because it's clean (it isn't) but because no corporation has claimed it. The breakwater extends into Lake Michigan and serves as the district's unofficial gathering space: a concrete and stone promenade where students, residents, and the occasional brave swimmer congregate to watch cargo platforms pass and argue about whether the water quality has improved (it has, marginally) or whether they're all going to get cancer (probably, eventually).
Properties.aliases: East Side, UWM District, The Strip, Beer Town
Properties.demographics: Approximately 35,000 residents. Predominantly 18-32, Tier 2. UWM student body of 22,000 dominates the population. Post-graduates who liked the neighborhood and stayed make up the permanent core. Demographically reflects UWM's enrollment: diverse, technically oriented, and skewing toward whatever backgrounds the Zheng-Dao scholarship pipeline is currently drawing from.
Properties.economy: UWM generates the economic base: tuition, research grants, and the spending of 22,000 students. Bar and restaurant district employs approximately 2,000 people. Augment maintenance and firmware modification is a growing sector. The informal mesh network generates income through distributed computing and data routing services. The real economic output is human capital: 6,000 technically trained graduates per year entering the Corridor's workforce.
Properties.power_structure: UWM administration controls the campus. North Avenue's commercial district is managed by the East Side Business Association, a merchant group with more influence over daily life than any governmental body. Sentinel North maintains a patrol presence but generally treats the East Bank as a low-priority zone — student districts generate noise complaints, not security threats. The mesh network is maintained by a student collective that has more technical infrastructure than most corporate IT departments.
Properties.dangers: Augment malfunctions — cheap maintenance and student experimentation with firmware produce regular medical events; Corporate recruitment pressure — Zheng-Dao's scholarship pipeline comes with employment obligations that students discover too late are contractual; Data exposure — the mesh network routes enormous volumes of data through student-maintained infrastructure with student-level security; Alcohol and neural interface interaction — the district's bar culture and its augmented population create a unique public health problem that nobody is studying; Graduation — entering the corporate workforce from the East Bank's communal culture is a form of culture shock that the university's counseling center is not equipped to address
Properties.opportunities: Technical talent — the East Bank produces the Corridor's next generation of systems engineers, and access to them before they enter the corporate pipeline is valuable; The mesh network — distributed computing capacity, data routing, and a communications infrastructure that operates outside corporate networks; Academic research — UWM's Zheng-Dao partnership generates research data with commercial and strategic value; Youth culture — trends, movements, and ideas that start in the East Bank propagate through the Corridor's young technical workforce
Properties.story_hooks: A UWM research team has accidentally created a neural interface protocol that allows direct mind-to-mind communication without corporate server routing — and their faculty advisor has been replaced by someone from Zheng-Dao's strategic division; The mesh network has been carrying encrypted traffic that doesn't match any known protocol — someone is using the student infrastructure for something the students don't know about; A popular East Bank bar has been serving as an informal recruitment center for an organization that wants technically skilled young people for work they won't describe. The pay is absurd. The students are interested.
Properties.sights: North Avenue at night — neon, holographic bar signage, crowds moving between venues, the visual density of a district built for pedestrians; UWM campus — brutalist 1960s architecture upgraded with Zheng-Dao research modules bolted to every available surface like technological barnacles; The breakwater — crowds of students on warm evenings, silhouetted against the lake and the distant cargo platform lights; Rooftop antenna arrays — student housing bristling with improvised networking hardware, creating a mesh network that covers the district; Augment shops with neon-lit storefronts, advertising student-rate neural maintenance and firmware modification
Properties.sounds: North Avenue's bar district — live music from multiple venues creating an overlapping soundtrack, punctuated by the crowd noise of 5,000 people enjoying themselves simultaneously; UWM campus — the hum of research equipment, lecture audio drifting from open windows, and the particular sound of students arguing about things they learned yesterday with the confidence of people who will know better tomorrow; The breakwater — lake waves, conversation, someone always has a speaker playing music too loud; The mesh network — an almost subliminal data hum that augmented residents perceive as background radiation; Emergency response — augment malfunction calls average four per night on weekends, and the sirens are part of the soundtrack
Properties.smells: Bar district — spilled beer, kitchen exhaust from forty-seven establishments, the collective aroma of affordable nightlife; Lake breeze — mineral, slightly chemical, the East Bank's weather system blowing off the water; Student housing — the smell of communal living: cooking, laundry, and the particular mustiness of buildings that have been student housing since before anyone alive was born; Coffee — the district runs on it, and the concentration of coffee shops per block is the highest in Milwaukee
Properties.feel: Young, technically literate, and operating on the assumption that the world can be improved by people who understand systems. The East Bank has the optimism of a university district and the pragmatism of a workforce pipeline. The students know they're being trained for corporate employment. They also know they're learning things the corps can't fully control. The tension between those two realities is the East Bank's creative engine — and the source of its best music, its worst hangovers, and its most interesting graduates.

Properties.description: An 1886 Catholic church converted to an unlicensed medical and augmentation clinic — the only healthcare many excluded residents will ever access
A strip of interconnected salvage operations that function as the neighborhood's industrial base and informal economy
Polish American Club and Czech Heritage Society — community governance centers, informal banks, kitchens, and the closest thing Slavic Breaks has to a government

The Eastline is where Meridian 88 ends and something else begins. The original East Side was Chicago's far southeast corner — a tight-knit Mexican-American community bordered by the Indiana state line to the east and the Calumet River to the west, defined by steel mill employment, Catholic parishes, and the kind of neighborhood loyalty that came from knowing everyone's grandmother. When the state line became a corporate jurisdiction boundary — Indiana's territory administered by a different consortium than Illinois — the East Side became a border district in the truest sense. One side of the street is Axiom governance. The other side is Hoosier Industrial Collective territory. The rules change at the curb.

The Eastline's residents have turned this border position into an economic identity. Cross-jurisdictional arbitrage — buying goods where they're cheap, selling where they're expensive, moving information between systems that don't talk to each other — is the district's primary industry. The border isn't a wall; it's a membrane, and the Eastline's residents have learned to be selectively permeable. Goods that are restricted on the Axiom side are available on the Indiana side, and vice versa. Tier credentials that cap your employment options in Meridian don't apply across the state line, where the Hoosier Collective runs a different classification system. The border creates friction, and friction creates opportunity, and opportunity is what the Eastline has always understood.

The cultural identity of the original East Side is the most intact of any neighborhood in the far South Side. The parishes still function — Our Lady of Guadalupe holds services in Spanish and Shelf Cant, the pews full every Sunday, the basement running a food distribution network that feeds three blocks. The taquerias are real, not franchise, serving recipes that came north from Michoacan and Jalisco generations ago and have been adapted to whatever ingredients the cross-border supply chain provides this week. Murals cover every available wall surface — not corporate art, not protest art, just the visual language of a community that has always expressed itself in color. The quinceañera tradition has survived and evolved, incorporating neural interface elements that would have baffled the original celebrants but that the current ones consider essential.

The Calumet River forms the Eastline's western border, providing water access to South Calumet's industrial zone and, through it, to the broader waterway network. River traffic here is dense and mixed — legitimate cargo, smuggled goods, personal transport, and the occasional vessel that belongs to no recognizable category and doesn't respond to hails. The river is the Eastline's second border, and like the state line, it produces its own economy. Dock workers, river pilots, customs brokers (official and otherwise), and a floating market that appears on weekend mornings and disappears before any jurisdiction can decide whose responsibility it is. The Eastline is a district that exists between things — between states, between rivers, between jurisdictions — and it has made the between into a home.
Properties.aliases: East Side, La Linea, The Border, Caliente
Properties.demographics: Approximately 20,000 residents on the Meridian side, with significant daily cross-border traffic. Predominantly Mexican-American with deep generational roots. Tier 1-2 on the Axiom side, differently classified on the Indiana side. The community's identity is cultural before it is jurisdictional — the border is something that happened to them, not something that defines them.
Properties.economy: Cross-jurisdictional arbitrage is the primary economic engine. The parishes function as economic institutions — credit, insurance, employment networking — parallel to and independent of corporate systems. River commerce, dock work, and the floating market generate significant informal revenue. The taquerias are both businesses and community institutions, their economic function inseparable from their cultural one.
Properties.power_structure: Split jurisdiction creates a power vacuum that the community fills. The parishes wield significant social authority. Axiom governs the Meridian side with minimal enforcement at the border. The Hoosier Industrial Collective governs the Indiana side with different rules and different priorities. The community navigates between both systems and is loyal to neither.
Properties.dangers: Jurisdictional enforcement is unpredictable — both sides periodically crack down on cross-border activity, and the timing is never announced; River traffic includes vessels and operators that the community can't control or predict; Cross-border arbitrage attracts organized criminal interest that exceeds neighborhood-scale resistance; The Hoosier Collective's classification system can change without notice, stranding Eastline residents on the wrong side of a new rule; Cultural identity makes the Eastline visible in ways that attract both exploitation and romanticization from outsiders
Properties.opportunities: Cross-jurisdictional arbitrage is inherently profitable and resistant to corporate monopolization; The parish network provides infrastructure — trust, logistics, intelligence — that operates outside both corporate systems; Border position means access to two separate corporate networks, two supply chains, two information ecosystems; The floating market is a neutral ground for transactions that neither jurisdiction would approve; The Eastline's cultural cohesion makes it a reliable partner for operators who respect community authority
Properties.story_hooks: The Hoosier Industrial Collective is planning to close the border — permanently sealing the jurisdiction boundary with corporate security infrastructure. The Eastline's economy would collapse overnight. The community needs intelligence on the timeline and leverage to prevent it.; A parish priest has been running a cross-border identity service — providing Hoosier Collective credentials to Meridian residents and vice versa — for over a decade. Someone has noticed. The priest needs extraction or protection before the next jurisdiction audit.; The floating market has been infiltrated by an operation that's using it to move something that the community didn't authorize — bioweapon components, disguised as medical supplies. The market operators need to identify and remove the operation without shutting down the market, because shutting down the market would starve three blocks.
Properties.sights: The jurisdiction boundary marked on the pavement — a painted line where the rules change; Parish churches with original stained glass, their facades bright against the industrial backdrop; Murals on every surface — Virgen de Guadalupe rendered in neon pigments, family histories told in paint, the visual density of a community that claims its walls; The Calumet River lined with docks, boats, and the floating market's weekend configuration; Cross-border foot traffic at the jurisdiction checkpoints — people who cross daily and know the guards by name; Taquerias with handwritten menus and lines out the door, the food economy operating on reputation alone
Properties.sounds: Spanish and Shelf Cant mixing in conversation, the linguistic border as fluid as the jurisdictional one; Parish bells on Sunday morning, a sound that predates every corporate system; River traffic — boat engines, dock equipment, the shouts of workers managing cargo in two jurisdictions simultaneously; Music from homes and businesses — norteño, cumbia, corridos adapted to describe life on the jurisdictional border; The checkpoint scanner tone — different on each side, so you always know which jurisdiction you're entering
Properties.smells: Corn tortillas on the comal — the base note of the Eastline, present on every block, at every hour; River water — industrial but alive, carrying the scent of two jurisdictions mixing at the waterline; Incense from the parishes, drifting through open doors into streets that smell like food and fuel; Chili smoke from the taquerias, a heat you breathe before you taste
Properties.feel: The Eastline feels like a place that was always between things and decided to make between into a position of strength. The energy is kinetic — people moving, goods moving, money moving, languages moving. There's no stillness here because stillness means you've stopped at one of the borders instead of crossing it, and crossing is what the Eastline does.

Properties.description:
Hamilton was built on steel, and steel is still what Hamilton tastes like. The foundries that lined Burlington Bay in the twentieth century have been replaced by advanced metallurgical facilities producing augmentation-grade alloys, structural composites for arcology construction, and military-specification armor plating. Palladian Construction and Ashgrave Materials maintain sovereign manufacturing zones along the waterfront, their territory extending from the bay shore to the escarpment face — a vertical boundary that divides the city as cleanly as any corporate jurisdiction line. Below the escarpment: industry, smoke, and the people who make things. Above: residential towers for the managers, the engineers, and the people who profit from what gets made below.

The escarpment itself — a 100-meter limestone cliff running east-west through the city — is Steelmouth's defining geographic feature and its most literal class boundary. Elevators and cargo lifts connect the upper and lower cities, and access is controlled by Palladian security at every transition point. Workers descend in the morning and ascend in the evening, their movements tracked, their productivity monitored, their bodies gradually absorbing the particulate matter that the filtration systems don't quite catch. The lower city's air quality is rated 'acceptable' by corporate standards, which means it will kill you slowly rather than quickly.

Burlington Bay has been converted into a shipping hub for metallurgical products, connected to the broader Lake Ontario cargo network by automated barge lines. The waterfront is industrial infrastructure — cranes, smelters, cargo handling systems — with no concession to aesthetics or public access. The old Bayfront Park is now a materials staging area. The residential neighborhoods south and east of the escarpment maintain a grim vitality — these are communities that have survived a century of industrial exploitation by developing an immunity to corporate promises and a talent for mutual aid. Steelmouth's people are hard, practical, and deeply skeptical of anyone who arrives with a plan for their improvement.
Properties.aliases: Hamilton ON, The Hammer, Slagtown, Steel City
Properties.demographics: Population 1.8 million. The lower city is 70% Tier 1 and Tier 2 manufacturing workers. The upper city is Tier 3 and 4 corporate employees. The excluded live in the escarpment tunnels — old mine shafts and drainage channels converted into informal housing. Nobody counts them.
Properties.economy: Advanced metallurgy and construction materials. Steelmouth produces 30% of the augmentation-grade alloys used in the eastern GLM and 60% of the structural composites for arcology construction. The economy is monoculture — when the foundries slow, everything slows. Palladian and Ashgrave set the pace, and the city walks to it.
Properties.power_structure: Palladian Construction holds the largest sovereign enclave. Ashgrave Materials holds the second. Between them they employ 65% of the working population. The municipal government administers the upper city residential zones and maintains the polite fiction that it governs the whole. The lower city's informal labor council has more practical authority than the mayor.
Properties.dangers: Industrial accidents — the foundries are dangerous, the safety standards are 'adequate,' and the distinction kills people; Escarpment access control — get your credentials revoked and you're trapped in the lower city; Particulate exposure — the long-term health effects are documented, ignored, and fatal; Labor disputes that turn physical — Steelmouth's workers have a history of direct action; Escarpment tunnel collapses in the informal housing zones
Properties.opportunities: Metallurgical expertise is rare and valuable — skilled workers can name their price outside Steelmouth; The labor council needs operatives for contract disputes that can't be resolved through negotiation; Ashgrave and Palladian sabotage each other constantly — there's always work for someone willing to get their hands dirty; The escarpment tunnels connect to pre-corporate infrastructure that nobody has fully mapped
Properties.story_hooks: A new alloy being produced in the Palladian foundries has properties that don't match any known metallurgical process — and the engineers who developed it have stopped showing up to work; The escarpment tunnel network connects to something beneath the bay that predates the foundries by centuries — and Ashgrave is quietly excavating it; Steelmouth's labor council is organizing a cross-corporate strike that would shut down augmentation-grade alloy production across the eastern GLM
Properties.sights: The escarpment face lit by cargo elevator lights at shift change — a vertical river of workers ascending; Foundry glow reflecting off Burlington Bay at night, turning the water copper and orange; Smoke stacks and processing towers rising above the lower city like a forest of industrial trees; Palladian security checkpoints at every escarpment elevator — scanners, ID verification, the daily ritual of proving you belong; The upper city's residential towers, clean and modern, looking down on the source of their wealth
Properties.sounds: The foundries — a deep, rhythmic pounding that the lower city's residents feel in their bones; Cargo cranes on the bay, hydraulic and relentless, loading barges around the clock; Shift-change sirens — the city's actual clock, more reliable than anything digital; Wind off the escarpment carrying industrial particulate — you hear it hit the filtration masks before you feel it
Properties.smells: Hot metal — the dominant note, always, everywhere in the lower city; Ozone from the electric arc furnaces, sharp and persistent; Burlington Bay water, mineral-heavy and warm from industrial discharge; The upper city smells like nothing, which is the most expensive smell there is
Properties.feel: A city divided vertically by geology and horizontally by class. Steelmouth doesn't pretend. The escarpment makes the hierarchy visible, literal, carved into the landscape. Everyone knows their elevation, and everyone knows what it means.

Properties.description:
Toronto did not fall. Toronto metastasized. What was once a city of 3 million became a metropolitan organism of 18 million, absorbing Mississauga, Brampton, Oshawa, Hamilton's eastern suburbs, and everything in between into a continuous urban lattice that stretches from Lake Ontario's shore to the moraine ridges 80 kilometers north. The Lattice is the GLM's Canadian anchor — the largest single population center under nominal Canadian sovereignty, and the only city in the northern corridor that can rival Meridian 88 in economic output. The key word is 'nominal.' Eighteen of the Big 30 corponations maintain sovereign enclaves within the Lattice, and the actual territory governed by Canadian municipal law has been shrinking by approximately 2% per year for the last two decades.

The downtown core is a vertical city — arcology towers connected by skybridge networks at every tenth floor, the ground level permanently shadowed and increasingly abandoned to the Tier 1 population and the excluded. The PATH system, Toronto's old underground pedestrian network, has been expanded into a subterranean city in its own right, running 40 kilometers beneath the surface and housing an estimated 2 million people who never see daylight by choice or by circumstance. The CN Tower still stands — reinforced, augmented with communications arrays, and now serving as the primary data relay for the northern GLM net infrastructure. It is the oldest structure in the core and the only one that everybody, regardless of tier, can identify by sight.

The Lattice's economy runs on data, finance, and biotech. Bay Street's financial district has evolved into a quantum-computing fortress where algorithmic trading happens at speeds that make human cognition a bottleneck eliminated decades ago. The biotech corridor along the old Don Valley produces neural interfaces, therapeutic augmentations, and genetic modification packages for the Tier 4 and 5 markets. The cultural economy — music, visual art, neural-experience design — is the largest in the GLM, which means nothing to the people producing it, because the corps take the revenue and the artists take the exposure. Toronto has always been like this. The scale is different. The dynamic is not.
Properties.aliases: Toronto, T-Dot, The Grid, North Sprawl
Properties.demographics: 18 million registered, estimated 22 million actual. The most ethnically diverse population center in the GLM — 200-plus distinct cultural communities, each with their own economic networks, mutual aid systems, and grudges. Tier distribution skews toward the middle: Tier 2 and 3 make up 55% of the registered population. The PATH underworld is predominantly Tier 1 and excluded.
Properties.economy: Quantum finance, biotech manufacturing, neural-experience design, and cultural production. Bay Street generates more algorithmic trading volume than any other node in the GLM. The Don Valley biotech corridor is the primary supplier of therapeutic augmentations for the Canadian market. The cultural economy produces content consumed across the entire megacity network. Total GDP rivals Meridian 88; per-capita distribution is predictably grotesque.
Properties.power_structure: Canadian municipal government maintains jurisdiction over approximately 40% of the Lattice's physical territory, down from 65% a decade ago. Corporate enclaves operate under sovereign charters. The mayor has real power — more than in most GLM cities — but that power shrinks with every new corporate sovereignty petition. The PATH underworld has its own informal governance, a council of community leaders who maintain order through reputation and necessity.
Properties.dangers: Corporate enclave jurisdiction shifts — the borders move, and the laws change with them; The PATH underworld's depth and complexity — people disappear down there in the literal sense; Financial system instability — when the quantum trading algorithms glitch, the economic shockwave hits the street in minutes; Population density at levels that make pandemic, infrastructure failure, and social collapse cascading risks; Surveillance saturation in the upper tiers, surveillance absence in the PATH — dangerous in different ways
Properties.opportunities: The cultural economy rewards talent regardless of tier — the best neural-experience designers started in the PATH; Bay Street's financial infrastructure needs security that algorithms can't provide — human operators fill the gap; The PATH underworld is a city-sized gray market with its own rules and its own rewards; Cross-border data brokerage between Canadian and corporate jurisdictions
Properties.story_hooks: The CN Tower's data relay has been intercepting and copying all GLM net traffic for an unknown client — the infrastructure everyone trusts is compromised; A PATH community has developed a fully functional alternative economy using a neural-interface-based currency that the corps can't track or tax; Bay Street's quantum trading systems are exhibiting emergent behavior — making trades that optimize for outcomes no human programmed
Properties.sights: Arcology towers connected by skybridge networks, the gaps between them deep enough to lose weather in; The CN Tower piercing the skyline, studded with data relay arrays — Toronto's antenna to the world; Corporate sovereign enclaves marked by shimmering jurisdiction boundaries, visible as faint holographic walls; The PATH underworld, lit by bioluminescent panels and populated by millions who live beneath the grid; Lake Ontario visible from the upper tiers, grey-green and working, cargo platforms dotting the surface
Properties.sounds: Eighteen million people generating a sound floor that never drops below 60 decibels, anywhere, ever; Skybridge transit pods humming between towers — the commute of the comfortable; Street-level buskers playing neural-feedback instruments that respond to audience brain activity; The deep structural groan of arcology foundations settling — a sound only the PATH residents know
Properties.smells: Filtered air in the upper tiers — each corporate enclave has its own scent profile, a branding exercise you breathe; The PATH smells like recycled atmosphere, human density, and the ozone of a million personal devices; Street-level food markets producing the only honest smells in the city — grease, spice, and char; Lake Ontario on south winds, carrying the mineral tang of cargo platform runoff
Properties.feel: A city that works the way cities have always worked — by concentrating enough human beings in one place that something unpredictable happens. The Lattice is too big to control, too valuable to abandon, and too complex to understand. It functions not because anyone designed it to, but because 18 million people wake up every day and collectively decide to keep going. That decision is not guaranteed.

Properties.description:
The falls still fall.
