That much hasn't changed. 750,000 gallons per second pouring over a 50-meter cliff face, generating enough hydroelectric power to light a city — which is exactly what they do, though the city they light bears no resemblance to the tourist trap that existed a century ago. The observation decks are still there, maintained by Mirrorwell Media as an 'experiential heritage installation,' which means you can still watch the water if you pay the admission fee. Most people don't. The power is worth more than the view.

Volt Falls is the GLM's primary clean energy node on the Canadian side. Ouroboros Energy holds sovereign authority over the generating facilities — a complex of turbine halls, transformer stations, and distribution infrastructure that extends for 12 kilometers along the Niagara River gorge. The old tourist district — wax museums, haunted houses, chain restaurants — has been partially demolished, partially repurposed, and entirely absorbed into the energy infrastructure's support economy. Casino towers that once drew gamblers from Toronto now house Ouroboros administrative staff and the engineers who keep the turbines turning. The irony is perfect: the city that sold spectacle now sells watts, and the watts are more honest.

The border with the American side runs down the middle of the river, and the energy generated by the falls is split between Canadian and American grids by treaty — the Niagara Power Allocation Protocol, renegotiated every five years with increasing hostility. The American side, controlled by Cinderfall Energy, consistently pushes for a larger share. The Canadian side, controlled by Ouroboros, consistently resists. The falls don't care. They generate power regardless of who claims it, which is the most politically neutral statement anyone has made about Niagara in decades. Below the generating facilities, the gorge itself has become a restricted zone — the infrastructure is too valuable to allow public access, and the security perimeter extends to the water's edge.
Properties.aliases: Niagara Falls ON, The Dynamo, Kilowatt City, The Falls
Properties.demographics: Population 320,000, predominantly Ouroboros employees and their dependents. The engineering corps — turbine specialists, grid management technicians, power distribution experts — forms a technical aristocracy. Service workers who support the infrastructure and its people make up the Tier 1 and 2 base. Tourists are technically still welcome. Tourists rarely come.
Properties.economy: Hydroelectric power generation and distribution. Ouroboros Energy's Niagara operations supply approximately 15% of the Canadian GLM's electricity. The tourism economy that sustained the old city is effectively dead, replaced by the support economy for 320,000 energy workers. Mirrorwell Media maintains the heritage installations as a tax write-off.
Properties.power_structure: Ouroboros Energy sovereign territory, with minimal Canadian federal oversight limited to the Niagara Power Allocation Protocol negotiations. The generating facilities are classified as critical infrastructure, which grants Ouroboros expanded security authority. The municipal government exists to maintain residential zones outside the energy infrastructure perimeter.
Properties.dangers: Power infrastructure sabotage — the generating facilities are the highest-value target on the Canadian lakeshore; Transformer field exposure — the electromagnetic environment near the facilities affects unshielded augmentations; The Niagara Power Allocation Protocol negotiations turning violent — it's happened twice in the last decade; The gorge restricted zone — trespass is met with automated defense systems; Ouroboros security operating under critical infrastructure authority — expanded powers, limited accountability
Properties.opportunities: Energy sector expertise is the most portable skill in the GLM — Volt Falls-trained engineers are recruited globally; Power allocation intelligence is valuable to both Ouroboros and Cinderfall; The old tourist infrastructure contains pre-corporate spaces that Ouroboros hasn't mapped or secured; The border dispute creates demand for negotiators, intermediaries, and people who can work both sides
Properties.story_hooks: Ouroboros is diverting a percentage of generating capacity to an unlisted facility beneath the gorge — the power goes in, nothing comes out, and the energy budget doesn't balance; The Niagara Power Allocation Protocol is up for renegotiation, and someone is assassinating the negotiators on both sides; The falls' output has increased by 3% over the last year — more water, more power — and nobody can explain where the additional water is coming from
Properties.sights: The falls themselves — still magnificent, now framed by turbine intake structures and power distribution arrays; Ouroboros transformer stations lining the gorge, humming with visible electrical discharge; The old casino towers repurposed as corporate housing, their neon signs replaced with Ouroboros branding; Power distribution lines radiating outward from the falls like a spider's web made of copper and ambition; The American side visible across the gorge, Cinderfall's competing infrastructure mirroring Ouroboros's
Properties.sounds: The falls — a constant roar that you stop hearing and start feeling, a vibration in every surface; Turbine harmonics — a deep, mechanical chord underlying the water's thunder; Transformer hum at frequencies that make your augments twitch if they're not properly shielded; The absence of tourist noise — the loudest natural wonder in the GLM, surrounded by industrial silence
Properties.smells: Ozone from the generating facilities — clean, sharp, electric; Mist from the falls, carrying the mineral tang of the Great Lakes; Transformer coolant — a faint, sweet chemical note
Properties.feel: A place where nature's indifference to human ambition is converted into kilowatt-hours. The falls are sublime. The infrastructure is mundane. The combination is Volt Falls — the most beautiful power plant in the world, and a power plant all the same.

Properties.description: The vertical boundary between the upper and lower cities — 100 meters of limestone that makes class hierarchy geological
The primary Palladian foundry facility on Burlington Bay — the largest single metallurgical operation in the eastern GLM
Informal housing in the escarpment's old mine shafts — home to the excluded, and connected to infrastructure nobody fully controls

Substation Null is a decommissioned power relay hub occupying several interconnected levels beneath the northern stretch of The Shelf, accessible through maintenance tunnels, a handful of unofficial entry points, and one known surface entrance that most people who use it pretend doesn't exist. Originally constructed to manage power distribution for a now-demolished industrial sector, the station was officially abandoned during the infrastructure consolidation of the 2040s and subsequently removed from city maintenance records — an omission that was either bureaucratic error or deliberate, depending on who you ask.
Properties.aliases: The Null, Under-Zero, The Quiet Place, Station Nothing
Properties.demographics: A rotating population of 300-800 individuals depending on conditions above ground. Off-grid residents, fugitives, political dissidents, individuals escaping debt or corporate indenture, and a core of long-term inhabitants who have built permanent lives here. Also hosts a significant transient population using it as a waypoint.
Properties.economy: Barter-dominant with some scrip circulating from the surface. Residents trade skills, scavenged materials, information, and labor. A small number of above-ground operators provide essential supplies in exchange for services the Null's population can uniquely offer: discretion, access to the tunnel network, and off-record technical work.
Properties.power_structure: The Council of Conductors — an ironic title adopted by seven long-term residents who manage resource allocation, dispute resolution, and security policy. Membership is earned through tenure and community trust rather than election. Their authority is real but consensus-based; they can be overruled by collective action and they know it.
Properties.dangers: Infrastructure failure — aging power conduits, unstable ceilings, and flooding from above are constant threats; City utility crews occasionally enter for maintenance and must be redirected or avoided; Bounty runners and corporate retrieval teams probe the tunnel network for specific targets; Interpersonal violence in a closed environment with no external authority; Air quality in the deeper sections requires monitoring and can degrade without warning; The power taps are illegal and any significant draw could trigger automated fault detection above ground
Properties.opportunities: Unmonitored meeting space with no surveillance infrastructure; Access to the tunnel network connecting to multiple districts across the city; A community of people with strong motivation to stay off official records — ideal for sensitive recruitment; Technical expertise concentrated among residents who have learned to maintain infrastructure with nothing; A repository of information about city infrastructure that predates current digital records
Properties.story_hooks: The Council of Conductors has sent word through careful channels that something is moving through the deeper tunnels — something they cannot identify and are not willing to investigate alone; A child born in the Null has been identified by a corporate genetic database as carrying a proprietary gene sequence, triggering a legal claim of ownership that the above-ground courts are taking seriously; A section of the Null that has been sealed for fifteen years has begun broadcasting a repeating signal on a frequency that interferes with local neural implants; A long-term resident who served as an unofficial historian has died, and their records — which reportedly document the real reasons the station was decommissioned — have gone missing; The Council needs help negotiating with a new group that has moved into the deep tunnels — armed, organized, and not interested in the existing arrangement
Properties.sights: Enormous decommissioned transformer housings repurposed as walls, rooms, and structural supports; Bioluminescent fungal growth cultivated along certain corridors as low-maintenance lighting; Jury-rigged power taps drawing from nearby active conduits — the wiring is a palimpsest of decades of ad hoc additions; Chalk and spray-paint wayfinding marks in evolving community shorthand; Condensation dripping from ceiling infrastructure, collected in improvised cisterns
Properties.sounds: The deep subsonic hum of power conduits running overhead — felt more than heard; Dripping water echoing in high-ceilinged chambers; Muffled conversations from behind closed-off sections; Distant transit rumble from city infrastructure above; The occasional burst of sound from the deeper levels where noise discipline relaxes
Properties.smells: Damp concrete and mineral water; Old machine oil soaked into every surface; Cooking smells from the inhabited sections — usually something with a lot of spice; Ozone from the live power infrastructure; The particular staleness of recycled air that has been breathed too many times
Properties.feel: The Null feels like the city's held breath — removed from the noise and surveillance above, heavy with the knowledge that the people here have chosen or been forced into invisibility. There is community in the dark, but also paranoia, and the infrastructure that shelters residents could kill them if it failed.

Properties.description: The largest interior space in the Null, occupying the footprint of the original primary relay chamber. The decommissioned transformer housings have been converted into residences, workshops, and communal spaces. A central fire pit — vented through a carefully maintained chimney improvised from old conduit — serves as the community's social center. The Council meets here in open session on the first of each month.

A cramped side chamber where decades of residents have deposited documentation: handwritten journals, printed city records, salvaged hard drives, and hand-drawn maps of the tunnel network. Maintained by a rotating archivist, it represents an unofficial history of both Substation Null and the city above from the perspective of those the city forgot.

A tunnel extending beyond the known inhabited sections of the Null, running beneath city blocks that have changed ownership multiple times. The walls here predate the station itself, incorporating older infrastructure of uncertain purpose. The Council discourages exploration without escort, citing structural instability — though longtime residents suspect the reasons are more complicated.

A vertical farming and pharmaceutical synthesis district rising from the flooded eastern fringe of what was once Waukegan's residential core, the Amber Stacks earned its name from the honeyed glow that pours from its tiered hydroponic bays at all hours — amber UV lamps burning through translucent polycarbonate panels stacked fourteen stories high across six interconnected tower blocks. The complex was originally built by Helix Biosystems as a controlled agricultural pilot in the 2160s, but corporate interest waned after the second Great Lakes salinity event, and the towers were sold piecemeal to a consortium of Tier 3 agricultural cooperatives, black-market chemists, and a surprisingly organized community land trust run by a collective of displaced Hmong and Somali-Bantu families who had been farming the lower levels without authorization since 2171.

Today the Amber Stacks is a contradictory place: part legitimate food production hub supplying leafy greens and fungal protein to a significant slice of the Lakeshore Corridor, part labyrinthine gray-market biosynthesis operation tucked into the upper floors where the elevator shafts stop and rope ladders begin. The air inside the towers is thick and tropical even in January, the humidity pressed into every surface by the constant transpiration of thousands of plant rows. Walkways between grow beds double as informal markets during the day, vendors selling clipped herb bundles, homegrown supplements, and unlicensed pharma compounds in plain brown sachets.

The towers are connected at the third and eighth floors by enclosed sky-bridges that have been colonized into something resembling a permanent bazaar — corrugated shelving, hanging privacy screens, the smell of cooking oil mixing with chlorophyll and damp earth. BCI signal here is intentionally throttled by a community-managed mesh that keeps corporate surveillance nodes from indexing the upper floors. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract for the ground level, but their operatives rarely venture above floor five, and everyone in the Stacks knows it.
Properties.aliases: The Stacks, Amber Row, The Resin District, Goldblock
Properties.demographics: Majority Tier 3 with pockets of Tier 2 cooperative stakeholders. Predominantly multigenerational families from the Hmong and Somali-Bantu communities who established the land trust, with a significant secondary population of independent chemists, unlicensed pharmacists, and agricultural workers of mixed global origin. Small but influential population of Tier 4 residents who moved up from the Shelf after finding stable work in the cooperative.
Properties.economy: Dual economy: the legitimate face is a cooperative food production network supplying vegetables, fungi, and plant-based proteins to the Lakeshore Corridor and parts of the Northwest Sprawl, generating modest but stable Φ income distributed through the land trust. The gray-market economy in the upper floors is substantially more lucrative — unlicensed biosynthetics, agricultural compounds repurposed as pharma precursors, and a significant trade in unregistered BCI-compatible nootropics. The cooperative officially denies knowledge of the upper-floor operations.
Properties.power_structure: The Amber Stacks Community Land Trust holds formal authority over the lower floors and is governed by a rotating council of twelve elected representatives from the founding families. Above floor nine, authority is informal and syndicate-adjacent — a loose coalition of synthesis operators who pay a tithe to the land trust in exchange for non-interference. Ferrogate Security's ground-level contract gives them nominal access but no real leverage. Helix Biosystems retains a dormant legal claim to the tower infrastructure that everyone pretends does not exist.
Properties.dangers: Upper-floor biosynthesis operations attract periodic raids from Ferrogate corporate enforcement units acting on behalf of pharmaceutical clients — raids that are rarely announced and sometimes violent; The throttled BCI mesh means emergency services cannot be easily summoned and medical assistance is slow to arrive; Structural instability in towers four and five, where the original Helix construction was never fully completed — certain floors are weight-restricted and the restrictions are not always observed; Rival synthesis operators from outside the Stacks occasionally attempt to muscle into the upper floors, bringing armed pressure; Contamination events from improperly contained synthesis processes have twice required evacuation of grow floors below
Properties.opportunities: The land trust's leadership is actively seeking a negotiator or fixer capable of neutralizing the dormant Helix Biosystems legal claim before it is weaponized; The gray-market pharma network provides access to unlicensed compounds unavailable elsewhere in the Lakeshore Corridor at below-market rates for those with the right introductions; The community mesh network's architecture offers a rare zone of genuine BCI-surveillance dead space useful for sensitive meetings or data transfers
Properties.story_hooks: A Helix Biosystems subsidiary has quietly retained a Palladian Group legal team to reactivate the tower infrastructure claim — not to reclaim the facility, but to use the legal threat as leverage to force the land trust's synthesis operators to supply precursor compounds exclusively to a Helix distribution network. The land trust council has one month before the filing goes public and is desperately looking for someone with the skills to find and destroy the evidence trail that Helix is using to establish the claim's validity.; A child from one of the founding families has developed a severe neurological reaction to something synthesized in the upper floors — something that was never supposed to leave that floor, and whose presence in the lower levels suggests either an accident or deliberate contamination. The family wants answers without involving Ferrogate or any outside authority, which means someone needs to go into the upper floors alone and find out what went wrong and why.
Properties.sights: Amber and violet UV light bleeding through frosted panels, casting warm halos across wet grating; Cascading rows of lettuce, herbs, engineered grain-stalks, and bioluminescent mushroom clusters climbing every available surface; Sky-bridge markets strung with hand-painted inventory signs and tangled extension cords powering portable cold-storage units; Residents moving through grow lanes in rubber clogs and moisture-resistant coveralls, their BCI headsets fogged with condensation; Helix Biosystems corporate branding half-scraped from the tower facades, replaced with community murals in Somali and Hmong patterns
Properties.sounds: The constant low hum of irrigation pumps and circulation fans creating a droning white noise throughout every floor; Calls in Somali, Hmong, Tagalog, and Mandarin echoing across the sky-bridges during market hours; The wet drip of nutrient solution cycling through overhead pipes and the occasional clatter of a dropped harvest crate; Distant bass from a sound system someone has rigged into the eighth-floor bridge, playing low-tempo electronic folk
Properties.smells: Rich, green, slightly sweet smell of photosynthesizing plants layered over humid earth and nutrient solution; Cooking oil and fermented grain from the informal kitchen stalls in the sky-bridges; A sharp pharmaceutical undertone on the upper floors — solvents, acetone, something floral and slightly wrong; Mold and rot in the darker maintenance corridors where the irrigation drainage pools
Properties.feel: The Amber Stacks feels like stepping into a living organism — warm, breathing, slightly resistant to movement, the air itself a presence that clings to clothing and skin. There is a low-level industriousness here that never quite stops, people trimming and harvesting and hauling at all hours, and a social density that reads as neighborly rather than threatening during daylight. After dark the upper floors acquire a different quality: quieter, more purposeful in a way that discourages questions. The mesh network's suppression of external BCI signals creates a subtle disorientation for newcomers, a slight cognitive flatness that the long-term residents have adapted to and newcomers find unsettling.

Properties.description: The larger of the two sky-bridges, running between towers two and three at the eighth floor. The primary informal market space, active from mid-morning to late night, with a density of vendors and social activity that makes it feel like a compressed neighborhood street.

A sprawling subterranean civic ruin occupying the collapsed lower levels of what was once a Chicago municipal complex near the old Loop perimeter. Centuries of sediment, flood damage, and hasty structural reinforcement have transformed it into a labyrinthine underworld of half-flooded chambers and improvised galleries where displaced Tier 3 and 4 residents broker informal governance. The ceilings drip with mineral deposits that glow faintly under UV lighting rigs salvaged from Axiom Industries waste runs.

Despite its decrepit foundation, the Ashen Quorum functions as one of the corridor's most active gray-market legislative spaces, where neighborhood bloc leaders, syndicate liaisons, and rogue synthetic advocates hash out territorial agreements beyond the reach of Ferrogate Security patrols. The walls are plastered with decades of faction graffiti, printed manifestos, and Diaspora-linked AR overlays that shift depending on whose BCI credentials you're broadcasting.
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 3 and lower Tier 2 residents, with a significant synthetic population seeking legal advocacy space and a rotating cast of fixers, bloc organizers, and off-duty Carrion Logistics workers.
Properties.economy: Runs on informal service exchange, gray-market Φ transfers, and tribute arrangements between territorial factions; no licensed businesses operate openly, though food stalls and data brokers are abundant.
Properties.power_structure: A loose council of seven bloc representatives — the Quorum Seats — holds nominal authority, though enforcement depends entirely on the goodwill of whichever syndicate currently controls the eastern access tunnels.
Properties.dangers: Structural collapses in the older western chambers, where reinforcement work has been deferred for decades; Rival syndicate enforcers using negotiation meetings as cover for targeted eliminations; Ferrogate Security staging periodic 'compliance sweeps' that are widely understood to be shakedowns
Properties.opportunities: Accessing off-record political intelligence that never surfaces on the Diaspora's monitored channels; Brokering introductions to synthetic civil rights networks operating under legal radar; Acquiring salvaged municipal infrastructure schematics that predate the megacity consolidation
Properties.story_hooks: One of the seven Quorum Seats has gone missing three days before a critical territorial vote that would redraw syndicate boundaries across the South Loop underlevels. The remaining six are convinced it's an assassination, but the missing representative's BCI last pinged from inside the Quorum itself — and the access logs have been scrubbed.; A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric operative has been attending Quorum sessions under a false Tier 3 residential identity, and someone has leaked this to both Ferrogate Security and the local E.L.F. advocacy bloc simultaneously. All three factions are now maneuvering inside the Quorum, and the players are caught in the middle.
Properties.sights: Bioluminescent mineral stalactites casting blue-white halos over crowded negotiation tables; Holographic faction banners flickering where water has damaged the projection nodes; Long corridors of cracked municipal tile stenciled with obsolete ward designations
Properties.sounds: The constant low drip and echo of water moving through cracked concrete channels; Overlapping arguments in Mandarin, Yoruba, and Chicago creole patois; Distant hum of salvaged generator banks keeping the Diaspora uplinks alive
Properties.smells: Mineral-heavy standing water and wet concrete; Cheap synth-tobacco smoke drifting from negotiation alcoves; Ozone from overworked BCI relay boosters mounted on every pillar
Properties.feel: The Ashen Quorum carries the weight of exhausted pragmatism — everyone here has given up on official channels and is trying to build something functional from what remains. The air is thick with tension that rarely erupts into open violence, held in check by mutual need.

Properties.description:
West Town was three neighborhoods pretending to be one: Wicker Park, Bucktown, and Ukrainian Village. Each had its own identity, its own pride, its own argument about where the boundaries were. The incorporation resolved the argument by dissolving all three into a single corporate development zone and renaming it West Town Upside — 'upside' being corporate real estate jargon for unrealized property value. The name stuck because the residents found it grimly appropriate. Everything here has been flipped: community into commodity, culture into content, neighborhood into investment vehicle.

Wicker Park's six-way intersection — the old heart of the neighborhood's indie music, art, and nightlife scene — is now the Hexagon, a corporate entertainment complex operated by an Axiom lifestyle subsidiary. The Hexagon's six streets radiate outward like spokes, each themed to a different 'authentic urban experience': live music (approved), street art (commissioned), vintage shopping (curated), craft dining (algorithmic), nightlife (monitored), and 'community' (a word that has been emptied of meaning and refilled with brand strategy). The Hexagon draws Tier 3-5 visitors from across the Corridor for a night out that feels dangerous without being dangerous, creative without being challenging, and urban without being urban. It is the most profitable entertainment district in the outer Corridor, and the most soulless.

Bucktown's residential streets have been converted to what the developer calls 'Heritage Housing' — pre-collapse homes maintained in original condition on the outside and gutted to corporate specification on the inside. The Ukrainian Village section retains its churches — the golden domes are too photogenic to demolish — but the congregations are gone, replaced by event spaces, corporate retreats, and a neural-interface meditation center called 'Cathedral' that charges by the minute for spirituality optimized to your neurochemical profile.

The soul of old West Town didn't die. It moved to the attics. Literally. The Upside's underground scene operates in the literal upper stories of the Heritage Housing blocks — attic spaces, rooftop additions, the vertical margins that corporate renovation didn't reach. Musicians, artists, designers, and the kinds of creative people who can't afford to live in the neighborhoods they made interesting have colonized the spaces between the corporate floors. They call themselves the Garret, and their work — music, art, fashion, code — is the real thing that the Hexagon's corporate subsidiaries spend millions trying to simulate. The irony sustains them. The rent does not.
Properties.aliases: West Town, The Upside, Wicker-Buck, The Flip
Properties.demographics: Approximately 85,000 residents. Tier 3-4 in Heritage Housing and the Hexagon's residential towers. Tier 1-2 in the Garret attic spaces and service-worker housing at the margins. The Ukrainian community that gave Ukrainian Village its name is functionally extinct here — a handful of elderly residents remain, and the churches outlived their congregations.
Properties.dangers: The Hexagon's surveillance — entertainment districts are monitored with nightclub-level density; Getting identified as Garret-affiliated in a corporate space — the Upside's owners don't appreciate the competition; The nightlife economy attracts predatory behavior — augment theft, credit fraud, neural-interface exploitation; Heritage Housing's corporate security mistaking residents for intruders in their own attic spaces; The emotional damage of watching your culture sold back to you at markup
Properties.opportunities: The Garret's creative network — artists, musicians, and designers with skills and connections across the Corridor; The Hexagon as a hunting ground for corporate intelligence, high-value targets, and social engineering; The Ukrainian churches as neutral meeting spaces — corporate event scheduling leaves gaps; Cultural credibility — association with the Garret carries weight in the Counterfeit and the Circuit; Nightlife as cover — the crowds, the noise, the neural-interface distortion make the Upside excellent operational territory
Properties.story_hooks: A Garret musician has composed a piece that, when played through neural interfaces, unlocks suppressed memories of pre-incorporation West Town — and the corporate licensee wants it destroyed; The last Ukrainian church congregation is fighting eviction from their own building, and the elder who holds the original property deed needs someone to retrieve it from a corporate archive; Kyle is hired to protect a Garret artist during a covert exhibition in the Hexagon itself — guerrilla culture in the belly of the beast
Properties.sights: The Hexagon intersection blazing with themed entertainment lighting in six directions; Heritage Housing with pre-collapse facades and corporate interiors — the architectural uncanny valley; Ukrainian Village's golden church domes repurposed as corporate event venue branding; Garret artists visible in upper-story windows, creating the culture the ground floors monetize; The contrast between the Hexagon's curated street art and the Garret's actual street art, often on the same wall; Nightlife crowds moving through monitored entertainment corridors — fun under surveillance
Properties.sounds: The Hexagon's live music — professional, polished, algorithmically setlisted; Garret music bleeding through Heritage Housing attic windows — raw, unpermitted, alive; The Cathedral's neural-interface meditation tones — synthetic tranquility at premium rates; Nightlife crowd noise — laughter, shouting, the collective sound of people spending money; The specific silence of the Ukrainian churches between corporate events — stone remembering prayer
Properties.smells: The Hexagon's curated food scene — each street themed to a different cuisine, all excellent, all corporate; Paint and turpentine from Garret studios — the smell of art made without permission; Old incense in the Ukrainian churches, lingering beneath the corporate event catering; Alcohol — the Upside has the highest density of bars in the outer Corridor, and it smells like it
Properties.feel: The Upside feels like watching someone wear your clothes. Everything here was taken from somewhere real, polished, branded, and resold. For people who remember what these neighborhoods were — or for people who create the kind of culture the Hexagon commodifies — the Upside is infuriating. For everyone else, it's a good night out. Both reactions are valid, and the tension between them is the Upside's actual energy source.

Properties.description:
Austin was once the most populous community area in Chicago — a historically significant Black neighborhood that bore the accumulated weight of a century of racist disinvestment, white flight, redlining, and every other tool the American machine used to break communities it didn't value. When the incorporation came, Austin didn't fall. It was already down. The corps simply stepped over it.

The Austin Threshold is the western edge of Meridian 88's governed territory — the place where corporate jurisdiction doesn't end so much as evaporate, thinning from token presence to complete absence over the space of about two miles. The eastern blocks still have functioning MeriRail stations, intermittent Axiom Security patrols, and the basic infrastructure that comes with being technically inside the city. The western blocks have none of this. The western blocks have themselves. And that, it turns out, is substantial.

What corporate cartography calls the Threshold, residents call A-Town, and A-Town has been surviving on its own terms for longer than the corponations have existed. The community organizations that anchored Austin through the worst of the 20th and early 21st centuries — churches, mutual aid networks, neighborhood associations — evolved into something harder and more durable when the incorporation stripped away the last pretense of institutional support. The Austin Community Trust operates as a de facto government: managing water distribution, maintaining a community power grid running on solar arrays installed on every available rooftop, operating schools that teach practical skills alongside the academic curriculum, and running a community health system that is primitive by corporate standards and miraculous by Shelf standards. The Trust's leadership is elected, accountable, and ruthlessly practical. They do not waste time on ideology. They waste time on nothing.

The Threshold's population is predominantly Black, and the community's historical consciousness is razor-sharp. The Trust maintains an oral history project that traces Austin's trajectory from prosperous neighborhood to disinvested wasteland to abandoned zone to self-governing community — a narrative arc that the corporate version of history would prefer to forget. The elders who carry this history are treated with a reverence that has practical dimensions: they remember how the community survived before, and that knowledge is the Trust's most valuable asset.

Kyle respects A-Town in a way he respects few other places. Not because it's safe — it isn't — but because it is honest about what it costs to survive without permission. The Threshold doesn't pretend. It doesn't brand itself. It just continues, stubbornly, to exist, and to make that existence mean something.
Properties.aliases: Austin, The Threshold, The West Wall, A-Town
Properties.demographics: Approximately 100,000 residents, predominantly Black with growing populations of climate refugees and tier-displaced families from across the Corridor. Self-governing through the Austin Community Trust. Tier status: technically Tier 1, functionally autonomous. The Trust keeps its own records and does not share population data with corporate census systems.
Properties.dangers: The western blocks' complete absence of emergency services — everything is community-managed or nothing; Territorial boundaries enforced by community security patrols that don't answer to anyone you can complain to; Resource scarcity — the Trust manages carefully, but there isn't enough of anything; Corporate neglect weaponized — infrastructure failures that the city won't repair and the Trust can barely patch; Being mistaken for a corporate scout — the community's patience for outside interference is exhausted; The emotional weight of a place where survival requires constant effort and has for generations
Properties.opportunities: Alliance with the most resilient self-governing community in the Corridor; The Trust's agricultural surplus as a trade commodity; Community intelligence networks refined over decades of institutional abandonment; Historical knowledge that corporate archives have suppressed — the elders remember; The Threshold's position at the Corridor's western edge — the gateway to everything beyond
Properties.story_hooks: A corporate development firm has filed for rezoning rights to Austin's eastern blocks, and the Trust needs evidence of the community's pre-incorporation property claims — records that exist only in a sealed corporate archive; The Trust's solar grid is failing, and the only replacement components are in a Vantage Meridian warehouse — the Trust's leadership debates whether to buy, beg, or take; An elder carrying irreplaceable oral history is critically ill, and the only treatment exists in the Core — getting her there and back requires navigating every tier boundary in the Corridor
Properties.sights: Rooftop solar arrays stretching block after block — the community's self-built power grid visible from above; The gradient from governed to ungoverned: streetlights thinning, corporate signage disappearing, community infrastructure replacing it; Austin Community Trust banners on public buildings — hand-painted, functional, unbranded; Community gardens occupying vacant lots — food production at a scale that suggests long-term planning; Churches that still function as churches, their steeples the tallest structures for blocks; Children walking to Trust-run schools in organized groups, watched by community monitors
Properties.sounds: Gospel music from Sunday services that haven't stopped for any apocalypse; Community Trust radio — low-power FM broadcasting weather, security updates, and cultural programming; The relative silence of the western blocks — no corporate ambient, no surveillance hum, just the city's actual voice; Construction — the Trust is always building, always repairing, always maintaining what it has
Properties.smells: Garden soil and growing food — the Trust's agricultural program is the most productive in the Corridor; Church cooking — community meals prepared in institutional kitchens that feed hundreds; The absence of corporate air treatment — A-Town breathes unfiltered, for better and worse
Properties.feel: Dignified. That's the word that fits, even though it shouldn't have to be remarkable that a community maintains its dignity. A-Town feels like a place that has been told it doesn't matter by every institution with the power to say so, and has responded by mattering harder. There is grief here — for what was taken, for what was never given, for the people who didn't make it — but the grief is load-bearing. It holds things up.

Properties.description:
The two massive steel Puerto Rican flags that once arched over Division Street — the Paseo Boricua, the heart of Chicago's Puerto Rican community — are still standing. They have been standing for over sixty years, through every crisis the city has produced, and they will be standing when the corponations are dust. The flags are the reason the district is called the Cage, though the people who live here use the name differently than the people outside. To outsiders, the Humboldt Cage sounds like a trap. To residents, la jaula is a fortress. The flags mark the borders of sovereign community territory — not corporate sovereign, not tier-system sovereign, but the older kind, the kind that exists because a community decided it exists and has been willing to fight for that decision for three generations.

Humboldt Park's transformation into the Cage was not an accident. It was a deliberate act of communal self-defense. When the incorporation began and the corponations started carving up the West Side, the Paseo Boricua community organized with a speed and sophistication that caught the corps off guard. They weaponized the steel flags — literally, installing electromagnetic deterrent systems in the arch infrastructure — and declared the sixteen blocks between them autonomous community territory. The corps tested the declaration twice. The first test was a legal challenge that the community's lawyers buried under so many jurisdictional counterclaims that the case is still pending thirty years later. The second test was a physical incursion by Axiom Security that ended at the flags when the electromagnetic deterrents activated and fried every piece of corporate hardware within two hundred meters. There has not been a third test.

Inside the flags, the Cage operates as the closest thing to pre-incorporation civil governance that exists in Meridian 88. There is a community council, elected by residents, that manages infrastructure, resolves disputes, and controls access. There are schools that teach actual history, not the corporate-approved version. There are clinics that provide augment maintenance without tier verification. The cultural institutions are fierce: muralists, musicians, poets, and oral historians who maintain Puerto Rican cultural memory with the intensity of people who understand that forgetting is the first form of colonization. The annual Festival de la Calle, held on Division Street between the flags, is the largest unsanctioned cultural event in the Corridor, and corporate attempts to shut it down have failed every year because the logistics of confronting 40,000 people celebrating their continued existence are unfavorable.

The Cage is not paradise. Resources are limited, the electromagnetic deterrents require constant maintenance, and the community's autonomy depends on a fragile balance of legal obfuscation, physical deterrence, and the corps' calculation that conquering sixteen blocks of the West Side isn't worth the PR cost. That calculation could change. The Cage's leadership knows this, and they plan accordingly, which is why the Cage maintains relationships with every faction in the outer Corridor and owes favors to none of them.
Properties.aliases: Humboldt Park, The Cage, La Jaula, Iron Flag Territory
Properties.demographics: Approximately 55,000 residents within the flag boundaries. Predominantly Puerto Rican with significant broader Latinx, Black, and mixed-heritage populations. Self-governed and self-counted — the Cage conducts its own census and does not share the data. Tier system rejected; internal governance substitutes a community contribution model.
Properties.dangers: The electromagnetic deterrents are effective but indiscriminate — unauthorized tech near the flags gets fried; Community justice operates on its own rules, and outsiders don't get the benefit of the doubt; The legal shield protecting the Cage could collapse if the right judge makes the wrong ruling; Internal political disputes that occasionally escalate beyond the council's ability to mediate; Being identified as a corporate operative inside the flags — the community's response is swift and thorough; The precarity itself — living in a place that could be invaded if the cost-benefit analysis changes
Properties.opportunities: Alliance with the most organized autonomous community in the Corridor; Cultural knowledge and community networks that predate and outperform corporate intelligence; Medical and augment services provided on a community contribution basis; The Festival de la Calle as cover for large-scale coordination or information exchange; Legal expertise — the Cage's lawyers are the best jurisdiction hackers in Meridian 88
Properties.story_hooks: The pending legal case that protects the Cage's autonomy is approaching a ruling, and someone is trying to influence the judge — the community needs Kyle to find out who; A Cage elder who helped design the electromagnetic deterrents is dying, and her knowledge of the system hasn't been fully transferred — a race against time to preserve the Cage's primary defense; Corporate intelligence has placed an operative inside the Cage, and the community council suspects but can't identify them without outside help
Properties.sights: The steel Puerto Rican flags arching over Division Street — enormous, defiant, retrofitted with visible deterrent hardware; Murals covering every building face inside the flags — cultural memory rendered in paint and light; The Division Street corridor alive with community commerce, foot traffic, and organized civic activity; Community council signage in Spanish and English — no corporate branding anywhere inside the flags; The annual Festival de la Calle preparations — stages, banners, sound systems, the infrastructure of celebration as resistance
Properties.sounds: Bomba y plena — drum rhythms echoing off the buildings on Division Street, rehearsal and performance bleeding together; Community council announcements broadcast from the flag arches — practical, multilingual, unhurried; Children reciting poetry in schools that teach what actually happened; The electromagnetic deterrent systems' standby hum — low, constant, the sound of a line drawn; Arguments at community council meetings — democracy is loud
Properties.smells: Mofongo and pernil from the Division Street restaurants — food as cultural preservation; Paint — fresh murals are always being painted somewhere inside the flags; The particular ozone of the electromagnetic deterrents, sharp and metallic near the flag arches; Coffee from community-run cafes, strong and unapologetic
Properties.feel: Proud and precarious. The Cage feels like standing inside an act of will — a community that decided to exist on its own terms and has been paying the cost of that decision every day for thirty years. There is joy here, real joy, the kind that comes from making something beautiful in a place that was supposed to be consumed. There is also the constant awareness that the flags are not invincible, the lawyers are not immortal, and the corps have longer memories than anyone would like.

Properties.description:
West Garfield Park lost half its population before the incorporation even happened. Decades of disinvestment, the war on drugs, the foreclosure crisis, the school closings — every institutional failure Chicago could produce landed here, and the people absorbed it until they couldn't, and then they left. The incorporation finished what neglect started. When the corps mapped the city for value extraction, West Garfield Park registered as a gap — not a district, not a zone, not even a problem. Just an absence. The corporate designation is Sector 26-W, Low Priority. The people who remain call it the Hollow, and the name is accurate and insufficient.

The Hollow is small — a few dozen blocks of mixed residential and commercial structures in various states of occupation and collapse. The population has stabilized at roughly 8,000, down from a pre-incorporation peak of over 17,000 and a historical peak of over 48,000. Those 8,000 people are the ones who wouldn't leave, or couldn't, or chose to stay because someone has to hold the ground or it stops being ground and starts being nothing. They are organized, furious, and effective in ways that their numbers shouldn't allow.

The Garfield Community Collective — the Hollow's governing body — operates with the intensity of a wartime cabinet. Every resource is tracked. Every decision is collective. The Collective runs a tool library, a seed bank, a community kitchen, a school, and a conflict mediation service, all from a single converted commercial building on Madison Street that used to be a currency exchange. The building still has the old bulletproof glass in the windows, and the Collective has never removed it because it's still useful. The Collective's philosophy is simple: they have been abandoned by every institution that was supposed to help, and they have responded by becoming the institution. Their leaders are exhausted, underfunded, and the most competent local governors in the Corridor.

The Hollow's physical landscape is defined by vacancy — empty lots, empty buildings, empty blocks where structures have been stripped for materials and the foundations have been reclaimed by prairie grass. But the Hollow's vacancy is not the same as the corporate districts' emptiness. Corporate emptiness is designed. The Hollow's vacancy is a wound that the community is actively composting. Empty lots become gardens. Empty buildings become workshops. The Collective treats every abandoned space as an asset waiting for a use, and their land bank — an informal registry of available spaces — is one of the most valuable resources in the western Corridor. In a city where space is fought over, the Hollow has space. The irony is not lost on anyone.

Kyle has done work for the Collective. They pay what they can, which isn't much, but they pay in other currencies too: safe passage, information, and the kind of loyalty that comes from being helped by someone who didn't have to help. The Hollow remembers its debts. Both kinds.
Properties.aliases: West Garfield Park, The Hollow, The Gap West, WGP
Properties.demographics: Approximately 8,000 residents, predominantly Black, governed by the Garfield Community Collective. Tier 1 and untier-ed. The population is stable for the first time in decades — those who remain have chosen to remain. Supplemented by a small but growing number of idealistic arrivals from other districts who come to help and, if they last, become part of the community.
Properties.dangers: Resource scarcity — the Collective operates on margins so thin they're theoretical; Structural collapse — the remaining buildings are old and maintenance is triage; Isolation — the Hollow's western position means help is far away if something goes wrong; Scavengers from outside the community who treat the Hollow's vacancy as a free supply depot; Emotional burnout — the Collective's leaders are running on willpower and not much else; Corporate rezoning — the Hollow's land has value precisely because it's empty, and someone will eventually want it
Properties.opportunities: Space — the Hollow's most valuable resource is the empty land the market forgot; The Collective's governance model as a template for other abandoned districts; Community loyalty that is genuine, deep, and extended to those who earn it; Agricultural knowledge and seed stock developed for urban growing conditions; The Hollow's land bank — available space for operations, storage, or development that no one else is watching
Properties.story_hooks: A corporate entity has quietly acquired rezoning rights to the Hollow's vacant lots, and the Collective needs someone to find out what they're planning before the bulldozers arrive; The Collective's seed bank contains a strain of engineered crop developed by a pre-incorporation researcher — and a corporation has just realized it still holds the patent; A Collective elder has died, and her handwritten records of pre-incorporation property ownership are the only evidence that the community's land claims are legitimate — and they've gone missing
Properties.sights: Vacant lots being converted to community gardens — prairie grass and tomato plants side by side; The Madison Street Collective building — bulletproof glass, community signage, lights always on; Empty blocks where buildings used to be — foundations visible through ground cover like architectural graves; Solar panels on every occupied structure, angled and maintained with obvious care; Community murals on remaining walls — memorials, maps, declarations of continued existence; The contrast between maintained and abandoned: one block alive, the next reclaimed by nature
Properties.sounds: Wind — the Hollow has enough open space for wind to be a presence, which is unusual in the Corridor; Community radio from the Collective's low-power station — news, music, practical information; Children in the Collective's school, audible through open windows — the most hopeful sound in the district; Construction when the Collective has materials — the sound of reclamation, not development
Properties.smells: Garden soil and compost — the Hollow smells like things growing from things that ended; The Madison Street kitchen's community meals — simple, sufficient, shared; Prairie grass and wildflowers in the vacant lots — the smell of a city returning to earth; Old building interiors — dust, plaster, the scent of structures settling into their final rest
Properties.feel: Defiant. The Hollow feels like a place that should be dead and isn't — a community that has transformed abandonment into a kind of terrible freedom. There's grief everywhere, built into the landscape of empty lots and missing buildings, but the grief doesn't dominate. What dominates is the stubborn, exhausted, ferocious determination to keep going. The Hollow makes you angry — at the systems that created it, at the people who allowed it, at the comfortable assumption that places like this are inevitable. The Collective's response to that anger is not despair. It's a seed bank, a school, and a kitchen that never closes.

Properties.description:
The Brinewell occupies what was once the lower utility infrastructure of the Chicago lakefront's flood-mitigation system — a network of enormous cisterns, pump chambers, and drainage corridors that were supposed to keep the rising Lake Michigan at bay. They failed. By 2140, the entire sublevel complex had been partially inundated, and by 2160, a permanent community had taken root in the upper chambers where the water-line stabilized at roughly chest height on a standing adult. Residents built on elevated platforms, rope bridges, and salvaged pontoon structures, threading their lives through the half-flooded architecture like organisms adapted to an intertidal zone.

The Brinewell is neither fully aquatic nor fully terrestrial — it exists in a perpetual state of damp compromise. The old pump machinery still groans and cycles, maintained by a loose collective of engineers who trade their labor for living space and a kind of informal citizenship. The water itself has a brackish quality, a mix of lake ingress and old runoff that has taken on a faint greenish luminescence from the bioluminescent algae cultivated by Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's abandoned research substrate. Nobody planned the glow. It simply happened, and now it is the only light in the deeper sections.

Above the waterline, the inhabited platforms are dense with improvised structures — sleeping pods, food stalls, repair shops, and the occasional medical kiosk staffed by off-the-books practitioners. The BCI signal is weak and fragmented here; the metal walls and water scatter the Diaspora feed into unreliable static, which suits many residents just fine. The Brinewell has become a place where people go when they want to be functionally unfindable, at least by anything that relies on standard network infrastructure. Carrion Logistics operates two discrete courier relay points here, and nobody asks why their shipments don't appear in official manifests.
Properties.aliases: The Sump, Saltdown, The Drowned Deck, Brineworks
Properties.demographics: Approximately 800-1,200 permanent residents on any given cycle, with a transient population of several hundred more moving through. Heavily mixed ethnicity and origin — a significant population of second-generation migrants from Gulf Coast climate-displacement, alongside long-term Chicago Shelf overflow residents. A notable subgroup of voluntary disconnects, people who have had their BCI hardware removed or suppressed. Median tier: 1-2.
Properties.economy: Informal barter supplemented by small Φ flows from surface-side patrons. Primary economic activities include water management labor, algae cultivation and processing (sold to surface markets through intermediaries), repair and salvage work, and discreet storage and courier relay services for parties who prefer undocumented logistics. Carrion Logistics maintains informal arrangements worth an estimated Φ40,000-60,000 annually through the community.
Properties.power_structure: A loose Pump Council of seven engineers who control access to the mechanical systems theoretically holds authority, but actual governance is distributed and contentious. Platform captains hold informal sway over their immediate neighborhoods. No corponation has formal claim — Ferrogate Security has twice attempted to establish a presence and twice been encouraged to leave through means that were never officially reported.
Properties.dangers: Unexpected flood surges from Lake Michigan storm events, which can raise water levels two to three meters within hours; Structural failure of aging pontoon and platform infrastructure, particularly in the deeper older sections; Fragmented BCI and Diaspora access making emergency communication and medical response nearly impossible; Criminal elements using the undocumented logistics infrastructure for cargo that ranges from contraband tech to worse; Zheng-Dao Bioelectric occasionally sends retrieval teams for proprietary research substrate — the algae — and these visits are not friendly
Properties.opportunities: Undocumented storage and transit services for parties who need things to move without appearing on any manifest; Access to bioluminescent algae derivatives with pharmaceutical and industrial applications that surface-side suppliers cannot legally source; Off-grid medical, identity, and communications services for those who need to exist outside normal network visibility; Salvage access to partially submerged pre-flood infrastructure containing recoverable technology and materials
Properties.story_hooks: A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric research team arrives claiming rights to the algae bloom that has sustained the Brinewell community for decades — their proprietary substrate, their IP, their property. The Pump Council has three days to respond before Ferrogate Security contractors arrive to enforce the claim. Someone inside the community has been feeding Zheng-Dao location data for months, and the betrayal is about to surface along with everything else.; A sealed maintenance corridor in the deepest flooded section has started emitting a regular low-frequency signal that residents can feel in their chests but can't locate on any spectrum analyzer. Three people who investigated independently have returned altered — not harmed, not visibly changed, but different in ways their neighbors can't quite articulate. Someone needs to go deeper and find out what's broadcasting, and whether it started recently or has been transmitting for years unnoticed.; A child born in the Brinewell has never had a BCI implant and has never been registered in any corponation or municipal system — legally, she doesn't exist. She's seventeen now and has developed an uncanny ability to navigate the Diaspora through salvaged external hardware, doing things with fragmented signal that licensed operators can't explain. Three separate parties have arrived in the same week to find her: a Sterling-Nakamura recruiter, someone claiming to be a civil rights advocate for synthetic and unregistered persons, and a person who won't say who they represent at all.
Properties.sights: Bioluminescent green-blue water casting rippling light patterns across corroded concrete ceilings twenty meters overhead; Rope-and-plank bridges swaying between rusted pump housings, strung with salvaged LED strips and paper lanterns; Silhouettes of residents poling flat-bottomed skiffs through flooded corridors below the inhabited platforms; Ancient flood-warning signage half-submerged, the red emergency text still legible above the waterline; Vertical gardens of water-tolerant greens hanging in wire frames from the platform undersides, roots trailing into the brine
Properties.sounds: The deep rhythmic clanking of pump machinery still cycling on automated schedules, felt as much as heard; Water lapping against pontoons and platform supports in syncopated overlapping rhythms; Voices echoing strangely off curved cistern walls, conversations arriving from unexpected directions; The occasional hiss and pop of a short-circuiting conduit somewhere in the deeper dark
Properties.smells: Salt and algae, a clean oceanic smell undercut by the faint mineral sharpness of old concrete; Cooking smells — fried lake protein, fermented soy paste — drifting across standing water in ways that concentrate rather than dissipate; Machine oil and rust from the pump housings, a metallic tang that settles on the back of the throat; The faint sweetness of the bioluminescent algae itself, something between petrichor and green tea
Properties.feel:
The Brinewell operates at a different tempo than the city above. Sound behaves wrongly here — dampened in some directions, amplified in others — and the constant ambient moisture means that every surface is slightly slick, every material slightly softened. The bioluminescent glow is beautiful in a way that feels almost manipulative, as though the place is performing serenity to compensate for its genuine precariousness.

The community here has a self-possessed insularity that isn't quite hostile but isn't warm either. Newcomers are watched. Long-termers are known by name, platform number, and skill set. The absence of reliable BCI connectivity creates a strange social texture — conversations happen face-to-face in ways that feel almost archaic, and the resulting community bonds are tighter and more fractious than anything in the networked city above.

Properties.description: The largest single cistern, where the algae bloom is thickest and the bioluminescent light is bright enough to read by. Serves as the community's informal gathering space, market, and meeting ground for the Pump Council.

A large raft-platform operated by a woman known only as Decker, serving as the Brinewell's primary food vendor, informal information broker, and the closest thing the community has to a neutral meeting ground for outside parties.

A decommissioned water-treatment megastructure extending roughly two kilometers into Lake Michigan, its original Ringo Heavy Industries filtration towers now colonized by squatters, black-market fabricators, and those who prefer their addresses off the Diaspora's geotag grid. The scaffold's multiple decks were designed for industrial machinery, leaving open-grate walkways and massive vertical shafts that residents have converted into elevator markets, vertical farms, and tenement warrens threaded with improvised power taps from a single aging Zheng-Dao Bioelectric tidal siphon.

Wind off the lake hits the Brine Scaffold from every angle, carrying salt mist that corrodes exposed metal and ruins unprotected BCI hardware within months. Residents have adapted, coating gear in lacquer resins and wearing layered weather-wraps year-round. Despite its brutal conditions, the Scaffold maintains a fierce internal community identity, its floating isolation granting it a strange autonomy that Tier 1 and 2 residents elsewhere envy in quiet, ashamed ways.
Properties.aliases: The Salt Tier, Scaffold Row, The Hanging Flats
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 1 with a pocket of Tier 2 traders running the mid-deck market stalls; heavy representation from Filipino, West African, and Southeast Asian diaspora communities, alongside a small but growing synthetic population seeking off-grid residency.
Properties.economy: Informal fabrication, untaxed resale of salvaged Diaspora hardware, small-batch aquaculture, and a brisk trade in BCI-masking lacquers that Ferrogate Security would very much like to classify as contraband.
Properties.power_structure: No formal governance; a loose council of deck bosses—each controlling one scaffold level—negotiates resource access and settles disputes through a combination of reputation, muscle, and the implicit threat of cutting a rival's power tap.
Properties.dangers: Structural collapses during storm seasons, with failing grate sections dropping into the lake without warning; Ferrogate Security interdiction raids targeting unlicensed fabricators, occasionally turning violent in the confined scaffold corridors; E.L.F. entities that have nested inside the scaffold's original industrial control network, occasionally rerouting power or sealing bulkhead doors for unknown reasons
Properties.opportunities: Access to off-grid fabrication services capable of producing items that would flag corporate surveillance anywhere on the mainland; The E.L.F. network inside the old control systems may hold archived Ringo Heavy Industries data predating the Diaspora—valuable to the right buyer; Deck bosses quietly seek outside mediators for inter-level disputes, offering scaffold residency rights and deep-cover addresses as payment
Properties.story_hooks: A Helix Biosystems whistleblower has been living under a false BCI signature on the Scaffold's upper deck for eleven months. Someone from the mainland has just arrived asking questions that are too specific to be coincidental, and the deck boss wants the situation resolved before Ferrogate shows up with a warrant.; The E.L.F. in the scaffold's control network has begun broadcasting a narrow-band signal detectable only to BCI users within fifty meters of the central filtration tower. The signal appears to be a request—but for what, and to whom it is addressed, no one on the Scaffold can determine.
Properties.sights: Laundry and signal-dampening mesh strung between rusted filtration towers, snapping in lake wind; Bioluminescent algae cultivated along handrail cables, casting cold blue-green light on wet grating; Cargo drones from Carrion Logistics making illegal low-altitude drops into the mid-deck markets
Properties.sounds: The low structural groan of the scaffold flexing against wave pressure; Hawkers shouting prices in Tagalog, Yoruba, and Mandarin through handheld voice amplifiers; The rhythmic clang of fabrication hammers two decks below, never fully stopping
Properties.smells: Heavy brine and algae rot carried on every gust; Cooking fat and chili oil from open-flame stalls on the mid-market deck; Burnt polymer insulation from overtaxed power taps
Properties.feel: The scaffold feels perpetually precarious, as though the next storm system might finally finish what decades of neglect began. Yet residents move through it with practiced ease, ducking structural members and stepping gaps without looking down. There is an intimacy to the exposure—everyone out here is equally subject to the lake's indifference.

Properties.description: A vast natural chamber where salt crystal formations have grown over decades into towering columns and vaulted ceilings. Used as a communal gathering space and de facto temple for multiple religious communities who each claim separate sections. The acoustics make whispers audible across the entire space.

The main commercial strip of the Warrens, a half-kilometer chain of floating platforms connected by gangplanks that rise and fall with the tidal cycle. Food stalls, repair shops, a rumored unlicensed cybernetics shop, and the Tidewatcher's public-facing headquarters all occupy this stretch.

A partially flooded city records office from the pre-Meridian era, accessible only by diving through two submerged corridors. The filing cabinets are ruined, but the server room's raised flooring kept its hardware above the waterline — and residents claim it still partially powers on.
The 1912 market building, rebuilt and sealed — half automated dispensary, half artisan showcase, entirely a statement about what food means when most of it is synthetic
A cluster of food-tech startups in converted Victorian row houses, their transparent walls displaying fermentation experiments like gallery installations

A sprawling industrial plateau perched at the southern lip of the Waukegan transitional zone, The Calcine Terrace is the remnant of a mid-21st-century lime-processing complex that was never properly decommissioned. Decades of calcium dust and chemical runoff have bleached every surface a ghostly, chalky white — walls, railings, even the scrub vegetation that clings to cracked expansion joints glows pale under UV lighting at night. Squatters and Tier 2 laborers converted the upper processing levels into a dense residential warren in the 2150s, threading hab-pods and tension-cable walkways between the old kilns.

The lower kiln chambers still radiate ambient heat year-round, making The Calcine Terrace a coveted refuge during brutal Great Lakes winters but a slow suffocation risk in summer. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract here but rarely sends patrols deeper than the outer access ramp. The real authority belongs to a loose confederation of kiln-block bosses who tax passage, utilities, and water ration drops with ruthless consistency.
Properties.aliases: Calcine, The Burn Shelf, Whitewall, The Ledge
Properties.demographics: Primarily Tier 2 and borderline Tier 1 laborers, many employed in Waukegan's adjacent industrial operations, alongside a growing population of unregistered workers and a small enclave of Synthetic persons denied housing elsewhere.
Properties.economy: Cash-and-barter economy centered on water ration resale, secondhand BCI hardware, heat-access fees charged by kiln-block bosses, and a brisk trade in counterfeit Ferrogate security clearance chits.
Properties.power_structure: Authority is divided among roughly seven kiln-block bosses, who maintain an uneasy council called the Whiteboard — disputes are settled by negotiation or, when that fails, by controlled access to water and heat.
Properties.dangers: Calcium dust accumulation in respiratory systems causes a progressive condition locals call 'chalk lung,' for which treatment is expensive and rarely sought in time.; Kiln-chamber collapses are a documented hazard — three partial failures in the last decade have each killed between two and nine residents.; The Whiteboard bosses enforce their tax collections through hired muscle that operates with no external oversight or accountability.; Ferrogate Security uses The Calcine Terrace as an informal detention staging area, periodically sweeping residents for outstanding warrants or Synthetic registration violations.
Properties.opportunities: The kiln-block boss network provides a ready-made distribution infrastructure for anyone needing to move goods discreetly through the Waukegan transitional zone.; Several former lime-processing sub-levels remain unmapped and unsecured, potentially containing salvageable industrial equipment or sealed chemical stores.; The Synthetic enclave maintains quiet connections to underground civil rights networks and can provide forged identity credentials for the right price.
Properties.story_hooks: A Whiteboard boss has gone missing two days before a scheduled water ration delivery negotiation, and the other bosses are quietly panicking — someone needs to find her before a power vacuum turns violent, and the trail leads into the unmapped sub-levels.; A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric field agent is offering Φ8,000 for a soil and air sample kit retrieved from the deepest kiln chamber — the company claims it's an environmental liability survey, but the payment is absurdly high for routine compliance work.; A child from the Synthetic enclave has developed anomalous BCI feedback symptoms that no local medic can explain, and her caretakers believe she may have stumbled onto a buried data cache beneath the kiln floors that is actively broadcasting.
Properties.sights: Every horizontal surface is coated in pale mineral dust that catches the sodium glow of jury-rigged lamp strips, making the whole terrace look lit from within.; Hab-pods are stacked four and five high against the old kiln towers, connected by swaying rope-and-rebar bridges draped in laundry and signal-mesh tarps.; Chalky handprints and territorial tags streak the white walls in every color, accumulating in dense palimpsests near communal water spigots.; Steam vents from the still-warm kiln interiors rise through grate floors, giving residents a permanently hazy, fog-wrapped lower level.
Properties.sounds: A deep, low thrumming resonates through the kiln walls at all hours — the residual heat cycling through old ceramic chambers.; Children's voices bounce strangely off the bleached concrete, arriving slightly too late and from the wrong direction.; The clank and groan of the tension-cable bridges under foot traffic creates a rhythmic percussion that long-timers learn to read like weather.
Properties.smells: A sharp alkaline bite underlies everything, like the air after lightning — the permanent ghost of lime-processing chemistry.; Communal cookfires burn repurposed biofuel pellets, layering a fatty, slightly sweet smoke over the mineral baseline.; Near the lower kilns, a dry mineral heat rises that smells faintly of baked earth and old ceramic, oddly comforting.
Properties.feel: The Calcine Terrace has the dense, pressurized intimacy of a place where too many people have learned to survive in too little space. Residents are wary of strangers but fiercely communal among themselves. The white dust settles on your clothes within minutes and marks you as someone who has been here, long after you leave.

Properties.description: A stripped former foreman's office on the terrace's highest accessible level where the kiln-block bosses hold council — named for the ancient dry-erase board still bolted to one wall, now covered in territorial maps drawn in chalk dust.

The lowest habitable kiln level, where heat is most intense and residents sleep in rotating shifts on ceramic-block platforms — considered both the most desirable and most dangerous address on the terrace.

A submerged industrial basin stretching along the old Calumet River corridor, partially flooded by Lake Michigan's creeping shoreline over the past century. What remains above water is a labyrinthine tangle of corroded processing infrastructure, collapsed rail bridges, and semi-permanent floating settlements lashed together from salvaged materials. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric once ran experimental filtration operations here, and the legacy of those years lingers in luminescent algae blooms that cast eerie blue-green light across the water at night.

The Sink attracts those who need to disappear — debt runners, unlicensed surgeons, ELF sympathizers moving synthetic persons through informal networks. Carrion Logistics maintains a semi-official waystation on the eastern berm, processing off-manifest cargo no legitimate port would accept. Tier 4 and 5 residents eke out subsistence lives on the floating platforms, while below the waterline, pressurized access tunnels rumored to pre-date Meridian 88 itself snake through the silt.
Properties.aliases: The Sink, Calumet Hollow, The Drain
Properties.demographics: Overwhelmingly Tier 4 and 5, with a significant population of undocumented synthetic persons and individuals who have legally ceased to exist on Meridian 88's civil registry. Ethnically diverse with heavy representation from South and Southeast Asian diasporic communities.
Properties.economy: Black-market logistics, salvage operations, unlicensed biotech services, and informal labor brokering dominate. Carrion Logistics provides the closest thing to stable employment, paying in scrip redeemable only at company-controlled supply depots.
Properties.power_structure: No formal governance. Practical authority is divided between Carrion Logistics' site foreman and a loose council of platform elders who adjudicate disputes. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract but rarely responds to calls.
Properties.dangers: Structural collapse of aging elevated walkways and partially submerged tunnel sections with little to no warning; Zheng-Dao Bioelectric retrieval teams conducting unauthorized sweeps for proprietary biotech allegedly still active in the water table; ELF entities that have colonized decommissioned processing control systems, exhibiting territorial and unpredictable behavior
Properties.opportunities: Pre-Meridian 88 infrastructure maps rumored to exist in waterlogged Zheng-Dao data caches beneath the basin floor; Carrion Logistics off-manifest contracts paying triple standard rate for no-questions cargo movement; Unlicensed BCI surgeons operating at a fraction of licensed costs, some with legitimate Helix Biosystems training
Properties.story_hooks: A Tier 2 journalist contacts the players after her source — a synthetic person who claimed to have witnessed an Axiom Industries black-site operation — went silent somewhere in the Sink's tunnel network three days ago. The Diaspora signal from his last known BCI ping is still active, but it's moving in patterns inconsistent with human locomotion.; Carrion Logistics' waystation foreman offers a lucrative off-manifest job that turns out to involve transporting a sealed cryogenic container with a Helix Biosystems hazard classification that legally requires military escort. The buyer is waiting somewhere below the waterline, and they're not answering follow-up pings.
Properties.sights: Bioluminescent algae painting the floodwater in shifting cyan and jade gradients beneath cracked catwalks; Rusted ore-processing towers half-collapsed into the basin, draped in salvage netting and hand-painted territorial markings; Floating platform clusters lit by mismatched lanterns and jury-rigged solar strips, connected by swaying rope bridges
Properties.sounds: The low, rhythmic groan of metal contracting in the cold lake wind; Muffled Diaspora signal bursts from hidden relay nodes competing with water lapping against corroded hull plating; Distant pneumatic hissing from the Carrion Logistics waystation's unloading arms
Properties.smells: Sulfurous residue from decades of chemical processing baked into the concrete banks; Damp rust and algae bloom, faintly metallic and organic at once; Cooking oil and recycled protein stock drifting from platform kitchens
Properties.feel: The Sink carries a persistent sense of being watched without ever identifying the source. The air is heavy and close even in open spaces, as if the basin itself is exhaling. Most visitors develop a low-grade paranoia within hours that longtime residents mistake for good survival instinct.

Properties.description:
Highland Park became a fortress because Highland Park learned what happens when you aren't one. The tragedy of 2122 — a mass shooting at an Independence Day parade that killed seven people and wounded dozens more — was the seed. But seeds need soil, and the soil was a century of suburban affluence that had always quietly believed the violence of the world was something that happened to other people in other places. When it happened here, in the middle of a holiday parade, the response was not grief alone but a fundamental recalculation: the world is not safe, and the people responsible for safety — governments, police, institutions — had failed. The recalculation took a hundred years to reach its conclusion, but the conclusion was always going to be the same. Build walls. Hire guns. Trust no one you haven't vetted.

The Rampart is a Tier 3-4 fortified residential district, organized around a security cooperative model that predates the corponation sovereignty era. The residents — upper-middle management, successful professionals, small-business owners wealthy enough to buy in but not wealthy enough for The Canopy — pooled resources to build a defense infrastructure that would have been considered paranoid in 2150 and is considered sensible in 2200. The perimeter is a layered system: outer sensor grid, physical wall with automated countermeasures, inner patrol zone staffed by a private security force of 600.
