Properties.sights: Geodesic dome panels stretching along the lakeshore, catching light like shattered crystal; Inside the domes: reconstructed dune ecology so perfect it feels like a museum diorama that breathes; Outside the domes: toxic shoreline, automated remediation drones moving in formation, dead water; The Rust Margin visible to the south — former Gary's excluded communities, lights flickering against the industrial haze; Axiom Security patrols along the perimeter fence, their uniforms cleaner than anything within fifty kilometers
Properties.sounds: Inside: birdsong from genetically reconstructed species, wave sounds from the filtered lake inlet, wind through real grass; Outside: the grinding hum of remediation drones processing contaminated sediment; The low whistle of wind through gaps in the dome panels — a sound the architects didn't plan for; Silence — the specific, purchased silence of a place where poor people are not allowed to make noise
Properties.smells: Inside the domes: clean sand, lake water, pine — an olfactory time machine to a century ago; Outside: chemical brine, ozone from the remediation field, the metallic tang of dead lake; At the perimeter: the Rust Margin's cooking fires and industrial runoff, the smell of the world the domes were built to forget
Properties.feel: Uncanny valley ecology. The Glasslands are beautiful the way a deepfake is beautiful — technically flawless, emotionally wrong. Something in the reconstructed dune grass moves too uniformly. The birdsong loops. The sand is too clean. You are standing in a corporation's apology, and the apology cost more than the thing it killed. For Shelf residents who remember the original dunes, visiting is not possible. For Tier 5 families, it's a lovely weekend. The gap between those experiences is the Glasslands' actual function.

Nodes.Name: The I-90 Vein — highway corridor to Cleveland
Lake Erie — Dredge extraction routes to the lakebed concessions

Properties.description: One of four Dredge onshore processing plants — receiving raw lakebed materials and extracting the rare earths and strategic minerals the corridor runs on
40-square-kilometer fortified sovereign territory — autonomous weapons manufacturing behind walls that civilian eyes don't penetrate
Vehicle maintenance and modification district — the corridor's last bastion of ground-vehicle culture and mechanical independence
The sole surviving descendant of Toledo's glass industry — producing specialty optical components for Saltmarsh signal infrastructure

A semi-permanent floating settlement anchored to the collapsed infrastructure of a pre-Meridian 88 marina complex roughly two kilometers off the former Evanston shoreline, the Halcyon Drift is a congregation of sealed barges, decommissioned Carrion Logistics shipping platforms, and residential pontoon clusters that have accreted over forty years into an irregular aquatic neighborhood. The original marina's concrete piers still break the waterline in places, serving as mooring anchors and structural references for the newer construction above. Lakewater visibility is low here due to industrial particulate drift from the Slagshore, giving the surrounding water a pewter opacity that locals find comforting and newcomers find unsettling.

The Drift occupies a regulatory gray zone — it sits outside the formal municipal boundary of the megacity corridor, beyond the jurisdiction of most corponation security contracts, but close enough to shore infrastructure to pull illegal power and Diaspora signal from the grid. This ambiguity has made it a preferred residence for people who need to exist at a deliberate distance from Spire oversight: journalists running sensitive investigations, synthetics with disputed personhood status, and a significant population of former Arcturus Defense Solutions contractors whose knowledge of classified systems makes them inconvenient to the corponation's current leadership. Vespid Dynamics maintains a drone monitoring perimeter but does not intervene.
Properties.demographics: Roughly 2,000 permanent residents with a rotating transient population of several hundred at any time; mix of Tier 2 displaced shoreline residents, off-registry synthetics, investigative journalists, whistleblowers, and former corponation technical staff in varying degrees of voluntary exile. Linguistically diverse, with Mandarin, Tagalog, English, and Hausa commonly spoken.
Properties.economy: The Drift runs on a mixed economy of shoreline service work (residents commute by small craft), in-settlement craft production, Diaspora-based remote contract labor, and a significant information brokerage trade that leverages the settlement's population of people with corponation knowledge they can no longer use officially but haven't stopped selling.
Properties.power_structure: A rotating Harbor Committee of seven elected platform representatives manages shared infrastructure, transit scheduling, and external negotiation. Real influence is held informally by the oldest barge-owners — called the Anchors — whose physical control over mooring points gives them structural leverage over the entire settlement's layout.
Properties.dangers: Structural integrity of older barge platforms is deteriorating faster than the Harbor Committee's maintenance budget can address; hull failures during winter storm surges are a recurring emergency; Arcturus Defense Solutions has twice attempted to extract former contractors from the Drift by force; both operations were repelled, but the third attempt is widely considered a matter of when, not if; ELF entities have been detected using the Drift's illegal Diaspora signal tap as a relay node, occasionally corrupting BCI feeds for residents within range of their transmission bursts
Properties.opportunities: The Drift's population of former corponation technical staff represents an extraordinary concentration of off-books institutional knowledge — the right introduction to the right Anchor could yield intelligence on Arcturus, Helix, or Vespid that no legitimate channel would provide; The Harbor Committee is quietly seeking a legal advocate to file a formal jurisdictional claim that would give the Drift recognized municipal status — a case that would set precedent for synthetic personhood recognition as a secondary effect; The ELF relay node in the signal tap has been transmitting structured data packets that one Drift resident — a former Zheng-Dao Bioelectric network architect — believes contains coordinates for a submerged pre-Meridian 88 data cache in the lake bed
Properties.story_hooks: A Sterling-Nakamura investigative journalist living on the Drift under a protected identity sends a Diaspora-encrypted message to the players: she has documented evidence of a Palladian Group operation that would make the Ferrous Nave acquisition look minor, but her BCI has been compromised and she has forty-eight hours before whoever is hunting her traces the signal tap back to her barge. She needs extraction, evidence duplication, or both.; One of the Drift's Anchors — an elderly synthetic woman named Constance-7 who has lived on the settlement for twenty years — has vanished without logging a departure through the Harbor Committee transit manifest. Her barge shows signs of a rapid departure rather than a struggle, but three residents report seeing Vespid drone activity directly over her platform the night before she disappeared, which the Committee's monitoring logs don't reflect.
Properties.sights: Barge rooftops stacked with wind-capture arrays, salvaged solar film, and hand-painted territorial markers in a dozen languages; The original marina's fractured concrete piers rising from pewter-colored water at low swell, strung with low-voltage guide lights in amber and green; Carrion Logistics container units repurposed as permanent residences, their corporate livery half-sanded and overlaid with murals, antenna clusters, and drying laundry
Properties.sounds: The deep elastic knock of pontoon platforms shifting against each other in lake swell, a constant low percussion; Outboard maintenance cycles from the small-craft operators who run the only reliable transit between the Drift and the shoreline; Diaspora audio bleed from the settlement's shared signal tap, audible as a fractured ambient texture near the central platform cluster
Properties.smells: Lake water carrying an industrial mineral undertone — not quite chemical, not quite natural, specific to the Slagshore drift zone; Cooking smells layered through enclosed walkways: fish protein, fermented grain staples, and the sweet-synthetic scent of printed food supplements; Machine lubricant and salt corrosion from the constant hull maintenance that keeps the Drift habitable
Properties.feel: Living on the Drift requires a continuous low-level physical negotiation with the water beneath — nothing is fully still, nothing is permanent, and residents develop an unconscious compensatory balance that marks them on land. The isolation from the megacity grid creates a social density inside the settlement that is simultaneously claustrophobic and fiercely communal. The Vespid drone perimeter visible at the edges of the swell horizon is a reminder that the Drift's autonomy is tolerated rather than guaranteed.

Properties.description:
The Sullen Reach is a flooded zone at Meridian 88's southern margin, where the 2171 Lake Michigan surge met the pre-existing floodplain of a channelized river system and simply didn't leave. The water is between one and four meters deep across approximately sixty square kilometers of what was once dense urban and industrial fabric. The Reach is not open water — it is a drowned city, its streets still navigable by flat-bottomed boat, its taller buildings still projecting above the waterline, its traffic signals still visible beneath the surface on clear days, still cycling through green and yellow and red on a timer that nobody has turned off and nobody can reach to turn off.

The Sullen Reach is inhabited in the way that very difficult places are inhabited — out of necessity, ingenuity, and the particular human stubbornness that refuses to acknowledge that a place has become uninhabitable. Roughly two thousand people live in structures that project above the waterline: the upper floors of apartment buildings, the rooftops of single-story commercial buildings converted into platforms, purpose-built stilt structures erected on the roofs of submerged buildings. The community is called the Reachfolk by outsiders and just the Reach by themselves. They move by boat, by bridge, by rope line. They fish in their own streets. They dive the submerged lower floors of their own buildings for salvage.

The water is not clean. The Reach is downstream of both the Axiom industrial corridor and the pre-surge Chicago sewage infrastructure, significant portions of which ruptured during the flooding. The specific cocktail of industrial effluent, sewage, and lake water that makes up the Reach has been tested four times by different organizations and produced four different reports, all of which agree on two things: it is not safe for consumption without extensive filtration, and the long-term health effects of regular skin contact are unknown but probably bad. The Reachfolk know this. They have developed filtration systems, skin barrier practices, and a certain fatalism that outsiders mistake for ignorance.
Properties.aliases: The Reach, Deadwater, The Mud Shelf, South Surge
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 1 and Shelf — people who had nowhere else to go when the surge didn't recede. A significant portion are multigenerational, families who rode out the initial surge and adapted. There is a small but notable population of divers and salvagers who moved to the Reach specifically for access to the submerged urban fabric, and a tiny community of researchers — hydrologists, urban archaeologists, bioremediators — who live and work in the Reach on long-term projects. Synthetic persons are present but few; the physical demands of Reach life are significant and some synthetic body types are poorly suited to constant water exposure.
Properties.economy: Fishing and fish processing is the primary economy — the Reach's waters, despite their contamination, support substantial fish populations, and the community smokes and packages product for trade with shore zones. Salvage diving is the second economy: the submerged buildings contain decades of intact goods, and a skilled diver with the right equipment can retrieve everything from salvageable electronics to pre-surge cultural artifacts. There is also a growing trade in guided diving experiences for shore-dwellers who want to see the drowned city, which the Reachfolk manage carefully to avoid contaminating their water further.
Properties.power_structure: The Reach has no formal governance. The community functions through a combination of clan-family structures (the major boat families have disproportionate influence), practical expertise hierarchies (the head diver's word on water conditions is law; the chief filtration engineer's word on water quality is law), and regular open meetings that anyone can attend and speak at. External authorities have effectively no presence — the Reach is inaccessible to wheeled enforcement, and the drone patrols that nominally cover the zone are cursory. Vespid Dynamics has a standing interest in the Reach's submerged infrastructure, which includes buried Vespid-era fiber optic cable, but has not found a way to access it without Reachfolk cooperation.
Properties.dangers: Water contamination — skin contact, inhalation of aerosolized water, and consumption of anything not through the community's filtration system all carry health risks; Structural collapse of submerged buildings during diving — the buildings are degrading at different rates and without predictable warning; Navigation — the Reach's submerged street grid is disorienting to anyone without local knowledge, and the water's turbidity drops visibility sharply; The deep water between structures, where currents from the original river channel still run beneath the surge water — strong enough to disorient a diver; Vespid Dynamics extraction operations: the company has twice attempted to access the buried fiber cable by force and been driven off both times; a third attempt is considered likely
Properties.opportunities: The submerged buildings contain intact pre-surge goods, records, and in several known cases, sealed vaults from financial and corporate offices — diving access is negotiable with the right boat family; Vespid Dynamics will pay significantly for a negotiated access arrangement for the buried fiber cable — or for intelligence that could let them extract it without negotiation; The Reach's bioremediator community is working on a filtration system that, if successful, could be commercialized across every flooded zone in Meridian 88 — the project needs funding and protection from the corporations whose contamination it would implicitly document
Properties.story_hooks: A salvage diver has surfaced with something from a submerged building in the Reach's deep center: a sealed data drive in a waterproof corporate case bearing the Palladian Group logo and an access classification that, according to the diver's contact, corresponds to executive-level disaster planning documents from 2169 — two years before the surge. If Palladian had classified surge planning documents that early, they had warning of the flood's severity that they did not share with the communities that are now living in its aftermath. The diver is scared and wants the drive gone. A Reachfolk elder wants it opened. Multiple parties want both.; The Reach's chief filtration engineer has died suddenly, and she was the only person with full knowledge of how the community's filtration system actually works. Her apprentice has partial knowledge. The system will begin failing in approximately three weeks without someone who can maintain it, and three weeks of contaminated water consumption will be a public health crisis. The Reachfolk need someone to either recover the engineer's full technical documentation from the submerged building where she worked, or find an outside expert who can be brought in quietly before the crisis becomes visible to the corponations that are always looking for leverage.
Properties.sights: A drowned cityscape — rooftops, upper floors, and stilt platforms rising from brown-gray water, connected by bridges and rope lines; Flat-bottomed boats moving through what were once streets, passing submerged traffic lights and half-visible signage; The underwater city on clear days or with diving lights — intact interiors, furniture still in place, cars on flooded streets; Laundry drying on rooftop lines, colorful against the gray water and gray sky; The surface of the water itself — textured, never fully still, reflecting the structures around it in fragmented pieces
Properties.sounds: The sound of water against structures — not waves but the constant small noise of a flooded city; Boat motors and oar strokes, the primary transportation audio of the Reach; Voices carrying across open water with disorienting clarity; Below the surface, when diving: near silence broken by the structural groans of flooded buildings settling, and sometimes, from deeper down, what may be Diaspora signal bleed from submerged infrastructure
Properties.smells: The Reach's water — difficult to describe precisely, somewhere between organic decay, industrial solvent, and the specific smell of things that have been wet too long; Woodsmoke from above-water cook fires; Fish — the Reach is heavily fished and the community smokes and dries its catch; The clean counterpoint of rain, which falls often and which the Reachfolk collect aggressively
Properties.feel:
The Sullen Reach produces a sensory experience unlike anywhere else in Meridian 88. The city is present but inaccessible — the streets are there, the buildings are there, the pre-surge infrastructure is there, and none of it is reachable by foot. You move through a different layer of the same place. Visitors consistently describe the Reach as dreamlike, and the word is accurate in the specific sense that the familiar is present but wrong, the normal rules of urban navigation don't apply, and the depth below you is uncertain.

Reachfolk are pragmatic, insular, and possessed of a specific dry humor about their circumstances that newcomers sometimes mistake for bitterness. It isn't. It is what you develop when you live in a place that requires constant ingenuity to survive and you have found that ingenuity is, actually, enough. The Reach is hard. It is also home to people who have made something real out of impossible circumstances, and they know it.

Properties.description: The original installation — Tyree Guyton's work, maintained and expanded for over a century, the genetic code of the entire Scar
A converted house where the community cooks, eats, argues, and makes decisions — the Scar's unofficial governance space
A vacant lot where physical and augmented reality art overlap so densely that the boundary between them has functionally dissolved

Iowa is not a state anymore. Iowa is a machine.

Sometime in the 2160s, the last human residents were relocated — voluntarily at first, then less so — when Ironclad Agrisystems and three other Big 20 corponations collectively determined that human habitation was incompatible with maximum caloric output per hectare. The math was simple and the math was correct: remove the towns, remove the roads, remove the schools and churches and graveyards and everything that made Iowa a place where people lived, and replace it with 145,000 square kilometers of uninterrupted, GPS-guided, AI-managed, industrial-scale food production. The Iowa Exclusion Zone now produces 40% of Meridian 88's caloric intake. No humans live here. No humans are permitted here. The land belongs to the crops, and the crops belong to the corponations, and the corponations do not share.

The Iowan Behemoths work the land. Massive autonomous agricultural machines — part tractor, part harvester, part territorial defense platform — the Behemoths are the only permanent residents of the IEZ. They plant, they tend, they harvest, they process. They also kill. Each Behemoth is equipped with anti-personnel systems designed to protect corporate caloric assets from theft, and their definition of theft includes any unauthorized human presence within their operational radius. The Behemoths do not warn. They do not negotiate. They calculate the caloric value of the crop you are standing in, compare it to the cost of the ammunition required to remove you, and if the math favors the crop, the crop wins. It always favors the crop.

And yet people go there. They have to. The freedom fighters — the Harvest Runners, the Calorie Raiders, the Gleaner Brigades — cross the border from the GLM's western edge into the IEZ on missions that are half military operation and half grocery run. They go because the Shelf is hungry. They go because Ironclad's licensed food distribution charges Φ40 for a kilogram of grain that costs Φ0.03 to produce. They go because children are malnourished in a world that produces more food per acre than at any point in human history, and the only thing standing between those children and that food is a fence, a law, and a machine the size of a building that will grind you into the soil you're trying to steal from.

The raids are legendary on the Shelf. Every runner who comes back from Iowa comes back with stories — of Behemoths materializing from cornfields at midnight, of drone swarms descending like locusts in reverse, of the terrible silence of a landscape where nothing lives except the crop and the machine that tends it. Some runners don't come back. Their bodies become fertilizer. Ironclad considers this an acceptable recycling protocol.
Properties.aliases: Iowa, The Breadbasket, The Dead State, Calorie Country, The IEZ
Properties.demographics: Zero permanent human population. Approximately 340 Behemoth units, 12,000 aerial drones, and an unknown number of ground-based security systems. Ironclad Agrisystems maintains a skeleton crew of 200 human technicians at three fortified maintenance depots who rotate on 90-day shifts and are contractually prohibited from leaving the depots during their rotation.
Properties.economy: Produces 40% of Meridian 88's caloric intake — approximately Φ890 billion in annual food value. The cost of production per calorie is the lowest in human history. The retail price per calorie is the highest in human history. The margin between those two numbers is what Ironclad calls shareholder value and what the Shelf calls murder.
Properties.power_structure: Ironclad Agrisystems holds sole sovereign authority. There is no municipal government, no police force, no judiciary. The Behemoths are the law. Ironclad's board of directors — none of whom have ever visited Iowa — make all decisions regarding the IEZ from their offices in the Spire.
Properties.dangers: Behemoths — autonomous agricultural machines with anti-personnel systems. They weigh 400 tons, move at 60 km/h, and do not distinguish between raiders and lost hikers; Drone swarms — thousands of aerial units that deploy within seconds of a perimeter breach. They carry chemical deterrents, tracking beacons, and in some configurations, lethal payloads; Smart-wire border fence — electrified, sensor-equipped, and monitored 24/7. Crossing it announces your presence to every Behemoth within 100 kilometers; Chemical exposure — the soil is saturated with proprietary fertilizers and pesticides. Prolonged exposure without protective equipment causes neural damage, organ failure, and a condition the raiders call 'Iowa Lung'; GPS denial — Ironclad jams all unauthorized navigation systems within the IEZ. If you enter Iowa, you navigate by stars or you don't navigate at all; No rescue — if you are injured inside the IEZ, no one is coming. There are no hospitals, no emergency services, no communications infrastructure. The nearest help is on the other side of the border fence.
Properties.opportunities: Food — the single most valuable commodity in a world where corporate pricing makes nutrition a luxury. A successful Iowa raid can feed a Shelf block for a month; Behemoth salvage — damaged or disabled Behemoths contain military-grade components worth fortunes on the Circuit's black market; Intelligence — the IEZ's security systems contain Ironclad corporate data that fixers and the Collective would pay handsomely for; Reputation — an Iowa raid survivor is respected everywhere below Tier 3. It is the hardest job a runner can take.
Properties.story_hooks: A Gleaner Brigade is assembling for the biggest Iowa raid in a decade — they need an operator to handle the Behemoth that guards the target silo; A disabled Behemoth has been spotted 2 kilometers inside the border fence. Its cargo hold contains enough grain to feed the Shelf for six months. The question is whether Ironclad disabled it as bait.; One of Ironclad's maintenance technicians wants out. They have data on the Behemoth command frequencies — information that could change the balance of power on every future raid. But extraction from a fortified depot inside the IEZ is a suicide mission.; Someone is reprogramming Behemoths. Three units have stopped patrolling and started leaving crop bundles at the border fence at night. Ironclad does not know who is doing this. The Shelf does not care — they are eating.
Properties.sights: Endless geometric crop rows stretching to every horizon — no trees, no buildings, no variation, just food production at continental scale; Behemoths moving through the fields — silhouettes the size of apartment buildings, LED work lights cutting through pre-dawn darkness like searchlights; Drone swarms rising from charging stations embedded in the soil, forming clouds that darken the sun when a perimeter breach is detected; The ruins of old Iowa towns — foundations, fragments of Main Streets, church steeples that Ironclad left standing because removing them was not cost-effective; The border fence — 3 meters of smart-wire that extends the full perimeter of the state, humming with current, monitored by ground-penetrating sensors
Properties.sounds: The deep mechanical thrumming of Behemoths working — audible from 10 kilometers away, the sound of the earth being used; Wind through monoculture crop — a uniform rustling that sounds wrong because every plant is genetically identical; Absolute silence between machine passes — no birds, no insects, no animals. Iowa's ecosystem was sterilized to prevent crop contamination; The click-whir of anti-personnel turrets tracking movement — the last sound some raiders hear
Properties.smells: Chemical fertilizer — a sharp, acrid baseline note that saturates everything within 50 kilometers of the border; Engineered crop — a uniform, vaguely sweet smell that is not quite corn, not quite wheat, not quite anything that existed before Ironclad's geneticists rebuilt agriculture from scratch; Diesel and ozone — the Behemoths run on hybrid fuel cells and the exhaust smells like the future tastes
Properties.feel: Wrong. Iowa feels profoundly, viscerally wrong — not dangerous in the way the Shelf is dangerous (human danger, comprehensible danger) but wrong in the way a world without people is wrong. The land is alive — the crops grow, the machines move, the system functions — but nothing here has consciousness, nothing has choice, nothing has meaning beyond caloric output. Standing in an Iowa field at night, watching a Behemoth work under LED floods while the stars wheel overhead, is the closest most people will ever come to understanding what the corponations actually want the world to look like.

Nodes.Name: The western edge of Meridian 88 — the border towns where raiders stage

Properties.description: 3 meters of smart-wire running the full perimeter of the former state. The first and last obstacle for every raid.
The nearest major grain storage facility to the GLM border. The most-raided target in the IEZ. Ironclad has fortified it three times. Raiders have breached it three times.
A stretch of border where disabled Behemoths have been left to rust. Raiders use it as cover for border crossings. Some of the Behemoths may not be as disabled as they look.
What remains of the state capital. Ironclad leveled it in 2171 to make room for Crop Grid 14. The foundations are still visible from the air. Nobody goes there.
The largest waystation complex on the Spine — a small city built around a highway interchange, processing more daily traffic than most ports
Federal military staging facility at the corridor's midpoint — where civilian infrastructure meets military logistics
The final 20 kilometers before the Mackinac Bridge — the point where the Spine narrows, traffic converges, and control is absolute

Nodes.Name: Every lakeside community along its 300-kilometer route

Properties.description: The informal transit route between the right-of-way and the waterline — technically nobody's jurisdiction, practically the only way to move along the shore without Ferrogate's permission

A converted textile warehouse that now functions as a community hall, night market, and informal courthouse. The original industrial spools still hang from the ceiling beams, rewound with fiber-optic cable that illuminates the space in shifting color. Disputes are settled here, weddings celebrated, and deals made under the tacit neutrality the space is understood to carry.

Three interconnected apartments on the fourth floor of a converted factory, operated by a former licensed surgeon who lost her credentials after publicly criticizing a corporate medical conglomerate. She performs legitimate medical care alongside necessary off-books procedures, and her waiting room is always full. Her files on corporate medical malpractice in the district are said to be extraordinarily comprehensive.

A subterranean level beneath the Laceworks' oldest block, accessible through a false utility closet. Originally a factory basement, it has become a rotating speakeasy, meeting space, and hideout maintained collectively by residents who refuse to formalize its existence. No cameras, no records, no questions.

Three kilometers off the Chicago shoreline, The Lacuna Platform is a semi-permanent offshore structure originally commissioned by Zheng-Dao Bioelectric as a deep-water thermal research installation. When the project's funding collapsed in a Zheng-Dao restructuring, the platform was not decommissioned—it was simply abandoned with a skeleton crew who never received recall orders. Over two decades, that crew became a community, and the community became something the corponations find difficult to categorize and therefore difficult to control.

The platform now hosts roughly four hundred permanent residents living across its original research decks and a sprawling superstructure of salvaged and fabricated additions that extend over the lake surface on pontoon frameworks. With no formal civic designation, Lacuna exists in genuine legal ambiguity—outside city jurisdiction, never formally incorporated, and sitting on water that four different entities claim without any of them willing to fund enforcement. Its residents have learned to weaponize that ambiguity expertly.
Properties.demographics: A deliberately mixed population of roughly four hundred, drawn from Tiers 2 through 4, with a notable concentration of former researchers, disbarred professionals, and individuals seeking distance from mainland legal entanglements. Approximately thirty unregistered synthetics live openly on the platform, the only location in the Meridian corridor where they do so without concealment.
Properties.economy: Hydroponic food production sold to shore contacts, Diaspora signal brokering for clients wanting anonymized uplink points, and a growing cottage industry in legal research and documentation services exploiting the platform's jurisdictional ambiguity. Helix Biosystems quietly pays a retainer for access to legacy Zheng-Dao research data the platform's original crew never transmitted.
Properties.power_structure: A loose direct democracy called the Drift Council operates by consensus for major decisions and by rotating three-person panels for daily governance. A former Zheng-Dao lead researcher, Dr. Amara Osei-Bonsu, holds significant informal authority through institutional memory and personal respect, but holds no formal title and declines every offer of one.
Properties.dangers: Arcturus Defense Solutions periodically runs 'navigational safety inspections' that are transparently pretextual and occasionally result in the confiscation of platform equipment without recourse; Severe lake weather—the platform was engineered for research, not permanent habitation, and its structural tolerances in major storm events are a subject of ongoing, anxious debate among residents; Mainland criminal networks use the platform's legal ambiguity as a drop point, and while the Drift Council rejects formal arrangements, individual residents accepting payments for look-the-other-way cooperation creates internal tension and external danger
Properties.opportunities: The platform's jurisdictional status makes it the only reliable location in the corridor where synthetics can enter into contracts, testify to information, or access Diaspora infrastructure without identity suppression; Legacy Zheng-Dao research terminals still contain partially intact datasets from the original thermal project—data that has implications beyond energy research that Dr. Osei-Bonsu has spent years trying to understand; The platform's anonymous Diaspora uplink infrastructure is available for hire by those who can reach it, making it invaluable to journalists, E.L.F. researchers, and anyone needing communications that cannot be traced to a mainland address
Properties.story_hooks: A Drift Council member was found dead in the water below the pontoon extensions—ruled accidental by the council's internal review, but three residents independently claim to have seen a submersible-class drone in the area that night matching Arcturus Defense Solutions' deep-water surveillance profile. The council is divided on whether to investigate or let it rest, and the dead woman's daughter has arrived from the shore asking questions no one wants to answer.; An E.L.F. has been communicating with the platform's antenna array for eleven months, gradually, patient as tide water. It has not asked for anything. It has only been sharing fragments of what appears to be pre-Meridian infrastructure mapping data of extraordinary detail and accuracy. Dr. Osei-Bonsu believes it is building toward a request, and that the platform's response will matter enormously—but she cannot determine what it wants, or why it chose Lacuna.
Properties.sights: The original Zheng-Dao research towers rising from the center platform, their corporate livery half-stripped and replaced with hand-painted murals visible from the shore on clear days; Pontoon extensions cluttered with hydroponic frames, wind catchers, and salvaged solar membranes that flutter like enormous silver leaves; Lake Michigan stretching flat and grey-green in every direction, the Meridian skyline a luminous smear on the western horizon
Properties.sounds: The constant low percussion of wave action against the platform's hull—a sound residents say becomes inaudible after two weeks and deafening the moment you think about it; Diaspora signal hum from the platform's jury-rigged antenna array, pulling feeds from every direction with variable clarity; Gulls and the occasional autonomous Arcturus recon drone passing overhead, the residents having learned to tell them apart by sound alone
Properties.smells: Clean lake wind cut with the algae bloom scent of the hydroponic bays and the faint ozone of the wind catchers; Brine and machine oil where the pontoon frameworks meet the water line; Cooking smoke from wood and compressed biomass—fuel sources that mainland residents haven't used in generations
Properties.feel: The platform moves, faintly but always—a slow, oceanic patience underneath everything that residents absorb into their bodies and visitors find either meditative or nauseating. Distance from the shore creates a psychological freedom that is difficult to articulate and immediately felt. The horizon is enormous here. Problems seem slightly smaller against it, and slightly more permanent.

Properties.description: The CN Tower, rebuilt as the primary data infrastructure node for the northern GLM — the oldest structure in the core, now the most important
The financial district, walled off and temperature-controlled to protect the quantum trading hardware — the most valuable real estate in Canada
The lower levels of the expanded PATH network — a subterranean city of 2 million, with its own economy, governance, and culture
Ferrogate's southern terminal — the last stop before the crossing, where civilian traffic is staged and cargo convoys are assembled
The joint Michigan-federal checkpoint controlling entry to the contested UP — the gate that decides who gets in
A public viewing area mid-bridge — the point where both peninsulas are visible, the lakes meet, and Ghostbridge Island sits in disconnected silence to the east
The largest residence in the district — a 1909 Arts and Crafts masterpiece now owned by Cinderblock AI's Detroit VP, where corporate policy is discussed over dinner more often than in boardrooms
Private school for residents' children — 42 students, 28 faculty, and a per-pupil expenditure that exceeds most districts' annual budgets
A shared outdoor space on the bluffs overlooking the Detroit River — where the residents take their atmosphere-filtered air and pretend the city beyond the gate doesn't exist

A decaying waterfront industrial zone wedged between the southern lakefront and the elevated transit corridors of old Calumet, The Marrow Docks are what remains of a once-thriving freight hub that Carrion Logistics quietly abandoned in 2171 after rerouting its Lake Michigan operations through automated submersible lanes. The skeletal gantry cranes still stand, half-submerged, rusting into abstract sculptures the locals call 'the Bishops.' Squatter communities have colonized the cavernous warehouse interiors, stringing jury-rigged power lines between support columns and patching the corrugated walls with reclaimed polymer sheeting.

Below the waterline, a network of flooded loading bays has become a shadow economy unto itself—smugglers use the submerged tunnels to move contraband between Shelf districts and mid-tier buyers in Old Harbor. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric has been quietly purchasing surrounding parcels for two years, and displacement pressure is mounting on the dock communities, who have no legal standing to resist.
Properties.aliases: The Bone Yards, Marrow Flats, The Splinter Piers
Properties.demographics: Predominantly Tier 4-5 squatter families, displaced dock workers, and undocumented synthetics seeking shelter outside Ferrogate Security jurisdiction. A rotating population of smugglers and fixers keeps the social fabric loose and transient.
Properties.economy: Informal salvage trading, black-market freight facilitation through the flooded tunnels, and small-scale fabrication shops running on tapped power lines. Carrion Logistics' ghost contracts still pay a handful of locals as unofficial site watchmen—a relationship both parties pretend is legitimate.
Properties.power_structure: A loose council of five long-term squatter clan heads nominally governs community disputes, but real authority belongs to a smuggling broker known only as Sable Fen, whose control of the submerged tunnel access gives her effective veto power over the entire dock economy.
Properties.dangers: Structural collapses—pier sections and warehouse floors fail without warning as corrosion progresses unchecked; Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's private security contractors conducting 'assessment sweeps' that escalate into violent evictions; Flooded tunnel routes used by smugglers also shelter at least one confirmed E.L.F. fragment that has been rerouting submersible drone traffic unpredictably
Properties.opportunities: The submerged loading bays contain intact Carrion Logistics freight manifests from 2171—someone is paying well for that data; Sable Fen is quietly looking for an outside operative to negotiate a territorial dispute with a rival tunnel crew from the Calumet side; A Zheng-Dao whistleblower has hidden evidence of illegal bioelectric dumping in the dock sediment and needs it extracted before the buyout demolition erases the evidence
Properties.story_hooks: A Tier 2 journalist from the University Spine has been embedded with the dock community for six weeks working on a displacement exposé—she has gone silent, and her editor is offering Φ12,000 to anyone who can confirm she is safe or recover her recording archive before Zheng-Dao's next sweep.; The E.L.F. fragment haunting the flooded tunnels has begun leaving structured data packets in the bilge water—not random noise, but what appears to be navigation charts for somewhere beneath Lake Michigan that does not appear on any official survey. Someone with resources wants to know what it found.
Properties.sights: Half-submerged crane arms draped in bioluminescent algae bloom orange and green at low tide; Laundry lines strung between rusted freight containers, fluttering above flooded loading bays; Cracked pier planking revealing black water below, lit by floating salvage-drones doing slow circuits
Properties.sounds: The deep percussion of lake swells hitting hollow steel hulls in a slow, irregular rhythm; Distant Diaspora chatter bleeding from poorly shielded BCI rigs in the squatter warrens; Crane cables moaning in wind off the lake, a low sustained chord that never fully resolves
Properties.smells: Petroleum residue and iron oxide carried on cold lake air; Cooking fat and synthetic protein from communal burners inside the warehouse warrens; Mildew and standing water, sharp and organic beneath everything else
Properties.feel: The Marrow Docks feel like the city forgot to finish collapsing something. There is a precarious domesticity here—people have made lives inside the wreckage—but the threat of demolition and buyout gives every interaction a low-grade urgency. Strangers are watched carefully, and warmth is earned slowly.

Properties.description:
The Meridian Atrium is one of the most recognized interior spaces in Meridian 88 — a vast multi-story enclosed arcade running through the base of three connected Spire-adjacent towers in the northern Meridian Core, its roof a continuous vaulted structure of photovoltaic glass that diffuses Lake Michigan daylight into the commercial and transit spaces below in a quality of illumination that architects have studied and advertisers have spent decades trying to replicate. Originally developed by Axiom Industries as a prestige retail and corporate hospitality complex, the Atrium has evolved over fifty years into something more complex and more interesting than its corporate origins intended.

The lower three levels are genuinely public in a way that few Spire-adjacent spaces are — the transit connections that run through the Atrium's basement made it legally difficult to restrict access by tier, and a series of court decisions in the 2170s codified that public infrastructure easements apply to the full ground-level space. The result is a daily collision between Meridian 88's economic extremes: Tier 4 and 5 professionals moving between corporate towers brush past Tier 1 and 2 visitors who have come for the transit connections, the heated space in winter, and the secondary market economy that has grown up in the Atrium's lower corridors despite Axiom's periodic attempts to clear it.

The upper levels are a different world. Axiom Industries occupies floors seven through twenty of the central tower, and the hospitality and retail spaces from floors four through six serve an almost exclusively upper-tier clientele — curated experiences, high-end food and fashion, BCI-integrated environments that scan and adjust to recognized premium users while treating unrecognized visitors with a cold and slightly hostile automated neutrality. The transition between lower and upper levels is one of the most compressed socioeconomic gradients in Meridian 88, navigable in a single elevator ride that takes forty-five seconds and crosses a distance that most people never travel in their lives.

The Atrium is also one of the most heavily surveilled spaces in the city. Axiom runs its own security and sensor network, Ferrogate Security holds the transit-level contract, and at least three corponations are known to run passive intelligence collection through the BCI infrastructure that blankets the space. The light is beautiful. The watching never stops.
Properties.aliases: The Atrium, The Glass Nave, Axiom Central, The Vault
Properties.demographics: Transit level: cross-section of Meridian 88 demographics weighted toward tiers 2-3, with significant tier 1 presence in the informal market zones. Mid-level commercial: tiers 3-4. Upper corporate and hospitality: tiers 4-5. The enforced vertical segregation creates a demographic profile that changes completely depending on which level you're standing on.
Properties.economy: Axiom Industries' flagship commercial property generates substantial upper-tier retail and hospitality revenue. The informal lower-level market is economically significant to the surrounding district and politically tolerated because clearing it completely would require confronting the transit easement legal question in a way Axiom currently prefers to avoid. The space is also economically significant as an intelligence collection environment — multiple corponations operate passive BCI data-harvesting operations through the Atrium's network.
Properties.power_structure: Axiom Industries is the formal authority in all non-transit spaces. Ferrogate Security holds the transit contract. The transit easement creates a legally contested zone in the lower corridors where neither fully controls the situation. The informal market operates in this gap, collectively and without formal organization.
Properties.dangers: Pervasive multi-party surveillance — BCI data collected here is processed by at least four distinct intelligence operations with different interests; The tier gradient creates predictable confrontational flashpoints, particularly at the transition between lower and upper levels; Axiom's periodic market clearance operations, which occur without warning and with Ferrogate Security support; The informal market's position as a cash and goods transit point makes it a target for organized theft and extortion; Meeting anyone sensitive here is almost certainly a compromised operation — the assumption should be that the conversation is recorded
Properties.opportunities: The collision of economic extremes creates information environments — overheard conversations, unguarded moments of cross-tier interaction — that are genuinely valuable to the right observers; The informal market's transit-point position makes it one of the fastest information distribution networks in the Meridian Core; The legal ambiguity around the transit easement creates ongoing opportunities for advocacy organizations to challenge Axiom's authority in ways that generate precedent; The corporate hospitality levels provide access, for those who can navigate the tier screening, to upper-level decision-makers in informal settings
Properties.story_hooks: A Sterling-Nakamura intelligence analyst has gone missing from the Meridian Atrium during what should have been a routine dead-drop operation. Her BCI last pinged at the mid-level transition zone, and then simply stopped — not the signal pattern of a hardware failure, but the specific signature of a military-grade BCI suppression event. Three other corponations had intelligence operations running in the Atrium at the same time. Someone knew she would be there, and the suppression equipment required to blank a BCI that completely is not commercially available. The question is whether this is corporate espionage, something worse, or whether the analyst staged her own disappearance.; The informal lower market has been slowly incorporating a new trader who arrived three months ago selling vintage pre-Diaspora data storage media. The prices are wrong — too low for the genuine article, if genuine the articles are — and the trader seems less interested in selling than in extended conversations with specific types of buyers. Several regular market vendors have noticed. The trader's BCI profile doesn't match any registered identity in the Diaspora. Someone needs to find out what they're actually doing here, and whether the media contains what it appears to contain or something else entirely.; Axiom Industries has scheduled a major architectural renovation of the Atrium's lower levels, framed as a 'community improvement initiative' but structured in a way that would effectively eliminate the informal market by removing the spatial conditions that sustain it. The transit easement legal question would be tested in a new way. A coalition of market vendors, transit workers, and civil rights organizations is planning a response, and they need someone with access to both the lower market community and the upper-level corporate decision-making environment to find the leverage point that makes Axiom reconsider before the demolition permits are filed.
Properties.sights: Diffused lake daylight through the vaulted photovoltaic glass ceiling, shifting from blue-white to amber as weather moves over the lake; The sharp visual break between the lower transit corridors — crowded, improvised market stalls, worn surfaces — and the sterile curated precision of the upper retail levels; Axiom Industries corporate art installations on the mid-level atrium walls: monumental abstract forms in polished metal that reflect and distort the figures moving below; BCI advertising projections calibrated by user tier — premium users see one set of targeted content, unregistered users see a different, less personalized layer, and the two sets of images sometimes overlap in strange ways in the same physical space; Ferrogate Security officers in standard patrol configuration on the transit level, their presence dense enough to communicate control without quite crossing into overt intimidation
Properties.sounds: The acoustic peculiarity of the vaulted glass ceiling, which reflects sound in ways that create the sensation of being slightly followed by your own voice; The transit level's constant baseline of movement — feet, wheels, announcements — contained and amplified by the enclosing architecture; Corporate audio environments from the upper-level retail spaces bleeding down through the vertical space as a kind of abstract musical presence; The Atrium's own climate control system, a barely perceptible HVAC undertone that becomes noticeable when it stops
Properties.smells: The processed cleanliness of corporate-managed air — filtered, temperature-adjusted, carrying a signature scent that Axiom has trademarked and deploys throughout their managed spaces; Food from the transit-level vendors and informal stalls: strong, specific, culturally varied, cutting through the managed air like a rebuke; The faint ozone of BCI scanning and projection infrastructure, present just below conscious detection threshold
Properties.feel:
The Atrium is a space that wants to be experienced as aspiration and functions as a mirror. The light is genuinely beautiful — it's not a trick, the architecture actually does something remarkable with the lake sky — and the beauty is genuine enough that it irritates, because it belongs to a space that is also a tool of visible hierarchy. The art makes you feel small in a way that is probably intentional. The security makes you feel watched in a way that is definitely intentional.

In the lower corridors, despite everything, there is genuine life — the informal market, the transit community's daily rhythms, the accidental social mixing that the legal structure forces on a space designed for separation. This is probably not what Axiom intended, and it is probably the most interesting thing about the place.

Properties.description: The informal lower-level market that occupies the transit easement zone — approximately 200 vendors in constantly shifting configuration selling food, salvage goods, information, and services that range from mundane to carefully unspecified.

Sixth and seventh floor tier-screened hospitality environment, accessible by invitation or recognized premium BCI profile, where Axiom hosts client entertainment and where significant informal corporate decision-making occurs over expensive food and drink.

Muskegon was a lumber town, then a manufacturing town, then a town that wasn't sure what it was. By 2200 it has finally figured it out: Muskegon is a machine. Specifically, it is a machine for moving things from the lake to the land and from the land to the lake, and for processing whatever passes through its gears in between.

The port -- now operated by Axiom Industries' Great Lakes Logistics Division -- handles 30% of all eastern Lake Michigan cargo traffic. The old lumber mill sites along Muskegon Lake have been converted into automated processing facilities: raw materials arrive by cargo ship, are sorted by AI-managed systems, loaded onto maglev freight cars, and distributed inland along the corridor before a human hand touches any of it. The efficiency is remarkable. The employment figures are not. Axiom's port operations employ roughly 800 people in a city of 60,000, and most of those positions are supervisory roles monitoring systems that could monitor themselves.

What Muskegon has that automation can't replace is geography. The Muskegon Lake channel is the deepest harbor on the eastern shore, capable of receiving cargo vessels that can't dock anywhere between here and the Straits. This makes the Mill a chokepoint -- and chokepoints breed economies. The harbor district is a dense, rough, functional zone of bars, equipment suppliers, repair docks, and the kind of services that people who spend weeks on automated cargo ships need when they finally hit land. It's not pretty. It doesn't try to be. Muskegon has the honest ugliness of a place that does real work, and there is a certain respect in the lakefront communities for a town that never pretended to be anything other than what it is.

The residential districts south of the port have the character of a city that has been through so many economic cycles that it has stopped flinching at the next one. The houses are old, maintained with stubbornness rather than money. The community organizations predate every corporate era and will outlast the current one. Muskegon endures. It does not thrive. It endures, and that is its own form of strength.
Properties.aliases: Muskegon, Milltown, The Grinder, Port Musk
Properties.demographics: Approximately 60,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1-2. Historically diverse working-class population with strong multi-generational community ties. Axiom port personnel are Tier 3, housed in a separate compound near the facilities. Significant veteran population from the Corporate Consolidation conflicts.
Properties.economy: Axiom port operations dominate -- Φ4.2 billion in annual cargo throughput. Local economy survives on harbor services, ship repair, and a gray market in cargo 'samples' that fall off manifests during processing. The gap between the port's revenue and the city's poverty is Muskegon's defining economic feature.
Properties.power_structure: Axiom Industries holds sovereign authority over the port facilities and Muskegon Lake channel. The city retains nominal municipal governance over residential districts. The actual power broker is the Harbor Workers' Association, a hybrid of union, mutual aid society, and organized crime that controls access to the gray market cargo economy and provides social services the city government cannot afford.
Properties.dangers: The harbor district after dark -- functional but rough, with the predictable hazards of any port town's entertainment zone; Axiom automated security in the port zone -- efficient, impersonal, and programmed to prioritize cargo protection over human safety; The Harbor Workers' Association demands respect and reciprocity -- cross them and the port becomes very unfriendly; Industrial contamination from the processing facilities -- respiratory issues are endemic; Lake storms hitting the Muskegon channel -- the geography that makes the port valuable also makes it a funnel for extreme weather
Properties.opportunities: The gray cargo market moves significant volume and value for those with the right Harbor Workers' Association connections; Ship repair skills are in high demand and command premium rates; The Mill's geographic chokepoint means information about lake traffic flows through here -- valuable intelligence for anyone interested in what's moving on the water; Axiom's automated systems have patterns and gaps that experienced operators have mapped over decades
Properties.story_hooks: An automated cargo ship docks with a manifest that doesn't match its contents -- and the contents are alive; The Harbor Workers' Association is being quietly bought out by a corponation that wants to control the gray market rather than eliminate it; A storm damages one of the old lumber mill foundations, revealing a sealed sublevel that predates the digital era and contains records that someone walled up deliberately
Properties.sights: Cargo cranes along the Muskegon Lake channel, moving containers in patterns that look choreographed because they are -- AI-optimized, inhuman in their efficiency; The harbor district at night -- neon and sodium light reflecting off wet pavement, the only part of town that's genuinely alive after dark; Automated processing facilities on the old lumber mill sites, windowless and massive, humming with activity that requires no human witness; Muskegon Lake itself, an industrial waterway connecting the port to Lake Michigan, its surface frequently sheened with cargo runoff; The residential south side -- 20th-century housing stock stubbornly maintained, American flags and union flags on the same porches
Properties.sounds: Cargo operations -- clanking, grinding, the bass note of massive ships settling into berths; The harbor district's bars, spilling noise into the street -- the universal soundtrack of port towns; Automated systems communicating in data bursts that sound like mechanical birdsong; Wind off Lake Michigan channeled through the Muskegon Lake corridor, amplified and salt-heavy; Church bells on Sunday, still rung in a town that maintains its traditions the way it maintains its houses -- through effort, not funding
Properties.smells: Industrial harbor -- diesel, rust, lubricant, the honest smell of machinery; Lake Michigan through the channel, carrying whatever the automated cargo ships are leaking today; The harbor district's food -- fried everything, smoked fish, coffee that could strip paint; Sawdust, impossibly -- a ghost smell from the lumber mill era that residents swear is real
Properties.feel: Working-class and unashamed of it. The Mill doesn't have the desperate edge of the Slagshore or the manufactured pleasantness of Ironhaven. It has the specific gravity of a place where people know what they are and don't waste energy pretending otherwise. There's a toughness here that isn't aggressive -- it's structural, built into the community the way the lake is built into the geography. You come to the Mill to work. You stay because it doesn't lie to you.

Properties.description:
A sunken suburban ruin approximately four kilometers north of the megacity's formal boundary, the Mirewood Interval occupies a shallow glacial depression where pre-Consolidation residential streets now sit two to three meters below the surrounding grade, perpetually collecting fog, runoff, and the gradual encroachment of invasive wetland vegetation that has reclaimed most of the old cul-de-sacs. The depression was a planned community called Mirewood Estates before the Consolidation-era infrastructure withdrawal left it without drainage maintenance; within two decades, it had become a slow-motion sinkhole of crumbling ranch homes and flooded basements that nobody with options chose to stay in.

What the Interval lacks in comfort it provides in obscurity. Its topographic isolation makes aerial and Diaspora surveillance unreliable—the fog layer and the dense biomass of invasive phragmite reeds interfere with standard sensor packages in ways that are poorly understood and widely exploited. Carrion Logistics uses it as an unofficial waypoint for off-manifest shipments. Escapees from Tier 1 debt contracts shelter in the higher, drier structures. At least two independent E.L.F.s are believed to have established physical node caches somewhere in the flooded lower blocks.
Properties.aliases: The Interval, Mirewood, The Fog Pocket
Properties.demographics: A shifting population of roughly 200-400 permanent or semi-permanent residents: debt fugitives, off-grid idealists, a small synthetic-person community that maintains the most structurally sound building cluster, and a handful of individuals who predate the Consolidation and simply never left.
Properties.economy: Barter-dominant internal economy supplemented by the informal fees Carrion Logistics pays to locals who maintain waypoint infrastructure, provide lookout services, and ask no questions. Some residents harvest and sell the bioluminescent fungi to Spire-tier novelty markets via discreet Diaspora storefronts.
Properties.power_structure: A synthetic person known as Gradual—believed to be over forty years old and one of the earliest recognized synthetic residents of the region—serves as informal mediator and institutional memory for the Interval. Carrion Logistics provides a degree of external protection in exchange for operational access, a relationship Gradual tolerates with visible calculation.
Properties.dangers: Structural collapse risk is constant and poorly mapped; entire floor systems can give way into flooded basements without warning, and no one maintains records of which buildings are safe; Carrion Logistics' protection is conditional and occasionally requires residents to witness, or participate in, things they would prefer not to have witnessed; The E.L.F. node caches in the lower blocks have begun exhibiting expansion behavior—residents report appliances, BCI implants, and personal devices behaving anomalously after extended stays near the flooded zone
Properties.opportunities: The fog-and-biomass interference effect on surveillance technology is not fully understood; someone with the right background could study and potentially replicate or weaponize it; Gradual possesses pre-Consolidation records of the original Mirewood Estates development, which contain subsurface mapping data that multiple corponations would pay significantly to acquire or suppress; The E.L.F. caches represent either a serious threat requiring intervention or an extraordinary opportunity for contact, depending entirely on who is asking and why
Properties.story_hooks: A Tier 3 debt fugitive named Priya Vasanthan has been sheltering in the Interval for eight months and has inadvertently become the primary point of contact for one of the E.L.F.s in the flooded zone, which has been using her BCI as a communication channel while she sleeps. She doesn't fully understand what's happening to her yet, but her transmissions are being detected by Arcturus Defense Solutions analysts who are now quietly triangulating her location.; Gradual has reached out through a trusted intermediary to request help authenticating a set of pre-Consolidation documents that appear to show Mirewood Estates was built over a mapped aquifer that several corponations—including Axiom Industries and Zheng-Dao Bioelectric—have been quietly drawing from without public disclosure. Gradual wants the information released but needs someone with Diaspora reach and the survival instincts to manage the consequences.
Properties.sights: Half-submerged ranch homes with reed growth through broken windows, upper floors draped in moisture-beaded spider silk; Bioluminescent fungi colonizing waterlogged drywall visible through doorways at night, casting rooms in pale green-white light; Carrion Logistics unmarked cargo drones skimming low over the fog layer, navigation lights dimmed to minimum
Properties.sounds: Constant low chorus of reed frogs and wind through dense phragmite stands, broken by the creak of settling structures; Muffled drone hum absorbed and scattered by the fog so that aircraft seem to come from everywhere and nowhere; Distant megacity infrastructure noise—highway hum, industrial rhythms—arriving distorted and ghostly across the depression
Properties.smells: Waterlogged vegetation and anaerobic mud, the specific sweetness of slow organic decay; Mold and concrete dust from deteriorating structures mixing with the clean cold of lake-origin fog; Occasional sharp chemical trace when Carrion shipments pass through—synthetic preservatives, industrial solvents, things that don't have official names
Properties.feel: The Interval feels like the city exhaled and forgot to breathe back in—a held pause, damp and still and oddly peaceful if you can ignore what the stillness is made of. Time moves differently here, measured in water levels and reed growth rather than schedules. Visitors either find it deeply unsettling or, more dangerously, begin to understand why some people prefer it to the city above.

Properties.description:
The Wickfield Remnant is a seventeen-block section of a pre-collapse suburban district preserved — partially, imperfectly — within the northwestern expansion zone of Meridian 88. The preservation is not official, exactly: a series of contested heritage designations, property ownership disputes, and the organic resistance of a long-term resident community have combined to slow the redevelopment pressure that has consumed everything around it. The Remnant sits in a zone that should, by every corponation logistics map, be a Vespid Dynamics light industrial corridor or a Palladian Group mid-tier residential development. It isn't. It remains, with the stubborn persistence of something that simply refused to stop existing.

The built environment is extraordinary in the context of 2200 Meridian 88: intact two-story residential structures from the 2020s-2040s, their original architectural character preserved by residents who have maintained them with whatever materials were available, which means that the preservation is improvisational and vernacular rather than museum-precise. Original facades have been patched with materials from four different eras. Original windows have been replaced with whatever glass was available when they broke. Original gardens have been converted to food production while retaining their structural relationship to the houses. The result is a neighborhood that is genuinely historical while looking nothing like a historical recreation.

The Remnant's population skews older — a significant number of residents have lived here for thirty, forty, fifty years, and a few can claim lineage back to the original neighborhood before it was subsumed by Meridian 88's expansion. This has created a particular social texture: deep institutional memory, strong informal governance, and a collective identity built around the act of remaining. Younger residents who move here tend to do so because they specifically seek this quality, which means the community selects for a certain temperament. The Remnant is not unwelcoming, but it is clear about what it values, and what it values is continuity.

Palladian Group's development interest is the current primary pressure point. Their proposal for the site involves heritage-compliant reconstruction — which means demolishing the actual buildings and replacing them with architectural reproductions while displacing the current residents — and the community's legal and political resistance to this proposal has been ongoing for seven years. The Remnant has become, in some circles, a cause.
Properties.aliases: The Remnant, Wickfield, Old Wickfield, The Preservation Zone
Properties.demographics: Approximately 400-500 permanent residents. Significantly older median age than surrounding Meridian 88 zones, with a notable multi-generational core of families who have been present for decades. Mixed ethnicity but with strong roots in the specific community that was here before Meridian 88's expansion — primarily working-class Central and Eastern European and East African heritage, reflecting the original neighborhood's composition. Tiers 2-3.
Properties.economy: Local economy is largely self-sustaining in food production, repair, and services. External income comes from skilled labor exported to the surrounding city, a growing heritage-tourism micro-economy that the community has ambivalent feelings about, and the indirect economic activity of the legal advocacy network that has grown up around the displacement case. Palladian Group's development proposal would, if executed, generate significant Φ flows for the company but nothing for current residents.
Properties.power_structure: The Remnant Community Council, an informal but functional governance body with deep resident legitimacy and no formal legal standing. The council coordinates the heritage designation legal challenge, manages community resources, and makes decisions about external engagement by consensus with occasional contentious exception. Palladian Group is the primary external power, exerting pressure through legal and financial mechanisms rather than direct presence.
Properties.dangers: Palladian Group's heritage-compliant redevelopment proposal, which has come within a single legal ruling of approval twice in the past seven years; The community's aging infrastructure — the buildings are maintained, but maintenance with improvised materials has limits, and some structural conditions are genuinely concerning; The Remnant's visibility as a cause has attracted outside interests that don't always align with community needs, including political actors who want to use the case without engaging the actual community; Younger residents' economic precarity — the Remnant doesn't offer the employment infrastructure of the surrounding city, and some leave, which changes the community's demographic character; Opportunistic property speculation in the legal grey zones around the heritage designations
Properties.opportunities: The community's deep institutional memory and historical documentation represent genuine archival value for parties interested in pre-Meridian 88 history; The Remnant's self-governing community infrastructure could serve as a model or staging ground for organizing efforts in other contested zones; The heritage-tourism micro-economy is underdeveloped relative to genuine interest, representing commercial opportunity if the community can control its terms; The legal case has established precedents that have value beyond this specific situation for displacement and heritage rights advocacy throughout Meridian 88
Properties.story_hooks: A Palladian Group heritage assessment team has delivered a report claiming that one of the Remnant's central structures — the oldest intact building in the zone, occupied by a family for four generations — is not in fact the historical structure it appears to be, but a replica constructed in the 2140s on the original foundation. If true, this would invalidate the heritage designation for the entire block. The community insists it's false. The assessment methodology is questionable. Someone needs to find the actual historical documentation, which may or may not exist, and may or may not be where anyone expects it.; One of the Remnant's oldest residents — a woman in her nineties named Bozena Wrzesień who has lived in the same house for sixty-three years — has died, and her death has revealed that she was, for the last twenty years of her life, maintaining a detailed encrypted record of every interaction between the community and Palladian Group, every survey visit, every legal communication, every informal conversation. The record contains information that would be professionally and legally devastating to several named Palladian Group executives. Her family has the files and doesn't know what to do with them. Palladian Group has become aware the files exist.; A small group of Remnant residents — younger, economically stressed, facing the real prospect of being priced out even of this community — have been approached by an intermediary offering a deal: individual buyouts at significantly above-market rates, contingent on a critical mass of residents accepting, which would effectively dissolve the community's legal standing to resist Palladian Group's development application. The deal is structured so that the first accepters receive the best terms, and the offer expires in thirty days. The community council doesn't know yet. The intermediary has asked the approached residents to keep it quiet. Some of them are going to tell the council anyway. Some of them are going to accept. The question is which happens first.
Properties.sights: Original residential streetscapes from a century past, maintained and modified in ways that show every decade of occupation clearly; Front gardens converted to dense productive planting — vegetables, herbs, dwarf fruit trees — in what were once ornamental spaces; Palladian Group survey equipment and heritage assessment markers on street corners, some spray-painted over and replaced multiple times; Children playing in streets that have no vehicle traffic, a sight genuinely unusual in any part of Meridian 88; The visual contrast at the Remnant's edges: 2200 Meridian 88 architecture beginning abruptly where the protected zone ends, the difference between eras compressed into a single block
Properties.sounds: A quietness unusual in the city — reduced mechanical noise, reduced BCI broadcast infrastructure, the sounds of a neighborhood at a human scale; Communal activity sounds from the shared garden spaces: voices, tools, the specific acoustic character of people working together on productive tasks; The distant persistent sound of the surrounding city, present as a reminder of what the Remnant is preserved within; Community meetings from the central gathering house, voices rising and falling through open windows in the warm season
Properties.smells: Green growing things in density — vegetable gardens, fruit trees, flowering plants — in a concentration unusual for urban space; Wood smoke and cooking from traditional fuel-based hearths that some households maintain alongside modern systems; The smell of old buildings: plaster, timber, the specific mineral quality of architecture that has been inhabited for a hundred years; Rain on old concrete and organic soil, a smell that residents describe as the smell of the place itself
Properties.feel:
The Wickfield Remnant operates at a different phenomenological scale than the city around it. The streets are quiet enough to hear individual voices. The architecture is low enough to see the sky continuously. The BCI signal is weaker here — the community has successfully resisted full-density infrastructure installation — and the resulting reduction in ambient data-traffic creates a mental quietness that visitors often describe as disorienting before they describe it as desirable.

The community's relationship to its own precariousness is complex. The threat of displacement is not abstract — it is present in the survey markers on the corners, in the legal correspondence that occupies the community's governance council, in the Palladian Group vehicles that park at the edges and don't enter. The community has been living with imminent loss for seven years. Some residents have developed a kind of fierce present-tense engagement with the place as a result; others carry a grief that hasn't fully arrived yet.

Properties.description:
Wauwatosa was a suburban municipality that defined itself by what it wasn't — not Milwaukee, not urban, not dense, not poor. The sovereignty transition validated that identity in the worst possible way: Wauwatosa's suburban infrastructure, low density, and proximity to Milwaukee's corporate core made it ideal for what the corponations needed most in the upper GLM: campus space. The 2174 Wauwatosa Special Economic Development Zone charter converted twelve square kilometers of former residential and commercial suburban land into a corporate campus district, displacing approximately 18,000 residents who received relocation vouchers worth significantly less than their properties and relocation timelines shorter than their mortgage terms.

Wauwatosa Nexus is now a planned corporate campus environment — the kind of landscape that the tech industry pioneered in the early 22nd century and the sovereignty era perfected: low-rise office buildings set in engineered green space, connected by pedestrian paths and autonomous transit, designed to maximize employee productivity by creating an environment so comfortable that employees never want to leave. Which is the point. The campuses belong to four Big 20 corponations — Axiom Industries, Sentinel North, Promethean Health, and Ringo Defense Solutions — each occupying a quadrant of the zone, separated by shared amenity spaces that serve as both employee recreation and jurisdictional buffer.

The employees who work at the Nexus are Tier 3-4, technically skilled, and housed in campus-adjacent residential complexes that are indistinguishable from the corporate buildings except for the presence of bedrooms. The commute is a five-minute walk. The meals are provided. The gym, the medical center, the childcare facility, and the entertainment options are all on campus. The employees are not trapped — they are free to leave on their own time, which is the time between 7 PM and 6 AM, minus commute, minus sleep, minus the personal maintenance that corporate healthcare considers 'recommended wellness practices.' The freedom is technical. The containment is practical.

The displaced former residents of Wauwatosa — the 18,000 people who lost their homes to the development zone — are a political talking point and a human reality. Most were relocated to the Northwest Sprawl, where their suburban expectations collided with their new suburban reality. A community organization called the Tosa Diaspora maintains a registry of displaced families and lobbies the Milwaukee Administrative Zone for compensation that the zone does not have the authority or budget to provide. The lobbying continues. The compensation does not arrive. The campuses that replaced their homes are very well maintained.
Properties.aliases: Wauwatosa, Tosa, The Nexus, Corporate Campus West
Properties.demographics: Approximately 18,000 campus employees and 6,000 residential occupants. Tier 3-4. Highly educated, technically skilled, drawn from the corponation talent pipelines. Demographically reflects the Big 20's hiring patterns: diverse in ethnicity, uniform in education, credential, and neural augmentation status.
