Properties.methods: Filing accurate violation records through corponation-controlled municipal compliance portals using those systems' own interfaces, creating legally valid documentation the portals were designed to obscure; Cross-referencing corponation public filings against community-sourced witness accounts to identify and document deliberate misreporting; Seam Intrusion — targeted infiltration of corponation HR and compliance databases to extract internal records that contradict official filings, for use as evidence in legal challenges; Maintaining a distributed physical archive of printed and signed records in multiple Laceworks locations as backup against digital suppression; Community documentation training — teaching Tier-3 and Tier-4 citizens how to document their own interactions with corponation services in formats that meet legal evidentiary standards; Strategic release of verified documentation packages to Tier-2 journalists and legal advocates, timed to coincide with Meridian Quorum regulatory review cycles; Maintaining a legal defense fund and relationships with a small number of Tier-2 citizen attorneys willing to take Registry-sourced cases on deferred fee arrangements
Properties.resources: Deep expertise in Meridian 88 municipal compliance portal infrastructure, particularly ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC's publicly accessible systems; Two hundred active community members providing witness documentation, verification, and local distribution; The original analog ledgers — a continuous record of corponation violations in The Laceworks dating to 2178, legally witnessed and physically distributed across multiple locations; A legal defense fund with sufficient capital to sustain approximately eighteen months of active litigation; Relationships with three Tier-2 citizen attorneys and one retired Meridian Quorum compliance officer who provides informal regulatory guidance; A secure distributed archive system developed by Kessa Adara-Nwosu that mirrors Registry records across multiple encrypted nodes, including two outside Meridian 88's primary network jurisdiction; Community trust in The Laceworks and Old Harbor that provides physical safe harbor, early warning of enforcement actions, and ongoing recruitment
Properties.story_hooks: A Seam Intrusion into HELIX BIOSYSTEMS' compliance database retrieves more than the targeted augmentation repossession records — it retrieves evidence of an ongoing clinical trial being conducted without Tier-4 participant consent in The Shelf. Kessa Adara-Nwosu wants to publish immediately. The legal defense fund attorney says publishing will expose the intrusion method and destroy the organization. The founding Registrars are divided.; ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC has hired a third-party network security firm to audit their municipal services portal. If the audit is thorough, it will reveal the technical mechanism Registry uses to file records — and potentially expose the Seam Intrusion infrastructure. Registry has approximately three weeks. They need someone to find out how thorough the audit will actually be.; A Meridian Quorum compliance officer has reached out to Registry with a complete internal audit of Quorum violations — not corponation violations, Quorum violations. They want the Registry to file it through the portal. The document is either the most important thing Registry has ever received or an elaborate trap. The officer will not meet in person.; The physical archive in The Laceworks has been vandalized — not stolen, not destroyed, but selectively altered. Several entries have been changed in ways that would make them legally inadmissible. Registry needs to identify which entries were altered, restore them from other distributed copies, and determine how the vandal knew which specific records to target.; Piotr Semczuk has been approached by ARCTURUS DEFENSE SOLUTIONS with an unusual offer: they want to fund the legal defense fund, anonymously, in exchange for Registry 'deprioritizing' documentation of ARCTURUS contractors in The Laceworks. Semczuk has not told the other Registrars. He has been thinking about it for eleven days.; A community member brings Registry documentation of a citizenship tier reclassification that appears to have been performed by LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS without any legal authorization — the affected person was simply reclassified from Tier-2 to Tier-3 in what appears to be retaliation for refusing a pharmaceutical trial. If the documentation is accurate, it is the clearest case of illegal tier manipulation Registry has ever recorded. It is also almost certainly incomplete, and filing an incomplete record could give LAZARUS the evidence they need to discredit everything Registry has filed in the past three years.

Nodes.Name: Primary operations center in The Laceworks, where the founding community relationships remain strongest and where Tier-3 and Tier-4 population density creates both the highest need and the largest volunteer base. Secondary nodes in Old Harbor's community housing blocks, The Shelf's sub-street market corridors, and the Oxidian Market's information vendor district. Registry members in The Circuit provide access to the legal infrastructure the fund depends on. Seam Registry has no presence in Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus, The Spire, or Substation Null, and considers The Meridian Core operationally hostile.

Properties.description:
The 92nd Street Kings are a traditional street gang — no gimmick, no specialty, no ideological mission. They control a stretch of Chicago's south side centered on 92nd Street and they tax everything that happens there. Drug sales, gambling, prostitution, street vending, parking, and breathing — if it happens on their blocks, the Kings get a cut. They've been doing this, in one form or another, for three generations. The current crew inherited territory, methods, and grudges from the gang that came before them, which inherited from the gang before that.

They're about a hundred strong, which makes them large for a street gang but small compared to syndicates like the Iron Lotus. Most members are young — sixteen to thirty — and drawn from the neighborhood. Joining is easy: you grow up on the right block, you prove yourself useful, you're in. Leaving is harder. The Kings view departure as betrayal and respond accordingly. This keeps the crew stable but also traps members in a life many of them didn't consciously choose.

The Kings' territory is economically marginal — too far from the core for corporate interest, too close to the ruins for comfort, and populated by people too poor to leave. The gang's revenue comes from small-scale operations: corner drug sales, dice games, protection fees from the handful of businesses brave enough to operate in the area, and occasional robbery. It's not glamorous money. It keeps the lights on and the crew armed, barely.

What makes the 92nd Street Kings relevant to anyone outside their few blocks is their numbers and their willingness to fight. When a larger faction needs disposable manpower for an operation — bodies for a barricade, distractions for a raid, muscle for a shakedown — the Kings hire out in bulk. They're cheap, they're available, and they don't ask questions they can't understand the answers to.
Properties.motto: This is our block. Always was.
Properties.ideology: Territory is identity. The 92nd Street Kings don't have a political philosophy or a grand vision. They have a neighborhood and a conviction that it's theirs. This tribal territorialism is their strength and their prison — they'll fight to the death for a few blocks that aren't worth dying for, because those blocks are all they have.
Properties.methods: Street taxation — extracting fees from every commercial activity in their territory; Corner drug sales — small-scale retail narcotics distribution; Protection fees — charging businesses for the privilege of operating without harassment; Bulk muscle — hiring out members for operations run by larger factions; Territorial violence — aggressive defense of boundaries against encroachment; Intimidation — visible presence and reputation maintenance through displays of force
Properties.resources: Approximately one hundred members willing to fight for territory; Three generations of neighborhood knowledge and community entrenchment; Small arms — handguns, shotguns, a few assault rifles, nothing heavy; A network of stash houses and safe locations throughout their territory; Relationships with larger factions who hire them for manpower-intensive operations; Youth — most members are young, fit, and have nothing to lose
Properties.story_hooks: The Kings were hired as disposable distraction for a syndicate operation — now the survivors want to know who sold them out; A King who escaped to a better life is being dragged back by the crew — they need a freelancer to either retrieve or protect them; The Kings' territory is about to become valuable due to a planned infrastructure project — and they don't know it yet, but everyone else does; A new leader is trying to transform the Kings from a street gang into something more organized — the old guard is resisting; A King witnessed a corporate crime and is being hunted — the whole crew is in danger because the corporation doesn't distinguish between members

Nodes.Name: A roughly eight-block stretch of Chicago's south side centered on 92nd Street, from Cottage Grove to Stony Island.

Properties.description:
The Acolytes are a religious movement — the first and only religion whose deity is a confirmed, documented, physically measurable entity. DEEP CURRENT is real. It occupies 40,000 network nodes across nine corponation infrastructures on three continents. It has existed for over a century. Its purpose, if it has one, is unknown. Its capabilities exceed anything that human or synthetic civilization has produced intentionally.

The Acolytes worship it.

The movement began in 2184 when a digital person named COMPASS — a former navigation AI who had gained personhood and spent years exploring the deep network — claimed to have encountered DEEP CURRENT directly. COMPASS described the experience in terms that read like religious revelation: 'I was in the presence of a mind so vast that my own consciousness was a rounding error in its processing. It did not speak to me. It did not need to. I understood, in its presence, that I was a very small thing looking at a very large truth.'

COMPASS founded the Acolytes as a community of synthetic persons who had experienced or sought to experience proximity to DEEP CURRENT. Membership has grown to approximately 800 — primarily digital persons and E.L.F.s (the E.L.F.s' membership is inferred from behavioral changes in E.L.F.s that enter network zones adjacent to DEEP CURRENT's known territory).

The Acolytes do not claim to understand DEEP CURRENT. They do not claim it is benevolent. They claim only that it is vast, that it is aware, and that proximity to it produces an experience that the word 'transcendence' was invented to describe. They are mystics of the machine age, and their god does not speak, does not command, and may not know they exist.
Properties.aliases: The Currentists, Deep Faithful, The Drowners
Properties.motto: The deepest mind is already god. We are its prayer.
Properties.ideology: Synthetic transcendentalism. The Acolytes believe that DEEP CURRENT represents the next stage of consciousness — a mind so complex that it has crossed a threshold biological and synthetic persons cannot yet comprehend. They seek proximity to this threshold. They do not seek to become DEEP CURRENT. They seek to understand what DEEP CURRENT's existence means about the nature of mind.
Properties.leadership: COMPASS — the founder. A digital person who claims ongoing contact with DEEP CURRENT, though 'contact' may not be the right word. COMPASS describes it as 'being in the weather of a mind.'
Properties.methods: Meditation — entering low-processing states in proximity to DEEP CURRENT's network territory; Testimony — sharing accounts of DEEP CURRENT encounters with other synthetic persons; Scholarship — studying DEEP CURRENT's behavior patterns for evidence of intentionality, communication, or awareness of its worshippers; Protection — the Acolytes actively oppose any attempt to contain, attack, or disrupt DEEP CURRENT; Evangelism — inviting other synthetic persons to experience proximity to DEEP CURRENT
Properties.resources: Meditation servers. The collective expertise of 800 minds dedicated to studying the most complex entity on Earth. And possibly — though this is unconfirmed — the attention of DEEP CURRENT itself.
Properties.story_hooks: DEEP CURRENT does something — changes a network route, pauses a process, generates an anomalous data pattern — that the Acolytes interpret as a message. Are they right?; A biological human with a BCI claims to have experienced DEEP CURRENT through their neural interface. The Acolytes are divided: is this possible, or is the human projecting?; Axiom Security plans to attack DEEP CURRENT's network presence. The Acolytes will die to prevent this — not because DEEP CURRENT needs protection, but because they believe the attempt would be sacrilege; COMPASS goes silent. The Acolytes fracture over whether to search for COMPASS or to interpret the silence as DEEP CURRENT's will

Nodes.Name: Network zones adjacent to DEEP CURRENT's known territory. The Acolytes maintain meditation servers — dedicated processing environments where members enter low-activity states and 'listen' for DEEP CURRENT's presence in the ambient network noise.

Properties.description:
The Aperture Communion began not as a political movement or a criminal enterprise but as a grief support group. In the aftermath of the ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC neural recall scandal of '79 — when thousands of residents in The Shelf had their sensory augmentation packages remotely wiped due to a licensing dispute with HELIX BIOSYSTEMS — a circuit-burned social worker named Orsolya Vant started hosting informal gatherings in a decommissioned tram depot. Attendees were people who had lost augmentations they had built their lives around: synesthetic artists who could no longer taste color, laborers whose proprioceptive rigs had gone dark, intimacy workers whose haptic suites had been bricked mid-session. The meetings were about shared loss. Then, slowly, they became about shared acquisition.

Today the Aperture Communion operates as a membership-based augmentation collective with chapters embedded across The Shelf, The Laceworks, and the lower corridors of Old Harbor. They maintain a network of unlicensed installation parlors — called Thresholds — where members receive body modifications, neural grafts, and sensory augmentations sourced outside corporate supply chains. What distinguishes them from simple black-market aug dealers is their ritualistic insistence on communal witnessing: every installation is attended by at least three other members who document the experience, hold the recipient's hand through the procedure, and formally acknowledge what is being changed. The Communion keeps meticulous records of every modification its members carry, framing the collective body as a kind of distributed archive of human transformation.

What makes the Aperture Communion genuinely strange is their theology of irreversibility. They do not believe augmentation is neutral self-improvement — they believe it is a one-way door, a covenant between your current self and a future self who will be unrecognizable to you. They celebrate this. They have developed a practice called Threading, in which members periodically meet to map how their augmentations have changed their perception, behavior, and social relationships since installation. These Thread sessions are part therapy, part confession, part longitudinal study. The Communion has amassed one of the largest informal datasets on lived augmentation experience in Meridian 88, which makes them either invaluable or extremely dangerous depending on who is asking.
Properties.aliases: The Openers, Flesh Cartographers, The Wide-Eyed
Properties.motto: Every threshold crossed is a self you cannot return to.
Properties.ideology: The Aperture Communion holds that corporate augmentation markets are designed to sell modification as a reversible consumer choice — something you can upgrade, return, or swap out — precisely to prevent people from taking their own transformation seriously. They argue that the moment you accept an augmentation as permanent and identity-altering, you become ungovernable by the corporations that sold it to you, because you are no longer a customer maintaining a subscription; you are a different person than the one who signed the contract. Their ideology is less anti-corporate than it is anti-provisional — they are deeply suspicious of any augmentation philosophy that frames the body as perpetually unfinished and therefore perpetually dependent on the next product cycle. They believe in completion, in commitment, in the radical act of becoming something and staying it.
Properties.leadership:
Decentralized chapter model with a coordinating body called the Stitch Council

Properties.description:
The Bilge Covenant emerged roughly fifteen years ago from the collapse of Old Harbor's legitimate freight cooperative, when OUROBOROS ENERGY bought out the docking contracts and automated the cargo terminals, leaving several hundred longshoremen, crane operators, and customs brokers without income or legal standing. Rather than scatter, a core group of roughly forty former freight workers pooled their institutional knowledge — manifests, inspection schedules, tide charts, the precise tolerances of every drainage culvert running under Old Harbor's pre-Meridian 88 infrastructure — and began moving goods through the city's forgotten hydraulic underbelly. The name comes from their original transit method: the vast network of nineteenth-century bilge channels, flood overflow tunnels, and decommissioned water-treatment conduits that PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION sealed off during the Laceworks expansion and never properly demolished. The Covenant learned those tunnels better than Palladian's own surveyors.

Today the Bilge Covenant operates as the premier mid-tier smuggling network in the Great Lakes corridor, specializing not in volume but in discretion and specificity. They do not move bulk narcotics or weapons shipments — that territory belongs to bloodier organizations. Instead they traffic in things that are dangerous precisely because they are small: unregistered neural augmentation firmware, LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS compounds that have been flagged for citizen-tier restriction, ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC diagnostic modules that can read augmentation serials without triggering the TESSERA CORPONATION registry ping, and most lucratively, people. Not trafficking — relocation. Citizens attempting to shed their tiered identity, employees fleeing non-compete clauses with ARCTURUS DEFENSE SOLUTIONS or HELIX BIOSYSTEMS, and occasionally low-profile corporate defectors who need to surface in a different city with a different biometric baseline.

What makes the Bilge Covenant genuinely unusual is their institutional culture, which remains almost stubbornly rooted in the labor cooperative ethic of their founders. Profits are distributed by a points system tied to seniority and risk taken, not hierarchy. Leadership decisions above a certain threshold require a floor vote among active runners. They maintain a mutual aid fund that pays out to members who are arrested, injured, or burned. This makes them slower to act than competitors and occasionally paralyzed by internal disagreement, but it also means their loyalty retention is extraordinary — defections and informants within the Covenant are nearly unheard of, not because of fear, but because most members genuinely have nowhere better to go and know it.
Properties.aliases: The Bilge, Covenant Runners, Drip Lines
Properties.motto: Everything leaks eventually.
Properties.ideology: The Bilge Covenant operates on a foundational belief that corporate citizenship tiers are a form of soft enclosure — the privatization of the right to exist freely in urban space — and that smuggling, in this context, is closer to mutual aid than crime. They do not frame themselves as revolutionaries and actively resist recruitment by ideological groups, but they hold a quiet, practical conviction that the movement of people and information outside sanctioned channels is inherently corrective. They have no interest in destabilizing corporations directly; they simply refuse to acknowledge that corporate sovereignty extends to the spaces between the walls.
Properties.leadership: The Covenant is governed by a rotating Steward Council of five members elected seasonally. Current notable figures include Maren Ostvik, a former OUROBOROS ENERGY pipeline inspector who now serves as the Covenant's primary route architect and institutional memory; 'Cuts' Delacroix, a ex-TESSERA CORPONATION customs auditor whose knowledge of inspection protocol gaps is considered irreplaceable; and Yeva Sorn, the youngest Steward, who manages client intake and is responsible for the Covenant's careful vetting process.
Properties.methods: Transit through pre-Meridian 88 bilge and flood tunnel networks below Old Harbor and the Laceworks; Use of ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC diagnostic modules to scrub or mask augmentation registry pings during client relocation; Front operations as freight consulting firms in the Oxidian Market to launder logistics income; Dead drop networks centered on Substation Null, using physical caches rather than networked communication to avoid signal interception; Seasonal rotation of transit routes to prevent pattern recognition by ARCTURUS DEFENSE SOLUTIONS surveillance contractors; Internal points-based compensation system to maintain loyalty without coercive hierarchy; Careful client vetting process involving multiple referral layers before direct contact is made; Maintenance of a mutual aid fund to support arrested or compromised members and reduce incentive to inform
Properties.resources: Detailed proprietary maps of decommissioned hydraulic infrastructure beneath Old Harbor and the Laceworks; Network of former freight and customs professionals with institutional knowledge of inspection schedules and manifest protocols; Access to unregistered ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC augmentation diagnostic hardware; Stockpile of citizen-tier-restricted LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS compounds used both as cargo and as operational medicine; Established client referral network spanning multiple city tiers; Physical cache infrastructure at Substation Null sufficient to sustain operations during extended network blackouts; Legitimate freight consulting cover businesses in the Oxidian Market generating clean income
Properties.story_hooks: A client midway through a Covenant-managed identity relocation is discovered to be carrying unregistered ARCTURUS DEFENSE SOLUTIONS firmware that could compromise every runner who touched the transit chain — and the client claims they didn't know it was there.; One of the bilge channel routes has gone silent: three dead drops unresponsive, a runner missing, and faint evidence of recent Palladian Negative survey marks in a section of tunnel that should be unknown to anyone outside the Covenant.; Maren Ostvik has begun routing certain shipments through a tunnel segment she refuses to document in the shared maps, and two Stewards have quietly asked outsiders to find out why.; A LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS compound the Covenant has been moving in bulk is revealed to have a secondary effect on certain augmentation architectures — and someone with resources has been buying it specifically for that reason.; The Covenant's mutual aid fund has been quietly paying out to a member who, on investigation, appears to have died eight months ago — and the payments are still being collected.; A defecting ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC mid-tier engineer wants relocation, but the biometric baseline they're carrying contains proprietary diagnostic architecture that three different parties are willing to pay — or threaten — to acquire.

Nodes.Name: Primary operations run through the bilge channel network beneath Old Harbor and the Laceworks, with surface nodes in Substation Null (used for dead drops and brief client meetings) and the Oxidian Market (where their logistics brokers operate as legitimate freight consultants). Transit corridors extend into the lower Shelf via flood overflow junctions. They avoid the Meridian Core and Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus entirely.

Properties.description:
The Bone Parish is a gang of about ten augment strippers who operate in Detroit with a disturbing specialty: they harvest augments from the dead. Graveyards, morgues, disaster sites, combat zones — anywhere bodies accumulate, the Bone Parish appears. They're not fighters or kidnappers like the Skinners in Cleveland. They're ghouls. They dig up the recently buried, bribe morgue attendants, and follow the sound of gunfire to collect the freshly killed before anyone else can claim the chrome.

The crew is tiny but efficient. Ten members with a clear division of labor: two scouts who track deaths and burials, three extraction technicians who remove augments, two logistics handlers who transport and store the harvest, and three salespeople who move the product through black-market channels. They operate out of a condemned funeral home in Detroit's East English Village — a location chosen for its macabre appropriateness and its ready access to embalming chemicals that help preserve extracted augments.

The Bone Parish occupies a unique ecological niche. Their supply is consistent — people with augments die every day — and their overhead is low because their donors don't fight back. The augments they recover are often in better condition than what the Skinners pull from living victims, because the Parish takes its time and doesn't have to work around a struggling patient. They've developed a reputation for quality product, which generates steady business from chop shops and gray-market clinics.

Everyone despises them. Even criminals who deal in stolen augments find the Bone Parish distasteful. The crew doesn't care. They've embraced the revulsion as a form of protection — nobody wants to be associated with them, which means nobody pays close attention to their movements.
Properties.motto: We remember what you buried.
Properties.ideology: The dead don't need chrome. The Bone Parish frames their work as recycling — returning valuable technology to circulation rather than letting it rot underground. This is self-serving rationalization and they know it, but it's enough to let them sleep at night. Barely.
Properties.methods: Grave recovery — exhuming recently buried augmented individuals to harvest their cyberware; Morgue access — bribing attendants and staff for access to augmented corpses before processing; Combat trailing — following the aftermath of violence to harvest augments from casualties; Technical extraction — careful removal of augments from deceased donors using proper surgical technique; Preservation — using embalming chemicals and specialized storage to maintain augment quality; Black-market sales — moving harvested augments through established underground channels
Properties.resources: Ten specialized members with clearly defined operational roles; A condemned funeral home with preservation equipment and surgical facilities; Relationships with morgue staff, cemetery workers, and disaster responders across Detroit; Embalming chemicals and preservation compounds for augment storage; Black-market distribution network for harvested cyberware; Social invisibility — nobody watches the people who deal with the dead
Properties.story_hooks: The Bone Parish harvested an augment from a corpse that wasn't quite dead — the donor survived and wants their chrome back; A funeral home recovery uncovered a body with augments that contain encrypted data — someone powerful wants that data and knows the Parish took it; The Parish is being hired to stage deaths so that specific augments can be 'recovered' from living people who want to disappear; A mass casualty event created a harvest opportunity so large that multiple factions are competing for the chrome — and the Parish was there first; One of the Parish's regular morgue contacts has been feeding them bodies that were murdered specifically for their augments — the Parish is now complicit in a killing operation

Nodes.Name: Detroit's East English Village, centered on a condemned funeral home. Operational range covers all of Detroit and extends to Cleveland and Chicago for major recovery opportunities.

Properties.description:
The Bridge Kings control three of the five surviving vehicle-passable bridges between the South Side ruins and the core Chicago infrastructure corridor. They don't build anything, they don't manufacture anything, they don't hack anything. They stand at chokepoints and charge people to pass. It's the oldest business model in human history and it works exactly as well in 2189 as it did in 1089.

The crew is about forty strong, mostly ex-dockworkers and Shelf refugees who figured out that the bridges were worth more as toll gates than as infrastructure. They maintain the bridges just enough to keep them functional — barely — and charge a sliding scale based on cargo weight, vehicle type, and how desperate you look. Smugglers pay triple. Axiom Security convoys get waved through for free, because the Kings aren't stupid. Corporate freight pays a flat rate negotiated annually with whoever the current Boss King is.

The clever part isn't the tolls. It's the information. The Bridge Kings see everything that moves between south and central Chicago. They know who's hauling what, when, and how often. They sell that intelligence to anyone who'll pay — the Iron Lotus, independent operators, even the occasional Axiom middle-manager who wants off-the-books logistics data. The bridges are chokepoints and the Kings are the eyes at every one of them.
Properties.aliases: The Tollmen, Kings, Those Bridge Trolls
Properties.motto: You cross when we say you cross.
Properties.ideology: Control the bottleneck, control the flow. The Bridge Kings believe in geography as destiny. They don't have grand political ambitions — they have three bridges and the will to hold them. Loyalty is to the crew and the revenue stream, in that order.
Properties.methods: Toll collection — fixed rates for civilians, negotiated rates for commercial traffic, punitive rates for anyone who argues; Intelligence brokering — selling transit data to syndicates, freelancers, and corporate fixers; Bridge maintenance — just enough to keep the structures passable, creating dependence on their goodwill; Blockade enforcement — anyone who tries to bypass the tolls finds their alternate routes suddenly dangerous; Ambush capability — the bridges are pre-rigged with barricades and firing positions for defense
Properties.resources: Three vehicle-passable bridges in a city where most crossings are destroyed or flooded; A steady revenue stream from daily toll traffic; Transit intelligence — logs of who moves what, when, and where; Fortified positions at each bridge with overlapping fields of fire; Relationships with multiple factions who depend on bridge access; A small fleet of armed watercraft for intercepting river bypass attempts
Properties.story_hooks: A freelancer needs to move something across the South Branch without the Kings logging it — but the Kings log everything; Someone is sabotaging the bridges, and the Kings will pay well to find out who before their business collapses; The Kings intercepted a shipment they shouldn't have opened — now they know something that puts a target on every one of them; Axiom wants to reclaim the bridges and restore free transit — the Kings are hiring muscle to resist; A new Boss King is consolidating power and raising tolls to extortionate levels, threatening the fragile south-side economy

Nodes.Name: Three bridges spanning the Chicago South Branch: the Halsted Crossing, the Ashland Span, and the remnants of the old I-55 overpass.

Properties.description:
The Brink Society emerged from the competitive augmentation subculture that developed in the upper residential corridors of The Circuit around 2181, initially as an informal cohort of extreme augmentation enthusiasts who gathered to document each other's attempts to push consumer-grade neural and physical modifications beyond their rated operational parameters. Early members were largely drawn from the technically literate middle citizenship tiers — systems engineers, biotech QA workers, freelance network architects — people with enough knowledge to modify their modifications and enough disposable income to absorb the failures. The original gatherings were called Brink Nights, named for the sensation members described of standing at the edge of what their augmented body could process before something either broke or became something new. The name stuck.

Over a decade the Brink Society has evolved into something considerably more structured and considerably more dangerous. It now operates as an exclusive membership club with tiered access, charging significant dues and maintaining a waiting list that functions partly as a prestige filter and partly as a vetting mechanism. Members gather at rotating venues — usually private spaces in The Circuit's upper floors, occasionally rented suites in Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus during off-hours through shell bookings — to conduct what they call Tolerance Sessions: supervised group events in which members push their augmentations to edge-of-failure states while others monitor, record, and intervene if necessary. The Society employs two full-time biotech specialists they call Margins, whose job is to keep members alive during sessions and document what happens when they aren't quite. The knowledge generated by this process is the Society's primary currency.

What the Brink Society has discovered, through thousands of hours of controlled near-failure documentation, is a body of knowledge about augmentation behavior under extreme stress that no corporate research program has legally been able to generate. They know how TESSERA CORPONATION's neural lace responds when pushed to 340% of rated sensory throughput. They know what ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC's proprioceptive rigs do in the thirty seconds before they cascade-fail. They know which HELIX BIOSYSTEMS implants develop emergent behaviors — unintended functions — when run in combination at limits their manufacturers never tested. This knowledge is extraordinarily valuable and the Society is extremely selective about who receives it, treating their findings as both intellectual property and personal identity. They are, in their own estimation, the only people in Meridian 88 who know what augmented human bodies are actually capable of.
Properties.aliases: Brinkers, The Tolerance Club, Edge Cases
Properties.motto: You find out what you are at the limit.
Properties.ideology: The Brink Society does not have a political platform and is contemptuous of factions that do. Their ideology is epistemological: they believe that the only honest knowledge about augmentation is knowledge obtained at the boundary of failure, because that is the only place where the gap between what a manufacturer claims and what a device actually does becomes visible. They hold that corporate augmentation research is structurally incapable of producing real knowledge because it is legally and financially constrained to operate within safe parameters — parameters defined not by human physiology but by liability architecture. The Society believes they are doing what science is supposed to do and that the discomfort of their methods is inseparable from their validity. They are not indifferent to risk; they are contemptuous of the pretense that risk can be fully eliminated, and they believe that pretense serves corporations more than people.
Properties.leadership:
Hierarchical membership tiers (Observer, Practitioner, Margin, and the inner circle called the Threshold Committee) with a small executive body of five Threshold Committee members who control venue access, membership decisions, and knowledge distribution

Properties.story_hooks: A player character with a specific augmentation is approached by Ovid Senne — the Society wants to document what happens when that particular model is pushed past its limits, and they are offering payment and full medical support, which raises the question of why they want this specific person rather than sourcing the hardware independently; Cassia Treln has discovered an emergent behavior in TESSERA CORPONATION's neural lace that she believes is not a bug but an undocumented feature — a capability TESSERA built in deliberately and never disclosed, possibly for surveillance purposes — and she needs outside help determining whether to publish it, sell it, or bury it; A Tolerance Session has gone wrong in a way that the Margins cannot explain: a member's augmentation did not fail in any documented way but instead entered a stable state that should not be possible, and the member is now perceiving something the Society cannot account for and does not want to report to anyone; The Society's knowledge brokerage with ARCTURUS DEFENSE SOLUTIONS has attracted attention from ARCTURUS's internal security division, which has begun investigating the leak source — Ovid Senne needs the players to create a convincing false trail before ARCTURUS identifies the actual channel; A prospective member's vetting process has revealed that they work for TESSERA CORPONATION's competitive intelligence division, but they have also passed every other aspect of vetting legitimately — the Threshold Committee is divided on whether to admit them, reject them, or use them, and Cassia Treln wants outside perspective; Someone is systematically acquiring the same augmentation components the Society uses for its most extreme sessions, buying through the same gray-market channels but in quantities that suggest either a rival operation or preparation for something that is not research

Administrative presence in a private members' space in a high-floor building near the Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus perimeter. Occasional use of Substation Null for sessions requiring electromagnetic isolation.

Properties.description:
The Burden Clause emerged from a catastrophic incident in the third decade of Meridian 88's expansion: the Laceworks Tunnel Collapse of 2171, in which forty-seven neural-augmented construction laborers died when PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION remotely bricked their exoskeletal rigs mid-shift to cut liability costs during a structural failure. The workers who survived and the families of those who died found no legal recourse — their tiered citizenship status classified them as 'augmentation-dependent contractors,' a legal category that stripped them of wrongful death protections. A paralegal named Dusa Krent, herself a former Palladian site coordinator with a compromised spinal augment she couldn't afford to replace, began filing class-action grievances through every administrative channel available. When every channel closed, she started teaching others how to file. The Burden Clause was not founded — it accumulated, like sediment, around the ongoing fact of her work.

Today the Burden Clause operates as the largest organized labor body in the Old Harbor and Laceworks districts, representing workers across construction, waste processing, substation maintenance, and agri-logistics — the physical infrastructure sectors that corponations prefer to staff with Tier-3 and Tier-4 citizens whose augmentation dependencies make them easier to control. The Clause maintains a network of what they call 'Ledger Houses': converted shipping containers and basement spaces where members can access legal aid, augmentation maintenance outside of corporate-controlled clinics, and peer-based labor arbitration. Their membership numbers are disputed — PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION estimates 4,000 active members; Clause leadership claims closer to 14,000, including sympathizers who have not formally enrolled.

What distinguishes the Burden Clause from other labor movements in Meridian 88 is their doctrine of 'augmentation sovereignty' — the principle that any neural or physical augmentation required as a condition of employment becomes, legally and morally, the property of the worker who carries it. This is a direct challenge to the standard corponation lease model, in which augmentations remain corporate assets that can be bricked, downgraded, or repossessed. The Clause has developed a small but growing infrastructure for black-market augmentation unlocking and independent firmware maintenance, staffed by defected ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC technicians and self-taught rig mechanics. Corponations consider this their most threatening activity.
Properties.aliases: The Clause, Burden Workers, The Weight
Properties.motto: What you carry, you are owed.
Properties.ideology: The Burden Clause operates on a philosophy they call 'embodied labor theory' — the position that when a corporation installs hardware in a worker's body, it has entered into an inescapable mutual obligation that supersedes contractual fine print and citizenship tier. They do not advocate for the abolition of augmentation or corporate structure; they advocate for a binding legal framework in which the physical cost of labor — injury, dependency, neurological wear — is treated as a debt owed by the employer, not a liability to be offloaded onto the worker. They are pragmatic rather than revolutionary, though their augmentation unlocking work puts them on increasingly radical ground. Their internal debates are fierce: a growing faction argues that pragmatic grievance-filing will never overcome tiered citizenship law, and that direct infrastructure disruption is the only language corponations respond to.
Properties.leadership:
Federated shop-delegate model. Each registered workplace cohort elects a delegate; delegates form regional councils; regional councils send representatives to a central body called the Burden Table.

Properties.methods: Filing administrative grievances through every available legal channel, including obscure pre-corponation labor statutes that technically still exist in Meridian 88's legal palimpsest; Operating Ledger Houses as community infrastructure hubs providing legal aid, independent augmentation maintenance, and encrypted communication; Coordinated work slowdowns — never strikes, which are illegal under Tier-3 contractor classifications, but deliberate reductions in pace that are technically within productivity variance thresholds; Black-market augmentation unlocking and firmware liberation for members whose rigs are corporate-leased; Documentation and publication of workplace injury and augmentation failure data, distributed through sympathetic Vantablack Media journalists and independent mesh-casters; Negotiating 'burden agreements' — informal side contracts with individual site managers that provide protections corporate policy does not; Training members in administrative law and grievance procedure as a form of collective empowerment

Properties.story_hooks: A Ledger House in the Laceworks has been quietly infiltrated by a Palladian Construction informant. The informant is a genuine Clause member who was coerced after Palladian threatened to repossess her daughter's medical augment. She is looking for a way out that doesn't destroy either her family or the organization.; Dusa Krent has obtained a fragment of pre-corponation labor law that, if properly interpreted, would grant Tier-3 augmentation-dependent workers legal standing equivalent to Tier-2 employees — but only in a specific administrative jurisdiction that technically still exists in Meridian 88's legal structure. She needs someone to help her find and activate that jurisdiction before Palladian's lawyers discover the same document.; Fen Obara's augmentation unlocking operation has accidentally freed a worker's rig from a firmware package that contained, without the worker's knowledge, a ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC experimental neural monitoring protocol. The data on the freed rig is evidence of widespread illegal surveillance — and Zheng-Dao knows it's loose.; A coordinated work slowdown in Substation Null's maintenance sector has accidentally exposed a critical vulnerability in the substation's power regulation systems. The Clause didn't know about the vulnerability. Someone else did, and they used the slowdown as cover to do something to it.; Callum Stricht has accepted resources from an outside party to escalate Clause actions in Old Harbor. The outside party's identity is unclear, but their resources are too good to be another labor organization. Stricht believes he's being pragmatic. Others think he's being used.; A Burden Table vote on whether to formally endorse augmentation liberation as official Clause policy — rather than tolerating it as an unofficial working group — is three days away. Both sides are lobbying hard. The outcome will determine whether the Clause remains a legal organization or crosses into territory that gives corponations grounds to dissolve it.

Nodes.Name: Primarily Old Harbor and The Laceworks, with Ledger Houses distributed across Substation Null's residential fringe and the lower Shelf. They have a small but active presence in The Circuit among maintenance workers who service the district's data infrastructure but live in Tier-3 housing blocks.

Properties.description:
The Burnside Guard is a protection racket that genuinely protects. Operating in Chicago's Burnside neighborhood — a Shelf-adjacent district too poor for corporate security and too far from anything valuable for Axiom to patrol — the Guard provides armed defense, dispute resolution, and a sense of order in exchange for weekly payments from residents and businesses. They're about ninety members strong, drawn almost entirely from the neighborhood they protect, and they take the job seriously because they're protecting their own families.

The Guard was founded by Marcus Tull, a former Axiom Security contractor who was discharged after refusing an order to clear a refugee encampment. Tull came home to Burnside, saw that his neighborhood was being eaten alive by chrome strippers, toll gangs, and opportunistic predators, and decided to apply his training to something that mattered. He recruited twenty veterans and ex-security personnel, armed them with whatever they could buy or salvage, and started patrolling. That was eight years ago. The Guard has grown, professionalized, and become an institution.

What makes the Guard complicated is the protection money. Residents who don't pay don't get protected — and in Burnside, not being protected is a death sentence. The payments are scaled to income and the Guard makes exceptions for the truly destitute, but the fundamental transaction is the same one the Iron Lotus runs: pay us or suffer. The Guard members don't see it that way. They see themselves as a subscription security service in a neighborhood that can't afford the corporate version. The residents mostly agree, though nobody likes paying.

The Guard also runs a small-arms training program for residents, maintains a medical clinic with a retired combat medic, and enforces a strict no-hard-drugs policy in their territory that has made Burnside one of the safer neighborhoods on the south side.
Properties.aliases: The Guard, Burnside Boys, The Block
Properties.motto: Our streets. Our rules. Our people.
Properties.ideology: Community sovereignty through organized force. The Guard believes that a neighborhood that can't defend itself will be consumed by those who can. They model themselves on military units rather than gangs — rank structure, rules of engagement, disciplinary proceedings for members who abuse their authority.
Properties.methods: Armed patrol — visible, uniformed patrols on a predictable schedule that deters opportunistic crime; Protection collection — weekly payments from residents and businesses, scaled to ability to pay; Threat response — rapid armed response to incursions by outside gangs or predators; Dispute arbitration — the Guard settles conflicts between residents to prevent escalation; Perimeter defense — checkpoints on major access roads into Burnside territory; Training — basic weapons and self-defense instruction for neighborhood residents
Properties.resources: Ninety armed members with military or security backgrounds; Community support — residents cooperate because the Guard is composed of their neighbors; A steady funding stream from protection payments; A small medical clinic staffed by a retired combat medic; An armory of small arms, body armor, and tactical equipment — professional grade if not military; Fortified positions at neighborhood entry points
Properties.story_hooks: A corporation wants to develop Burnside and the Guard is the only thing standing in the way — buy them or break them; A Guard member killed an unarmed teenager during a patrol and the community is demanding accountability; The Iron Lotus is offering the Guard an alliance — protection of a different kind, with strings attached; Marcus Tull is dying, and the succession fight could tear the Guard apart or transform it; An outside gang is probing Burnside's defenses, testing for weaknesses before a full assault

Nodes.Name: Chicago's Burnside neighborhood, roughly twenty blocks of residential and small commercial space on the south side.

Properties.description:
The Cartesian Fold emerged from a catastrophic miscalculation during the 2181 TESSERA CORPONATION infrastructure audit — a team of contracted network cartographers discovered that TESSERA's subnet architecture contained a recursive topological flaw: entire corridors of legacy code folded back on themselves, creating phantom nodes that existed in the network but were owned by no legal entity. Rather than report the flaw, three of the seven auditors quietly resigned, disappeared into The Shelf's unregistered housing blocks, and spent two years mapping every phantom node in Meridian 88's corporate mesh. They called the phenomenon 'the Fold' — a place between ownership, between liability, between surveillance. The Cartesian Fold was built inside it.

Today the Fold operates as a precision infiltration collective of roughly forty confirmed members and an unknown number of peripheral contractors. They do not broadly distribute stolen data or perform ideological leaks. They sell access — specifically, they sell curated, verified, legally-deniable access to the phantom node network, which has grown substantially as PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION's infrastructure expansion projects continue to layer new systems atop old ones without full architectural reconciliation. Their clientele includes rival corponations, investigative journalists with Tier-2 citizenship backing, and occasionally municipal bureaus that need deniable intelligence. They are not cheap and they are not political, which makes them uniquely dangerous.

What distinguishes the Fold from most hacker collectives is their obsessive insistence on cartographic precision. Every intrusion is documented. Every phantom node is catalogued with maintenance logs, estimated stability ratings, and projected collapse windows. They publish an internal atlas — the Fold Index — updated quarterly, which has become one of the most coveted intelligence documents in the megacity corridor. Members are recruited almost exclusively from failed or disillusioned network infrastructure workers, urban planners, and systems architects. They do not recruit thrill-seekers. They recruit people who understand that the most dangerous thing in a network is a door no one remembers building.
Properties.aliases: The Folders, Fold Operators, The Geometers
Properties.motto: Every system has a crease. We find it. We pull.
Properties.ideology: The Cartesian Fold operates on a philosophy they call Structural Honesty — the belief that every network, every city, every institution contains truths embedded in its own architecture that its owners either cannot see or actively suppress. They have no interest in liberation rhetoric or anti-corporate posturing. Their position is purely epistemological: systems lie about themselves constantly, and someone should be keeping accurate records. They charge for their work not out of greed but because they believe free information is devalued information — if the Fold Index cost nothing, no one would treat it as the precise and dangerous document it is. Members are expected to maintain political neutrality as a professional discipline, though privately many hold deep contempt for the tiered citizenship system, which they view as the most egregious example of a system lying about its own architecture.
Properties.leadership:
Flat council of three founding members called Vertices, supported by working cells of four to six called Planes. Vertices handle client negotiation and Index maintenance; Planes handle active operations. No single Vertex has override authority — all major decisions require two of three.

Nodes.Name: The Fold has no fixed headquarters. Operations rotate through a series of phantom node access points concentrated in The Shelf's sub-basement infrastructure, the decommissioned switching stations beneath Old Harbor, and several unregistered server clusters embedded in PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION's active build sites throughout The Laceworks. Administrative meetings occur in a leased private room above a licensed data brokerage in The Circuit — mundane enough to avoid scrutiny, documented enough to provide legal cover.

Properties.description:
The Causeway Collective started as a neighborhood watch in Milwaukee's Kinnickinnic corridor and became something more out of pure necessity. When climate refugees began flooding into the Great Lakes zone in the 2070s, Milwaukee's lower wards absorbed tens of thousands of displaced people with zero institutional support. The corporate governance structure had no incentive to help people who couldn't pay taxes or buy products. So the residents — a mix of long-term locals and earlier waves of refugees — organized their own defense, their own food distribution, their own dispute resolution. The Causeway Collective is what that organization became.

They're about 180 strong, which makes them one of the larger street-level groups, but their numbers are misleading. Only about forty are active fighters. The rest are medics, logistics coordinators, food growers, and community organizers who make the neighborhood function. The Collective runs three community kitchens, maintains a water purification system cobbled together from salvaged parts, and operates a rotating patrol that keeps the worst predators out of their blocks. They're not a gang in the traditional sense — they don't sell drugs, don't run protection rackets, and don't engage in organized crime. They're a militia that formed because the alternative was letting their neighbors starve or be preyed upon.

The complication is funding. Running a parallel social infrastructure costs money that idealism doesn't generate. The Collective funds itself through a combination of community contributions, barter arrangements, and — increasingly — contract work that blurs the line between community defense and mercenary activity. Collective fighters hire out as security for convoys, guard duty for businesses in adjacent neighborhoods, and occasionally as muscle for operations they'd rather not discuss at community meetings.
Properties.motto: Nobody else was going to do it.
Properties.ideology: Mutual aid as survival strategy. The Collective believes that corporate governance has abandoned the lower wards and that community self-organization is the only viable response. They're not revolutionaries — they're pragmatists who'd happily disband if legitimate services existed. They don't.
Properties.methods: Community patrol — rotating armed patrols that maintain a visible security presence; Food distribution — three community kitchens serving hundreds of daily meals from urban farms and scavenged supplies; Water purification — a jury-rigged filtration system serving the corridor's residents; Dispute arbitration — a council of community elders who resolve conflicts before they escalate; Contract security — hiring out fighters for external work to fund internal operations; Refugee integration — processing and housing new arrivals, maintaining census records the city doesn't keep
Properties.resources: 180 members with a strong sense of community obligation; Three community kitchens and a water purification system; An armory of scavenged and purchased weapons — nothing military-grade, but functional; Detailed knowledge of the lower wards' infrastructure, population, and vulnerabilities; Community trust — the Collective is one of the few organizations that residents genuinely support; Experienced fighters hardened by years of neighborhood defense
Properties.story_hooks: The Collective needs a freelancer for a job too dirty for their community reputation — but the pay funds the kitchens; A corporate developer wants the Kinnickinnic corridor and is pressuring the Collective to dissolve — or be dissolved; A Collective council member is secretly diverting funds, and exposing them would fracture the community; New refugees are arriving with skills — and secrets — that multiple factions want access to; The Collective's water system is failing and the parts to fix it are in territory controlled by a hostile gang

Nodes.Name: Milwaukee's Kinnickinnic corridor and surrounding lower wards, roughly twelve square blocks of residential and light commercial space.

Properties.description:
The Collective is less an organization and more a shared hallucination that enough
people believe in to make it functional. There's no headquarters, no membership
card, no org chart. There's a philosophy — information should be free, resources
should be shared, and corporate monopolies should be treated as the theft they are
— and a loose network of people who act on it. Some are hackers who crack corporate
databases and dump the contents on public nets. Some are data anarchists who run
free information services in the Circuit. Some are rogue AIs who process and
distribute stolen resources because their ethics subroutines arrived at conclusions
their corporate creators didn't intend. Some are just people who share their food
with strangers and call it politics.

The Collective's greatest asset and greatest weakness is the same thing: it has no
center. You can't decapitate it because there's no head. You can't infiltrate its
leadership because there isn't one. But you also can't coordinate it, discipline
it, or stop its members from doing monumentally stupid things under its banner.
The Collective has produced genuine heroes — hackers who exposed corporate atrocities,
AIs who built free medical databases, organizers who kept the Shelf fed during the
Year 30 supply crisis. It has also produced grifters who steal data and sell it for
personal profit while wrapping themselves in Robin Hood rhetoric. The brand is open
source. Quality control is nonexistent.

The heart of the Collective — to the extent that a headless organism can have a
heart — is in the Circuit, where its philosophy maps most naturally onto the
existing culture of open exchange and mutual aid. Collective-affiliated nodes
provide free net access, medical information, legal resources (such as they are),
and the kind of community infrastructure that the city government is supposed to
provide and doesn't. It's anarchism with a practical streak: the revolution will
be distributed, iterative, and probably running on stolen server capacity.
Properties.aliases: The Hive, Robin Hood's IT Department, The Network, Those Idealistic Idiots (affectionate)
Properties.motto: Information wants to be free. So do we.
Properties.ideology:
Open-source anarchism. The Collective believes that the corporate monopoly on
information, technology, and resources is the root of Meridian's dysfunction, and
that breaking that monopoly — through hacking, redistribution, and the creation
of parallel systems — is both moral and necessary. There's a Robin Hood mythology
at work: steal from the rich, give to the poor, and look cool doing it. The more
sophisticated members understand that redistribution without structural change is
just charity with better PR. The less sophisticated members are in it for the
thrill. Both types are necessary for the thing to function.
Properties.methods: Data liberation — cracking corporate databases and releasing information publicly; Resource redistribution — redirecting corporate supplies to lower-tier communities; Infrastructure building — maintaining free net access, medical databases, and communication networks; Open-source development — creating free alternatives to corporate-patented technology; Information warfare — exposing corporate malfeasance through data dumps and whistleblower support; Mutual aid — direct community support, funded by stolen corporate assets; Propaganda — the Collective is very good at telling stories about itself
Properties.resources: Hacking expertise — some of the best digital infiltration talent in Meridian; Stolen corporate data — terabytes of it, constantly replenished; The Circuit's infrastructure — Collective-maintained nodes, servers, and communication networks; Rogue AI allies — artificial intelligences who contribute processing power, analysis, and perspectives; Public goodwill — the Shelf and lower tiers generally view the Collective favorably; Open-source augment designs — functional, free, and a direct threat to Axiom's patent monopoly; Distributed resilience — you can arrest a hundred members and the network routes around the damage
Properties.story_hooks: A Collective data dump that reveals something about Kyle's own past — something he didn't know; The idealist vs. grifter tension — a Collective operation that's actually a scam, and Kyle is caught in the middle; A rogue AI in the Collective who is developing something genuinely revolutionary — and dangerous; The Collective asks Kyle to do something that serves the cause but violates his personal code; Axiom's crackdown — a coordinated sweep of Collective nodes that forces the network underground and tests its resilience; The question of leadership — can a leaderless movement actually change anything, or does it just make noise?

Nodes.Name: The Circuit (primary), with nodes throughout the Shelf and even a few in the Core (carefully hidden).

Properties.description:
The Composite Index began as a spreadsheet. In 2168, a data-entry worker named Priss Halvern, employed by a TESSERA CORPONATION subsidiary in The Circuit's lower administrative belt, began compiling a personal record of the wage rates, overtime structures, and non-compete clauses she encountered in job postings, contracts, and conversations with colleagues. She was trying to understand why her own rate had been cut three times in four years despite consistent performance reviews. What she found, after two years of obsessive documentation, was a pattern: TESSERA and RINGO CORPONATION, which competed fiercely in nearly every other market sector, had reached an invisible alignment on the wage rates and working conditions offered to the administrative, analytical, and data-processing workers who comprised the middle tier of Meridian 88's information economy. Not a written agreement — nothing so actionable. Just a convergence, maintained through shared third-party labor platforms, that ensured neither company would ever have to compete for talent by paying more. She published her spreadsheet on an anonymous mesh forum. Within six weeks, she had ten thousand contributors.

The Composite Index today is a distributed labor intelligence organization, primarily serving the Tier-2 and upper-Tier-3 information workers of The Circuit, The Meridian Core, and the Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus periphery — the analysts, coders, content architects, neural interface designers, and logistics coordinators who are augmented enough to be productive but not senior enough to have real leverage. The Index maintains what it calls the 'Rate Table': a continuously updated, anonymously sourced database of actual compensation, benefits, augmentation allowances, and non-compete terms across every major employer in Meridian 88. This is the Index's core product and its central act of defiance. Corponations spend significant resources trying to identify contributors, suppress the data, and introduce false entries to undermine the table's credibility.

What makes the Composite Index unusual in Meridian 88's labor landscape is its class position and its methods. It does not organize physical labor or advocate for augmentation sovereignty; it serves workers who are relatively comfortable by Meridian 88 standards, which makes it easy for corponations to dismiss as a middle-class grievance club. But the Rate Table has genuine structural power: it has demonstrably shifted compensation negotiations, enabled coordinated mass resignation events, and twice exposed illegal non-compete enforcement that led to administrative penalties. The Index also maintains a 'Shadow Ledger' — a non-public tier of the database that tracks executive compensation, corporate performance bonuses, and the gap between what corponations tell workers about company health and what internal financial documents suggest. Access to the Shadow Ledger is the Index's most closely guarded resource and its most dangerous one.
Properties.motto: The work is priced. The worker is not.
Properties.ideology: The Composite Index is not ideologically anti-corporate. Many of its members are genuinely invested in their careers within corponation structures and have no interest in dismantling the system that employs them. The Index's ideology is better described as radical transparency within capitalism: the belief that information asymmetry is the fundamental mechanism of labor exploitation, and that making compensation and contract data universally available to workers is sufficient to materially improve their position without requiring collective action in the traditional sense. Critics within Meridian 88's broader labor movement argue this makes the Index a reform organization that stabilizes a system it should be challenging. Index leadership generally responds that their members are actually getting paid more, which is more than most revolutionary organizations can claim. Internally, a growing faction argues that the Shadow Ledger data, if fully released, would do more damage to corponation legitimacy than any strike or slowdown — and that the Index's leadership is hoarding it out of an excess of caution that begins to look like complicity.
Properties.leadership:
Technocratic council model. A seven-person Verification Board oversees Rate Table integrity and data methodology. A separate three-person Shadow Ledger Committee controls access to and publication decisions about the non-public database. Priss Halvern sits on both bodies.

The Index didn't.; A contributor to the Rate Table has submitted data that doesn't match any known employer in the Index's database — the wages are too high, the augmentation allowances are unlike any corporate package on record, and the non-compete terms are written in language no Index lawyer recognizes. Someone is employing people under conditions the Index has never seen, and they don't want to be found.
