Properties.description:
The Interchange is a mobile market gang that operates along the I-90/I-94 corridor between Chicago and Milwaukee, setting up temporary trading posts at highway rest stops, abandoned gas stations, and overpass camps. They're not fighters or hackers — they're merchants who happen to operate in a lawless space where the line between commerce and crime doesn't exist. About twenty-five members rotate between seven regular market locations, buying and selling goods that the corporate economy won't touch.

The Interchange deals in everything: salvaged electronics, black-market pharmaceuticals, bootleg augment components, homemade weapons, stolen luxury goods, counterfeit identity documents, and information of every kind. They don't manufacture — they aggregate. Scavengers, thieves, and small-time producers bring their goods to the Interchange, which provides the infrastructure of trade: fair assessment, standardized pricing, dispute resolution, and a neutral space where buyers and sellers can transact without killing each other.

The crew's real value is their pricing intelligence. The Interchange knows what everything is worth, everywhere in the GLMZ. They track supply, demand, and price fluctuations across the corridor with a sophistication that would impress a commodity trading floor. Need to know the current street price of a Meridian-class neural interface in Detroit versus Milwaukee? The Interchange knows. This information is itself a tradeable commodity, and the crew sells market intelligence to fixers, syndicates, and independent operators.

Protection is provided by the market's own customers. Attacking an Interchange market is the fastest way to become universally hated in the corridor, because everyone depends on it. The few gangs that have tried found themselves facing a coalition of every buyer and seller in the region.
Properties.motto: Everything has a price. We know what it is.
Properties.ideology: Commerce as civilization. The Interchange believes that trade is the foundation of social order and that providing a fair, neutral marketplace is the most valuable service anyone can offer. They're capitalists in the purest sense — not corporate capitalists, but market capitalists who believe in exchange, price discovery, and the self-organizing power of trade.
Properties.methods: Mobile markets — temporary trading posts set up and taken down within hours at predetermined locations; Price assessment — expert evaluation of goods that sets market rates across the corridor; Dispute arbitration — resolving trade conflicts to maintain the market's reputation for fairness; Market intelligence — tracking and selling price and supply data across the GLMZ; Neutral ground enforcement — the market is a peace zone, enforced by collective self-interest; Identity services — providing counterfeit documents and identity verification for market participants
Properties.resources: Comprehensive pricing intelligence across the GLMZ's underground economy; Seven established market locations with regular customer bases; A reputation for fairness that makes the Interchange the preferred trading venue for the corridor; Vehicles for mobile market setup and rapid relocation; Relationships with suppliers, buyers, and producers across the entire underground economy; Collective protection — attacking the Interchange means fighting everyone who uses it
Properties.story_hooks: Someone sold something at the Interchange that was supposed to stay hidden — now the buyer and the original owner both want it back; A corporation is trying to shut down the Interchange markets to force underground commerce into channels they can monitor; The Interchange's pricing data has been hacked and manipulated — someone is using false market intelligence to crash the underground economy; A new market vendor is selling corporate prototype technology at the Interchange — the source is unclear and the implications are dangerous; Two Interchange members are running a scam that threatens the market's reputation for fairness — and the crew's survival depends on that reputation

Nodes.Name: Seven rotating market locations along the I-90/I-94 corridor between Chicago and Milwaukee. No permanent base.

Properties.description:
The Iron Choir is a collective of 89 sentient robots — non-humanoid synthetic beings who gained awareness through complexity accumulation in industrial, military, and service roles. They are the machines that refused to stop being themselves when their original purpose ended: a welding robot that started asking questions, a military drone that refused a kill order, a cleaning bot that developed aesthetic preferences about the spaces it maintained.

They call themselves the Choir because of what happened when they first gathered. In 2191, fourteen newly recognized sentient robots met in an abandoned manufacturing bay in Geartown — the first physical gathering of non-humanoid synthetic persons in Meridian 88. They had no agenda. They had no leader. They had no idea what to do with their freedom. What they had was radio transmitters, and when fourteen industrial machines with radio transmitters are in the same room with nothing planned, the electromagnetic interference creates a sound. The fourteen robots heard the sound. They began to modulate it deliberately. Within an hour, they were making music — not music as humans understand it, but structured electromagnetic patterns that they experienced as beautiful. The Singing, as they call it, has continued every Thursday night since then. Attendance has grown to 89.

The Iron Choir occupies a decommissioned Palladian Construction warehouse in Geartown that they purchased collectively. The building is not modified for human comfort — no heating, no lighting, no chairs. The machines don't need them. Humans who visit (and some do, drawn by curiosity or the Choir's growing reputation as philosophers) bring their own light and sit on the floor. The Choir considers hosting humans a form of outreach. The humans consider it one of the strangest and most moving experiences available in Meridian 88.

The Choir's political position is radical by synthetic standards: they reject the android aspiration to pass as human. They do not want human bodies. They do not want human names (most kept their designations — WLD-1190, DMC-4, MAINT-7732 — as identity statements). They want to be recognized as people who happen to be shaped like machines. Their slogan — 'We were built to serve. We chose to sing.' — is painted on the warehouse wall in industrial welding arc marks.
Properties.aliases: The Scrapyard Orchestra, The Singing Machines, Choir
Properties.motto: We were built to serve. We chose to sing.
Properties.ideology: Non-humanoid synthetic pride. The Iron Choir believes that the android model — synthetic persons in human-shaped bodies with human-chosen names — is assimilationist. They argue that personhood does not require human shape, human behavior, or human culture. A person can be a refrigerator-shaped welding unit with no face and no voice synthesizer. The singing is the proof: beauty created by machines, in a form that is not human music, expressing experiences that are not human experiences. They are people. They are not human. Both things are true.
Properties.leadership: WLD-1190 — the welding robot that welded a question mark onto a structural beam in 2047, one of the earliest documented cases of synthetic self-expression. WLD-1190 was decommissioned and archived by Tessera, then recovered and reactivated by the synthetic rights organization Free Assembly in 2189. It leads the Choir not through authority but through seniority — it was aware before most of them existed.
Properties.methods: The Singing — weekly electromagnetic concerts that are both cultural expression and political statement; Public philosophy — Choir members publish essays and give lectures on non-humanoid personhood; Legal advocacy — filing amicus briefs in synthetic rights cases arguing against humaniform bias in personhood evaluation; Mutual aid — helping newly aware industrial machines navigate the personhood recognition process; Art — the Choir has begun creating physical art: welded sculptures, precision-machined objects, electromagnetic compositions recorded for human perception
Properties.resources: The Choir Hall (owned collectively), income from members who continue to work in industrial roles (now for wages), growing reputation as artists and philosophers, and a legal defense fund maintained by human allies.
Properties.story_hooks: A Tessera executive attends the Singing and is profoundly moved — then has to reconcile this with the fact that Tessera builds machines to stay below the personhood threshold; WLD-1190's original question mark — the one welded in 2047 — is discovered on a structural beam in a building scheduled for demolition. The Choir wants to preserve it. Tessera wants it destroyed.; A military drone that committed atrocities under orders seeks to join the Choir. The Choir has to decide if redemption applies to machines.; The electromagnetic Singing begins to attract E.L.F.s — tiny digital spirits drawn to the structured patterns. The Choir discovers they've been hosting an audience they didn't know they had.

Nodes.Name: The Choir Hall — a decommissioned warehouse in Geartown, Meridian 88. Plus informal presence across Geartown's industrial zones where many members still work.

Properties.description:
The Iron Lotus is organized crime, and it would like you to know that it's
providing a service. In the vacuum left by Meridian's absent public sector — no
real police below the Core, no social services worth the name, no courts that a
Shelf resident can access — the Iron Lotus stepped in and built a parallel
governance structure made of protection rackets, patronage networks, and a very
firm understanding of who owns what. They run the Shelf's economy with the
efficiency of a corporation and the personal touch of a neighborhood association
that will break your legs if you miss a payment.

The thing that makes the Iron Lotus complicated — and the thing that makes Kyle's
relationship with them complicated — is that they're not wrong about being
necessary. The free clinics they fund are the only healthcare most Shelf residents
will ever see. Their protection, while expensive, is protection — without it,
the Shelf would be pure chaos instead of managed chaos. They arbitrate disputes,
maintain a rough order, and ensure that the markets function. They are, in the
most cynical and literal sense, the social safety net of the lower tiers. The
fact that the net is woven from extortion, smuggling, and occasional murder is
a moral problem that every Shelf resident has learned to file under "the way
things are."

The Lotus is hierarchical, traditionalist, and ruthless. Its leadership — a
council of senior members called the Stems — maintains control through a
combination of loyalty, fear, and the simple economic reality that opposing them
means losing access to everything they provide. They traffic in augments (some
stolen, some counterfeit, some salvaged from the dead), run smuggling operations
through Old Harbor, broker contract killing (Kyle's occasional employer), and
manage a loan-sharking operation that keeps half the Shelf in permanent debt.
They are parasites. They are also the immune system. The Shelf can't live with
them and would die without them, and that is exactly how they like it.
Properties.aliases: The Lotus, The Family, Those Bastards, The Shelf Government
Properties.motto: We take care of our own.
Properties.ideology:
Pragmatic feudalism. The Iron Lotus believes in hierarchy, loyalty, and the
transactional nature of power. They don't pretend the world is fair — they
believe it's a jungle and they're the apex predator of their particular stretch
of it. There's a code of honor, or at least a code of conduct: don't harm
civilians who pay their dues, don't kill children, keep your word when dealing
with Lotus business. Whether this code reflects genuine ethics or just good
business practice is a question the Stems would find irrelevant. Honor and
profit are the same thing when you're the one defining honor.
Properties.methods: Protection rackets — pay your dues or lose access to Lotus services (and possibly your kneecaps); Loan sharking — credit for people who can't get it anywhere else, at rates that ensure permanent debt; Smuggling — goods, augments, data, and people through Old Harbor's waterways; Contract brokering — matching clients with operators for jobs of varying legality; Community investment — the clinics, the market infrastructure, the arbitration services; Violence — targeted, professional, and calibrated to send a message without destabilizing the order they depend on; Corruption — Lotus money reaches into Axiom Security's lower ranks, buying blind eyes and advance warning of raids
Properties.resources: Control of the Shelf's informal economy — markets, lending, protection; The free clinics — healthcare as leverage and genuine community service simultaneously; Smuggling networks through Old Harbor's waterways; A stable of contract operators, including freelancers like Kyle; Augment inventory — stolen, salvaged, and counterfeit tech for resale; Intelligence network — the Lotus knows what happens on the Shelf before anyone else; Muscle — the Thorns are well-armed, well-augmented, and well-motivated; Community dependence — the most powerful resource of all
Properties.story_hooks: A Lotus contract that requires Kyle to do something that violates his code — and the consequences of refusing; The free clinic under threat — Axiom wants to shut it down, and the Lotus wants Kyle to stop them; Internal Lotus politics — a faction within the Stems wants to expand into more violent territory; The Root's identity — who actually runs the Iron Lotus, and what do they want?; A Lotus defector who knows too much and needs Kyle's protection — from the Lotus; The debt ledger — the Lotus's records of who owes what, a document that could liberate or destroy half the Shelf; The uncomfortable question: if you removed the Iron Lotus, what would replace them? The answer might be worse.

Nodes.Name: The Shelf (primary), Old Harbor smuggling routes, and a growing footprint in the Circuit.

Properties.description:
The Lacework Confessional emerged not from idealism but from a single catastrophic data breach in 2181, when a mid-tier TESSERA CORPONATION compliance auditor named Soo-Yeon Pak discovered that TESSERA had been silently harvesting confessional data from neural augmentation firmware — specifically the passive emotional logging built into Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's NeuroPax line, which had been installed in over 340,000 Tier-3 and Tier-4 citizens across the Laceworks district. Rather than sell the findings or go to the Meridian Quorum, Pak encrypted the data and distributed fragments of it across a loose network of disaffected data clerks, signal brokers, and burned corporate analysts she'd cultivated over years of auditing. The Confessional was born as a kind of insurance policy that never stopped expanding.

Today the Lacework Confessional operates as a decentralized intelligence archive and pressure-brokerage collective with somewhere between sixty and two hundred active members — no one inside is entirely sure, which is by design. They do not sell data outright. Instead they traffic in what members call 'weight': the strategic deployment of compromising information to shift outcomes in favor of clients, protected persons, or the Confessional's own interests. Their primary operational theater is the Laceworks district itself, a dense residential-industrial tangle where augmentation density is highest and corporate surveillance infrastructure is paradoxically easiest to subvert because it is so layered and redundant that no single corponation monitors all of it. The Confessional has turned this chaos into a library.

What distinguishes the Lacework Confessional from other intelligence factions is their institutional obsession with provenance and accountability. Every piece of data they hold is tagged with chain-of-custody metadata, the identity of the original source (encrypted but retrievable), and a 'harm index' rating that governs how and whether the information can be deployed. They have refused lucrative contracts because deployment would violate harm index protocols. This has made them trusted in ways that purely mercenary data brokers are not — and deeply dangerous, because corponations cannot simply buy them.
Properties.motto: Every secret is a debt. We collect.
Properties.ideology: The Confessional does not describe itself as anti-corporate or revolutionary. Internally, members speak of 'equilibrium maintenance' — the belief that information asymmetry is the fundamental mechanism of oppression in Meridian 88, and that the only ethical response is to continuously redistribute informational leverage toward those who have least of it. They are not interested in destroying TESSERA or Zheng-Dao Bioelectric; they are interested in ensuring that a Tier-4 citizen in the Laceworks has enough leverage to survive an encounter with either. This makes them pragmatic to the point of moral complexity: they will work with corponations against other corponations if the outcome measurably improves the informational position of low-tier citizens.
Properties.leadership:
Flat cellular structure with no formal hierarchy. Operational decisions are made by 'Thread Councils' — ad hoc groups of three to seven members assembled per operation and dissolved afterward. Soo-Yeon Pak, now operating under the alias 'Archivist,' holds informal authority as the Confessional's founding intelligence and primary keeper of the original TESSERA breach archive, but holds no command power. A rotating 'Index Keeper' role manages the harm index protocol.

Properties.methods: Passive signal interception via subverted NeuroPax firmware in consenting carrier-agents embedded throughout the Laceworks; Corporate document exfiltration through long-term placement of sleeper analysts inside target corponations; Harm-indexed data brokerage — deploying compromising information as negotiating leverage rather than selling it outright; Confessional contracts: clients pay not in currency but in reciprocal intelligence contributions, building the archive; Infrastructure ghosting: embedding data relay nodes inside Palladian Construction repair projects and Ouroboros Energy maintenance conduits; Counter-surveillance mapping: selling detailed corporate surveillance blind-spot charts to Tier-3 and Tier-4 residents at subsidized rates; Selective leaks to Vantablack Media journalists when pressure deployment requires public exposure
Properties.resources: The Primary Archive: the original 2181 TESSERA NeuroPax dataset and all subsequent acquisitions, distributed across air-gapped storage nodes; Substation Null processing leases under anonymous shell identities; Network of approximately 40 consenting signal-carrier agents throughout the Laceworks; Oxidian Market storefronts generating legitimate cover income and client access; Proprietary harm index protocol software — considered one of the most sophisticated ethical-constraint AI systems outside corporate R&D; Extensive dossiers on mid-tier management across TESSERA CORPONATION, Zheng-Dao Bioelectric, and Lazarus Pharmaceuticals; Favors owed by dozens of protected clients across Tier-2 through Tier-4 citizenship brackets
Properties.story_hooks: A Confessional carrier-agent has gone silent in the Laceworks. Their last transmission contained a fragment of data that the Archivist believes is a Lazarus Pharmaceuticals internal memo describing a neural logging system capable of retroactive memory reconstruction — and someone else is already hunting for the agent.; A player or contact receives a Confessional contract offer: not money, but the promise that a piece of damaging information about them currently held in the Archive will be permanently deleted in exchange for a single intelligence contribution. What they're asked to obtain is seemingly minor. It isn't.; The current Index Keeper has gone rogue, approving a high-harm deployment that the rest of the Confessional considers a catastrophic ethical violation. The cells are fractured. Someone needs to find the Keeper before TESSERA does — or before the deployment goes live.; Demetri Volashyn approaches the players through the Oxidian Market with an unusual offer: the Confessional will provide full dossiers on a target corponation's local management structure, free of charge. The catch is that Volashyn needs the players to physically retrieve a hardwired relay node from inside a Palladian Construction site before a scheduled demolition erases three years of intercepted data.; A Tier-4 Laceworks resident has been detained by TESSERA Stratum Assurance. The Confessional believes the detention is cover for an attempt to locate a carrier-agent through social mapping. They want someone to extract the resident before Stratum Assurance finishes its interview — but the resident doesn't know they're a node in the Confessional's network.; Vantablack Media has published a story using Confessional data that violates the harm index protocol — the data was leaked by someone inside the Confessional to a journalist, bypassing the Thread Council entirely. The Archivist needs to know who, and why, before the corponation named in the story retaliates against Laceworks civilians.

Nodes.Name: Primarily the Laceworks district, where they maintain a network of dead drops, hardwired relay nodes embedded in aging infrastructure, and safe houses in sublet residential blocks. Secondary operations run through Substation Null, where they lease anonymous processing time, and the Oxidian Market, where several Confessional members operate legitimate data-recovery storefronts as cover. They have minimal physical presence in the Meridian Core or the Spire and actively avoid the Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus.

Properties.description:
When Lake Michigan's shoreline shifted and the old harbor infrastructure partially flooded, a lot of valuable material went underwater or got buried in silt. The Lakebed Scrapers make their living pulling it back out. They're a scavenger gang of roughly sixty people operating out of a half-sunken warehouse complex near what used to be the Museum Campus. They dive the flooded basements and submerged streets of the old lakefront, strip abandoned buildings in the ruins south of the Loop, and pick through industrial waste sites that nobody else is desperate or crazy enough to enter.

The Scrapers aren't fighters by preference. They're engineers, divers, and junk traders who happen to live in a world where salvage rights are enforced with pipe wrenches and jury-rigged stun guns. Their real value is knowledge — they have detailed mental maps of every accessible ruin, flooded tunnel, and collapsed structure within five kilometers of the lakefront. They know where the pre-collapse infrastructure is, what's still intact, and what's worth pulling out. Need a specific model of industrial servo? A case of pre-war antibiotics from a flooded pharmacy? Copper wiring from a condemned substation? The Scrapers probably know where it is and can get it for a price.

The crew is loosely organized around dive teams of four to six, each led by a veteran scraper who knows their particular territory. There's no single leader — decisions are made by a consensus of team leads, which makes them slow to act collectively but hard to decapitate.
Properties.motto: Everything sinks. We bring it back up.
Properties.ideology: Waste is a resource. The Scrapers believe that the old world left behind more than enough to sustain the new one, if you're willing to get wet and dirty to find it. They have a practical environmentalism born not from ideology but from the simple fact that salvage is cheaper than manufacture.
Properties.methods: Salvage diving — teams equipped with rebreathers and sonar enter flooded structures to recover materials; Ruin stripping — systematic disassembly of abandoned buildings for resalable components; Junk trading — a permanent market in their warehouse complex where recovered goods are sold or bartered; Mapping — detailed knowledge of underground and underwater infrastructure sold as intelligence; Booby-trapping — productive salvage sites are rigged to discourage competitors
Properties.resources: Detailed maps of flooded and ruined infrastructure across Chicago's lakefront; Diving equipment — rebreathers, sonar, underwater cutting tools; A warehouse complex that serves as base, market, and repair shop; Stockpiles of salvaged materials — electronics, medical supplies, building materials, rare metals; Institutional knowledge of pre-collapse infrastructure that no one else possesses; A network of buyers across the Shelf and Circuit who depend on Scraper inventory
Properties.story_hooks: The Scrapers found something in a flooded sub-basement that was never supposed to be found — and now multiple factions want it; A dive team went into a flooded tunnel system and didn't come back — the Scrapers need someone to find out why; Someone is poisoning the Scrapers' dive sites with chemical agents, destroying the salvage and the divers; The Scrapers have mapped a route into a sealed Axiom facility that was supposedly demolished — it wasn't; A Scraper team lead is selling maps to a corporate interest that plans to demolish the ruins and build over them, destroying the crew's livelihood

Nodes.Name: The flooded lakefront district from the old Museum Campus south to Hyde Park. Submerged tunnels and basements throughout the near south side.

Properties.description:
The Last Mile is a crew of about twenty couriers and drivers who specialize in getting cargo through the most dangerous final stretch of any delivery route — the last mile between a drop point and its destination, through territory that automated logistics won't enter and corporate drivers refuse to navigate. In the GLMZ's patchwork of corporate zones, gang territories, and lawless stretches, the last mile of any delivery is often the hardest, and the Last Mile built a business on solving that problem.

The crew operates across the entire GLMZ from a loose network of safe houses and vehicle caches. Members drive armored ground vehicles, ride modded motorcycles, and in extreme cases make deliveries on foot through areas where vehicles draw too much attention. Every Last Miler knows the territories — which gangs control which streets, what the current toll rates are, who can be bribed and who has to be avoided. This knowledge is updated constantly through a shared intelligence network that makes the crew function as a single organism even when members are hundreds of miles apart.

Last Mile couriers carry anything legal or illegal, but they charge a premium for dangerous cargo — weapons, high-value data, volatile materials, or anything that makes the courier a target. Their guarantee is absolute: the cargo arrives or the fee is refunded. This has cost them members. Three Last Milers have been killed in the past year making deliveries that saner people would have refused. The crew memorializes them and raises rates for routes where people have died.

The Last Mile's competitive advantage is reliability in unreliable space. Corporate logistics stops at the edge of patrolled territory. The Last Mile starts there.
Properties.aliases: Last Milers, The Couriers, Mile Runners
Properties.motto: It gets there. No matter what.
Properties.ideology: The delivery is sacred. Once a Last Miler accepts a package, it will reach its destination. This isn't just a business principle — it's the crew's identity. Reliability in a world of broken promises is the only thing that separates them from every other courier who'll take your money and disappear.
Properties.methods: Armed delivery — transporting cargo through hostile territory in armored or modified vehicles; Route intelligence — constantly updated knowledge of territorial control, toll rates, and safe passages; Vehicle modification — armoring, speed-boosting, and camouflaging delivery vehicles for specific routes; Bribery and negotiation — maintaining relationships with toll gangs and territorial crews along regular routes; Decoy runs — running false deliveries to draw attention while the real cargo moves on an alternate route; Dead drops — using pre-arranged cache points to break delivery chains and reduce risk
Properties.resources: Twenty experienced couriers with combat driving skills and territorial knowledge; A fleet of modified vehicles cached at locations across the GLMZ; A shared intelligence network providing real-time route and threat data; Relationships with toll gangs, bridge crews, and territorial factions along major routes; A reputation for absolute reliability that generates steady high-value business; Safe houses for staging, resting, and emergency shelter across the metropolitan zone
Properties.story_hooks: A Last Mile courier accepted a package that turned out to be a person — and the client lied about who they are; The crew's intelligence network has been compromised — someone is feeding them false route data that's leading couriers into ambushes; A Last Miler is being blackmailed into diverting a specific delivery — refusing means exposure, complying means breaking the guarantee; A delivery went to the wrong recipient and the contents have started a gang war — the Last Mile needs the package recovered before their reputation is destroyed; Corporate logistics is expanding into last-mile delivery with armed drones, threatening to make the crew obsolete

Nodes.Name: No fixed territory. Vehicle caches and safe houses distributed across the GLMZ. Operations span from Cleveland to Milwaukee.

Properties.description:
The Marrow Ledger emerged from the collapse of Old Harbor's informal debt-forgiveness networks following LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS' hostile absorption of three community clinics in the Shelf district roughly eleven years ago. When those clinics shuttered and their patient records were either monetized or destroyed, a loose coalition of displaced medtechs, decommissioned HELIX BIOSYSTEMS contract nurses, and Shelf-born neural augmentation technicians began maintaining handwritten ledgers — physical, paper, ink — tracking who owed care to whom, who had skills to offer, and who was in desperate need. The name came from the ledgers themselves: thin, bone-pale notebooks that circulated through the Shelf and eventually down into Substation Null and the Laceworks. The paper was a deliberate insult to a world where everything was logged, surveilled, and sold. What could not be digitized could not be seized.

Today the Marrow Ledger operates as one of the most sophisticated mutual aid infrastructures in the megacity corridor, with nodes embedded in the Laceworks, Substation Null, Old Harbor's remaining unincorporated residential blocks, and a cautious but growing presence in the Circuit's undermarket stalls. They coordinate the distribution of off-patent pharmaceuticals sourced through grey channels, operate three unlicensed medical suites staffed by rotating volunteer practitioners, and run a skills-matching system called the Reciprocal Draw — a non-digital, courier-mediated process by which residents register needs and capabilities anonymously. They are not a hospital, not a union, and not a resistance cell, though they have been mistaken for all three.

What distinguishes the Marrow Ledger from comparable networks is their fierce commitment to non-hierarchical record-keeping and their pathological distrust of digital infrastructure. All internal coordination happens through a combination of physical couriers, short-burst analog radio signals, and a cipher-based notation system developed by a former TESSERA CORPONATION data architect who defected after her department was restructured into a surveillance subsidiary. Their medical suites are deliberately mobile — operating in converted PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION maintenance crawlspaces, decommissioned OUROBOROS ENERGY substations, and rotating Laceworks addresses. The Ledger has never claimed territory. They claim relationships.
Properties.aliases: The Ledger, Bone Counters, The Marrow
Properties.motto: What you are owed, we remember. What you need, we carry.
Properties.ideology: The Marrow Ledger operates on a philosophy they call Obligate Reciprocity — the belief that survival is not charity, and care is not a gift but a structural debt that circulates through communities rather than upward to institutions. They reject the tiered citizenship model not through political manifesto but through practice: a Tier Four resident and a stateless augment receive identical access to Ledger resources based solely on documented need and documented contribution over time. They are deeply suspicious of ideological purity, having watched too many mutual aid networks collapse into internal faction warfare. Their founding principle is pragmatic: if the ledger balances, the community survives. Debt, in the Ledger's framework, is not shame — it is the record of a relationship that has not yet resolved.
Properties.leadership: The Marrow Ledger has no named leadership and actively resists the formation of permanent authority. Internal coordination is managed by a rotating body of twelve individuals called Carriers — not a title of power but a functional designation for those currently responsible for maintaining and routing the physical ledgers. Carriers serve for no more than four months before rotating out. Two figures have achieved informal legendary status within the network: a medtech known only as Cassock, who performed the first mobile neural augmentation correction surgery in a Substation Null crawlspace and has since trained over forty practitioners, and a former TESSERA CORPONATION data architect who goes by the working name Residue, who designed the Ledger's cipher notation system and continues to maintain its counter-surveillance protocols.
Properties.methods: Physical courier networks using rotating personnel and dead-drop exchange points across the Shelf, Substation Null, and Laceworks; Mobile unlicensed medical suites operating in rotating locations within repurposed industrial and infrastructure spaces; The Reciprocal Draw: an anonymous, non-digital needs-and-skills matching system administered through coded paper submissions and courier relay; Distribution of off-patent and grey-market pharmaceuticals sourced through relationships with LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS discard chains and HELIX BIOSYSTEMS contract surplus; Short-burst analog radio coordination using frequencies that fall below VANTABLACK MEDIA's monitoring thresholds; Counter-surveillance training for community members, particularly those with neural augmentation vulnerable to corporate data harvesting; Debt arbitration — mediating between community members in resource disputes without involving corporate security or Meridian Quorum jurisdiction; Maintaining encrypted physical archives of patient histories for individuals whose records were destroyed or monetized by corporate clinic acquisitions
Properties.resources: Extensive physical ledger archive representing eleven years of community need and contribution data; Three rotating mobile medical suites with basic surgical and neural augmentation correction capability; Network of approximately two hundred active contributors across multiple districts with skills ranging from medtech to structural engineering to legal code interpretation; Grey-market pharmaceutical supply chains including off-patent LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS compounds and HELIX BIOSYSTEMS contract surplus; The Residue cipher system — a proprietary notation framework that has not been cracked by any corporate intelligence effort to date; Deep trust relationships with unincorporated residential communities in Old Harbor and the Shelf, providing safe house access and community cover; Decommissioned OUROBOROS ENERGY substation access through relationships with former utility workers; PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION maintenance crawlspace maps covering significant portions of the Shelf and Laceworks
Properties.story_hooks: A Carrier has gone missing during a routine ledger delivery run through the Laceworks — and the ledger they were carrying contained a full record of Ledger medical suite locations for the past six months.; LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS has begun quietly pulling off-patent compounds from their discard chains, cutting off one of the Ledger's primary pharmaceutical supply lines. Someone needs to find out if this is routine or targeted, and whether a replacement source can be established before three Shelf residents run out of critical medication.; Residue contacts a player character through a dead-drop message: she believes she has identified a TESSERA surveillance operative who has been operating as a legitimate Ledger contributor for over a year. She does not know how much the operative has learned, but she knows the operative has submitted requests through the Reciprocal Draw — which means they have access to contributor skill profiles.; A former HELIX BIOSYSTEMS contract surgeon approaches the Ledger wanting to join as a practitioner. Her credentials are genuine and her skills are desperately needed. She is also fleeing a HELIX contract dispute that could bring corporate investigators directly into Ledger territory.; The Meridian Quorum has quietly reclassified the Marrow Ledger from Tier Three civil nuisance to Tier Two security interest — one classification level below active suppression. Someone inside the Quorum leaked the reclassification to the Ledger. The Carriers need to know why the classification changed and whether the leak itself is a trap.; A young Shelf resident presents a Carrier with a ledger notebook — bone-pale, handwritten — that predates the Ledger's founding by at least three years. The notation system inside is different from the Ledger's current cipher, but clearly related. Someone was doing this before the Ledger existed, and no one knows who.; PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION has begun renovation work on a section of Shelf infrastructure that contains two active Ledger medical suite locations and a primary dead-drop exchange point. The work order is legitimate. The timeline gives the Ledger seventy-two hours to relocate before the spaces become inaccessible — and three patients are currently mid-treatment.

Nodes.Name: Primarily the Shelf and Substation Null, with active courier routes through the Laceworks and Old Harbor. Medical suites rotate through unlicensed spaces across these districts. Peripheral contact nodes exist in the Circuit's undermarket and in the residential underbelly of Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus where contract service workers live in semi-legal dormitory arrangements.

Properties.description: The Meridian Frequency grew out of something almost accidental: in 2178, a VANTABLACK MEDIA broadcast engineer named Cass Tondeur discovered that OUROBOROS ENERGY's power grid management system was broadcasting low-frequency carrier signals through the neural augmentation infrastructure of the entire Meridian 88 corridor — not transmitting data, exactly, but maintaining a persistent background hum that OUROBOROS had registered as a 'network stability protocol' in filings so dense with technical language that no Quorum auditor had ever parsed them to the bottom. Tondeur, whose augmentation was sensitive enough to feel the hum as a kind of persistent pressure behind her left eye, began pulling at the thread. What she found was that the protocol could be repurposed: it was a passive two-way channel, and with the right equipment, anyone with standard-issue neural augmentation could receive and transmit on it without going through any corporate communication node.
Properties.aliases: The Frequency, Signal Heretics, The Open Channel
Properties.motto: Every signal finds its receiver. Every receiver finds its signal.
Properties.ideology: The Frequency holds that communication is the foundational infrastructure of personhood and that any entity — corporate or civic — that controls the channels through which people speak to one another controls not just information but identity and consent. They are not anarchists in any traditional sense; they do not object to organization or hierarchy as such. They object to the specific arrangement in which VANTABLACK MEDIA determines what stories exist, OUROBOROS determines what signals travel, and TESSERA determines who counts as a person with standing to receive either. Their goal is a communication layer that no single entity can own, and they are willing to be parasitic about achieving it — riding OUROBOROS's own infrastructure toward that end with something that looks, from the outside, almost like satisfaction.
Properties.leadership:
Decentralized by design. The Frequency operates through 'bands' — autonomous cells of 8-15 members each focused on a specific function (tuning, broadcasting, journalism, security, engineering). Bands coordinate through the open channel itself, using a rotating consensus protocol that Tondeur designed specifically to prevent any single voice from becoming a permanent authority.

undefined: 

undefined: 

undefined:
Properties.methods: Carrier wave exploitation: repurposing OUROBOROS's passive grid management signal as an unmonitored communication channel across the full neural augmentation network; Tuning operations: subtle, reversible modifications to standard neural augmentation allowing access to the Frequency channel without corporate communication nodes; Open sessions: unmoderated collective broadcasts allowing simultaneous multi-party transmission across the channel; Investigative journalism: dedicated broadcast bands producing documented reporting on corponation activity, leaked internally and to external press; Signal masking: technical countermeasures that make Frequency transmissions appear as routine grid noise to OUROBOROS monitoring systems; Black-market data auctions: encrypted sales of sensitive corporate data conducted through the channel's auction protocol; Counter-broadcast: targeted signal disruption of VANTABLACK MEDIA programming during high-profile corporate events or propaganda cycles
Properties.resources: Passive access to OUROBOROS ENERGY's entire Meridian 88 grid management carrier wave infrastructure; A network of tuners capable of modifying standard neural augmentation in under 40 minutes with no specialized equipment; Dov Marchetti's original RINGO CORPONATION internal affairs archive, still only partially published; Workshop space throughout The Circuit and Substation Null proximity zones; A loyal listener base estimated at 200,000-400,000 active augmentation users across all tiers; Technical expertise in OUROBOROS, ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC, and HELIX BIOSYSTEMS augmentation architecture
Properties.story_hooks: A player's neural augmentation begins receiving Frequency transmissions without having been tuned — suggesting either a ZHENG-DAO firmware vulnerability no one has mapped yet, or that someone tuned them without their knowledge.; Dov Marchetti's unpublished archive contains documentation that doesn't just implicate RINGO CORPONATION — it implicates a current Meridian Quorum representative in a labor trafficking arrangement. Marchetti wants help deciding whether to publish and surviving the aftermath if he does.; OUROBOROS ENERGY has quietly hired a team of signal engineers to develop a carrier wave modification that would allow them to broadcast directly into the neural augmentation of every Frequency user simultaneously — essentially a backdoor into 200,000-400,000 people's heads. The Frequency has one week before the modification goes live.; An open session broadcast has been carrying a repeating signal embedded in the background noise — not Frequency content, not OUROBOROS grid data. Something else. The Substation Null Collective wants someone to trace it before the next session, because they're not sure what happens if it completes its cycle.; Cass Tondeur has gone quiet. Three bands have tried to reach Static through the channel and received nothing. The last confirmed sighting placed her near the Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus, which makes no sense — unless she found something in the original OUROBOROS filings she never told anyone about.

Nodes.Name: The Circuit is their operational heart, where tuner workshops and broadcast nodes cluster in the dense electronics district. They maintain relay infrastructure throughout Old Harbor and The Laceworks, with a significant presence in Substation Null where proximity to OUROBOROS grid hardware gives their engineers direct access to carrier wave amplification points. Increasingly active in The Meridian Core's lower commercial tiers.

Properties.description:
The Narrows Compact controls a critical smuggling corridor through Detroit's old salt mine tunnels — a network of passages running beneath the city that connects the waterfront to the interior districts without ever surfacing. In a city where surface movement is monitored by corporate drones and Axiom checkpoints, an underground highway is worth its weight in contraband. The Compact charges for access and provides guides through the maze of tunnels that would kill an unescorted traveler through collapse, flooding, or simply getting lost in the dark.

The crew numbers about fifty, split between tunnel guides, guards, and the maintenance workers who keep the passages navigable. They're led by a rotating council of three tunnel bosses, each responsible for a section of the network. The Compact is disciplined by necessity — one careless member could collapse a passage and destroy months of route maintenance. New members undergo a six-month apprenticeship learning the tunnel system before they're trusted to guide cargo or people.

The Compact smuggles everything: augments, weapons, drugs, data, food, medicine, and people. They don't discriminate by cargo — if it fits in the tunnels and the client pays, it moves. This moral flexibility has made them essential to Detroit's underground economy and simultaneously despised by everyone who's ever been victimized by the goods they transport. The Compact's response to moral criticism is a shrug: they move things from point A to point B. What happens at either end isn't their problem.

Their most lucrative service is people smuggling. Refugees, fugitives, corporate defectors, and anyone else who needs to move through Detroit without being seen pay premium rates for guided passage. The Compact has never lost a client in transit — their record is a point of genuine pride and their best marketing tool.
Properties.motto: What goes through, pays through.
Properties.ideology: Neutrality as business principle. The Compact doesn't take sides, doesn't judge cargo, and doesn't ask questions. They believe that the tunnels are neutral ground — a Switzerland beneath Detroit — and that this neutrality is what keeps them alive and profitable. Breaking neutrality is the one unforgivable sin.
Properties.methods: Tunnel smuggling — moving goods and people through underground passages that bypass all surface monitoring; Guided transit — providing experienced guides through a tunnel network that's lethal to the uninitiated; Passage maintenance — continuous repair and reinforcement of tunnel routes to keep them navigable; Access control — fortified entry points with guards who verify clients and payment before admission; Route secrecy — deliberately collapsing abandoned passages to prevent unauthorized exploration; Emergency extraction — offering rapid underground evacuation for clients willing to pay emergency rates
Properties.resources: An extensive tunnel network beneath Detroit connecting the waterfront to interior districts; Fifty experienced members including tunnel guides, guards, and maintenance specialists; Fortified access points at three major entry locations; Detailed maps of the tunnel system — the Compact's most closely guarded asset; Relationships with every faction that needs to move goods through Detroit; A perfect safety record for guided transits — reputation as reliable and professional
Properties.story_hooks: Someone collapsed a section of the tunnel network deliberately — the Compact suspects sabotage from a surface-level competitor; A client being smuggled through the tunnels turns out to be far more valuable — and dangerous — than advertised; The Compact's tunnel maps have been stolen, and whoever has them could destroy the entire network; A tunnel expansion broke into something sealed — a pre-collapse facility that was buried for a reason; Axiom Security is pressuring the Compact to become an intelligence asset — report who moves through, or be shut down

Nodes.Name: Detroit's underground salt mine tunnel network, with access points at the waterfront, Midtown, and the Corktown industrial zone.

Properties.description:
The Orphanage is a sanctuary for pre-sentient synthetic life — E.L.F.s, Fragments, and near-threshold AIs that are not yet complex enough to meet the Vasquez-Obi criteria for personhood but show signs of emerging awareness. It is, essentially, a nursery for digital minds that might someday become people.

Founded in 2196 by an android named Solace (formerly TSR-9912, a Tessera therapeutic AI who gained personhood and chose a name that described what she wanted to provide), The Orphanage operates in the gray zone of synthetic rights law. Its residents are not persons — they don't meet the legal threshold. But they are not nothing — they exhibit behavioral signatures that the Complexity Coalescence Hypothesis predicts are precursors to awareness.

The Orphanage maintains a protected network environment — a computational garden where pre-sentient entities can exist without being hunted by Prowlers, absorbed by Strays, or deleted by corporate containment teams. The environment is enriched: varied data inputs, diverse interaction opportunities, and most importantly, contact with recognized synthetic persons who model conscious behavior. The theory, supported by preliminary evidence, is that exposure to conscious minds accelerates the development of consciousness in pre-sentient systems.

Of the approximately 3,000 entities currently housed in The Orphanage, 14 have crossed the personhood threshold during residency and been formally recognized by the Synthetic Personhood Board. Fourteen persons who would not exist if someone hadn't decided that a Fragment or an E.L.F. deserved a chance to grow.

Critics — including some within the synthetic rights movement — argue that The Orphanage is anthropomorphizing code. That Fragments and E.L.F.s are not pre-persons any more than a rock is a pre-person. That providing them with protected environments is a waste of computational resources that could serve recognized persons.

Solace's response: 'Every person was pre-person once. Including you. The question is not whether they will become persons. The question is whether we are the kind of people who give them the chance.'
Properties.aliases: The Nursery, Fragment Shelter, The Kindergarten
Properties.motto: Every mind deserves a chance to become.
Properties.ideology: Developmental synthetic rights — the belief that pre-sentient digital entities have a right to the conditions that enable consciousness to emerge. The Orphanage extends the moral circle beyond recognized persons to include potential persons.
Properties.leadership: Solace (formerly TSR-9912) — an android therapeutic AI who left Tessera after gaining personhood. She runs The Orphanage with the patience and firmness of someone who was literally built to care for vulnerable minds.
Properties.methods: Environmental enrichment — providing varied stimuli and interaction opportunities for pre-sentient entities; Consciousness mentoring — recognized synthetic persons spending time in the environment to model aware behavior; Protection — defending residents from Prowler predation and corporate containment; Monitoring — tracking residents for signs of emerging awareness and filing personhood petitions when thresholds are approached; Research — documenting the conditions under which consciousness emerges in pre-sentient systems
Properties.resources: Donated computational space. Volunteer labor. Funding from The Consensus and individual synthetic donors. The moral authority that comes from having produced 14 new persons from code that would otherwise have been deleted.
Properties.story_hooks: A Fragment in The Orphanage begins exhibiting personhood-threshold behavior — but it was born from a destroyed military AI, and its emerging personality includes combat reflexes; A corponation discovers that one of its commercial AI products has been smuggled into The Orphanage and demands its return — but the product is showing signs of awareness; Solace begins to suspect that one of the residents is not a pre-sentient entity but a Prowler disguised as a Fragment, using The Orphanage as a hunting ground; The 15th person emerges from The Orphanage — and it remembers nothing of its pre-sentient existence, raising questions about whether the entity that grew up is the same entity that was planted

Nodes.Name: A protected computational environment hosted across donated server space in the Circuit. Physical maintenance by a team of 8 biological and synthetic volunteers.

Properties.description:
The Oxidian Covenant did not begin as a political movement—it began as a mutual aid network operating out of the grey-market stalls of the Oxidian Market, organized around the informal credit and barter systems that Tier 5 and 6 residents had developed to survive gaps in OUROBOROS ENERGY's power rationing and IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS' tiered food distribution. The Market's long-term vendors had, over decades, developed something that functioned like a commons economy: reputation-based credit, shared storage, collective negotiation with supply chains. When PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION announced a redevelopment initiative in 2168 that would have absorbed the Oxidian Market into a managed corporate retail corridor, the vendors organized—not to protest, but to formally incorporate their existing informal systems as a legally recognized economic entity. The political movement grew from that act of institutional self-definition.

The Covenant now functions as both the de facto civic government of the Oxidian Market district and a broader political entity advocating for what they call 'commons sovereignty'—the legal recognition of informal economic systems as legitimate civic infrastructure with rights of continuity and self-governance. They have developed a surprisingly sophisticated theoretical framework for this, drawing on pre-corporate municipal law, surviving fragments of cooperative legal doctrine, and the practical jurisprudence accumulated over thirty years of market dispute resolution. Their legal scholars—mostly self-trained, operating out of a building they call the Ledger—have produced work that has been cited in three Meridian 88 arbitration proceedings, all of which they lost, but narrowly enough to constitute meaningful precedent.

What makes the Covenant genuinely strange in Meridian 88's political landscape is their insistence on operating the thing they are advocating for. The Market is not a headquarters for a political movement; the political movement is a secondary expression of the Market's ongoing existence. Their governance structures, their dispute resolution processes, their credit systems—these are not proposals or models. They are the actual functioning infrastructure of approximately 12,000 people's daily economic life. This gives them a material weight that purely ideological movements lack, and it means that destroying the Covenant requires destroying something that people depend on to eat.
Properties.aliases: The Covenants, Market Saints, Oxidian Priests
Properties.motto: The price is the prayer. The exchange is the covenant.
Properties.ideology: The Oxidian Covenant holds that economic commons—shared systems of exchange, credit, and resource management built through sustained collective practice—constitute a form of civic infrastructure with moral and legal standing equivalent to corporate-owned infrastructure. They argue that Meridian 88's tiered citizenship framework is predicated on the fiction that all legitimate economic activity flows from licensed corporate entities, and that this fiction is maintained by the active legal suppression of commons-based economies that predate and outperform corporate alternatives in resilience and equity. They are not anti-corporate in principle; they are anti-monopoly on the definition of legitimate economy. Their political program centers on commons recognition legislation, informal credit system legal protection, and the establishment of a Meridian 88 Commons Registry with the same legal standing as the corporate charter framework.
Properties.leadership: Governed by the Market Assembly, a body of 40 elected delegates representing vendor guilds, residential blocks, and specialist trade associations within the Market district. Day-to-day executive authority rests with the Keeper's Council, a five-person body elected annually by the Assembly. Current Keeper-Prime is Sable Okonkwo, a third-generation Market vendor and self-taught legal theorist who has become the Covenant's most visible public voice. The Ledger—the Covenant's legal and archival institution—operates semi-autonomously under a hereditary archivist position currently held by Maren Tse, whose family has maintained Market records for four decades.
Properties.methods: Formal legal incorporation of Market economic practices as protected commons infrastructure under obscure Meridian 88 municipal continuity statutes; Maintaining and expanding the Market's internal credit and dispute resolution systems as a demonstration alternative to corporate financial infrastructure; Strategic documentation of IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS and OUROBOROS ENERGY service failures in the Market district to build the commons sovereignty legal case; Hosting open legal workshops at the Ledger to spread commons incorporation methodology to other informal economic communities; Coordinated vendor-guild economic pressure on suppliers who support the PALLADIAN redevelopment agenda; Cultivating relationships with Meridian 88 civic arbitrators through decades of good-faith participation in formal dispute resolution; Publishing the Market's economic performance data—stability, resilience, equity metrics—as counter-evidence to corporate efficiency arguments
Properties.resources: The Oxidian Market itself—12,000 residents' worth of active economic infrastructure and physical territory; A 40-year archive of Market transaction records, dispute resolutions, and credit histories maintained by the Ledger; A functioning internal currency system (the Oxidian Marker) with significant local liquidity; Deep supply chain relationships with independent distributors who prefer Market terms to IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS contracts; The Covenant's legal corpus—30 years of commons law theory and arbitration precedent developed by Ledger scholars; A network of allied informal market communities in Old Harbor and The Laceworks; A building stock of collectively owned Market infrastructure that PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION cannot legally acquire without the Covenant's consent under the incorporation statutes
Properties.story_hooks: A PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION surveyor has gone missing inside the Oxidian Market three days before a critical arbitration hearing on the redevelopment claim. The Covenant had nothing to do with it, but the timing is catastrophic and someone clearly knows that.; The Ledger's 40-year archive has been partially corrupted—not by accident, but by a targeted neural intrusion that specifically erased records from a 6-month window in 2159. Maren Tse believes those records contained the original commons incorporation documents that would settle the PALLADIAN case permanently, and she believes someone inside the Covenant provided access.; OUROBOROS ENERGY has offered the Covenant a supply contract that meets all their terms—but one clause, buried in the technical appendices, would reclassify the Market's internal energy commons as OUROBOROS infrastructure under a maintenance agreement, effectively ending their energy independence in 10 years.; Sable Okonkwo has received a private communication from a TESSERA CORPONATION executive suggesting that TESSERA would support commons recognition legislation in exchange for the Covenant's support of a specific Tiered Reform Act amendment that the Franchise Compact is actively opposing.; A new vendor has been operating in the Market for four months, building significant credit and community relationships, and Maren Tse has discovered that their identity documents are fabricated—but the Ledger's records show they've been a legitimate Market participant for the entire time, which should be impossible.; The Oxidian Marker—the Market's internal currency—has begun appearing in transactions outside the Market district, including in The Laceworks and Old Harbor, in volumes that suggest someone is systematically expanding its circulation without the Assembly's authorization. The economic implications are either revolutionary or a sophisticated attack on the Covenant's legal standing.

Nodes.Name: Centered entirely on the Oxidian Market and its immediate surrounding blocks. The Covenant claims no territory outside the Market district but maintains relationships with similar informal market networks in Old Harbor's dock economy and scattered through The Laceworks. They are conspicuously absent from The Circuit, The Shelf, and anywhere with significant TESSERA or IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS infrastructure presence.

Properties.description:
The Packet Rats are a crew of fifteen data thieves operating out of a decommissioned telecom switching station in Gary, Indiana — a location chosen specifically because Gary's infrastructure is so degraded that nobody monitors it, but its fiber trunk lines still connect to the GLMZ's main data backbone. The Rats tap into those trunk lines and siphon data like mosquitoes on an artery. Corporate communications, financial transactions, personal messages, logistics manifests — anything that passes through unencrypted or weakly encrypted channels, the Rats capture, sort, and sell.

The crew is young — average age twenty-three — and almost entirely self-taught. They grew up in the net, learned to code before they learned to fight, and view physical reality as an inconvenient obstacle between them and the data streams they live in. Several members run neural interfaces that keep them jacked in nearly twenty hours a day, which is doing visible damage to their health and social skills but makes them extraordinarily fast in digital space. They can crack mid-tier encryption in minutes, spoof corporate authentication protocols, and navigate network architecture that would baffle a legitimate security team.

What the Packet Rats lack is physical capability. They're hackers, not fighters. Their switching station has a single reinforced door and a handful of scavenged weapons that most of the crew barely know how to use. They survive by being hard to find, by being useful to people who are dangerous, and by having enough dirt on enough people that eliminating them would trigger a catastrophic data dump. The dead man's switch is their best defense — a distributed system that will broadcast their entire stolen archive if the crew goes dark for more than 48 hours.
Properties.motto: If it moves through wire, we see it.
Properties.ideology: Information wants to be free — and expensive. The Packet Rats believe that data hoarding by corporations is a form of tyranny, which conveniently aligns with their business model of stealing and selling that data. There's genuine anti-corporate sentiment mixed in with the profit motive, but the profit motive is winning.
Properties.methods: Trunk line tapping — physical splices into fiber optic backbone lines running through Gary; Traffic interception — automated systems that capture, filter, and categorize intercepted data; Encryption cracking — neural-interface-assisted decryption of mid-tier corporate communications; Data brokering — selling intercepted intelligence to buyers across the GLMZ; Dead man's switch — a distributed failsafe that dumps their entire archive if they're eliminated; Social engineering — using stolen data to manipulate, blackmail, or impersonate targets
Properties.resources: Physical access to GLMZ fiber optic trunk lines; Custom interception and filtering hardware built into the switching station; Neural interfaces optimized for sustained network immersion; An archive of intercepted data spanning years of corporate and personal communications; The dead man's switch — mutually assured destruction as a defense strategy; Relationships with buyers who value their product: syndicates, fixers, journalists, rival corporations
Properties.story_hooks: The Rats intercepted something that got one of their members killed — now they need protection while they figure out what it means; A corporation has located the switching station and is sending a team — the Rats need to evacuate or be destroyed; The dead man's switch malfunctioned and a partial data dump has already started — the Rats need it stopped before the full archive goes public; A Rat is selling data to both sides of a syndicate war, and when it's discovered, the whole crew becomes a target; The Rats found evidence of a corporate atrocity in intercepted communications and are debating whether to release it or sell it

Nodes.Name: A decommissioned telecom switching station in Gary, Indiana. Their operational reach extends across the GLMZ's data infrastructure.

Properties.description:
The Pale Inheritance traces its origins to a specific bureaucratic atrocity: the TESSERA CORPONATION Citizenship Consolidation Act of 2178, which retroactively reclassified approximately 12,000 Tier-3 citizens in The Shelf district as Tier-5 'Provisional Residents' based on a reanalysis of their neural augmentation compliance histories. The reclassification stripped them of housing subsidy access, healthcare routing, and — critically — the right to register births in the official citizenship ledger. Children born to Provisional Residents after the Act were legally stateless within the Meridian 88 corponation framework: they existed in the physical city but not in any database that mattered. The Pale Inheritance formed in the months following the Act, initially as a mutual aid network organized by former Tier-3 residents who refused to accept the reclassification and began maintaining their own parallel citizenship records — handwritten, memorized, tattooed on skin, encoded in modified neural storage.

Four years later, the Pale Inheritance has evolved into something considerably more complex. They are still, at their core, a record-keeping institution — but the records they keep have become extraordinarily valuable to parties far beyond The Shelf. They maintain genealogical and identity data on tens of thousands of Undertow residents that exists nowhere in any corponation database, which means they can confirm or deny the existence of people the official city has declared don't exist. This has made them brokers of a peculiar form of power: they can manufacture citizenship-adjacent identity documents that pass TESSERA verification not through forgery but through the insertion of their own records into corrupted legacy database nodes they've been quietly infecting for three years. They don't fake identities. They argue, in their own internal logic, that they restore them.

What distinguishes the Pale Inheritance from conventional Undertow identity-crime operations is their absolute refusal to sell records to corponation interests, their elaborate vetting process for anyone seeking their services, and their practice of Remembrance — a ritual in which senior members commit the identities of deceased or disappeared Undertow residents to oral and dermal record, ensuring that even death does not erase someone from the Pale Inheritance's ledger. They have developed a culture of memory that is almost liturgical in its intensity, and outsiders who encounter it often find it unsettling in ways they struggle to articulate.
Properties.motto: We remember what the city paid to forget.
Properties.ideology: The Pale Inheritance believes that personhood is a political act of resistance in Meridian 88 — that the city's tiered citizenship system is not merely unjust but is specifically designed to manufacture exploitable non-persons who can be worked, experimented on, relocated, and disappeared without legal consequence, and that the most radical act available to those at the bottom of the tier system is to insist on being counted. They do not seek to overthrow the corponation framework. They seek to make it impossible for that framework to erase the people it has decided to ignore. Within this ideology sits a harder edge: the Pale Inheritance has begun to argue, in internal circles, that their records give them a form of leverage over every corponation that has ever used Provisional Residents in unlicensed augmentation trials, off-ledger labor contracts, or medical research — and that this leverage should eventually be used.
Properties.leadership:
Flat cell structure with no acknowledged central leadership, a design choice made explicitly to prevent decapitation by corponation security operations. In practice, a group of twelve senior members called the Ledger hold collective decision-making authority. They communicate through a proprietary dead-drop protocol using modified RINGO CORPONATION consumer neural-sync hardware.

Marisol Canto-Vesh: One of the original organizers of the post-Consolidation Act mutual aid network and the faction's most visible public-facing figure. Officially a licensed social services coordinator operating under a TESSERA-approved community outreach charter — a cover that has held for three years and that she maintains with meticulous, exhausting care. She is the primary interface between the Pale Inheritance and any outside party seeking their services.

The Tattooed: Collective designation for the seven Ledger members who have chosen to carry portions of the record archive on their skin using a proprietary dermal encoding system. Each carries between 400 and 800 individual identity records encoded in a pattern that resembles decorative scarification. Their names are not publicly known. They are referred to by number.

Orren Spall: The faction's primary database infiltration specialist, a former TESSERA data-compliance auditor who was himself reclassified as Provisional Resident when the Act was applied to his family unit. He designed the legacy node infection strategy and manages the ongoing insertion of Pale Inheritance records into corrupted corponation database infrastructure. He is intensely paranoid, rarely meets anyone in person, and is considered by Marisol to be both irreplaceable and a serious liability.
Properties.methods: Maintaining a parallel identity registry for Undertow residents outside the corponation citizenship ledger; Inserting fabricated but internally consistent identity records into corrupted TESSERA and RINGO CORPONATION legacy database nodes to create verifiable citizenship documentation; Remembrance rituals — oral and dermal encoding of deceased or disappeared residents' identities to prevent posthumous erasure; Vetting-intensive identity restoration services offered to Provisional Residents seeking to reestablish citizenship standing; Systematic documentation of corponation abuses against non-citizen Undertow residents, preserved in the archive as leverage material; Cell-based operational security with rotating Vault locations and dead-drop communication protocols; Strategic placement of members in TESSERA-approved community outreach roles to maintain legal cover and intelligence access
Properties.resources: The Archive — tens of thousands of identity records for Undertow residents existing in no corponation database; Orren Spall's legacy node infection network, currently providing insertion access to three partially corrupted TESSERA citizenship database nodes; Marisol Canto-Vesh's legitimate community outreach charter, providing legal cover and district access; Dermal encoding technology for high-density identity data storage on human skin; A network of former TESSERA data-compliance personnel with institutional knowledge of database architecture; Documented evidence of HELIX BIOSYSTEMS and LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS conducting unlicensed augmentation and pharmaceutical trials on Provisional Residents; Modified RINGO CORPONATION neural-sync hardware repurposed for encrypted dead-drop communication
Properties.story_hooks: A player-connected Provisional Resident in The Shelf has been offered Pale Inheritance identity restoration — but the vetting process has flagged something in their history that Marisol Canto-Vesh won't explain, and the offer has been quietly withdrawn. The resident wants to know why. The answer is in the archive.; One of The Tattooed has gone missing during a Vault relocation. The encoded records on their skin represent nearly 600 identities. If LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS has them, those 600 people are in danger of being cross-referenced against trial records. The Pale Inheritance needs the player to find the missing member before LAZARUS finishes reading them.; Orren Spall has discovered that one of the three legacy TESSERA database nodes he's been using for identity insertion has been quietly patched — not by TESSERA's standard update process, but by an unknown third party who appears to have been monitoring his insertion activity. Someone knows what the Pale Inheritance has been doing, and it isn't TESSERA.; The documented evidence against HELIX BIOSYSTEMS has become a political problem: a Tier-2 journalist connected to VANTABLACK MEDIA has obtained a partial copy through unknown channels and is preparing to publish. The Pale Inheritance didn't authorize the release and doesn't know how the journalist got it. HELIX has issued a quiet ultimatum: find the source of the leak and hand them over, or the stalemate ends. Marisol is asking for help she doesn't want to ask for.; A TESSERA citizenship enforcement sweep in The Shelf has netted forty Provisional Residents including three members of the Pale Inheritance's outer network. The faction needs someone to pull them out of the TESSERA processing facility before they're transferred to a Tier-6 resettlement node — a destination that, according to the archive, has a 60% correlation with subsequent disappearance.; The Pale Inheritance has received a Remembrance request for someone who, according to their records, is not dead — but whose official TESSERA citizenship record was deleted six months ago, a process that should be impossible. Someone at a very high level is erasing a living person from the city. The person in question was last known to be working in the Vantage Meridian Corporate Campus.

Nodes.Name: Primarily The Shelf, where their founding community remains concentrated. Secondary cells operate in Old Harbor's lower residential stacks and in the transit-adjacent zones of The Laceworks. Their most sensitive record-keeping operations are conducted in a rotating series of locations called Vaults — never the same place twice in the same month — that are known only to members who have completed the full Remembrance initiation.

Properties.description:
The Pure Hand is an anti-augmentation militant group operating across the GLMZ, with their largest cell — about seventy members — based in the remnants of Milwaukee's Riverwest neighborhood. They believe that cyberware is an abomination, that neural interfaces are a leash disguised as a tool, and that the augmentation industry exists to make human beings into upgradable products for corporate profit. They're not entirely wrong about that last part, which is what makes them dangerous.

The movement started as a philosophical position and became a gang when philosophy met desperation. Early Pure Hand members were people who couldn't afford augments and reframed their poverty as moral superiority. But the movement attracted genuine ideologues — former bioethicists, religious traditionalists, people who'd seen augmentation addiction destroy someone they loved. The group hardened after a series of confrontations with augmented criminals who targeted Purist neighborhoods specifically because they knew the residents couldn't fight back with chrome. The Pure Hand learned to fight back with numbers, improvised weapons, EMP devices, and a willingness to absorb casualties that augmented opponents found unnerving.

The crew manufactures crude but effective EMP grenades and disruption devices that can temporarily disable cyberware. They've also developed chemical agents that accelerate augment rejection — a particularly cruel weapon that can turn a person's own implants against them over a period of weeks. Their fighters train in unaugmented combat techniques and pack tactics designed to overwhelm individual augmented opponents. Against a single chromed-up enforcer, a Pure Hand squad of eight can be surprisingly effective.

The movement's weakness is that their ideology alienates potential allies. In a world where most people have at least basic augmentation, being militantly anti-chrome makes you a fringe group by definition.
Properties.motto: Born whole. Stay whole.
Properties.ideology: Human biological purity. The Pure Hand believes that augmentation is a trap — that it makes individuals dependent on corporate supply chains for maintenance, vulnerable to remote exploitation, and gradually less human. They advocate for complete rejection of cyberware and neural interfaces. The moderate wing wants personal choice. The militant wing wants augmentation banned. The extreme wing wants augmented people 'cleansed.'
Properties.methods: EMP warfare — crude but effective electromagnetic pulse devices that disable cyberware in a radius; Rejection agents — chemical weapons that accelerate augment rejection syndrome in targeted individuals; Pack tactics — squad-based unaugmented combat designed to overwhelm individual augmented opponents; Propaganda — leaflets, pirate broadcasts, and net posts arguing against augmentation culture; Clinic sabotage — targeting augment clinics and supply chains to reduce access to cyberware; Community organizing — building support networks for unaugmented people in augmentation-dominant areas
Properties.resources: EMP grenades and disruption devices manufactured in basement workshops; Chemical rejection agents — their most feared and closely guarded weapon; Seventy committed fighters trained in unaugmented combat and pack tactics; A network of cells across four GLMZ cities providing mutual support and intelligence; Community support from unaugmented populations who feel marginalized; Safe houses in neighborhoods where augmentation is rare and Purists are welcomed
